# TypeScript orchestrator structure

> The official modular structure of a PSO orchestrator - src/.app for application-wide components, src/modules for business modules with MODULE.pso.ts and routes/ROUTES.pso.ts, controllers, services, providers, DTOs, contracts, mappers - and how PSO discovers, validates, compiles and serves it.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified.** The runtime, `pso validate`, Studio and the generators read this structure; a real build serves it (interceptors, `created()`/`noContent()`, module routes), and a build that mixes it with the 0.1 structure refuses to start (`PSO_STRUCTURE_MIXED`).

```tree title="The modular orchestrator"
gateway/
  src/
    .app/
      configs/  # app.config.ts: plain configuration modules, imported where needed
      contracts/  # *.contract.ts|json: contracts used by several modules
      decorators/  # *.decorator.ts: reusable metadata decorators
      filters/  # *.filter.ts: error filters named by routes
      guards/
        jwt.guard.ts  # generated: authentication / authorization
      interceptors/  # *.interceptor.ts: run around the actions of the routes that name them
      middlewares/  # *.middleware.ts: run before the actions of the routes that name them
    modules/
      products/
        MODULE.pso.ts  # generated: the module's controllers and providers
        routes/
          ROUTES.pso.ts  # generated: its endpoints and their access policy
        controllers/
          product.controller.ts  # generated
        services/
          product.service.ts  # generated
        providers/
          product.provider.ts  # generated: the call to the microservice
        contracts/
          product.contract.ts  # generated: the microservice API it depends on
        dto/
          request/
            create-product.dto.ts  # generated: validated bodies
          response/
            product.dto.ts  # generated: response contracts
        mappers/
          product.mapper.ts  # generated
    shared/  # reusable code of no single module
    main.ts  # generated: bootstrap() only
  tests/
  docs/
  package.json
  tsconfig.json
  README.md
```

Every directory above exists in a new project, with or without the reference CRUD (`--template empty`): an empty one holds a `.gitkeep`
so it survives version control. Placeholders are not evidence for structure detection. The container image's Dockerfile is written by
the first `pso docker:build`.

## Discovery and registration

The runtime and `pso validate` find modules as **directories** of `src/modules/` (the build's `dist/modules/`). A module counts only
through its `MODULE.pso.ts`, and an endpoint exists only if its `routes/ROUTES.pso.ts` declares it with a security policy: a decorated
controller method that no route names is never reachable. Nothing is discovered by scanning for decorators.

```ts
// src/modules/products/MODULE.pso.ts (generated)
export default defineModule({
  name: "products",
  controllers: [ProductController],
  providers: [ProductService, ProductProvider],
  routes: productsRoutes,
  imports: [],
  exports: [],
});
```

```ts
// src/modules/products/routes/ROUTES.pso.ts (excerpt)
{ method: "GET", path: "/products/options", controller: ProductController, action: "options", security: { public: true } },
{ method: "POST", path: "/products", controller: ProductController, action: "create",
  security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["products:write"] }, metadata: { services: ["catalog"] }, responses: { 201: "ProductResponse", 400: "problem", 409: "problem" } },
```

Application-wide components are found by kind in `.app/` (and module-local ones in `modules/<m>/guards|middlewares|filters|interceptors/`):
a route names them (`guards`, `middleware`, `interceptors`, `filters`), and an unknown name is a validation error before anything listens.

**Compilation.** TypeScript skips directories whose name starts with a dot even when they are listed, so `tsconfig.json` includes
`"src/.app/**/*"` explicitly (the template does; `pso structure:inspect` reports a project that does not). Docker builds copy `src/` whole,
`.app/` included.

## The components

| Component | Responsibility | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| controller | receive the request, delegate, choose the answer | parameters are validated by their decorators (`@Param("id", spec)`, `@Query(...)`, `@Body(Dto)`); no business logic |
| service | coordinate the operation | no persistence; no copy of rules the microservice owns |
| provider | call a microservice | `UpstreamClient` with the service NAME (discovery), `credentials: "caller"` to forward the user; translate 404/409/400 |
| DTO | the request/response contract | `@Dto()` with field decorators; unknown properties are rejected |
| contract | the microservice API the module depends on + its binding (`PRODUCT_SERVICE`) | types only |
| mapper | microservice record -> public response | copy only contract fields |
| routes | what is exposed and to whom | `public: true` or a guard; `metadata.services` names what the actions may call |

Answers: a returned value is JSON (200; 201 for POST). `created(body, location)` answers 201 with a `Location` header, `noContent()`
204, `withStatus(status, body, headers)` any 2xx/3xx. Errors are thrown: `new HttpError(409, "conflict", { detail })` becomes an RFC 9457
problem whose `detail` is that sentence; an `UpstreamCallError` left unhandled becomes a stable 502/503/504 problem.

## Secure microservice communication

```ts
// src/modules/products/providers/product.provider.ts (excerpt)
find(id: string): Promise<ProductRecord> {
  return translate(this.client.get<ProductRecord>(PRODUCT_SERVICE, "/products/:id", { params: { id }, credentials: "caller" }));
}
```

The destination is a workspace service name, never a URL: the client resolves it through PSO service discovery, applies the service's
endpoint prefix, uses its TLS and mutual TLS material (with the 0.2 infrastructure engine), propagates the correlation id and the trace,
and sends the caller's token only because the call asks for it and the route declared the service. The microservice validates the token
again: the orchestrator never replaces the service's own authorization.

## Interceptors

```ts
// src/.app/interceptors/timing.interceptor.ts (pso make:interceptor timing)
const interceptor: Interceptor = async (call, next) => {
  const started = performance.now();
  try { return await next(); }
  finally { log("info", "action timed", { route: `${call.route.method} ${call.route.path}`, ms: Math.round(performance.now() - started) }); }
};
```

A route opts in with `interceptors: ["timing"]`; interceptors run after guards and middleware, around the action, in the declared order,
and may return a different result.

## What goes wrong

- `PSO_STRUCTURE_MIXED`: the project has `src/routes/` (0.1) and `src/modules/` or `src/.app/`. Keep one: `pso structure:inspect`.
- `PSO_MISPLACED_RESOURCE`: a file is not where its kind lives (a controller next to MODULE.pso.ts, a service in `.app/`). Generate it with `pso make:<kind>`.
- `PSO_CRUD_UNBOUND` (warning): a CRUD module is bound to a service the workspace does not have yet; its routes answer 502 until it exists.

# Java microservice structure

> The official layered structure of a PSO Spring Boot microservice - application/rest, service, dto, mapper; infrastructure/persistence, entity, config, security, filter; shared - with transactions, Jakarta Validation, PostgreSQL and Flyway, Spring Security, RFC 9457 errors and tests.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified.** `pso create service <name>` generates this structure with the reference Product CRUD; its generated tests pass against a real (embedded) PostgreSQL with the real Flyway migration, real JWT validation and the real HTTP layer (16 tests; 24 after `pso make:crud order`).

```tree title="The layered Spring service"
catalog/
  src/
    main/
      java/com/pso/catalog/
        application/
          rest/
            ProductController.java  # generated: @RestController: HTTP, @Valid, @PreAuthorize, status codes, Location
          service/
            ProductService.java  # generated: @Service: business operations, @Transactional boundaries
          dto/
            request/
              CreateProductRequest.java  # generated: a record with Jakarta Validation
              UpdateProductRequest.java  # generated
            response/
              ProductResponse.java  # generated: a record (the entity never leaves the service)
              PageResponse.java  # generated: the stable paginated contract
          mapper/
            ProductMapper.java  # generated: request to entity to response
        infrastructure/
          entity/
            ProductEntity.java  # generated: the JPA entity
          persistence/
            ProductRepository.java  # generated: Spring Data JPA (+ JpaSpecificationExecutor)
            ProductSpecifications.java  # generated: database-level filters
          config/  # @Configuration classes (pso make:config)
          security/  # security integration beyond the starter
          filter/  # servlet filters (pso make:filter)
        shared/
          exception/
            ResourceNotFoundException.java  # generated: RFC 9457 problems with a safe detail
            ConflictException.java  # generated
            InvalidRequestException.java  # generated
          constant/  # constants
          validation/
            PageRequests.java  # generated: page, size and sort validation
        Application.java  # generated
      resources/db/migration/
        V1__create_products.sql  # generated: the table, constraints and indexes
    test/java/com/pso/catalog/application/rest/
      ProductControllerTests.java  # generated: the API tests
```

Every package above exists in a new service, also with `--template empty`: an empty one holds a `.gitkeep`. `infrastructure/client/`
is added by `pso make:client` when the service calls another one.

The base package comes from the project (`--package com.example.catalog` at creation; generators read it from the
`@SpringBootApplication` class). There is **no providers package, no modules package and no `.app` directory** in a Java service: those
are orchestrator concepts.

## Layers

**application** - what the service does. Controllers stay small: they validate (`@Valid @RequestBody`), authorize
(`@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_products:write')")`) and delegate. Services hold the business operations; each public method is a
transaction (`@Transactional`, reads `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`), and they coordinate repositories directly. Request and response
DTOs are records; mappers convert between them and entities.

**infrastructure** - how it is done technically: JPA entities, Spring Data repositories, `@Configuration` classes, security integration,
servlet filters and outbound clients (`PsoHttpClient`). No custom abstraction duplicates Spring.

**shared** - genuinely reusable code: the exceptions, `PageRequests`, constants.

## Persistence

Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate only validates the mapping (`spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: validate`, set by the template, never
`update`); timestamps are `TIMESTAMPTZ` and `hibernate.jdbc.time_zone: UTC`; money is `NUMERIC(p, s)` and `BigDecimal`. Uniqueness is a
database constraint, and the service turns its violation into a 409 even when two requests race past the first check:

```java
// application/service/ProductService.java (excerpt, generated)
@Transactional
public ProductResponse create(CreateProductRequest request) {
    if (repository.existsBySku(request.sku().strip())) {
        throw duplicateSku();
    }
    ProductEntity entity = mapper.toEntity(request);
    return mapper.toResponse(saveAndFlush(entity));       // writes now, so a constraint violation is reported here, as a 409
}
```

Lists are paginated, sorted and filtered **by the database** (`Specification` + `Pageable`); the sort field must be one the endpoint allows
and the page size has a maximum. A service with PostgreSQL runs against PostgreSQL, also locally (`pso docker:up` provisions it) and in
its tests (an embedded PostgreSQL): the generated `h2` profile is for services without a database of their own, and the migrations use
PostgreSQL features (expression indexes, `TIMESTAMPTZ`) that H2 does not reproduce.

## Validation and errors

Jakarta Validation on the request records (`@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Pattern`, `@Digits`, `@DecimalMin`); unknown JSON properties are
refused (`spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties: true` in the template). Every failure is an RFC 9457 problem with
the same shape as the orchestrator's: `validation_failed` (400, with the fields), `not_found` (404), `conflict` (409, with a detail),
`unauthorized` / `forbidden` (401 / 403). An application error is a `PsoProblemException` subclass (`shared/exception`): its detail is a
sentence you wrote, never an exception message or caller input. Unexpected exceptions are a generic 500 that reveals nothing.

## Security

The PSO security starter validates the JWT (issuer, audience, JWKS) before any controller runs; everything is denied unless a valid token
is present (`/actuator/health` is public). Scopes become `SCOPE_*` authorities for `@PreAuthorize`. The orchestrator forwards the
caller's token, and the service authorizes the same user again.

## Tests

Generated tests start the real application context: MockMvc for HTTP, `PsoTestJwt` (a local JWKS and real signed tokens), an embedded
PostgreSQL with the real migrations (`TestDatabaseConfig`). They cover the round trip, validation, duplicates (sequential and
concurrent), 404, 401/403, pagination, sorting and filtering. `./mvnw test` runs them.

## What goes wrong

- `Schema-validation: missing table [...]` at start-up: an entity without its migration. Hibernate validates, it never creates tables;
  add the table with `pso make:migration <name> --service <svc>`.
- `Validate failed: Migration checksum mismatch`: an applied migration was edited. Restore it and add a new `V<next>__` migration.
- `400 validation_failed` with `unknown property`: the client sent a field the record does not declare. Unknown properties are refused
  on purpose; add the field to the record if it belongs there.
- A `403` from the service after the orchestrator accepted the request: the token lacks the scope the service checks. The scopes of both
  sides are the same names (`products:read`, `products:write`); compare the route with the `@PreAuthorize`.

---

# The reference Product CRUD

> File by file, the Product CRUD that pso create service and pso create orchestrator generate - endpoints, security, validation, persistence, the request lifecycle from the orchestrator to PostgreSQL, how to run and call it locally, in Docker and from Studio, how to remove it and how to generate another resource the same way.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified.** Generated by the distributed CLI into a new workspace, built, started with real PostgreSQL and the identity provider in Docker, and called through the orchestrator and directly: every status below was observed, the data survived a restart, and the generated tests pass.

`pso create service catalog` generates a working Product API in the layered Java structure; `pso create orchestrator gateway` generates
the matching `products` module and binds it to the service that serves `/products`. Both are **examples to keep or remove**: nothing
in the framework depends on them, and `--template empty` creates the same projects without them.

## The resource

| Field | Type | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | UUID | assigned by the service |
| `sku` | string | required, 3-64 characters, upper-case letters, digits and inner hyphens (`KB-100`), **unique** (database constraint) |
| `name` | string | required, 1-120 characters |
| `description` | string | optional, at most 2000 characters |
| `price` | decimal | required, `>= 0`, at most 10 integer digits and 2 decimals (`NUMERIC(12,2)`, `BigDecimal`; sent as a string) |
| `active` | boolean | defaults to `true` |
| `createdAt`, `updatedAt` | timestamp | UTC (`TIMESTAMPTZ`), set by the service |

## Endpoints

| Method and path (orchestrator) | Scope | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /products/options` | public | 200: the sortable and filterable fields and the page limits (no data, no backend call) |
| `POST /products` | `products:write` | 201 + `Location`, 400, 401, 403, 409 (duplicate SKU) |
| `GET /products?page&size&sort&sku&name&active` | `products:read` | 200 (a page), 400 (bad page, size or sort field) |
| `GET /products/{id}` | `products:read` | 200, 400 (not a UUID), 404 |
| `PUT /products/{id}` | `products:write` | 200, 400, 404, 409 |
| `DELETE /products/{id}` | `products:write` | 204, 404 |

The microservice serves the same API under its prefix (`/catalog/products`), checks the token and the scopes **again**, and is reachable
only inside the workspace network: the browser and other clients use the orchestrator. Every error is an RFC 9457 problem
(`application/problem+json`) with the same shape on both sides; a duplicate SKU is `409 conflict` with the detail "a product with this
sku already exists" (the submitted value is not echoed).

## How a request flows

1. The orchestrator matches the route in `routes/ROUTES.pso.ts`; the `jwt` guard validates the token and the scope (401 / 403 here).
2. The controller validates parameters and the body with the DTO decorators (400 before anything is called) and delegates to the service.
3. `ProductProvider` calls the service **by name** (`UpstreamClient`, the binding constant `PRODUCT_SERVICE`) with the caller's token
   (`credentials: "caller"`) and the correlation id; it translates the service's 404 / 409 / 400 into the same problems.
4. In the microservice the PSO security starter validates the token again, `@PreAuthorize` checks the scope, `@Valid` validates the
   record, and `ProductService` runs the operation in a transaction.
5. PostgreSQL enforces the constraints (the unique SKU among them); pagination, sorting and filters run in the query.
6. The mapper returns the public response; the entity never leaves the service.

## The files

### Microservice (`catalog`)

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `application/rest/ProductController.java` | HTTP: `@Valid` bodies, `@PreAuthorize` scopes, 201 + `Location`, 204 |
| `application/service/ProductService.java` | the operations, each `@Transactional`; the SKU check plus the constraint violation turned into 409 |
| `application/dto/request/CreateProductRequest.java`, `UpdateProductRequest.java` | records with Jakarta Validation |
| `application/dto/response/ProductResponse.java`, `PageResponse.java` | the response record and the stable page contract |
| `application/mapper/ProductMapper.java` | request -> entity -> response |
| `infrastructure/entity/ProductEntity.java` | the JPA entity (`@Version`, UTC timestamps) |
| `infrastructure/persistence/ProductRepository.java`, `ProductSpecifications.java` | Spring Data + database-level filters |
| `shared/exception/*.java` | `ResourceNotFoundException`, `ConflictException`, `InvalidRequestException` (RFC 9457 problems) |
| `shared/validation/PageRequests.java` | page, size (maximum 100) and the allowed sort fields |
| `src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_products.sql` | the table, its constraints and indexes (Flyway; Hibernate only validates) |
| `src/test/java/.../application/rest/ProductControllerTests.java` | the API tests: real context, real JWTs, embedded PostgreSQL |
| `docs/reference-crud.md` | this list for the project, with the removal steps |

```sql
-- src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_products.sql (generated, excerpt)
CREATE TABLE products (
    id           UUID             PRIMARY KEY,
    sku          VARCHAR(64)      NOT NULL CHECK (char_length(sku) >= 3),
    price        NUMERIC(12, 2)   NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0.00 AND price <= 9999999999.99),
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ      NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT uk_products_sku UNIQUE (sku)
);
```

### Orchestrator (`gateway`)

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `src/modules/products/MODULE.pso.ts` | registers the controller and the providers |
| `src/modules/products/routes/ROUTES.pso.ts` | the six endpoints, their scopes and `metadata.services: ["catalog"]` |
| `controllers/product.controller.ts` | parameters and bodies validated by decorators; `created()` / `noContent()` |
| `services/product.service.ts` | coordinates; holds no rule the microservice owns |
| `providers/product.provider.ts` | the call to the microservice and the translation of its answers |
| `contracts/product.contract.ts` | the service's API types and the binding `PRODUCT_SERVICE` |
| `dto/request/create-product.dto.ts`, `update-product.dto.ts` | validated bodies (unknown properties refused) |
| `dto/response/product.dto.ts`, `product-page.dto.ts` | the response contracts |
| `mappers/product.mapper.ts` | service record -> public response |
| `docs/api/products.collection.json` | the Studio request collection (no credential in it) |
| `tests/products/product.mapper.test.ts` | the module's test |

```ts
// src/modules/products/routes/ROUTES.pso.ts (generated, excerpt)
{ method: "GET", path: "/products/options", controller: ProductController, action: "options", security: { public: true } },
{ method: "POST", path: "/products", controller: ProductController, action: "create",
  security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["products:write"] }, metadata: { services: ["catalog"] },
  responses: { 201: "ProductResponse", 400: "problem", 409: "problem" } },
```

## Binding the module to its service

The orchestrator finds the service that serves `/products` in `pso.workspace.json`; no service name is assumed. Created **before** the
service, the module still compiles and starts, `pso validate` warns `PSO_CRUD_UNBOUND`, and its routes answer `502` (`unknown_service`) while the start-up
log names the missing service and the fix; `pso create service` binds it as soon as the service exists. To bind it yourself:

```bash
pso crud:bind products --to catalog
```

## Running it

```bash
pso infra:init --identity keycloak --runtime docker --users "ana,bob:products:read"   # declare Docker, Keycloak, development users
pso docker:up --vendor        # PostgreSQL, Keycloak, the service, the orchestrator and the edge, provisioned by PSO
pso studio                    # API client: the "Reference requests" panel holds the collection, sent with the dev user
```

Locally without the containers of the projects: `./mvnw spring-boot:run` in `catalog` against a PostgreSQL database (`DB_URL`,
`DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`; the `h2` profile does not apply to this service) and `npm run dev` in `gateway`. `./mvnw test` and `npm test` run the generated tests. The database password and the development user
are generated per workspace into `.infra/` and never written into source or into the collection.

In Studio the collection's requests go to the **orchestrator** (`edge:api`): that is how clients use the API. A request sent directly
to the microservice is labelled as such and needs a token of its own: it is for diagnosing the service, not for clients.

## Requests and answers

Real requests through the orchestrator of a generated workspace, and the answers it gave (identifiers, timestamps and correlation
ids as returned; the token is a development user's). The microservice was stopped for the last one.

## Removing it

Delete the files listed above (the project's `docs/reference-crud.md` lists them for the project) and, if the table holds nothing you
need, add a migration that drops it (`pso make:migration drop-products`) instead of editing `V1`. Remove the `products` module
directory from the orchestrator. `pso validate` confirms the result.

## Another resource the same way

```bash
pso make:crud order --service catalog --orchestrator --fields "code:string:unique:length=3-32:filter:sort,total:decimal:precision=12:scale=2:min=0:sort"
```

generates the same set of files for `order` (the next migration number, its own scopes `orders:read` / `orders:write`, tests and a
collection): see [Generators](architecture/generators.md).

## What goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| every request `502 unknown_service` | the module is bound to a service the workspace does not have | `pso create service <name>` or `pso crud:bind products --to <service>` |
| `401` from the orchestrator | no token, or one from another issuer | send it with the development user from Studio, or a token of the workspace's identity provider |
| `403` | the token lacks `products:read` / `products:write` | grant the scope to the user in the identity provider |
| `409 conflict` on create | the SKU exists (also when two requests race: the database constraint decides) | use another SKU |
| `400` on list | a sort field the endpoint does not allow, or `size` above 100 | `GET /products/options` lists what is allowed |

# Generators in the official structures

> Which pso make commands exist for the modular orchestrator and the layered Java service, where each one writes, what it registers for you, and the rules every generator follows (structure detection, no overwrites, no mixing, transactional changes).

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified**: every generator below was run against a generated workspace; the results compiled, passed their tests and `pso validate`. Duplicates, overwrites and misplaced kinds are refused.

## Orchestrator (modular)

| Command | Writes | Registers |
|---|---|---|
| `pso make:module <m>` | `src/modules/<m>/MODULE.pso.ts`, `routes/ROUTES.pso.ts` | - |
| `pso make:controller <m> [name]` | `modules/<m>/controllers/<name>.controller.ts` | MODULE `controllers` |
| `pso make:route <m> <action> --method --path [--public \| --scopes]` | the action + its route | ROUTES entry (validated, rolled back on error) |
| `pso make:service <m> [name]` | `modules/<m>/services/<name>.service.ts` | MODULE `providers` |
| `pso make:provider <name> --module <m>` | `modules/<m>/providers/<name>.provider.ts` | MODULE `providers` |
| `pso make:dto <m> <name> [--response] [--fields ...]` | `modules/<m>/dto/request/` (or `response/`) | - |
| `pso make:mapper <m> <name>` | `modules/<m>/mappers/<name>.mapper.ts` | - |
| `pso make:contract <m> <name>` | `modules/<m>/contracts/<name>.contract.ts` | - |
| `pso make:guard <name>` / `<m> <name>` | `src/.app/guards/` / `modules/<m>/guards/` | named by routes |
| `pso make:middleware`, `make:filter`, `make:interceptor <name>` | `src/.app/middlewares/`, `filters/`, `interceptors/` | named by routes |
| `pso make:decorator`, `make:config <name>` | `src/.app/decorators/`, `configs/` | imported where used |

In the modular structure a provider, a service or a hook belongs to a module: `--module` (or the module argument) is required.

## Java service (layered)

| Command | Package |
|---|---|
| `pso make:controller <name> --service <svc>` | `application/rest` |
| `pso make:service`, `make:mapper` | `application/service`, `application/mapper` |
| `pso make:request <name>`, `make:response <name>` (`make:dto <name> [--response]`) | `application/dto/request`, `application/dto/response` |
| `pso make:entity <name>`, `make:repository <name>` | `infrastructure/entity`, `infrastructure/persistence` (a repository needs its entity) |
| `pso make:config`, `make:filter`, `make:client <service>` | `infrastructure/config`, `infrastructure/filter`, `infrastructure/client` |
| `pso make:exception <name>` | `shared/exception` |
| `pso make:event <name>`, `make:listener <name>`, `make:dispatch-event <event.name>`, `make:dispatch-handler <event.name>` | `application/event` (the Dispatch declaration itself goes to `src/main/resources/dispatch/<service>.events.json`) |
| `pso make:migration <name> --service <svc>` | `src/main/resources/db/migration/V<next>__<name>.sql` |

`make:port` and `make:adapter` belong to the 0.1 hexagonal layout and are refused in a layered service.

## A complete resource

```bash
pso make:crud order --service sales --orchestrator \
  --fields "code:string:unique:length=3-32:filter:sort,total:decimal:precision=12:scale=2:min=0:sort,paid:boolean:default=false:filter"
```

Writes the whole layered resource in `sales` (entity, the next Flyway migration with constraints and indexes, repository and filters,
request/response records, mapper, transactional service, controller with `orders:read` / `orders:write`, tests) and, with `--orchestrator`,
the `orders` module bound to `sales` (DTOs, contract, provider, service, mapper, controller, routes, a request collection for Studio,
a test). Fields: `name:type[:option]...` with types `string text integer long decimal boolean` and options `optional unique min=N max=N
length=MIN-MAX precision=P scale=S default=true|false sort filter`. Without `--fields` a resource has one required `name`.

`pso crud:bind <module> --to <service>` changes which service a CRUD module calls.

## Rules every generator follows

- It detects the project's runtime and structure and writes in that structure; a project that mixes conventions is refused.
- It never overwrites: an existing file, module or resource stops the command before anything is written.
- Changes to the orchestrator are validated as a whole and rolled back if they would leave it inconsistent.
- `--dry-run` shows the plan; `--json` gives it to CI.
- No generator edits framework-managed infrastructure (`.infra/`) or a project's configuration files beyond the registrations listed above.

## Limits

- `make:entity` writes the entity only: its table comes from a migration you add (`pso make:migration`), because Hibernate only
  validates the schema. In a service without a database `make:entity` and `make:repository` are refused with the command that adds one
  (`pso database:enable postgresql --service <svc>`, which also sets the validation of the schema).
- `make:crud` in a service created before this release may lack `spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties`; the
  command says so, and the generated unknown-property test is left out until the setting is added.
- `crud:bind` rebinds modules generated as CRUD modules (a `contracts/*.contract.ts` with a `*_SERVICE` constant); other modules name
  their services in their own routes and providers.

---

# Structure compatibility and migration

> How PSO recognises the 0.1 and the official structures, refuses projects that mix them, keeps 0.1 projects working, and plans (read-only) the migration of a project to the official structure with pso structure:inspect.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified**: 0.1 projects validate, generate and run as before; mixed projects are refused by `pso validate`, the generators and the runtime; `pso structure:inspect` produces the migration plan of a 0.1 project. Moving the files is deliberately left to the project's owner: PSO never restructures application code on its own.

## How the structure is decided

| Project | Official structure | 0.1 structure |
|---|---|---|
| orchestrator | `src/.app/` or `src/modules/<m>/` with module files | `src/routes/<m>/` with module files, or component files in `src/guards/`, `src/middlewares/`, ... |
| Spring service | `application/rest`, `application/service`, `application/dto`, `application/mapper`, `infrastructure/`, `shared/` | `routes/`, `contracts/`, `ports/`, `adapters/`, `persistence/`, `events/`, `configs/`, `security/`, or classes directly in `application/` |

The files decide. A project may also state it (`"structure": "modular" | "layered" | "legacy"` for the project in `pso.workspace.json`);
files that contradict the statement are an error. A new project with no file yet follows the official structure. Empty `.gitkeep`
placeholders are not evidence.

A project with files of both structures is **refused** (`PSO_STRUCTURE_MIXED`) by `pso validate`, by every generator and, for the
orchestrator, by the runtime: conventions are never mixed silently.

## Planning a migration

```bash
pso structure:inspect                     # every project
pso structure:inspect --service gateway   # one project, --json for tools
```

For a 0.1 project it lists every file to move and where, the files whose relative imports, route declarations, module registrations or
Java package declarations change with it, and what needs a decision (a hexagonal port has no layered equivalent). Nothing is moved.

For a 0.1 orchestrator with one resource (`pso create orchestrator gateway --structure legacy`, then `pso make:resource product`):

```text evidence="verified"
$ pso structure:inspect --service gateway
gateway (node): legacy
  migration plan to the modular structure (inspection only: nothing is moved):
    move    src/contracts/product.contract.json  ->  src/.app/contracts/product.contract.json
    move    src/guards/jwt.guard.ts  ->  src/.app/guards/jwt.guard.ts
    move    src/routes/product/MODULE.pso.ts  ->  src/modules/product/MODULE.pso.ts
    move    src/routes/product/ROUTES.pso.ts  ->  src/modules/product/routes/ROUTES.pso.ts
    move    src/routes/product/product.controller.ts  ->  src/modules/product/controllers/product.controller.ts
    update  src/routes/product/MODULE.pso.ts: 2 relative import(s) re-pointed; module registration (controllers/providers imports)
    update  src/routes/product/ROUTES.pso.ts: 1 relative import(s) re-pointed; 1 route declaration(s)
    update  tsconfig.json: add "src/.app/**/*" to "include" (TypeScript skips dot-directories otherwise)
  5 file(s) to move, 3 file(s) whose imports, package declarations or registrations change. Back up first (commit), move, then pso validate and the project's tests.
```

To migrate: commit (or back up) the project, move the files as listed, fix the imports and package declarations it names, then
`pso validate` and the project's own tests. Endpoints, security and behaviour do not change: routes and rules are paths, not files.

## Limits

- `structure:inspect` plans; it never moves, rewrites or deletes a file.
- A hexagonal port (`ports/`) has no layered equivalent: the plan lists it as a decision, not a move.
- Imports written with path aliases or computed at runtime are not followed; `pso validate` and the compiler report what remains after
  the move.

# A CRUD by hand in the 0.1 layout (compatibility)

> For projects that keep the 0.1 layout - a products API built piece by piece (Spring service, PostgreSQL, Flyway, validation, transactions, forwarding routes, tokens), with the real responses. New projects get the CRUD generated in the official structure.

By the end of this page you will have a **products API** running on your machine: a Spring Boot service that stores products in PostgreSQL, behind a PSO orchestrator that checks who is calling. You will create, list, read, update and delete products, look at the rows in the database after each step, and provoke every common error on purpose.

> [!NOTE]
> This tutorial builds the CRUD **by hand, piece by piece**, in the 0.1 layout (`--structure legacy --template empty`), to show what each
> file does. New projects get a complete CRUD generated in the official structure: `pso create service` and `pso create orchestrator`
> ([the reference CRUD](architecture/reference-crud.md)), or `pso make:crud` for another resource.

Everything here was run, in this order, on an empty folder. Output marked **Verified output** is copied from that run. Where a block is not from the run, it says so.

## What you will build

```architecture title="One request through the layers"
client (client)
  orchestrator, Node, :3000 (orchestrator) # Bearer token | checks the token and scope; exposes only declared routes
    catalog, Spring Boot, :8081 (service) # forwards | checks the token again, validates the body, runs the transaction
      PostgreSQL, :5432 (database)
```

| Public route (orchestrator) | Reaches the service as | Scope | Success |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /products` | `POST /catalog/products` | `products:write` | `201` and the created product |
| `GET /products` | `GET /catalog/products` | `products:read` | `200` and a list |
| `GET /products/:id` | `GET /catalog/products/{id}` | `products:read` | `200`, or `404` |
| `PUT /products/:id` | `PUT /catalog/products/{id}` | `products:write` | `200` and the updated product |
| `DELETE /products/:id` | `DELETE /catalog/products/{id}` | `products:write` | `204` |

The `/catalog` prefix is added once, by PSO, on the way to the service ([service prefix](spring/service-prefix.md)).

### Why it is built in layers

| Layer | Owns | Why it is separate |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator route | which URLs exist and who may call them | nothing is reachable until it is declared in `ROUTES.pso.ts` ([why](decisions/why-routes-pso-mandatory.md)) |
| Controller | parsing and the HTTP status | no business rules, no SQL |
| Service | the transaction | the only place that decides which changes happen together |
| Repository | data access | Spring Data generates it from an interface |
| Entity | how the data is stored | never sent to clients |
| Request and response records | the public contract | you can change the table without changing the API |
| Mapper | where fields cross the boundary | one visible place |
| Flyway migration | the schema | versioned like code, reviewed like code |

The orchestrator **may** validate bodies early ([DTO validation](orchestrator/dto-validation.md)), but the service always validates for itself: it must stay safe if it is ever called by something other than the orchestrator. This tutorial validates in the service. See [gateway or service validation](decisions/gateway-or-service-validation.md).

## Before you start

```bash
node --version      # 24 or newer
java -version       # 21 or newer
docker --version
pso --help         # confirms that the CLI starts and lists its commands
```

You also need `curl`. The examples use a Unix shell; on Windows use Git Bash, or translate the `curl` lines.

That one starter brings Spring Data JPA, Flyway and the PostgreSQL driver, with versions managed by the PSO BOM. The generated test dependencies include an embedded PostgreSQL, so the tests need no Docker.

## 4. Configure PostgreSQL

### 4.1 Start a database

The database of this tutorial is development infrastructure: it gets its own Compose file, `infra/postgres.compose.yml`. The name `docker-compose.yml` in the workspace root is reserved for the deployment of the application itself, which `pso docker:init` generates later ([Docker](devops/docker.md)); `docker:init` never replaces a file it did not write, so keeping the two apart is what lets you go from this tutorial to the deployment guide without a conflict.

```yml
// spring-crud/postgres.compose.yml
# Development database for the catalog service. The password is a throwaway for a container that listens on loopback only.
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: catalog
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: catalog-dev
      POSTGRES_DB: catalog
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - catalog-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U catalog -d catalog"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  catalog-data:
```

```bash
docker compose -f infra/postgres.compose.yml up -d --wait
```

```text evidence="expected"
 Container shop-db-1  Healthy
```

(`--wait` returns when the health check passes. The container name depends on your folder name.) The database listens on loopback only, and the password is a throwaway. Never reuse it.

### 4.2 Tell the service how to connect

The generated `application.yml` already reads the connection from the environment, so credentials are never in a file:

```yaml title="catalog/src/main/resources/application.yml (generated, excerpt)"
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/catalog}
    username: ${DB_USER:}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD:}
  flyway:
    enabled: true
```

Add a connection pool and make Flyway the only writer of the schema. Insert the first block under `datasource:` (after `password`) and the second under `spring:` next to `flyway:`:

```yml
// spring-crud/datasource-pool.yml
    hikari:                         # connection pool (HikariCP is Spring Boot's default)
      maximum-pool-size: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:10}   # size it from the database's connection limit divided by the number of instances
      minimum-idle: ${DB_POOL_MIN_IDLE:2}
      connection-timeout: 5000      # ms to wait for a free connection before failing fast
      max-lifetime: 1800000         # ms; keep it shorter than any idle-connection timeout in front of the database
```

```yml
// spring-crud/jpa.yml
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false             # no database access while the response is being rendered
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate            # Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate only checks that entities match it
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc:
          time_zone: UTC
```

| Setting | Why |
|---|---|
| `ddl-auto: validate` | Hibernate checks the entities against the schema and **never changes it** |
| `open-in-view: false` | no queries while the response is rendered: a lazy-loading mistake fails in the service instead of leaking a connection |
| `maximum-pool-size` | the database has a connection limit. A starting rule: `limit / instances`, minus a margin for tools |
| `connection-timeout` | when the pool is exhausted, fail in 5 s with a clear error instead of queueing requests behind a stuck query |
| `max-lifetime` | recycle connections before a firewall silently drops idle ones |

This is the complete file after the two insertions. It is a real generated file plus those two blocks; the test of this tutorial rebuilds it and checks that it is identical:

```yml
// spring-crud/application.yml
# catalog: PSO Spring Boot service. Every value below can be overridden by an environment variable (shown as ${VAR:default}).
# Unknown pso.* keys are an error at start-up (a misspelled security setting is never silently ignored).
# Reference: PSO Docs > Spring Boot > Configuration reference.
spring:
  application:
    name: catalog
  output:
    ansi:
      enabled: ${PSO_LOG_COLOR:detect}   # detect | always | never (NO_COLOR is not read by Spring; use never)
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/catalog}
    username: ${DB_USER:}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD:}
    hikari:                         # connection pool (HikariCP is Spring Boot's default)
      maximum-pool-size: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:10}   # size it from the database's connection limit divided by the number of instances
      minimum-idle: ${DB_POOL_MIN_IDLE:2}
      connection-timeout: 5000      # ms to wait for a free connection before failing fast

  flyway:

  # no default profile on purpose: choose one explicitly (local, dev, test, staging, prod, h2); `pso dev` uses local.

# Logging uses Spring Boot's own facilities (Logback). Console pattern: timestamp, level, [service,correlationId,traceId], logger, message.
```

## 5. The migration

Flyway applies every `V<number>__<name>.sql` file in `src/main/resources/db/migration/` exactly once, in order, and records it. The template shipped `V1`; yours is the next number:

```bash
pso make:migration create-products --service catalog
```

That creates `V1__create_products.sql`. Replace its content with:

```sql
// spring-crud/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_products.sql
-- Migrations are append-only: never edit an applied version, add a new one (V2__..., V3__...).
CREATE TABLE products (
    id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    sku         VARCHAR(32)  NOT NULL,
    name        VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
    price_cents BIGINT       NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents > 0),
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    version     BIGINT       NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    CONSTRAINT uq_products_sku UNIQUE (sku)
);
```

Why the table looks like this:

- The constraints (`NOT NULL`, `CHECK`, `UNIQUE`) live in the database too. The application validates for good messages; the database is the last line of defence when two requests race.
- `version` supports optimistic locking (step 6).
- Never edit a migration after it has been applied anywhere: Flyway stores a checksum and refuses to start if it changed. Add `V2__...` instead.

## 6. The domain: entity and repository

```java
// spring-crud/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/domain/Product.java
package com.pso.catalog.domain;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import jakarta.persistence.Version;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.UUID;

/** Persistence model. It is never returned from a controller: the API contract is ProductResponse. */
@Entity
@Table(name = "products")
public class Product {

    @Id
    private UUID id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 32, updatable = false)
    private String sku;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 120)
    private String name;

    @Column(name = "price_cents", nullable = false)
    private long priceCents;

    @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private Instant createdAt;

    @Column(name = "updated_at", nullable = false)
    private Instant updatedAt;

    @Version
    private long version;

    protected Product() {
        // required by JPA
    }

    public Product(String sku, String name, long priceCents) {
        this.id = UUID.randomUUID();
        this.sku = sku;
        this.name = name;
        this.priceCents = priceCents;
        this.createdAt = Instant.now();
        this.updatedAt = this.createdAt;
    }

    public void change(String name, long priceCents) {
        this.name = name;
        this.priceCents = priceCents;
        this.updatedAt = Instant.now();
    }

    public UUID getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public String getSku() {
        return sku;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public long getPriceCents() {
        return priceCents;
    }

    public Instant getCreatedAt() {
        return createdAt;
    }

    public Instant getUpdatedAt() {
        return updatedAt;
    }
}
```

- The constructor creates the id (a UUID), so the id is known before the insert and no round trip is needed to learn it.
- `@Version` is **optimistic locking**: if two requests update the same row from the same starting version, the second fails instead of silently overwriting the first.
- `sku` is `updatable = false`: the entity itself refuses to change it.

```java
// spring-crud/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/persistence/ProductRepository.java
package com.pso.catalog.persistence;

import com.pso.catalog.domain.Product;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

/** Spring Data generates the implementation. Derived queries are parameterised: values are never concatenated into SQL. */
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, UUID> {

    boolean existsBySku(String sku);
}
```

`existsBySku` is a **derived query**. Spring Data turns the method name into a parameterised statement, so request data is never concatenated into SQL.

## 7. The contract: request, update and response records

Three records describe what crosses the API. None of them is the entity.

```java
// spring-crud/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/contracts/ProductRequest.java
package com.pso.catalog.contracts;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Pattern;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Positive;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Size;

/**
 * What a client may send. The sku is part of the create request only: it identifies the product and cannot be changed afterwards,
 * so the update request leaves it out (an unknown "sku" in an update is ignored by Jackson's defaults in Spring Boot, never applied).
 */
public record ProductRequest(
        @NotBlank @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z0-9-]{3,32}", message = "must be 3-32 characters: A-Z, 0-9 or -") String sku,
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 120) String name,
        @Positive long priceCents) {
}
```

```java
// spring-crud/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/contracts/ProductUpdate.java
package com.pso.catalog.contracts;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Positive;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Size;

/** The fields a client may change on an existing product. */
public record ProductUpdate(@NotBlank @Size(max = 120) String name, @Positive long priceCents) {
}
```

```java
// spring-crud/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/contracts/ProductResponse.java
package com.pso.catalog.contracts;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.UUID;

/** The public contract. Internal columns (version) are deliberately absent. */
public record ProductResponse(UUID id, String sku, String name, long priceCents, Instant createdAt, Instant updatedAt) {
}
```

`ProductUpdate` has no `sku`: a sku cannot be changed, so the contract does not offer it. `ProductResponse` has no `version`: internal columns do not leak. If the entity were the API, adding a column would change what clients receive.

```java
// spring-crud/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/adapters/ProductMapper.java
package com.pso.catalog.adapters;

import com.pso.catalog.contracts.ProductRequest;
import com.pso.catalog.contracts.ProductResponse;
import com.pso.catalog.domain.Product;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

/** Hand-written mapping keeps the boundary explicit: every field that crosses it is a decision, not a side effect of reflection. */
@Component
public class ProductMapper {

    public Product toEntity(ProductRequest request) {
        return new Product(request.sku(), request.name().strip(), request.priceCents());
    }

    public ProductResponse toResponse(Product p) {
        return new ProductResponse(p.getId(), p.getSku(), p.getName(), p.getPriceCents(), p.getCreatedAt(), p.getUpdatedAt());
    }
}
```

## 8. The service: where the transaction lives

```java
// spring-crud/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/ProductService.java
package com.pso.catalog.application;

import com.pso.catalog.adapters.ProductMapper;
import com.pso.catalog.contracts.ProductRequest;
import com.pso.catalog.contracts.ProductResponse;
import com.pso.catalog.contracts.ProductUpdate;
import com.pso.catalog.domain.Product;
import com.pso.catalog.persistence.ProductRepository;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

/**
 * The transaction boundary. Each public method is one unit of work: either every change commits, or none does.
 * Reads are marked readOnly so the connection can skip dirty checking.
 */
@Service
public class ProductService {

    private final ProductRepository products;
    private final ProductMapper mapper;

    public ProductService(ProductRepository products, ProductMapper mapper) {
        this.products = products;
        this.mapper = mapper;
    }

    @Transactional
    public ProductResponse create(ProductRequest request) {
        if (products.existsBySku(request.sku())) {
            throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "a product with this sku already exists");
        }
        return mapper.toResponse(products.save(mapper.toEntity(request)));
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<ProductResponse> list() {
        return products.findAll().stream().map(mapper::toResponse).toList();
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public ProductResponse get(UUID id) {
        return mapper.toResponse(find(id));
    }

    @Transactional
    public ProductResponse update(UUID id, ProductUpdate update) {
        Product product = find(id);
        product.change(update.name().strip(), update.priceCents()); // dirty checking writes the UPDATE when the transaction commits
        return mapper.toResponse(product);
    }

    @Transactional
    public void delete(UUID id) {
        products.delete(find(id));
    }

    private Product find(UUID id) {
        return products.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
    }
}
```

- Each public method is **one transaction**. If `create` throws after checking for a duplicate, nothing is stored.
- `update` does not call `save`: the entity is *managed* inside the transaction, so changing it is enough. Hibernate writes one `UPDATE` at commit (dirty checking) and increments `version`.
- Reads use `readOnly = true`.
- Failures the caller can fix are `ResponseStatusException`s. PSO turns them into RFC 9457 problems with the status you chose.
- The `existsBySku` check gives a friendly `409`. Two simultaneous requests can both pass it; then the `UNIQUE` constraint rejects the second insert. That rare case surfaces as a generic error unless you map it.

## 9. The controller

```java
// spring-crud/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/routes/ProductController.java
package com.pso.catalog.routes;

import com.pso.catalog.application.ProductService;
import com.pso.catalog.contracts.ProductRequest;
import com.pso.catalog.contracts.ProductResponse;
import com.pso.catalog.contracts.ProductUpdate;
import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreAuthorize;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.DeleteMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PutMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ResponseStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

/** HTTP only: parse, validate, delegate. The service prefix (/catalog) is applied by PSO, so mappings do not repeat it. */
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/products")
public class ProductController {

    private final ProductService service;

    public ProductController(ProductService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @GetMapping
    @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_products:read')")
    public List<ProductResponse> list() {
        return service.list();
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_products:read')")
    public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable UUID id) {
        return service.get(id);
    }

    @PostMapping
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_products:write')")
    public ProductResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody ProductRequest request) {
        return service.create(request);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_products:write')")
    public ProductResponse update(@PathVariable UUID id, @Valid @RequestBody ProductUpdate update) {
        return service.update(id, update);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_products:write')")
    public void delete(@PathVariable UUID id) {
        service.delete(id);
    }
}
```

- `@Valid` runs Jakarta Validation on the body. A violation never reaches the service.
- `@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_products:read')")` requires the scope in the token. Anything not explicitly allowed requires authentication.
- Mappings do not include `/catalog`: PSO adds the prefix.
- Registration needs no extra file. Spring finds the `@RestController` by component scanning, and the PSO starters (already in `pom.xml`) configure security, errors and logging. Spring has no `MODULE.pso.ts`: that file exists only in orchestrators.

### Where each file goes

`pso validate` checks the layout, and it fails if a class is in the wrong directory: a mapper must live in `adapters/`, a repository in `persistence/`, services in `application/`, controllers in `routes/` and request or response records in `contracts/`. The example follows that layout, and its test runs `pso validate` before it compiles anything. The entity sits in `domain/`. See [Java project structure](microservices/project-structure.md).

Delete the example `PingController`, `PingService`, `PingDto`, `PingRequest` and their tests if you do not want them; the tutorial does not depend on them.

## 10. Compile and run the service's tests

```bash
cd catalog
./mvnw test
```

The tests (`ProductCrudTests`) start an in-process PostgreSQL, apply the real migrations and validate real signed tokens. No Docker is needed for them.

| Test | What it proves |
|---|---|
| `flywayAppliedTheProductsMigration` | version 2 ran |
| `createReadUpdateDeleteRoundTrip` | the happy path, the stored row after the update, `version` never exposed, `404` after delete |
| `invalidInputIsA400ProblemWithFieldErrorsAndNothingIsStored` | validation rejects and the row count is unchanged |
| `aDuplicateSkuIsA409...` | the friendly error, and the `UNIQUE` constraint rejecting a direct insert |
| `scopesAreEnforcedBeforeAnythingTouchesTheDatabase` | `403`/`401` and no row created by a read-only token |
| `aFailureInsideATransactionRollsEverythingBack` | a row inserted, then an exception: the row is gone |

```text evidence="verified"

```

That result comes from the framework's own run of exactly these files (`spring-crud-example.test.ts`).

## 11. Connect the orchestrator to the service

The orchestrator exposes nothing by default. You declare a **module**, one **controller** and one **route per operation**. The CLI keeps the three consistent:

```bash
cd ..
pso make:module products --service gateway
pso make:controller products --service gateway
pso make:route products list    --method GET    --path /    --guard jwt --scopes products:read  --upstream catalog --service gateway
pso make:route products findOne --method GET    --path /:id --guard jwt --scopes products:read  --upstream catalog --service gateway
pso make:route products create  --method POST   --path /    --guard jwt --scopes products:write --upstream catalog --service gateway
pso make:route products replace --method PUT    --path /:id --guard jwt --scopes products:write --upstream catalog --service gateway
pso make:route products remove  --method DELETE --path /:id --guard jwt --scopes products:write --upstream catalog --service gateway
```

On Windows with Git Bash, set `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` first, or Git Bash rewrites `/` and `/:id` into Windows paths and the CLI rejects them.

```tree title="gateway/src/routes/ after the commands"
gateway/src/routes/
  products/
    MODULE.pso.ts  # generated: declares the module and registers the controller
    ROUTES.pso.ts  # generated: the registry of exposed endpoints
    products.controller.ts  # generated: one action per route
```

These are the three generated files, in full:

```ts
// spring-crud/gateway/src/routes/products/MODULE.pso.ts
import { defineModule } from "@pso/core";
import productsRoutes from "./ROUTES.pso";
import { ProductsController } from "./products.controller";

export default defineModule({
  name: "products",
  controllers: [ProductsController],
  providers: [],
  routes: productsRoutes,
  imports: [],
  exports: []
});
```

```ts
// spring-crud/gateway/src/routes/products/ROUTES.pso.ts
import { defineRoutes } from "@pso/http";
import { ProductsController } from "./products.controller";

// The authoritative endpoint registry of this module: only routes listed here can be activated.
export default defineRoutes({
  routes: [
    {
      method: "GET",
      path: "/products",
      controller: ProductsController,
      action: "list",
      security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["products:read"] },
      metadata: { service: "catalog" }
    },
    {
      method: "GET",
      path: "/products/:id",
      controller: ProductsController,
      action: "findOne",
      security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["products:read"] },
      metadata: { service: "catalog" }
    },
    {
      method: "POST",
      path: "/products",
      controller: ProductsController,
      action: "create",
      security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["products:write"] },
      metadata: { service: "catalog" }
    },
    {
      method: "PUT",
      path: "/products/:id",
      controller: ProductsController,
      action: "replace",
      security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["products:write"] },
      metadata: { service: "catalog" }
    },
    {
      method: "DELETE",
      path: "/products/:id",
      controller: ProductsController,
      action: "remove",
      security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["products:write"] },
      metadata: { service: "catalog" }
    }
  ]
});
```

```ts
// spring-crud/gateway/src/routes/products/products.controller.ts
import { Controller, RestController, Get, Req, Res, Upstream, Param, Post, Put, Delete } from "@pso/http";
import { IncomingMessage, ServerResponse } from "node:http";

@Controller()
@RestController("/products")
export class ProductsController {
  constructor(private readonly upstream: Upstream) {}

  @Get("/")
  async list(@Req() req: IncomingMessage, @Res() res: ServerResponse) {
    return this.upstream.forward(req, res, "catalog");
  }

  @Get("/:id")
  async findOne(@Param("id") id: string, @Req() req: IncomingMessage, @Res() res: ServerResponse) {
    return this.upstream.forward(req, res, "catalog");
  }

  @Post("/")
  async create(@Req() req: IncomingMessage, @Res() res: ServerResponse) {
    return this.upstream.forward(req, res, "catalog");
  }

  @Put("/:id")
  async replace(@Param("id") id: string, @Req() req: IncomingMessage, @Res() res: ServerResponse) {
    return this.upstream.forward(req, res, "catalog");
  }

  @Delete("/:id")
  async remove(@Param("id") id: string, @Req() req: IncomingMessage, @Res() res: ServerResponse) {
    return this.upstream.forward(req, res, "catalog");
  }
}
```

How to read them:

- `MODULE.pso.ts` registers `ProductsController`. A controller missing here is diagnostic `PSO_MODULE_003`.
- Each entry in `ROUTES.pso.ts` is one reachable endpoint. Its `security` says which guard applies and which scopes the token needs. `metadata.service: "catalog"` names the upstream.
- Each controller action only forwards: `this.upstream.forward(req, res, "catalog")`. The gateway adds no logic; the service owns the data.
- `@Req()` and `@Res()` give the action the raw request and response so the body streams through unchanged.

Check that everything agrees:

```bash
pso validate
pso routes:list
```

```text evidence="verified"
catalog: 3 resource(s), digest 4731e3e29002
gateway: 4 resource(s), digest 01fa089139ce
OK
```

```text evidence="verified"
GET     /products                products.list           -> catalog        guard:jwt
POST    /products                products.create         -> catalog        guard:jwt
DELETE  /products/:id            products.remove         -> catalog        guard:jwt
GET     /products/:id            products.findOne        -> catalog        guard:jwt
PUT     /products/:id            products.replace        -> catalog        guard:jwt
```

(Your digests may differ.) Five routes, five rows: nothing else is exposed. Install the orchestrator's dependencies once:

```bash
cd gateway
npm install
cd ..
```

## 12. Give both services a way to verify tokens

Both services check the same tokens, signed by an issuer. In production that is your identity provider. For this tutorial you are the issuer:

```bash
pso security:keys --generate
```

```text evidence="verified"
generated k-20261108-d3a27b63 (ES256); private key: keys\k-20261108-d3a27b63.private.pem (owner-only ACL applied); public JWKS: keys\jwks.json
active    k-20261108-d3a27b63  ES256  2026-11-08T16:01:24.567Z
```

(The key id contains the date and a random suffix; yours differs.) The private key is ignored by git (`keys/*.private.pem`). Never commit it.

The Spring service reads the public key from a **JWKS URL** (`PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI`). Plain `http` is accepted only for loopback, for development. The orchestrator can use the same URL. Serve the generated file with this small script, which exists only for development:

```mjs
// spring-crud/dev-jwks.mjs
// Development only: serves keys/jwks.json on loopback so the Spring service can fetch the public key (production uses your identity provider's JWKS URL).
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

createServer((req, res) => {
  if (req.method === "GET" && req.url === "/jwks.json") {
    res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" });
    res.end(readFileSync(new URL("./keys/jwks.json", import.meta.url)));
  } else {
    res.writeHead(404).end();
  }
}).listen(8099, "127.0.0.1", () => console.log("JWKS on http://127.0.0.1:8099/jwks.json"));
```

And this script signs tokens with your private key, with the scopes you ask for:

```mjs
// spring-crud/dev-token.mjs
// Development only: signs a short-lived ES256 token with the private key generated by `pso security:keys --generate`.
// Usage: node dev-token.mjs "products:read products:write"
import { createPrivateKey, createSign } from "node:crypto";
import { readdirSync, readFileSync } from "node:fs";

const keyFile = readdirSync("keys").find((f) => f.endsWith(".private.pem"));
const kid = keyFile.replace(".private.pem", "");
const b64 = (v) => Buffer.from(typeof v === "string" ? v : JSON.stringify(v)).toString("base64url");
const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
const head = b64({ alg: "ES256", typ: "JWT", kid });
const body = b64({ iss: "https://shop.local", aud: "shop-api", sub: "alice", scope: process.argv[2] ?? "", iat: now, exp: now + 3600 });
const sig = createSign("SHA256").update(`${head}.${body}`).sign({ key: createPrivateKey(readFileSync(`keys/${keyFile}`)), dsaEncoding: "ieee-p1363" });
console.log(`${head}.${body}.${sig.toString("base64url")}`);
```

Create the orchestrator's environment file. `npm run dev` loads it; it contains no secret:

```ini title="gateway/.env"
PSO_JWT_ISSUER=https://shop.local
PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE=shop-api
PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI=http://127.0.0.1:8099/jwks.json
PSO_JWT_ALGORITHMS=ES256
PSO_WORKSPACE=../pso.workspace.json
```

## 13. Start everything

Open four terminals in the `shop` folder. Order matters: the database first, the JWKS server, the service, then the gateway.

```bash title="terminal 1"
docker compose -f infra/postgres.compose.yml up -d --wait
node dev-jwks.mjs
```

```bash title="terminal 2 - the Spring service"
cd catalog
export DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:5432/catalog DB_USER=catalog DB_PASSWORD=catalog-dev
export PSO_JWT_ISSUER=https://shop.local PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE=shop-api PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI=http://127.0.0.1:8099/jwks.json PSO_JWT_ALGORITHMS=ES256
./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=local
```

```bash title="terminal 3 - the orchestrator"
cd gateway
npm run dev
```

Alternatively, `pso dev` starts the services in dependency order and colours their logs, but it does not start the database or the JWKS server, and the environment above must be exported in the shell that runs it.

On an empty database the service applies both migrations and starts:

(Port 55433 is where the verification run's database listened; yours is 5432.) Restarting the service does not migrate again: Flyway logs `Successfully validated 2 migrations` and applies nothing.

The orchestrator logs one JSON line per event:

In a terminal, `pso dev` and `npm run dev` print the same events coloured and aligned ([logging](devops/logging.md)).
