# DTOs

> Data transfer classes for request bodies, how to generate them, and how @Body(Dto) validates them.

```ts
// users/dto/request/create-user.dto.ts
import { Dto, Required, Optional, StringField, MinLength, MaxLength, Email, IntegerField, Min } from "@pso/http";

@Dto()
export class CreateUserDto {
  @Required() @StringField() @MinLength(3) @MaxLength(80)
  name!: string;

  @Required() @Email()
  email!: string;

  @Optional() @IntegerField() @Min(18)
  age?: number;
}
```

```bash
pso make:dto users create-user --fields "name:string:min=3:max=80,email:email,age?:integer:min=18"
```

creates `src/modules/users/dto/request/create-user.dto.ts` with a `@Dto()` class like the one above. Without `--fields` the class is empty and accepts only `{}`. Field syntax: `name[?]:type[:min=N][:max=N]` with the types `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, `email`, `date`, `enum=a|b` and an optional `[]` suffix for arrays; `?` makes the field optional.

## What the runtime does with `@Body()` and `@Body(Dto)`

| Declaration | What the action receives |
|---|---|
| `@Body()` | the parsed JSON as it came (after size limit, content type and JSON parsing) |
| `@Body(CreateUserDto)` | an instance of `CreateUserDto` holding only declared, valid fields; invalid input is a `400` problem and the action is not called |

A class in the parameter type alone (`@Body() dto: CreateUserDto`) validates nothing: TypeScript types are erased at run time. The rules are the decorators. The complete guide, with nested objects, business validators, query/path parameters, limits and security notes, is [Validate request bodies with DTOs](orchestrator/dto-validation.md).

## The manual alternative

For a body whose shape is genuinely free-form, accept `unknown` with `@Body()` and check what you need yourself:

```typescript title="src/modules/users/controllers/users.controller.ts"
import { Body, Controller, HttpError, Post, RestController } from "@pso/http";
import { UsersService } from "../services/users.service";

@Controller()
@RestController("/users")
export class UsersController {
  constructor(private readonly usersService: UsersService) {}

  @Post("/")
  create(@Body() value: unknown) {
    if (typeof value !== "object" || value === null || Array.isArray(value))
      throw new HttpError(400, "Expected a JSON object");
    const name = (value as Record<string, unknown>)["name"];
    if (typeof name !== "string" || name.trim().length === 0)
      throw new HttpError(400, "name is required");
    return this.usersService.create({ name: name.trim() });
  }
}
```

This action still requires a matching `POST /users` entry in `ROUTES.pso.ts` and controller registration in `MODULE.pso.ts`. Check a missing `name`, a numeric `name`, invalid JSON and an oversized body separately: the first two are your action's `400`, while parsing and size limits happen before it runs. Spring service actions use Jakarta Validation for the equivalent field checks ([CRUD tutorial](tutorials/crud-api.md)).

## What generating a DTO does

Expected output (for the `orders` module, DTO `create-order`):

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso make:dto orders create-order --fields "customer:string:min=3:max=40,email:email,quantity:integer:min=1:max=100"
created    src/modules/orders/dto/request/create-order.dto.ts
```

The class it writes is shown in full on [Validate request bodies](orchestrator/dto-validation.md).

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| an empty class to fill by hand | `pso make:dto orders create-order` (it accepts only `{}` until you add fields) |
| optional fields | `age?:integer:min=18` in `--fields` |
| a fixed set of values | `role:enum=admin|user` |
| a DTO for a route | `pso make:route orders create --method POST --path / --dto create-order` |
| a Spring DTO | `pso make:dto customer-request --service catalog` (a record with Jakarta Validation) |

## Common mistakes

- Using the DTO class as a type only (`@Body() dto: CreateUserDto`): no validation happens.
- Reusing one DTO for create and update.
- Putting secrets in a DTO that is logged elsewhere (the framework does not log bodies).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Check | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| a request with a wrong field is accepted | the action does not use `@Body(Dto)`, so the gateway only parses JSON | the controller source | declare a `@Dto` class and use `@Body(Dto)` ([DTO validation](orchestrator/dto-validation.md)) |
| `400` with `PSO_VALIDATION_FAILED` and an `errors` list | the body violates the DTO | the `errors[].field` values in the answer | fix the client, or the DTO if it is too strict |
| the gateway accepts but the service answers `400` | the gateway validates early, the service always validates for itself | the service's own record annotations | keep both in step; the service is authoritative |
| unknown properties are rejected | strict mode is the default | the `is not allowed` entries | add the field to the DTO, or stop sending it |

## Next steps

- [Validate request bodies](orchestrator/dto-validation.md)
- [Controllers](orchestrator/controllers.md)

# Guards

> Authentication and authorization checks that run before a route's action, including the built-in jwt guard.

A guard is a function exported as the default of a `*.guard.ts` file. Its **name** is the file name without `.guard.ts`.

## The built-in `jwt` guard

The framework provides the `jwt` guard (package `@pso/security`). You do not write verification code; the generated file is only:

```typescript title="src/.app/guards/jwt.guard.ts"
import { JwtGuard } from "@pso/security";
export default JwtGuard.create();
```

If the file is absent the guard is registered automatically. Configuration lives in `pso.config.json` ([Security configuration](security/security-configuration.md)). An optional policy function adds an authorization decision after verification:

```typescript
export default JwtGuard.create({ policy: (p) => p.hasRole("staff") });
```

## Custom guards

```typescript title="src/modules/users/guards/users-key.guard.ts"
import type { Guard } from "@pso/http";

const guard: Guard = (req) => (req.headers["x-key"] === "k" ? true : { allow: false, status: 401 });
export default guard;
```

A guard returns `true` (allow), `false` or `{ allow: false, status: 401 }` (unauthenticated), `{ allow: false, status: 403 }` (forbidden), or `{ allow: true, principal }` to establish the caller's identity so declared scopes and roles are enforced by the framework. A project `jwt.guard.ts` that does not use `JwtGuard.create()` is **rejected by default**. To replace JWT verification, declare `security.authentication.provider: custom`, identify `customProvider` and use `CustomGuard.create`; see [Custom guards](security/authentication.md#custom-guards). A module-local guard for an additional condition does not replace the framework JWT verifier.

## Where guards live

- Global: `src/.app/guards/*.guard.ts`.
- Module-local: `src/modules/<module>/guards/*.guard.ts`. Names share one namespace; a duplicate stops start-up.

## Using a guard

In `ROUTES.pso.ts`: `security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["users:read"], roles: ["admin"] }`, or `guards: ["a", "b"]` (all must pass). With decorators: `@UseGuards("jwt")`, `@RequireScopes("users:read")`, `@RequireRoles("admin")`, `@Public()` and, for the identity, `@CurrentPrincipal()` ([Authorization](security/authorization.md)). Requirements add up across module, controller, action and route; a declaration can never weaken what a decorator demands (`PSO_ROUTE_007`), and an unknown guard name is `PSO_ROUTE_008`. A route with no policy inherits the default `jwt` guard.

```bash
pso make:guard authenticated            # src/.app/guards/authenticated.guard.ts
pso make:guard users users-key          # module-local
```

Generated custom guards deny by default (`() => false`); replace the body with real verification.

## Order of evaluation

Guards run in declared order and establish the principal; then scopes and roles are evaluated centrally (`401` vs `403`); then middleware; then the action.

## What generating a guard does

Expected output:

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso make:guard authenticated
created    src/.app/guards/authenticated.guard.ts

$ pso make:guard orders orders-key --service gw
created    src/modules/orders/guards/orders-key.guard.ts
```

and the generated file denies everything until you replace the body:

```typescript
import type { Guard } from "@pso/http";

// Deny by default: replace with real verification.
const guard: Guard = () => false;
export default guard;
```

A route that names a guard with no matching file is `PSO_ROUTE_008`.

## What a guard decision looks like to the caller and in the log

For the built-in `jwt` guard (expected):

```text evidence="expected"
no token                              -> 401  WARN [security] authentication failed  reason=missing_header route="GET /customers"
valid token, missing scope            -> 403  WARN [security] authorization denied  missing=scope:customers:read route="GET /customers"
```

A custom guard returns `false` or `{ allow: false, status: 401 | 403 }` to refuse; the response is the standard problem for that status.

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| the standard JWT check | `JwtGuard.create()` (generated by default); configure issuer, audience and keys |
| an extra authorization rule | `JwtGuard.create({ policy: (p) => p.hasRole("staff") })` |
| an API-key check for one module | a module-local guard in `src/modules/<module>/guards/` |
| to replace JWT verification entirely | a custom `jwt` guard **and** an explicit `custom` provider declaration; an undeclared replacement stops start-up ([authentication](security/authentication.md)) |

## Common mistakes

- Leaving the generated `() => false` in place and wondering why everything is `401`.
- Returning `true` for "unknown" states: fail closed.
- Doing authorization with scopes by hand inside actions: declare them on the route.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Check | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PSO_ROUTE_008` (unknown guard) | the route names a guard that is not defined, often a typo | `pso validate` shows `available:` | use an existing name; never remove the guard to silence it |
| `401` `PSO_AUTH_UNAUTHORIZED` | no token, a malformed token, or issuer, audience, algorithm or expiry do not match | the gateway log line for the request, and `pso security:validate` | send a valid token; align `PSO_JWT_ISSUER` and `PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE` |
| `403` `PSO_AUTH_FORBIDDEN` | the token is valid but lacks the route's scope | the gateway `warn` line "authorization denied" names the missing scope | issue the scope, or correct the route's `scopes` |
| the orchestrator refuses to start | the guard is used but issuer, audience or a key source is missing | `pso security:validate` | set `PSO_JWT_ISSUER`, `PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE` and one key source ([keys](security/keys-and-pem.md)) |

The first three were reproduced on a real workspace ([Validation errors, one by one](reference/diagnostics-catalog.md)); the log line of the fourth is in [Build a CRUD API](tutorials/crud-api.md).

## Next steps

- [Authentication](security/authentication.md)
- [Secure routing](security/secure-routing.md)

# Validate request bodies with DTOs

> Declare the shape of a request once with @Dto fields, bind it with @Body(Dto), and let the orchestrator reject invalid input before your action runs. Basic to production, with real output.

## What it is

`@Body(CreateOrderDto)` makes the orchestrator check the request body against a class you declared, field by field, **before your action is called**. If anything is wrong, the client gets a `400` `application/problem+json` response that lists every wrong field, and your code never runs.

```typescript
@Post("/")
create(@Body(CreateOrderDto) body: CreateOrderDto) { /* body is valid here */ }
```

`@Body()` without a class is unchanged: it passes the parsed JSON as it is. Nothing is inferred from TypeScript types, because types do not exist at run time. The rules are the decorators on the fields.

## Why it exists

Without it, every action starts with the same lines: is this an object, is `name` a string, is it long enough, did the client send fields I do not expect. Those lines get forgotten, written differently in each action, or written wrong. A declaration is shorter, is read by the framework, and produces the same error shape everywhere.

## When to use it, and when not to

| Use `@Body(Dto)` when | Do not use it when |
|---|---|
| the orchestrator itself handles the request | the action only forwards to a Spring service with `forward(...)`; the service validates (Jakarta Validation) and the body must reach it untouched |
| the body has a fixed, known shape | the body is free-form JSON on purpose (use `@Body()` and validate what you need) |
| you want one consistent 400 contract | the rule needs a database or another service (use a business validator, below, not a field rule) |

Forwarded routes keep working exactly as before. Validating in both places is allowed and harmless, but the Spring service stays the authority for its own data.

## Prerequisites

A workspace with an orchestrator and a module. If you have none yet, follow [your first orchestrator](getting-started/first-orchestrator.md).

## 1. Minimal example

```bash
pso make:module orders
pso make:controller orders --prefix /orders
pso make:dto orders create-order --fields "customer:string:min=3:max=40,email:email,quantity:integer:min=1:max=100"
pso make:route orders create --method POST --path / --scopes orders:write --dto create-order
```

What each command created:

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `src/modules/orders/MODULE.pso.ts` | the module: which controller and providers exist |
| `src/modules/orders/routes/ROUTES.pso.ts` | the authoritative route list: `POST /orders`, guarded, scope `orders:write` |
| `src/modules/orders/controllers/orders.controller.ts` | the action `create`, already using `@Body(CreateOrderDto)` |
| `src/modules/orders/dto/request/create-order.dto.ts` | the validated shape |

The generated DTO:

```typescript title="src/modules/orders/dto/request/create-order.dto.ts"
import { Dto, Required, StringField, IntegerField, Email, MinLength, MaxLength, Min, Max } from "@pso/http";

@Dto()
export class CreateOrderDto {
  @Required() @StringField() @MinLength(3) @MaxLength(40)
  customer!: string;

  @Required() @Email()
  email!: string;

  @Required() @IntegerField() @Min(1) @Max(100)
  quantity!: number;
}
```

The generated controller (the action body is yours to write; here it returns what it received):

```typescript title="src/modules/orders/controllers/orders.controller.ts"
import { Controller, RestController, Post, Body } from "@pso/http";
import { CreateOrderDto } from "../dto/request/create-order.dto";

@Controller()
@RestController("/orders")
export class OrdersController {

  @Post("/")
  async create(@Body(CreateOrderDto) body: CreateOrderDto) {
    return { accepted: true, customer: body.customer, quantity: body.quantity };
  }
}
```

### How to read it

- `@Dto()` marks the class as a validation contract. A class without it cannot be used in `@Body(...)`; the orchestrator refuses to start.
- Each field has a **type decorator** (`@StringField`, `@IntegerField`, `@Email`, ...) and any number of constraints (`@MinLength`, `@Min`, ...). A field with no type decorator is a start-up error, never a silent pass.
- Fields are required unless you say `@Optional()`. `@Required()` is the explicit way to say the default.
- `!` after the name is plain TypeScript ("assigned by the framework"): the framework creates the object, not a constructor.

## 2. Run it and see what happens

```bash
pso validate          # static checks, no code runs
npm run build         # compile the orchestrator
pso dev               # or: node dist/main.js
```

A valid request:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"customer":"Grace","email":"grace@example.com","quantity":3}'
```

```text evidence="illustrative"
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
x-correlation-id: 5b0d6f0e-4b1c-4a8e-9c0e-5e3d3f6a1c11

{"accepted":true,"customer":"Grace","quantity":3}
```

An invalid one (name too short, malformed e-mail, quantity below 1, and a property the DTO does not declare):

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -H "x-correlation-id: demo-corr-0001" \
  -d '{"customer":"Gr","email":"nope","quantity":0,"admin":true}'
```

```text evidence="expected"
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8
```

```json evidence="verified"
{
  "type": "urn:pso:problem:validation-failed",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "The request is not valid; see the errors member.",
  "code": "PSO_VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "error": "validation_failed",
  "instance": "/orders",
  "correlationId": "demo-corr-0001",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "admin",    "message": "is not allowed" },
    { "field": "customer", "message": "must have at least 3 characters" },
    { "field": "email",    "message": "must be a valid e-mail address" },
    { "field": "quantity", "message": "must be at least 1" }
  ]
}
```

What you see in the orchestrator terminal (default `pretty` format on a terminal; see [logging](devops/logging.md)):

```text evidence="expected"
2026-11-08 14:18:19.530 INFO  request (demo-corr-0001)  traceId=82b1e39923a376ea73ba19a092fca833 method=POST path=/orders status=201 ms=6.56
2026-11-08 14:18:19.536 INFO  request (demo-corr-0001)  traceId=d5bffcb133d75597de34f26b737428d9 method=POST path=/orders status=400 ms=1.17
```

The log line carries the method, path, status and correlation id. It does **not** carry the body: submitted values are never logged or echoed.

## 3. What happens internally

1. The request arrives. Authentication and authorization run first: an unauthenticated caller gets `401` and the body is never examined.
2. The body is read up to the configured size limit (`http.limits.maxBodyBytes`), and the content type must be `application/json` (`415` otherwise; invalid JSON is `400 invalid_json`).
3. The top level must be a JSON object.
4. For every declared field the framework checks presence, type, then constraints. Types are strict: `"3"` is not an integer. `null` is not "absent" (see `@Nullable`).
5. Properties that are not declared are reported (default) or dropped (`@Dto({ unknown: "strip" })`).
6. Only if the whole structure is valid do business validators (`@Validate`) run.
7. If anything failed, one `400` problem lists up to 50 errors and your action is not called. Otherwise the action receives an instance of your DTO class containing only the declared, valid fields. The class constructor is **not** run.

## 4. Choosing constraints

| Decorator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `@Required()` / `@Optional()` / `@Nullable()` | presence; `@Nullable` also accepts an explicit JSON `null` |
| `@StringField()` `@IntegerField()` `@NumberField()` `@BooleanField()` | exact JSON type (no coercion) |
| `@Email()` `@IsoDate()` | strings with a format: RFC-style e-mail up to 254 characters; ISO 8601 date or date-time with zone (the value stays a string) |
| `@MinLength(n)` `@MaxLength(n)` | string length in characters |
| `@Min(n)` `@Max(n)` | numeric range (inclusive) |
| `@Pattern(/re/)` | string must match; the expression must not use the `g` or `y` flag |
| `@OneOf("a", "b")` | the value must be one of these |
| `@ArrayOf("string")`, `@ArrayOf(ItemDto)` + `@MinItems` `@MaxItems` | arrays of scalars or of DTOs; up to 1000 items unless you lower or raise (max 10 000) with `@MaxItems` |
| `@Nested(AddressDto)` | an object validated by another `@Dto` class (up to 8 levels) |
| `@Message("text")` | replaces the messages of that field with a constant of yours |
| `@Validate(Rules)` | a business validator, see below |

Anything else is deliberately missing: the model is small so that every decorator means the same thing in every DTO.

## 5. Intermediate: nested objects and arrays

```typescript
@Dto()
export class AddressDto {
  @Required() @StringField() @MinLength(1) street!: string;
  @Required() @StringField() @MaxLength(40) city!: string;
}

@Dto()
export class CreateCustomerDto {
  @Required() @StringField() @MinLength(3) name!: string;
  @Optional() @Nested(AddressDto) address?: AddressDto;
  @Optional() @ArrayOf("string") @MaxItems(5) tags?: string[];
}
```

Errors carry the path: `address.city`, `tags[2]`. For DTOs that refer to each other, pass a function: `@Nested(() => CategoryDto)`.

## 6. Advanced: business validators that use services

A field rule is **structural** and pure: it needs nothing but the value. A rule such as "this SKU exists" needs a service. Keep it separate:

```typescript title="src/modules/orders/services/sku-rules.service.ts"
import { Injectable, type FieldValidator } from "@pso/http";
import { SkuCatalog } from "./sku-catalog.service";

@Injectable()
export class SkuRules implements FieldValidator {
  constructor(private readonly catalog: SkuCatalog) {}
  async validate(value: unknown): Promise<string | undefined> {
    return (await this.catalog.exists(String(value))) ? undefined : "is not a known SKU";
  }
}
```

```typescript
@Dto()
export class CreateOrderDto {
  @Required() @StringField() @Validate(SkuRules)
  sku!: string;
}
```

```typescript title="MODULE.pso.ts"
providers: [SkuCatalog, SkuRules],   // registration is explicit: a validator that is not listed stops the start-up
```

Properties of this design:

- Validators are **providers**, resolved by the same container as services, with the same constructor injection.
- They run **only after the structure is valid**, so garbage input never causes a query.
- They may be `async`. They return a message to reject or nothing to accept, and receive `{ object, path }` for cross-field rules (`ctx.object["startDate"]`).
- The framework never queries anything because a DTO exists. If a validator is not registered, the application refuses to start with the route and the class name:

```text evidence="expected"
2026-11-08 14:21:07.101 ERROR startup failed  error="POST /orders: validator SkuRules must be listed in the providers of module \"orders\"\nnothing was started" diagnostics=["PSO_DTO_VALIDATOR_UNREGISTERED"]
```

## 7. Path and query parameters

`@Param` and `@Query` accept an optional description. Conversion is explicit and strict (`"12abc"` is an error, never 12; `"012"` is rejected):

```typescript
@Get("/")
list(
  @Query("page", { type: "integer", min: 1, default: 1 }) page: number,
  @Query("sort", { oneOf: ["asc", "desc"], default: "asc" }) sort: string,
) { /* page is a number, sort is "asc" or "desc" */ }

@Get("/:id")
get(@Param("id", { type: "integer", min: 1 }) id: number) { /* ... */ }
```

A violation is the same `400` problem with the field named `query.page` or `path.id`. Without a second argument both decorators behave as before (a raw string).

## 8. Create, update and partial update

There is one DTO per intent. Reuse by composition, not by flags:

```typescript
@Dto() export class CreateUserDto { @Required() @StringField() name!: string; @Required() @Email() email!: string; }
@Dto() export class UpdateUserDto { @Required() @StringField() name!: string; }                 // PUT: replace what can change
@Dto() export class PatchUserDto  { @Optional() @StringField() name?: string; }                 // PATCH: only what was sent
```

`email` is missing from `UpdateUserDto`, so a client that sends it gets `"email": "is not allowed"`: the rule that "email cannot change" is the shape of the class. Validation groups and conditional "required if" rules are intentionally not part of this model; express them as separate DTOs or as a business validator.

## Files in a DTO

A DTO can also describe files. `@FileField` (one file) and `@FilesField` (several) read `multipart/form-data`; declaring one switches `@Body(Dto)` from JSON to multipart for that route. Ordinary fields in the same form are converted strictly to the type you declared (`"3"` becomes `3` for an `@IntegerField`, `"3x"` stays a string and fails). Limits are enforced while the body streams, and the declared content type is checked against the file's signature, not trusted.

```typescript
@Dto()
export class UploadDocumentDto {
  @FileField({ required: true, maxSize: "10MB", mimeTypes: ["application/pdf"], extensions: [".pdf"] })
  document!: PsoUploadedFile;

  @Required() @StringField() @MaxLength(80)
  title!: string;
}
```

Everything about it (options, errors, forwarding to a service, the CLI generators) is on [File uploads and downloads](orchestrator/file-uploads.md).

## 9. Production considerations

- **Unknown properties are rejected by default.** This prevents mass assignment ("I sent `isAdmin`") and surfaces client bugs. Use `@Dto({ unknown: "strip" })` only for DTOs that must tolerate newer clients, and know that the extra data is dropped silently.
- **Bounded work.** Up to 8 nesting levels, 1000 items per array by default, 50 errors per response (a `more errors were found` entry is added), and the body size limit applies before parsing.
- **Prototype pollution.** Fields named `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` cannot be declared; such keys in a request are reported as unknown properties and never copied; the result object has the DTO prototype and own properties only.
- **No data in errors.** Messages are constants. Only property **names** from the request are echoed, truncated to 64 printable characters.
- **Order is part of security.** Authentication, then authorization, then validation. An anonymous caller cannot probe your DTO.
- **Compatibility.** Routes that use `@Body()` do not change behavior.

## 10. Anti-patterns

| Do not | Do instead |
|---|---|
| annotate the parameter with a class and expect validation (`@Body() dto: CreateUserDto`) | pass the class to the decorator: `@Body(CreateUserDto)` |
| write `age?: number` and expect the question mark to make it optional | add `@Optional()`; TypeScript syntax is erased and is not read |
| query a database from a field rule | write a `@Validate` provider; keep structure pure |
| put request data into `@Message` text | use constants; the message is returned to the client |
| use one DTO for create and update with many `@Optional()` | one DTO per intent |
| validate in the orchestrator **and** assume the service no longer needs to | the service validates its own input (Jakarta Validation) |

## 11. Errors you may meet

| What you see | Meaning and fix |
|---|---|
| start-up: `... is used as a DTO but is not decorated with @Dto()` | add `@Dto()` to the class used in `@Body`, `@Nested` or `@ArrayOf` |
| start-up: `... has no type decorator` | add `@StringField()`, `@IntegerField()`, `@Email()`, ... |
| start-up: `field "x" already has the type string` | a field has two type decorators; keep one |
| start-up: `validator X must be listed in the providers of module "m"` | add the class to `providers` in `MODULE.pso.ts` |
| `400` with `"message": "is not allowed"` | the client sent a property the DTO does not declare |
| `400` with `"a JSON request body is required"` | the body was empty |
| `415` | the request was not `application/json` |
| `400 invalid_json` | the body is not valid JSON (before any DTO check) |

## 12. Spring Boot services: the equivalent

Spring services use **Jakarta Validation** (`@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Email`, `@Valid`), which the starter activates, and the same Problem Details contract. The two mechanisms are different implementations with a deliberately similar result: a `400` `application/problem+json` with `code: PSO_VALIDATION_FAILED`, a `correlationId`, and an `errors` list of `{ field, message }`. Message wording follows each library. See [PostgreSQL CRUD in Spring](spring/postgresql-crud.md) for a complete example with validation, persistence and tests.

## Next steps

- [DTO classes and `make:dto`](orchestrator/dtos.md)
- [The error standard (RFC 9457)](reference/error-standard.md)
- [Logging and correlation](devops/logging.md)

# File uploads and downloads

> Receive multipart uploads in the orchestrator, bind them to a DTO with @FileField, validate them while they stream, forward them to a Spring service and stream downloads back.

## What it is

The orchestrator receives `multipart/form-data`, binds files and ordinary fields to a `@Dto` class, checks them, and forwards the validated files to the Spring service that owns the business rules and the storage. You never parse a multipart body in a controller and you never see a physical path.

| Step | Where | Who |
|---|---|---|
| authenticate, authorize (scopes), rate limit | before the body is read | orchestrator |
| parse, bound, spool to private temporary files, validate | `@Body(Dto)` | orchestrator |
| rebuild a clean multipart request and stream it | `Upstream.forwardUpload` | orchestrator |
| business authorization, storage, metadata | the Spring service ([Storage](spring/storage.md)) | the service |

## 1. The upload DTO

```typescript
import { Dto, FileField, FilesField, MaxLength, PsoUploadedFile, Required, StringField } from "@pso/http";

@Dto()
export class UploadDocumentDto {
  @FileField({ required: true, maxSize: "10MB", mimeTypes: ["application/pdf"], extensions: [".pdf"] })
  document!: PsoUploadedFile;

  @FilesField({ required: false, maxFiles: 3, maxSize: "2MB", mimeTypes: ["image/png", "image/jpeg"] })
  attachments?: PsoUploadedFile[];

  @Required() @StringField() @MaxLength(80)
  title!: string;
}
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `required` | `true` | `false` makes the file optional |
| `maxSize` | `10MB` | per file, enforced **while the body streams** (`10MB` = 10 * 1024 * 1024 bytes) |
| `mimeTypes` | any | exact (`application/pdf`) or family (`image/*`); verified against the file signature |
| `extensions` | any | extensions of the sanitized filename, e.g. `[".pdf"]` |
| `allowEmpty` | `false` | accept a zero-byte file |
| `unverified` | `false` | trust the declared type for a listed type the framework cannot verify |
| `maxFiles` / `minFiles` (`@FilesField`) | `10` (max 100) / `1` | files in the field |

The content types the framework can verify by signature are `application/pdf`, `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/gif`, `image/webp`, `application/gzip`, `application/json`, `text/plain`, `text/csv`, `text/markdown` and the zip family (`application/zip`, OOXML and OpenDocument, EPUB). Listing any other type is a **start-up error** unless you set `unverified: true`, so trusting the client is always a visible decision. A zip-family signature cannot distinguish a `.docx` from another zip: the check proves "a zip container", not "a Word document".

A `PsoUploadedFile` has `field`, `filename` (sanitized), `contentType` (declared), `detectedType`, `size`, `sha256`, `stream()` and `buffer(maxBytes)`. The temporary path is not a property and is never serialized.

Files can only be declared at the top level of a DTO. Unknown form fields (and files in undeclared fields) follow the usual `@Dto({ unknown })` policy: rejected by default, their content is discarded and never written.

## 2. The routes

```typescript
@Controller()
@RestController("/employees")
export class DocumentsController {
  constructor(private readonly upstream: Upstream) {}

  @Post("/:id/documents")
  async upload(@Param("id") id: string, @Body(UploadDocumentDto) dto: UploadDocumentDto, @Req() req: IncomingMessage, @Res() res: ServerResponse) {
    return this.upstream.forwardUpload(req, res, "hr-service", dto, { path: `/employees/${id}/documents` });
  }

  @Get("/:id/documents/:fileId")
  async download(@Param("id") id: string, @Param("fileId") fileId: string, @Req() req: IncomingMessage, @Res() res: ServerResponse) {
    return this.upstream.forwardDownload(req, res, "hr-service", { path: `/employees/${id}/documents/${fileId}`, maxResponseBytes: 50_000_000 });
  }
}
```

Declare both in `ROUTES.pso.ts` with `security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: [...] }` and `metadata: { service: "hr-service" }` like any forwarded route. The generators write all of this:

```bash
pso make:dto documents upload-document --service gw \
  --fields "document:file:mime=application/pdf:size=10MB:ext=.pdf,title:string:max=80"
pso make:route documents upload --method POST --path /:id/documents --scopes documents:write \
  --upstream hr-service --dto upload-document --service gw
pso make:route documents download --method GET --path /:id/documents/:fileId --scopes documents:read \
  --upstream hr-service --download --max-download 50MB --service gw
```

`make:dto` refuses a file field without `mime=` (it never generates a field that accepts any file) and refuses types it cannot verify. `make:route` with a DTO that has file fields requires `--upstream`: the orchestrator forwards, the service stores. The Spring side is `pso make:files` ([Storage](spring/storage.md)).

## 3. Run it and see what happens

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/employees/42/documents \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "X-Correlation-ID: corr-upload-0001" \
  -F title="Employment contract" -F "document=@contract.pdf;type=application/pdf"
```

The service answers with the metadata and an opaque identifier; the orchestrator relays that response unchanged (status and body come from the service).

```http evidence="expected"
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json
x-correlation-id: corr-upload-0001

{"id":"f_FOnGV-Jgz67FK_f5LA9fnA","filename":"contract.pdf","contentType":"application/pdf","size":4216,"ownerRef":"employee:42", "checksumSha256":"f719...", "context":{"title":"Employment contract"}}
```

The identifier, size and checksum vary per run. Both of the following are asserted by tests that run the real orchestrator in front of the real Spring service (`storage-e2e.test.ts`): the file arrives byte for byte with its sanitized name, and the correlation id survives the whole chain.

## 4. How it behaves

- **Order.** Authentication, scope authorization, rate limits and the concurrency check happen **before** a byte of the body is read. An anonymous caller cannot make the orchestrator write anything to disk.
- **Streaming and backpressure.** The body is consumed chunk by chunk; the next chunk is not read until the previous one reached the file system. Memory does not grow with the file (a test streams 400 MB and asserts the retained memory plateaus).
- **Limits during streaming.** A lying `Content-Length` does not help: bytes are counted as they arrive. The budget of a route comes from its DTO (every `maxSize * maxFiles` plus the ordinary fields), never above `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`; the ordinary fields share `MAX_BODY_BYTES`; `MAX_MULTIPART_PARTS` bounds the parts; `MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS` bounds simultaneous uploads (`503` + `Retry-After`).
- **Private temporary files.** One `0700` directory per request, files named with random bytes (never the client\'s name), removed when the response ends: on success, on every error and when the client disconnects.
- **A fresh request to the service.** `forwardUpload` re-encodes only the validated, declared fields and files. The client\'s raw body, boundary, `Content-Type` and `x-pso-*` headers are never relayed; the bearer travels only as your [upstream policy](security/service-identity.md) allows, so the service authenticates the caller itself.
- **Compatibility.** `@Body()` and `@Body(Dto)` without file fields behave as before; a DTO with file fields answers `415` to a JSON body.

## 5. Errors

| Situation | Response |
|---|---|
| not `multipart/form-data` on an upload route | `415 PSO_HTTP_UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` |
| missing boundary, truncated or malformed parts, invalid UTF-8 in a field | `400 PSO_HTTP_MALFORMED_MULTIPART` |
| a field or file rule is not met (required, type, signature, extension, count, unexpected field) | `400 PSO_VALIDATION_FAILED` with `errors[]` naming the field, never the content |
| a file over `maxSize` | `413 PSO_FILE_TOO_LARGE` |
| the request over the route budget, `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` or `MAX_MULTIPART_PARTS` | `413 PSO_HTTP_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` |
| too many uploads at once | `503 PSO_SERVER_BUSY` + `Retry-After` |
| the service is down | `503 PSO_UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE`; temporary files are still removed |

The client closing the connection mid-upload cannot be answered; the partial files are removed and the request is counted with status `499` in the metrics.

## 6. Downloads

`forwardDownload` streams the service\'s response with backpressure. On a `2xx` it adds `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox`, `Cache-Control: private, no-store` and `Content-Disposition: attachment` when the service sent no disposition. Error responses are relayed untouched. The size cap is per call (`maxResponseBytes`); a plain `forward()` keeps `MAX_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE_BYTES`. Authorization of **who may read which file** belongs to the service: possessing an id grants nothing.

## Production considerations

- Raise `REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 30 s) if your largest legitimate upload needs longer on your slowest network.
- Keep `maxSize` and the Spring `pso.storage.upload.max-size` and `pso.limits.multipart.max-file-size` consistent: the smallest one wins and the others never see the file.
- Put the system temporary directory (`TMPDIR`) on a volume with room for `MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS * MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`.
- Malware scanning is not performed by the orchestrator; use the `ContentScanner` hook in the service.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What happens | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `@Body() dto: UploadDocumentDto` without the class in the decorator | no file binding | `@Body(UploadDocumentDto)` |
| `document: File` as the property type | the global DOM `File` is not the value | `PsoUploadedFile` |
| listing `application/msword` in `mimeTypes` | start-up error: no signature check | list verifiable types or set `unverified: true` knowingly |
| using `forward()` for an upload route that has a DTO | the body was already consumed and validated; the client\'s bytes are replayed unvalidated framing | `forwardUpload` |
| a `maxSize` above `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | files are refused by the route budget first | raise `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` deliberately |

## Next steps

- [Storage in Spring Boot services](spring/storage.md): where the files go and who may read them.
- [Validate request bodies with DTOs](orchestrator/dto-validation.md) and [Upstream clients](orchestrator/upstream-clients.md).

# Middleware and filters

> Named per-route middleware that runs after the guards and exception filters that turn errors into answers - generated, wired, run and verified end to end.

Both are **named** files that a route opts into. Nothing runs globally from `main.ts` ([why](decisions/why-minimal-bootstrap.md)). The examples on this page are run by the framework's test suite (`docs-middleware.test.ts`): the behavior described here is verified, not assumed.

## Middleware

A function exported by `src/.app/middlewares/<name>.middleware.ts`. Routes opt in by name (`middleware: ["audit"]` in `ROUTES.pso.ts`). It runs **after the guards**, so it only sees authenticated requests (public routes excepted). It may end the response; if it does, the action is not run.

```bash
pso make:middleware audit
```

```typescript title="src/.app/middlewares/audit.middleware.ts"
import type { Middleware } from "@pso/http";

const middleware: Middleware = (req, _res, route) => {
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: "audited", method: req.method, path: route.path }));
};
export default middleware;
```

Wire it in the route:

```typescript title="src/modules/orders/routes/ROUTES.pso.ts"
{
  method: "POST", path: "/orders", controller: OrdersController, action: "create",
  security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["customers:read"] },
  middleware: ["audit"],
  filters: ["conflict"]
}
```

### What happens (expected)

1. A `POST /orders` **without a token** answers `401`. The middleware did not run: the log contains no `audited` line.
2. The same request **with a valid token** answers `201` with the action's result, and the log shows:

```text evidence="expected"
{"msg":"audited","method":"POST","path":"/orders"}
```

The middleware sees the route (`route.path`) and the request; use it for audit trails, request enrichment or early refusal. For authentication and authorization use [guards](orchestrator/guards.md), so the decision is made in the same place for every route.

## Filters

A filter handles errors thrown by the action. Return `true` once the response has been written:

```bash
pso make:filter conflict
```

```typescript title="src/.app/filters/conflict.filter.ts"
import { HttpError, type Filter } from "@pso/http";

const filter: Filter = (err, _req, res) => {
  if (!(err instanceof HttpError) || err.status !== 409) return false;
  res.writeHead(409, { "content-type": "application/json" });
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: "conflict" }));
  return true;
};
export default filter;
```

Use it with `filters: ["conflict"]`. If the action throws `new HttpError(409, "duplicate")`, the answer is (expected):

```text evidence="expected"
HTTP 409 application/json
{"error":"conflict"}
```

and **not** the framework's default `application/problem+json` body. That is the point and the risk: a filter replaces the standard error contract for that route. Prefer keeping the standard ([error standard](reference/error-standard.md)) unless a client truly needs another shape. A filter that returns `false` leaves the error to the next filter and then to the framework; unhandled errors produce a generic `500` that never leaks internals.

## Failure: an unknown name

A route that names a middleware or filter that does not exist is `PSO_ROUTE_008`, caught by `pso validate` and again at start-up (verified: the process refuses to start and names the code).

## When to use which

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| to check who may call | a guard |
| to record, enrich or rate-shape every request of some routes | middleware |
| to translate one kind of error into a specific answer | a filter |
| a rule about the body's shape | a DTO ([validation](orchestrator/dto-validation.md)) |
| to apply something to every route | a global guard or the framework's own limits, not a middleware list copied everywhere |

## Common mistakes

- Expecting a middleware to run for a request the guard refused.
- Logging tokens or bodies in a middleware.
- Writing a filter that swallows errors it does not understand (return `false` for those).

## Next steps

- [Request and response lifecycle](orchestrator/request-lifecycle.md)
- [Guards](orchestrator/guards.md)

# Channels (real-time)

> Declare WebSocket channels with decorators, register them in MODULE.pso.ts, authorize every subscription against the resource, publish typed events from Spring Boot through Dispatch, and connect browsers with the client SDK.

## What it is

PSO Channels delivers real-time events to browsers over WebSocket, on the **same HTTP server** as your routes. Three responsibilities stay separate:

| Piece | Owns |
|---|---|
| **Channels** (`@pso/channels`) | connections, subscriptions, authorization, client commands, delivery, presence, limits, heartbeats |
| **Channel registry** (`channels: [...]` in `MODULE.pso.ts`) | which channel classes exist, their names, contracts and who may publish |
| **PSO Dispatch** | inter-service messaging, brokers, retries, dead letters, the transactional outbox |

Channels is **not a message broker**. A browser connection is not a durable queue: an event published while a client is offline is not replayed, and the SDK never claims otherwise.

## 1. Declare and register a channel

```typescript
import { Channel, OnSubscribe, OnEvent, OnDisconnect, Payload, Client, Context, ChannelParam } from "@pso/channels";
import type { ChannelClient, ChannelContext } from "@pso/channels";
import { Scopes } from "@pso/http";

@Channel("/recruitment", { visibility: "private" })
export class RecruitmentChannel {
  @OnSubscribe()
  @Scopes("recruitment:read")
  async authorize(@Context() context: ChannelContext): Promise<boolean> {
    return context.user !== null;
  }

  @OnEvent("candidate.subscribe")
  @Scopes("candidate:read")
  async subscribeCandidate(@Payload(CandidateSubscriptionDto) payload: CandidateSubscriptionDto, @Client() client: ChannelClient) {
    await client.join(`candidate.${payload.candidateId}`); // goes through the SAME authorization as a direct subscribe
    return { joined: payload.candidateId };
  }

  @OnDisconnect()
  async disconnect(@Client() client: ChannelClient): Promise<void> { /* optional cleanup */ }
}

@Channel("candidate.{candidateId}", { visibility: "private", publishers: ["recruitment-service"], events: { "candidate.updated": CandidateUpdatedDto } })
export class CandidateChannel {
  constructor(private readonly access: CandidateAccess) {}           // normal dependency injection

  @OnSubscribe()
  async authorize(@ChannelParam("candidateId") candidateId: string, @Context() context: ChannelContext): Promise<boolean> {
    return this.access.canRead(context.user, candidateId);          // the RESOURCE, not just "is logged in"
  }
}
```

```typescript
// src/modules/recruitment/MODULE.pso.ts
export default defineModule({
  name: "recruitment", controllers: [RecruitmentController], providers: [CandidateAccess],
  channels: [RecruitmentChannel, CandidateChannel],      // explicit: a decorated class that is not listed here stays INACTIVE
  routes, imports: [], exports: [],
});
```

Decorators only attach metadata. Nothing is scanned: a class is active only when a module lists it. Start-up refuses (naming the module and class): a class without `@Channel`, a channel registered twice or in two modules, two patterns that can match the same name (`zone.{id}` and `zone.north`), a duplicate handler, a `@ChannelParam` the pattern does not have, a `@Payload` that is not a `@Dto`, an internal channel with client handlers, a public channel handler without `@Public()`, and a **private or presence channel with parameters but no `@OnSubscribe`** (authentication alone never grants access to a resource).

Authentication and permissions reuse what you already know: handlers require an authenticated caller unless marked `@Public()`, and `@Scopes(...)` has the same meaning as on an HTTP action. Generate the files with:

```bash
pso make:channel recruitment candidate --service gw --pattern "candidate.{candidateId}" \
  --publisher recruitment-service --event candidate.updated --fields "candidateId:string,status:enum=APPLIED|INTERVIEW|HIRED"
pso channels:validate --service gw
```

The generated access provider **starts closed** (every subscription refused) until you write the rule.

| Visibility | Rule |
|---|---|
| `private` (default) | authenticated, scopes, then the channel's own `@OnSubscribe` |
| `public` | may be subscribed without authentication, only when you declare it; never publish sensitive data here |
| `presence` | private plus participant tracking (opaque subject ids, shown only to authorized subscribers, one participant for several connections) |
| `internal` | never subscribable by clients (it looks like a channel that does not exist); only declared publishers and in-process `onInternal` listeners |

## 2. Four separate decisions

| Decision | Where it is made |
|---|---|
| may this connection exist | origin check, authentication, `@OnConnect` |
| may it subscribe to this channel | visibility, `@Scopes`, `@OnSubscribe` with the resolved parameters; a denial and a resource that does not exist give the **same** `PSO_CHANNEL_FORBIDDEN` |
| may it send this client event | subscribed to the channel, `@Scopes`, `@OnEvent` exists, DTO valid |
| may a service publish | the channel's `publishers` list against the **publisher of the Dispatch message**, and the `events` contract. The publisher is authenticated only when Dispatch publisher trust is on (`dispatch.trust.mode`, see [Dispatch security](dispatch/security-and-observability.md)); without it the envelope's `source` is a claim any producer on the broker can write, and the orchestrator logs that once |

A client frame can only reach an `@OnEvent` method: there is no way to invoke a service method or to produce a `t:"event"` frame other clients receive. Client commands and server events use different frame types and different paths.

## 3. Publish from a Spring Boot service

```bash
pso channels:enable --service recruitment-service      # starter, pso.channels, the channels.publish event
pso channels:enable --service gw                       # the orchestrator side: Dispatch consumer + @pso/channels
pso make:notifier candidate --service recruitment-service --channel "candidate.{candidateId}" \
  --event candidate.updated --fields "candidateId:string,status:string" --durable
```

In a layered service `make:notifier` writes the payload record to `application/event/CandidateEvent.java` and the publishing service
to `application/service/CandidateNotifier.java`; a 0.1 service gets `events/` and `application/`.

```java
@Service
public class RecruitmentNotificationService {
    private final PsoChannelPublisher publisher;
    public RecruitmentNotificationService(PsoChannelPublisher publisher) { this.publisher = publisher; }

    public void notifyCandidateUpdated(UUID candidateId, CandidateStatus status) {
        publisher.publish("candidate." + candidateId, "candidate.updated", new CandidateUpdated(candidateId, status));
    }
}
```

```java
@Transactional
@ChannelPublish(channel = "candidate.{candidateId}", event = "candidate.updated", delivery = PsoChannelPublisher.Delivery.DURABLE)
public CandidateUpdated updateCandidate(UpdateCandidateCommand command) {
    Candidate c = repository.findById(command.candidateId()).orElseThrow();
    c.updateStatus(command.status());
    return new CandidateUpdated(c.getId(), c.getStatus());
}
```

The event travels as the Dispatch event `channels.publish`; the service never knows an orchestrator address or a connection. Dispatch must be enabled with a provider; the envelope `source` is the service's own name.

### Delivery semantics (explicit)

| `Delivery` | Behaviour | If something fails |
|---|---|---|
| `BEST_EFFORT` (default) | inside a transaction: sent **after commit**, never on rollback; outside one: sent now | after commit the transport can fail and the event is **lost** (logged, counted in `metrics().failedAfterCommit`) |
| `DURABLE` | written to the transactional **outbox in the same transaction** as your data and relayed with the framework's retries | no transaction or no outbox: it **fails**, it is never downgraded. At-least-once; stable event id; the orchestrator suppresses duplicates it already delivered. Not exactly-once |

`PsoChannelPublisher.publish` returns an `Outcome` (`SENT`, `SCHEDULED_AFTER_COMMIT`, `STORED_IN_OUTBOX` and what the transport acknowledged). `@ChannelPublish` publishes the **return value** once per invocation after the method returns normally (`null` publishes nothing, an exception publishes nothing, `{property}` placeholders in the channel come from the returned record). It works through the Spring proxy: self-invocation and private methods are not intercepted; void, primitive, String or collection returns are refused at start-up. Commit-before-publish is not delivery: a committed `BEST_EFFORT` event can still be lost, which is why `DURABLE` exists.

For consuming durable events between services keep using `@PsoEventHandler` and `@DispatchConsumer`: Channels has no listener annotation of its own.

## 4. Connect the browser

```typescript
import { createPsoChannels } from "@pso/channels-client";

const channels = createPsoChannels({ url: "/channels", getToken: () => session.accessToken() });
const subscription = channels.subscribe("candidate.3f2a", { onEvent(e) { console.log(e.type, e.payload); }, onError(err) { console.warn(err.code); } });
subscription.unsubscribe();
```

```typescript
import { PsoChannelsProvider, usePsoChannel } from "@pso/react-channels";   // React 18+ is a peer dependency

function Candidate({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const { status, connected, events, error } = usePsoChannel(`candidate.${id}`);
  ...
}
```

The token is sent in an `auth` frame after the socket opens (never in the URL), renewed before it expires, and repeated after every reconnect. Reconnection uses bounded exponential backoff with jitter; after reconnecting every active subscription is **requested again so the server re-authorizes it** (a subscription that is no longer allowed is reported through `onError`, not retried). There is no offline queue and no automatic replay of commands (`send()` rejects while disconnected), and no event replay. The hook subscribes once per mounted component, unsubscribes on unmount and when the channel changes, keeps a bounded event list (`maxEvents`) and survives StrictMode.

## Install the React integration

From the root of an **existing** React + TypeScript application (it never creates a project):

```bash
pso install:react channels                        # inside a PSO workspace the orchestrator contracts are found automatically
pso install:react channels --contracts ../gw      # or name the orchestrator folder
pso install:react channels --dry-run              # show the packages and files without changing anything
```

What it does, in order: finds the project root, confirms React 18 or later and a `tsconfig`, detects the package manager from the `packageManager` field or the lockfile (npm, pnpm or Yarn; a conflict between them is refused), reports whether the integration is not installed, partly installed or complete, installs the two official packages **with that package manager**, writes the application-owned files that do not exist yet, and type-checks them with the project's own TypeScript options. If the installation fails, `package.json` and the lockfile are restored and no file is written. Running it again changes nothing; deleting a generated file and running it again restores only that file. A file that already exists and was not written by PSO is never overwritten (the command stops and names it); it never edits `App.tsx` or your router, never installs globally and never runs a downloaded script.

| Installed | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `@pso/channels-client` | the framework-independent SDK: the single connection, authentication, reconnection, heartbeat, subscriptions (no dependencies) |
| `@pso/react-channels` | React 18+ bindings over the SDK: they only tie subscriptions to component lifecycles and never open a socket of their own |

| Generated (in `src/integrations/pso/`, or `--dir`) | Content |
|---|---|
| `client.ts` | how to obtain your **current access token** (`TokenProvider`) and where the orchestrator is (`VITE_PSO_CHANNELS_URL`, `REACT_APP_PSO_CHANNELS_URL`, or `globalThis.PSO_CHANNELS_URL`, by bundler; default `/channels` on the page's own origin) |
| `channels.ts` | typed hooks bound to the contracts: `PsoProvider`, `useChannel`, `sendCommand`, `channelName`, `usePsoConnection` |
| `types.ts` | the generated, client-safe contracts (marked `pso:generated`; regenerate with `pso channels:contracts --from <orchestrator>`) |

The files are small and import the SDK; nothing of the SDK is copied into your project. After installation the command prints the provider snippet to add by hand. This is the code the repository test runs, in a real React app, against a real orchestrator in a real browser:

```tsx
// channels/installed/main.tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { PsoProvider, useChannel, usePsoConnection } from "./integrations/pso/channels";

// Your application's session. Here the user comes from the URL and the token from a stand-in endpoint; use your authentication library.
const initialUser = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("user") ?? "alice";
const getAccessToken = (user: string) => async () => (await fetch(`/api/token?user=${user}`)).text();

function Candidate({ id }: { id: string }) {
  // Typed from the generated contract: `events` is a union discriminated by `type`, `candidateId` is the channel parameter.
  const { status, events, error } = useChannel("candidate.{candidateId}", { candidateId: id });
  return (
    <section>
      <p>channel: <b id="channel">{status}</b></p>
      {error && <p id="error">{error.message}</p>}
      <ul>
        {events.map((e) => (e.type === "candidate.updated" ? <li key={e.eventId}>{e.payload.candidateId} is now {e.payload.status}</li> : null))}
      </ul>
    </section>
  );
}

function Panel({ user, onSwitch }: { user: string; onSwitch: () => void }) {
  const [shown, setShown] = useState(true);
  const { state } = usePsoConnection(); // the shared connection: one WebSocket for the whole application
  return (
    <>
      <p>connection: <b id="state">{state}</b> user: <b id="who">{user}</b></p>
      <button id="toggle" onClick={() => setShown((s) => !s)}>toggle</button>
      <button id="bob" onClick={onSwitch}>switch user</button>
      {shown && <Candidate id="c1" />}
    </>
  );
}

function Shell() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(initialUser);
  // `sessionKey` changes with the user: the connection re-authenticates and the server re-authorizes every subscription.
  return (
    <PsoProvider getToken={getAccessToken(user)} sessionKey={user}>
      <Panel user={user} onSwitch={() => setUser("bob")} />
    </PsoProvider>
  );
}

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(<Shell />);
```

**Contracts and types.** `types.ts` lists the registered, non-internal channels with the type of each name parameter and the payload types of their server events and client commands, read statically from your `@Channel` classes and `@Dto` DTOs. It contains no publishers, scopes, authorization methods, unregistered or internal channels, and no addresses; generation warnings go to the console, never into the file. It makes `useChannel("candidate.{candidateId}", { candidateId })` type-checked and `events` a union discriminated by `type`. It is a typing aid, not access control: the server decides every subscription.

**Authentication.** The integration plugs into the authentication you already have: `getToken` returns your current access token (refresh it there). Nothing is stored in browser storage, the token is sent in an `auth` frame (never in the URL) after every connection and shortly before expiry, and `sessionKey` makes the connection re-authenticate when the user changes: the server re-authorizes every subscription (and, since a socket never changes identity, a different user reconnects). `enabled={false}` (for example while logged out) closes the connection. An expired token ends the authorized subscriptions; `usePsoConnection().error` and `useChannel(...).error` report it. Cookie sessions are not used by the protocol, so there is nothing for a cross-site WebSocket hijack to ride on; the orchestrator additionally refuses browser origins that are not in `allowedOrigins`. The client refuses `ws://` to any host except localhost: use `wss://` outside development.

| Environment | Setting |
|---|---|
| development | endpoint `ws://localhost:3000/channels`; the orchestrator accepts the same origin, or list your dev server in `PSO_CHANNELS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173` |
| production | `wss://api.example.com/channels` in the build-time variable; `PSO_CHANNELS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com`; `bus: redis` for several orchestrator instances |

Unsupported targets are refused with the reason: no `react` dependency, React older than 18, no `tsconfig`, TypeScript not installed, no `src/` folder (pass `--dir`), conflicting lockfiles, or a `--dir` outside the project. `--skip-install` writes only the files and prints the exact packages to add yourself.

## Front-end examples: connecting a page to the orchestrator

Both examples below are real files (`docs/examples/channels/`) that the repository tests run in a **real browser** (headless Edge or Chrome) against a **real orchestrator**: the page authenticates, subscribes to `candidate.c1`, receives the `candidate.updated` event the application publishes, and a second user who may not see that candidate gets `Not allowed.` and no events. A page served from an origin that is not in `allowedOrigins` is refused before the upgrade.

What the orchestrator needs, for either front end:

```bash
# the origin that serves your page (exact; no wildcard). Development accepts the same origin only.
PSO_CHANNELS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com
```

and a way for the page to get the **access token** your login already issues. The examples call `/api/token` as a stand-in for your login flow; replace `getToken` with your own function (it is called after every connection and shortly before expiry, so refresh the token there). The token travels in an `auth` frame, never in the URL.

### Plain HTML and JavaScript

The client SDK (`@pso/channels-client`) is a single dependency-free ES module. Copy `node_modules/@pso/channels-client/dist/index.js` next to the page as `client.js` (or let your bundler resolve `@pso/channels-client`).

```html
// channels/index.html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Candidate updates</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Candidate <span id="candidate">c1</span></h1>
  <p>Connection: <strong id="status">connecting</strong></p>
  <p id="error" role="alert" hidden></p>
  <ul id="events" aria-live="polite"></ul>

  <!-- the SDK is one dependency-free ES module: copy node_modules/@pso/channels-client/dist/index.js next to this page as client.js -->
  <script type="module" src="./app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
```

```js
// channels/app.js
import { createPsoChannels } from "./client.js";

// Where the orchestrator is, and who is logged in. In a real application the token comes from your login flow (the same access token
// your HTTP calls send); `/api/token` below is a stand-in for it.
const params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const candidateId = params.get("candidate") ?? "c1";
const orchestrator = params.get("orchestrator") ?? location.origin; // e.g. https://api.example.com

const statusEl = document.getElementById("status");
const errorEl = document.getElementById("error");
const eventsEl = document.getElementById("events");
document.getElementById("candidate").textContent = candidateId;

const channels = createPsoChannels({
  url: orchestrator.replace(/^http/, "ws") + "/channels",
  // called after every (re)connection and shortly before the token expires; the token never goes in the URL
  getToken: async () => (await fetch(`/api/token${location.search}`)).text(),
  onStateChange: (state) => { statusEl.textContent = state; },
  onError: (e) => showError(e.message),
});

function showError(message) { errorEl.textContent = message; errorEl.hidden = false; }

// The server authorizes THIS candidate for THIS user: a user who may not see it gets "Not allowed." and no events.
const subscription = channels.subscribe(`candidate.${candidateId}`, {
  onSubscribed: (active) => { statusEl.textContent = active ? "subscribed" : "not subscribed"; if (active) errorEl.hidden = true; },
  onEvent: (event) => {
    const li = document.createElement("li");
    li.textContent = `${event.type}: ${event.payload.candidateId} is now ${event.payload.status}`; // textContent, never innerHTML: payloads are data
    eventsEl.prepend(li);
  },
  onError: (e) => showError(e.message),
});

// stop cleanly when the page goes away
addEventListener("pagehide", () => { subscription.unsubscribe(); channels.close(); });
```

Open it with `?orchestrator=https://api.example.com&candidate=c1`. The page shows the connection state, the events (newest first) and, if the server refuses the subscription, the fixed message `Not allowed.`. It writes events with `textContent`, never `innerHTML`: payloads are data, not markup.

### React and TypeScript

The React adapter is `@pso/react-channels` (React 18 or later is a peer dependency; the core SDK never imports React). Create one client, provide it once, and use the hook where the data is needed.

```tsx
// channels/react/main.tsx
import { StrictMode } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { createPsoChannels } from "@pso/channels-client";
import { PsoChannelsProvider } from "@pso/react-channels";
import { CandidateEvents } from "./CandidateEvents";

// One client for the whole application. In a real app `getToken` returns your current access token (refresh it there);
// `/api/token` is a stand-in for your login flow.
const params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const orchestrator = params.get("orchestrator") ?? location.origin;

const channels = createPsoChannels({
  url: orchestrator.replace(/^http/, "ws") + "/channels",
  getToken: async () => (await fetch(`/api/token${location.search}`)).text(),
});

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <PsoChannelsProvider channels={channels}>
      <CandidateEvents candidateId={params.get("candidate") ?? "c1"} />
    </PsoChannelsProvider>
  </StrictMode>,
);
```

```tsx
// channels/react/CandidateEvents.tsx
import { usePsoChannel } from "@pso/react-channels";

/** The payload of the `candidate.updated` event: the same contract the Spring service publishes (CandidateUpdated). */
interface CandidateUpdated { candidateId: string; status: "APPLIED" | "INTERVIEW" | "HIRED" | "REJECTED" }

export function CandidateEvents({ candidateId }: { candidateId: string }) {
  // One subscription while this component is mounted; it follows `candidateId` and is removed on unmount (StrictMode safe).
  const { status, connected, events, error } = usePsoChannel<CandidateUpdated>(`candidate.${candidateId}`, { maxEvents: 50 });

  return (
    <section>
      <h1>Candidate {candidateId}</h1>
      <p>Connection: <strong data-testid="status">{status}</strong>{connected ? "" : " (waiting)"}</p>
      {error && <p role="alert">{error.message}</p>}
      <ul aria-live="polite">
        {[...events].reverse().map((e) => (
          <li key={e.eventId}>{e.type}: {e.payload.candidateId} is now {e.payload.status}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </section>
  );
}
```

The hook subscribes once while the component is mounted, follows `candidateId` when it changes, unsubscribes on unmount (also under `StrictMode`) and keeps at most `maxEvents` events. `status` is `loading`, `connected`, `disconnected` or `error`; an authorization refusal arrives as `error` with the fixed code and text. The example type-checks under `--strict`, and the event payload type mirrors the contract the Spring service publishes (`CandidateUpdated`).

### Both examples against the server side of this page

The orchestrator side is the `CandidateChannel` of section 1 (resource-level `@OnSubscribe`, `publishers: ["recruitment-service"]`); the service side is the notifier of section 3. The event the page shows is exactly the `candidate.updated` payload the Spring service sends through Dispatch. After a reconnect the page re-authenticates and the server re-authorizes the subscription, but it does not replay events missed while offline: fetch the current state over HTTP when the connection comes back.

## 5. Protocol, limits and errors

Version 1, JSON text frames, subprotocol `pso.channels.v1`. Client frames: `auth`, `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `event`, `ping`. Server frames: `ready`, `ack`, `error`, `event`, `presence`, `unsubscribed`, `pong`. A server event carries `eventId`, `type`, `channel`, `ts`, `correlationId` and `payload`; the internal `source` is never sent to browsers. Errors have a stable code and a fixed text and nothing else:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PSO_CHANNEL_UNAUTHENTICATED` / `_TOKEN_EXPIRED` | no valid identity / credentials expired (authorized subscriptions end; renew with an `auth` frame) |
| `PSO_CHANNEL_FORBIDDEN` | not allowed (also for a resource that does not exist) |
| `PSO_CHANNEL_INVALID_CHANNEL` | unknown, malformed or internal channel |
| `PSO_CHANNEL_UNKNOWN_EVENT`, `_INVALID_PAYLOAD` | no such `@OnEvent`; DTO errors with field **names** only |
| `PSO_CHANNEL_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`, `_RATE_LIMITED`, `_SUBSCRIPTION_LIMIT` | limits |
| `PSO_CHANNEL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION`, `_BAD_FRAME` | protocol errors |
| `PSO_CHANNEL_UNAVAILABLE`, `_INTERNAL`, `_SLOW_CONSUMER` | transport or server problems |

Before the upgrade the problems are HTTP (RFC 9457): `403` wrong Origin, `401` bad Authorization header, `404` wrong path, `503` full. After it they are protocol frames and close codes (`4401` unauthenticated, `4403` forbidden, `4408` idle, `4426` bad version, `4429` slow consumer, `1009` too big).

Authentication: an `Authorization: Bearer` header on the upgrade (non-browser clients) or an `auth` frame within `authTimeoutMs`; both use the framework's JWT verification (signature, issuer, audience, expiry). Renewal for another subject closes the connection. **Origin** is validated: allowed origins must be listed (development accepts the same origin only). Cookies are not used for authentication, so cross-site hijacking has nothing to ride on.

| Setting (`pso.config.json` `channels.*` or variable) | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` / `PSO_CHANNELS_ENABLED` | `true` when a module registers channels | `false` switches Channels off |
| `path` / `PSO_CHANNELS_PATH` | `/channels` | |
| `allowedOrigins` / `PSO_CHANNELS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` | none | exact origins; required in production; `*` refused |
| `allowAnonymous` | `false` | not allowed in production |
| `authTimeoutMs`, `heartbeatMs`, `idleTimeoutMs` | 10 s, 30 s, 15 min | ping/pong liveness and idle close |
| `maxConnections`, `maxSubscriptionsPerConnection` | 1000, 50 | |
| `maxMessageBytes` | 65536 | enforced while receiving (close `1009`) |
| `ratePerSecond`, `burst` | 20, 40 | token bucket per connection |
| `maxBufferedBytes` | 1 MiB | a client that cannot keep up is closed, never buffered without limit |
| `bus` / `PSO_CHANNELS_BUS`, `redisUrl` / `PSO_CHANNELS_REDIS_URL` | `local` | `redis` for several orchestrator instances |

Spring: `pso.channels.enabled`, `dispatch-event` (`channels.publish`), `max-payload` (`32KB`).

## 6. Several instances

`bus: local` delivers only to the connections of the instance that receives the event: right for development and a single orchestrator, **not distributed**. With several instances use `bus: redis`: every instance fans events out to the connections it owns (duplicates are suppressed by event id; there is no global connection table and no authorization state outside the instance). **Production refuses the local bus** unless `PSO_CHANNELS_ACK_SINGLE_INSTANCE=true` states that exactly one instance runs. The Redis bus is fire-and-forget. An event received from Redis gets the same checks as a local publication before any fan-out (envelope structure and size, registered channel, source allowed for that channel, declared event type and payload contract); a refused event is counted (`busRejected`), logged without its content and dropped, and a received event is never published again. Those checks prove an event is well-formed and permitted, not who sent it. Set `PSO_CHANNELS_BUS_SECRET` (at least 32 characters, the same value on every instance, environment only) to sign bus messages: an instance then delivers only messages with a valid signature (`PSO_CHANNELS_BUS_SECRET_PREVIOUS` keeps the old secret valid while rotating). Without the secret, anyone able to publish to the Redis topic can make instances deliver contract-valid events, so restrict the Redis user with ACLs; production logs a warning. Upgrade every instance before setting the secret: an instance with the secret drops unsigned messages. The bus, its validation and the signed mode are tested against a live Redis (`packages/channels/test/bus.test.ts`).

### Production policy for the two distributed boundaries

| Boundary | Production (`PSO_ENV` / `NODE_ENV` = `production`) | Explicit, insecure legacy switch | Development |
|---|---|---|---|
| Redis bus between instances | start-up is refused without `PSO_CHANNELS_BUS_SECRET` | `PSO_CHANNELS_BUS_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED=true` | no secret needed |
| Dispatch bridge (`ChannelDispatchConsumer`) | an event whose publisher is not **verified** by Dispatch trust is refused and logged; the envelope's `source` never authorizes a publication | `PSO_CHANNELS_BRIDGE_ALLOW_UNVERIFIED=true` | the claimed `source` is accepted, with one warning |

Both switches must be exactly `true`, are reported in the log (`INSECURE legacy mode`) and exist only to keep an existing installation running while keys are rolled out; neither is implied by an incomplete configuration. A weak or missing secret is an error, never a fallback to an unauthenticated bus.

To move a running fleet to a signed bus without losing events: (1) give every instance `PSO_CHANNELS_BUS_SECRET` together with `PSO_CHANNELS_BUS_ACCEPT_UNSIGNED=true`, one instance at a time (each signs what it publishes and still delivers unsigned messages, counting and logging every one); (2) when no `UNSIGNED message was accepted` warning appears any more, remove `PSO_CHANNELS_BUS_ACCEPT_UNSIGNED`. A message that carries a signature must always verify, also during the migration. For the bridge: give the publishing services `PSO_DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY`, the orchestrator `PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_KEY_<SERVICE>` and `dispatch.trust.mode: required` ([publisher authentication](dispatch/security-and-observability.md)).

## What was verified

The hub, registry, protocol, limits and configuration are unit tested with hostile inputs; heartbeats (a silent peer is terminated), the idle timeout, backpressure (a non-reading client is closed and released), presence and graceful shutdown are tested over real sockets; a real orchestrator process with real WebSockets and the client SDK is tested end to end (subscription, resource authorization, delivery, denial, cleanup, reconnection); the Spring publisher is tested with real transactions, the real outbox class and the real Dispatch runtime on its **in-memory adapter** (it proves what is handed to Dispatch and when, not broker behaviour). Not verified: a browser-based UI, the Redis bus, and the chain Spring service to a real broker to the orchestrator.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `pso install:react channels` says a file "was not written by PSO" | a file with that name already exists | move it, or choose another folder with `--dir` (it is never overwritten) |
| the installer reports conflicting lockfiles or a package manager mismatch | two lockfiles, or `packageManager` disagrees with the lockfile | keep one lockfile or fix the field |
| `types.ts` has no channels | no orchestrator was found | `pso channels:contracts --from <orchestrator>` |
| a decorated channel does nothing | not listed in `channels` of `MODULE.pso.ts` | register it; `pso channels:validate` warns |
| start-up: "needs an @OnSubscribe method that authorizes the requested resource" | resource channel without an authorizer | add `@OnSubscribe` with the rule |
| upgrade `403` from a browser | Origin not allowed | add the origin to `allowedOrigins` |
| closed with `4401` after a few seconds | no `auth` frame (or `getToken` failed) | pass `getToken` to the client |
| `PSO_CHANNEL_FORBIDDEN` for every resource | the generated access provider is closed | write `canSubscribe` |
| the page never connects and the console shows a refused WebSocket | the page origin is not in `allowedOrigins`, or a relative `url` points at the page server instead of the orchestrator | list the origin; pass the orchestrator address (`wss://api.example.com/channels`) |
| events from Spring never arrive | event not declared, Dispatch disabled, source not in `publishers` | `pso channels:enable`; enable Dispatch; list the service in `publishers` (refused events are logged as `channel event from dispatch dropped`) |
| events arrive on one instance only | `bus: local` with several instances | `bus: redis` |
| `DURABLE` fails | no transaction or no outbox | `@Transactional` and `pso.dispatch.outbox.enabled=true` |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| treating the channel name as a secret or as access control | authorize in `@OnSubscribe` against the resource |
| authorizing a parameterized channel with `context.user !== null` | check ownership, assignment or tenant |
| publishing sensitive data to a `public` channel | keep it private |
| expecting a reconnecting client to receive what it missed | it does not: fetch current state over HTTP after reconnecting |
| using Channels instead of Dispatch for service-to-service work | Dispatch consumers; Channels is for browsers |

- [Dispatch overview](dispatch/overview.md) and the [outbox](dispatch/outbox.md) for durable publication.
- [Validate request bodies with DTOs](orchestrator/dto-validation.md): the same `@Dto` classes validate `@Payload`.
