# Request and response lifecycle

> The exact order in which the orchestrator handles an HTTP request, which status each stage can answer, what is logged, and how to find the stage that rejected a request.

## What this page answers

When a request does not do what you expect, the first question is *which stage said no*. The answer is always in the status code, the `code` member of the error body and one log line. This page lists the stages in the order they run, so you can read an answer backwards to its cause.

**HTTP request lifecycle.** The order in which the PSO orchestrator runtime handles a request, as implemented in @pso/http.

1. **HTTP request** (arrives at the orchestrator): The runtime assigns a server-side correlation id (a client-supplied x-correlation-id is never trusted) and starts structured logging for the request.
2. **Rate limit** (per client address): A bounded token bucket keyed by the socket address (X-Forwarded-For is not trusted). Excess requests get 429 with Retry-After. Health probes are exempt. This is one protection layer, not DDoS protection.
3. **Route registry** (ROUTES.pso.ts): The request is matched by method and path against the validated routes only. An undeclared path, or a decorated method that is not in ROUTES.pso.ts, answers 404.
4. **Authentication** (guard: jwt): The guard named by the route verifies the bearer token: asymmetric signature, issuer, audience, expiry, not-before and subject. With no key configured it denies everything. Failure answers 401.
5. **Authorization** (scopes): The same guard checks the scopes required by the route. A valid token without the required scope answers 403.
6. **Middleware** (named, per route): Middleware listed on the route runs after the guards, so it only ever sees authenticated requests (public routes excepted). A middleware may end the response.
7. **Body and parameters** (@Param @Query @Body): Path and query parameters are read and, when the action declares @Body(), the JSON body is parsed with a size limit (400 invalid JSON, 413 too large, 415 wrong content type). Schema validation of DTOs is not built in.
8. **Controller** (the action): The decorated action runs. It stays thin: it delegates to a service or forwards to an upstream service with the injected Upstream provider.
9. **Service** (provider): Providers declared in MODULE.pso.ts hold the logic that belongs to the orchestrator. Domain logic belongs in the microservices.
10. **Response** (JSON + correlation id): The returned value is serialized as JSON (201 for POST, otherwise 200). Errors never leak internals: exception filters can handle them, otherwise a generic 500 is returned.
## The stages, in order

| # | Stage | What it checks | Outcome when it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Correlation | accepts an incoming `x-correlation-id` when it is 8 to 64 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`; otherwise generates a UUID (so even a refused request has an id) | never fails; a malformed id is replaced, never echoed |
| 2 | Limits and rate limit | connection and concurrency limits, header size, the token bucket for the client (and route, and principal when configured) | `431`, `503 server_busy`, `429` with `Retry-After` and `RateLimit-*` headers |
| 3 | Route registry | the method and path are declared in `ROUTES.pso.ts` and the controller is registered | `404` for anything not declared, including decorated but undeclared methods |
| 4 | Authentication | a valid token for guarded routes | `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` |
| 5 | Authorization | the scopes or roles the route requires | `403` |
| 6 | Middleware | your middleware, only for requests that passed the guards | whatever your middleware sends |
| 7 | Body and parameters | size limit, `application/json`, valid JSON, then the `@Dto` rules and any `@Param`/`@Query` descriptions | `413`, `415`, `400 invalid_json`, `400 PSO_VALIDATION_FAILED` with a field list |
| 8 | Action | your code | `200` (`201` for POST) with the returned value, the status of a thrown `HttpError`, otherwise `500` (nothing internal is returned) |
| 9 | Upstream (when the action forwards) | the service is known, reachable and answers in time | `502` unknown service or invalid answer, `503` unreachable, `504` timeout |
| 10 | Response | headers added to every answer, one log line | |

> [!NOTE]
> The order differs from some frameworks on purpose. Middleware runs **after** the guards, so it never processes an unauthenticated request on a guarded route. Validation runs after authorization, so an anonymous caller cannot probe the shape of your bodies. Rate limiting runs first because it is the cheapest way to refuse work.

## Every response

- `x-correlation-id`: the same value that appears in the error body (`correlationId`) and in the log line.
- Errors are `application/problem+json` with a stable `code` ([error standard](reference/error-standard.md)). A client-supplied correlation id is used **only if it is well-formed**; a value that is not is replaced with a generated one.
- One log line per request with the method, path, status, duration and trace id (never the body, headers or tokens). On a terminal:

```text evidence="expected"
2026-11-08 14:18:19.536 INFO  request (demo-corr-0001)  traceId=d5bffcb133d75597de34f26b737428d9 method=POST path=/orders status=400 ms=1.17
```

In production the same event is one JSON line ([logging](devops/logging.md)).

## Example: one request through every stage

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -H "x-correlation-id: trace-me-0001" -d '{"customer":"Gr","email":"nope","quantity":0}'
```

1. Correlation: `trace-me-0001` is well-formed, so it is kept.
2. Rate limit: allowed (`RateLimit-Remaining` is in the response headers).
3. Route registry: `POST /orders` is declared.
4. Authentication and authorization: the token is valid and carries `orders:write`.
5. Body: JSON object, within the size limit.
6. Validation: three fields break their rules. The action is **not** called.

```text evidence="expected"
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8
x-correlation-id: trace-me-0001
```

```json evidence="expected"
{ "type": "urn:pso:problem:validation-failed", "status": 400, "code": "PSO_VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "correlationId": "trace-me-0001", "instance": "/orders",
  "errors": [ { "field": "customer", "message": "must have at least 3 characters" },
              { "field": "email", "message": "must be a valid e-mail address" },
              { "field": "quantity", "message": "must be at least 1" } ] }
```

## Find the stage from the answer

| You see | The stage that answered | Look at |
|---|---|---|
| `429` | rate limit | `Retry-After`; the limits in `pso.config.json` ([rate limiting](security/rate-limiting.md)) |
| `404` with `PSO_HTTP_NOT_FOUND` | route registry | `pso routes:list`: the method and path must be declared |
| `401` | authentication | the token, issuer, audience and algorithms; the start-up line `security initialized` |
| `403` | authorization | the scopes the route declares versus the scopes in the token |
| `400` + `errors` | validation | the field names in `errors` |
| `400` + `invalid_json` / `415` / `413` | body parsing | content type, JSON syntax, `http.limits.maxBodyBytes` |
| `500` | your action | the response never contains the cause. In this version the log has only the `request ... status=500` line with the correlation id (verified: no message or stack is logged for an unexpected error), so reproduce it, or catch and log inside the action with `log("error", ...)` from `@pso/http` |
| `502` / `503` / `504` | upstream | whether the service is running at the address in `pso.workspace.json`; its own logs with the same correlation id |

## Anti-patterns

- Validating authentication inside an action: use a guard, so the decision happens at stage 4 and appears in the same place for every route.
- Throwing `HttpError` for conditions the framework already covers (a missing field is a validation problem, not `new HttpError(400, ...)`).
- Returning internal error text to "help" the caller. The `500` body is deliberately generic. Note that the runtime does not log the cause either, so log it yourself where you can add context (never the request body or a token).

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | Which stage answered | How to tell |
|---|---|---|
| `401`, `403` | the gateway, before any service | `instance` is the public path (`/products`), and the gateway log has a `warn` line for `403` |
| `400` `PSO_VALIDATION_FAILED` with `instance` `/catalog/...` | the **service** validated and the gateway passed the answer through | the `/catalog` prefix in `instance` |
| `404` with `instance` not starting with the prefix | the gateway has no such route | `pso routes:list` |
| `404` with the service prefix | the service answered | the id or path |
| `500` `PSO_INTERNAL_ERROR` | an unexpected error in the service, with no cause in the body | the service log under the same `correlationId` |

All five were observed in [Build a CRUD API](tutorials/crud-api.md). A response's `x-correlation-id` and the `correlationId` of its error body are the same id: search the logs for it.

## Next steps

- [Guards](orchestrator/guards.md) and [middleware and filters](orchestrator/middleware-and-filters.md)
- [Validate request bodies](orchestrator/dto-validation.md)
- [Logging](devops/logging.md)

# Dependency injection in the orchestrator

> A complete example - a service injected into a controller, exported and imported across modules - with the exact diagnostics for each mistake and the rules of the container.

The `users` module injects `UsersService` into `UsersController` through the constructor:

```typescript {4}
@Controller()
@RestController("/users")
export class UsersController {
  constructor(private readonly usersService: UsersService) {}
  // ...
}
```

`MODULE.pso.ts` lists `UsersService` in `providers`, so the dependency resolves. Remove it and `pso validate` fails:

```text evidence="expected"
PSO_MODULE_006

Dependency cannot be resolved.

Module: users
Controller: UsersController

Expected: UsersService listed in providers or exported by an imported module
Found: not available in this module

Module activation denied.
```

The orchestrator refuses to start with the same diagnostic, so the mistake cannot reach traffic.

## Step by step: share a provider between modules

1. Create the modules and the provider:

```bash
pso make:module pricing
pso make:service pricing --export        # PricingService, exported
pso make:module orders
pso make:controller orders
```

2. Make `orders` import `pricing` (edit `src/modules/orders/MODULE.pso.ts`):

```typescript
import pricingModule from "../pricing/MODULE.pso";
export default defineModule({ name: "orders", controllers: [OrdersController], providers: [], routes: ordersRoutes, imports: [pricingModule], exports: [] });
```

3. Inject it:

```typescript
constructor(private readonly pricing: PricingService) {}
```

4. Check. Verified: with the `imports` entry missing, `pso validate` printed `ERROR PSO_MODULE_006 gw/src/modules/orders/MODULE.pso.ts: Dependency cannot be resolved.` (Expected `PricingService` listed in providers or exported by an imported module; Found: not available in this module) and exited 1; with the import added it printed `OK` and exited 0. `pso validate` prints `OK`. If you forget the `imports` entry the diagnostic is `PSO_MODULE_006`; if you import a module that does not exist it is `PSO_MODULE_008`.

## A provider that needs another provider

```typescript
@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly pricing: PricingService) {}
}
```

Both in `providers` (or one exported by an imported module), `@Injectable()` on the class that has dependencies. The container builds them in dependency order. A cycle is `PSO_MODULE_007` and the message shows the path.

## Rules

- Constructor types are the contract. An interface or `any` becomes `Object` and is unresolvable.
- Providers are singletons per process.
- `Upstream` is built in: inject it anywhere without declaring it.
- Cycles (`A` needs `B` needs `A`) fail with `PSO_MODULE_007` before start-up.
- Spring Boot services use Spring's own container; none of this applies there.

## Alternatives when you need an abstraction

The container has no token-based or optional injection. Common ways to get the same effect:

| Need | Approach |
|---|---|
| swap an implementation in tests | extend the class and list the subclass under `providers` in a test module; or pass the dependency as a constructor argument in a unit test (no container) |
| two implementations of one idea | two classes with a shared abstract base class; inject the one you need by class |
| configuration | read it from configuration at the point of use, not from a provider tree |

## Common mistakes

- Depending on an interface type.
- Listing the same class in two modules instead of exporting it.
- Forgetting `@Injectable()` on a class with constructor parameters.

## Next steps

- [Services and providers](orchestrator/services-and-providers.md)
- [Module composition](concepts/module-composition.md)

# Remote service clients

> Forward requests to Spring Boot services with the built-in Upstream provider.

```typescript
@Get("/")
async findAll(@Req() req: IncomingMessage, @Res() res: ServerResponse) {
  return this.upstream.forward(req, res, "catalog");
}
```

with `metadata: { service: "catalog" }` on the route. `forward` refuses a service that differs from the route's declared one, so the route registry stays the single source of truth.

## Where services come from

| Environment | Source |
|---|---|
| Development | `pso.workspace.json` (the services' `port`, on `127.0.0.1`) |
| Production | `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>=host:port`, e.g. `PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG=catalog:8081` (what the generated Compose file sets) |

Nothing scans ports. A malformed `host:port` stops start-up. **Discovery never implies authorization**: the route's guard decides who may call.

## Request hygiene

- Client `x-pso-*`, `x-forwarded-for` and `x-correlation-id` headers are dropped; a fresh correlation id is sent.
- `Authorization` is forwarded only on guarded routes, so the service validates the token itself.
- Hop-by-hop headers are removed; the upstream timeout (`UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS`, default 5 s) and body limit apply.
- If an action consumed the body with `@Body()`, the raw body is re-sent. Actions generated by `make:route --upstream` and `make:resource` do not consume it.

## Failure modes

| Situation | Response |
|---|---|
| Upstream refused the connection or cannot be resolved | `503 upstream_unavailable` |
| Upstream timed out (connect, idle or total deadline) | `504 upstream_timeout` |
| Upstream reset the connection or sent an invalid response | `502 bad_gateway` |
| Upstream response larger than `MAX_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE_BYTES` (declared length) | `502 upstream_response_too_large` |
| Request body larger than `MAX_BODY_BYTES` | `413 payload_too_large` |
| Service name not registered | `502 unknown_service` |
| Route and action disagree on the service | `500` (a programming error) |

There are no automatic retries or circuit breakers in this version.

## Limits

Limits are read from environment variables at start-up and validated; an invalid value stops the process and names the variable. Streaming is enforced while bytes flow, so memory stays bounded.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MAX_BODY_BYTES` | 1048576 | request body; checked from `Content-Length` and while streaming |
| `MAX_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE_BYTES` | 10485760 | upstream response body |
| `MAX_HEADER_BYTES` | 16384 | request line plus headers (`431` when exceeded) |
| `UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS` | 5000 | connect and idle time of an upstream socket |
| `UPSTREAM_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS` | 30000 | deadline for the whole upstream exchange |
| `HEADERS_TIMEOUT_MS` / `REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` / `KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT_MS` | 10000 / 30000 / 5000 | client-side timeouts |
| `MAX_CONNECTIONS` | 1000 | open connections |
| `MAX_CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` | 0 (unlimited) | above this, requests get `503 server_busy` with `Retry-After` |
| `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 10485760 | a whole `multipart/form-data` request, counted while it streams (a DTO's own file limits apply inside it) |
| `MAX_MULTIPART_PARTS` | 50 | parts (fields and files) of one multipart request |
| `MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS` | 16 (0 = unlimited) | uploads being received at once; above this `503 server_busy` with `Retry-After` |

When an upstream response exceeds the limit **after** headers were sent (chunked streams), a second status is impossible: the stream is closed abnormally, the upstream transfer is terminated and a warning is logged. A client that disconnects cancels the upstream request. With `NODE_ENV=production` a critical limit set to more than 100 times its default is refused.

Each limit is also a configuration key (`http.limits.maxBodyBytes`, `http.limits.maxUpstreamResponseBytes`, `http.limits.upstreamTimeoutMs`, ...) that can be set in `pso.config.json`, per environment in `pso.config.<environment>.json`, or with `PSO_CFG_http__limits__<name>`; the variable in the table always wins. See [Rate limiting](security/rate-limiting.md) for the precedence rules and `http.rateLimit.*`.

TLS, mutual TLS, credential-forwarding policy per upstream and certificate rotation are described in [Service identity and mutual TLS](security/service-identity.md).

## Uploads and downloads

`forward()` relays the request exactly as it arrived. Files get two dedicated methods, both on the same `Upstream` provider, both bound to the route's declared `metadata.service`:

| Method | Use | What it guarantees |
|---|---|---|
| `forwardUpload(req, res, service, dto, { path })` | the DTO was bound with `@Body(Dto)` and has `@FileField` fields | a **new** multipart request is built from the validated fields and files (nothing of the client's body, `Content-Type`, boundary or identity headers is relayed), streamed from the temporary files with an exact `Content-Length`; correlation, trace and the credentials your upstream policy allows travel as in `forward()` |
| `forwardDownload(req, res, service, { path, maxResponseBytes })` | stream a stored file to the client | backpressure both ways, abort on client disconnect, a per-route size cap (default `MAX_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE_BYTES`), and on `2xx` responses `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox`, `Cache-Control: private, no-store` and `Content-Disposition: attachment` unless the service chose one |

See [File uploads and downloads](orchestrator/file-uploads.md) for a complete example.

## What the caller sees

When the upstream behaves, the gateway is transparent. When it does not, the answer is a standard problem with a stable code (verified for the unavailable case):

| Upstream condition | Answer |
|---|---|
| answers | the upstream's status and body |
| connection refused (service down) | `503 PSO_UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE` |
| does not answer in time | `504 PSO_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT` |
| unknown service name | `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN_SERVICE` |
| invalid or oversized answer | `502` (`PSO_UPSTREAM_BAD_GATEWAY`, `PSO_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE`) |
| TLS verification failed | `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_TLS` |

Verified body for the unavailable case:

```text evidence="verified"
HTTP 503 application/problem+json
{"type":"urn:pso:problem:upstream-unavailable","title":"Upstream unavailable","status":503,"detail":"An upstream service could not be reached.","code":"PSO_UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE","error":"upstream_unavailable","instance":"/customers","correlationId":"doc-corr-0004"}
```

## Troubleshooting a forward

1. `pso services:health`: is the service up? (verified output: `DOWN catalog http://127.0.0.1:8081/actuator/health`).
2. `pso routes:inspect <route>`: does the route point at the service and port you expect?
3. In production, is `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>=host:port` set (the service name in upper case, hyphens as underscores)?
4. Read the service's own log with the same correlation id: the orchestrator forwards `x-correlation-id`.
5. For timeouts, compare `http.limits.upstreamTimeoutMs` with the service's real latency before raising it.

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| a longer timeout for slow endpoints | raise `http.limits.upstreamTimeoutMs` for the gateway; fix the slow endpoint first |
| to forward the user's token | the default for guarded routes under the upstream's policy; bind it with `audience` ([service identity](security/service-identity.md)) |
| to never forward the token | `forward: "none"` for that upstream |
| TLS or mutual TLS to the service | per-upstream settings ([service identity](security/service-identity.md)) |

## Composing a response from several services: `UpstreamClient`

`Upstream.forward` hands the current request to **one** service. An action that needs data from several services (a customer summary built from the customers, orders and catalog services) uses `UpstreamClient` instead: it calls registered services by name and the action builds the response. The orchestrator coordinates; the business rules stay in the services.

```bash
pso make:route summary show --method GET --path /of/:id --compose customers,orders,catalog --scopes summary:read --service gateway
```

The generator injects the client and, in `ROUTES.pso.ts`, declares the services the action may call:

```ts title="src/modules/summary/routes/ROUTES.pso.ts (the generated entry)"
{
  method: "GET",
  path: "/summary/of/:id",
  controller: SummaryController,
  action: "show",
  security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["summary:read"] },
  metadata: { services: ["customers", "orders", "catalog"] }
}
```

```ts title="src/modules/summary/controllers/summary.controller.ts"
import { Controller, RestController, Get, Param, UpstreamClient } from "@pso/http";

interface Customer { id: string; name: string }
interface Order { id: string; productIds: string[] }
interface Product { id: string; title: string }

@Controller()
@RestController("/summary")
export class SummaryController {
  constructor(private readonly services: UpstreamClient) {}

  @Get("/of/:id")
  async show(@Param("id") id: string) {
    const customer = await this.services.get<Customer>("customers", "/customers/:id", { params: { id }, credentials: "caller" });
    const orders = await this.services.get<Order[]>("orders", "/orders", { query: { customerId: id } });
    const ids = [...new Set(orders.flatMap((o) => o.productIds))];
    const products = await Promise.all(ids.map((pid) => this.services.get<Product>("catalog", "/products/:id", { params: { id: pid } })));
    return { customer, orders, products };
  }
}
```

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Destination | the **name** of a registered service; there is no URL parameter. The path is relative to the service, and its endpoint prefix is applied once, by the client |
| Declaration | inside a request the service must be listed in the route's `metadata.services` (or be its `metadata.service`). A call to any other service is refused before anything is sent (`PSO_UPSTREAM_POLICY`, and the log names the missing declaration). `pso validate` refuses a name that is not a service of the workspace (`PSO_ROUTE_010`) |
| Path and query | `:name` segments are replaced from `params`, each encoded as one segment; `..`, `//`, `?`, `#` and encoded separators are refused; the query goes in `query` |
| Transport | the upstream's own TLS and mutual TLS configuration (the one `forward` uses); verification is never disabled; in production plain HTTP to another host is refused at start-up as for `forward` |
| Credentials | none by default. `credentials: "caller"` sends the bearer token of the current request, and only when the upstream policy, the transport and the token audience allow it; a refusal is an error, not a silent omission |
| Correlation | the correlation id and the trace of the current request travel with every call |
| Deadline | `timeoutMs` per call, at most (and by default) `http.limits.upstreamResponseTimeoutMs` |
| Cancellation | `signal` (an `AbortSignal`); and when the client of the current request disconnects, the calls made for it are aborted |
| Response | JSON (or `responseType: "text"`), read up to `maxResponseBytes` (default `http.limits.maxUpstreamResponseBytes`); redirects are never followed |
| Methods | `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete` return the parsed body; `call` returns `{ status, headers, data }` |

### Failures

Every failure is an `UpstreamCallError` with `service`, `kind` and, for an answer of the service, `status` and the parsed `problem`. Left unhandled it becomes a stable problem that never contains the service's response body:

| `kind` | What happened | Problem when unhandled |
|---|---|---|
| `status` (404) | the service answered 404 | `404 PSO_UPSTREAM_NOT_FOUND` |
| `status` (409) | the service answered 409 | `409 PSO_UPSTREAM_CONFLICT` |
| `status` (other 4xx, 3xx) | the service refused the request | `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_REJECTED` |
| `status` (5xx), `invalid_response` | the service failed or answered something else than JSON | `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_BAD_GATEWAY` |
| `timeout` | no answer within the deadline | `504 PSO_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT` |
| `unavailable` | the service could not be reached | `503 PSO_UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE` |
| `tls` | the certificate or the handshake was rejected | `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_TLS` |
| `response_too_large` | the answer exceeds the limit | `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE` |
| `policy`, `unknown_service` | refused before anything was sent | `500 PSO_UPSTREAM_POLICY`, `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_UNKNOWN_SERVICE` |

An action that knows what a downstream answer means translates it on purpose:

```ts
import { HttpError, UpstreamCallError } from "@pso/http";

try {
  return await this.services.get("customers", "/customers/:id", { params: { id } });
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof UpstreamCallError && e.is(404)) throw new HttpError(422, "unknown_customer");
  throw e;
}
```

Limits: one attempt per call (no retries, no circuit breaker), no distributed transaction and no saga: if the second call fails after the first one changed data, undoing it is the application's design decision.

## The service prefix outside the workspace: `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>_PREFIX`

With the workspace file the orchestrator knows each service's endpoint prefix. In a container there is no workspace file: the address comes from `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>` and the prefix from `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>_PREFIX`. Both `forward` and `UpstreamClient` put that prefix in front of the path.

```yaml title="what pso docker:init writes for the orchestrator"
PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG: "catalog:8081"
PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG_PREFIX: "/catalog"
```

In a deployment you write by hand, set both for every service that has a prefix. Without the prefix variable every forwarded path misses it and the service answers 404 for routes that work in development.

## Service and guard names checked by the compiler

```bash
pso types
```

writes `src/pso-types.d.ts` from `pso.workspace.json` and the guards of the project. From then on `metadata.service`, `metadata.services`, `security.guard`, `Upstream.forward` and `UpstreamClient` accept only names that exist, in the editor and in `npm run typecheck`. It is optional: without the file every string is accepted, as before, and `pso validate` and start-up keep checking either way. Run it again after adding a service or a guard (`pso types --check` in a pipeline).

## Common mistakes

- Raising the timeout instead of fixing the slow service.
- Forgetting that a route's `metadata.service` must equal the service the action forwards to (otherwise a `500` programming error).
- Declaring a service in the workspace but not setting `PSO_UPSTREAM_*` in production.

- [Service-to-service communication](microservices/service-to-service.md)
- [Request and response lifecycle](orchestrator/request-lifecycle.md)

# Spring Boot integration

> How PSO generates and manages Spring Boot services, which starters each generated service includes, and what stays plain Spring.

PSO generates standard Spring Boot 3.5 services (Java 21 target) and keeps them plain Spring: no custom container, and a developer who knows Spring Boot can read the result. Common infrastructure comes from the first-party [PSO starters](spring/overview.md) instead of copied classes.

| Included by `pso create service` | Notes |
|---|---|
| `pso-spring-boot-starter` | web, validation, actuator, typed `pso.*` configuration, [service prefix](spring/service-prefix.md), [request limits](spring/limits.md), correlation id |
| `pso-security-spring-boot-starter` | deny-by-default JWT resource server, authorization rules, [CORS](spring/security-and-cors.md) |
| `pso-http-spring-boot-starter` | [`PsoHttpClient`](spring/http-client.md) for secure outbound calls |
| Lombok | [conventions](spring/lombok.md), explicit annotation processing |
| `pso-test`, `spring-boot-starter-test`, `spring-security-test` | generated tests use real JWT validation |
| Project-local Maven Wrapper | Maven 3.9.9, SHA-256 pinned, no global Maven needed |
| Profiles | `local`, `dev`, `test`, `staging`, `prod`, `h2` ([configuration](spring/configuration.md)) |
| Database and dispatch | present but **off**: `pso.database.provider: none`, `pso.dispatch.enabled: false` |

Optional starters you add on demand: the persistence starter (`pso database:enable`), a Dispatch provider (`pso dispatch:install`), the Redis-backed rate limiter and the OpenTelemetry observability starter (`pso-observability-starter`, off unless an OTLP endpoint is configured; see [observability](devops/observability.md)).

PSO adds three things around Spring: the **workspace declaration** (port, prefix, dependencies, health path), the **generators** (`make:resource`, `make:controller`, `make:migration`, `database:enable`, ...) and **validation** (`pso validate`, `pso security:validate`).

## What "plain Spring" means in practice

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args); } }
```

The starters are ordinary auto-configuration: every bean backs off when you define your own, and nothing scans your packages. You can read the effective `pso.*` settings in any IDE (the autoconfigure artifact ships configuration metadata) and override anything with Spring's own mechanisms.

## Build and test

```powershell
pso java:install      # once: the PSO artifacts into your local Maven repository
cd catalog
.\mvnw.cmd test       # ./mvnw test on macOS and Linux
.\mvnw.cmd package
```

or from the workspace: `pso test --service catalog`, `pso build --service catalog`. A fresh generated service passes its tests (verified: 16 tests including a `product` resource, `BUILD SUCCESS`, about 11 s on a warm Maven cache). The artifacts are not published ([Maven BOM and SNAPSHOTs](spring/maven-bom.md)).

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| to start with a database | `pso create service orders --db postgres` |
| a different port | `pso create service orders --port 8090` |
| to run it | `./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=local` ([First microservice](getting-started/first-microservice.md)) |
| structured JSON logs | the `prod`/`staging` profiles ([Logging](devops/logging.md)) |

## Common mistakes

- Running without a profile and expecting local conveniences.
- Overriding a PSO bean without reading what it provided (for example replacing the security chain without keeping the deny-by-default rules): `pso security:check` flags a hand-written chain that ends in `permitAll()`.
- Calling the service on the wrong path: PSO adds the service prefix once, so `/catalog/ping`, not `/ping`.

## Next steps

- [Spring Boot starters](spring/overview.md)
- [Project structure](microservices/project-structure.md)
- [Security integration](microservices/security-integration.md)

# Java project structure

> The mandatory layered structure of a PSO Spring Boot service - application, infrastructure and shared packages - where each kind of class goes, what the generators write, and how 0.1 services are kept.

Every new PSO Spring Boot service uses the **layered** structure. It is the standard, not a suggestion: the generators write into it,
`pso validate` checks it, and the documentation, examples and AI context assume it. `pso create service <name>` creates it with the
reference Product CRUD, PostgreSQL and Flyway; `--template empty` creates the same packages without the example.

```tree title="A new service (pso create service catalog)"
catalog/
  pom.xml  # generated: Spring Boot 3.5, the PSO BOM 0.2.0-rc.3 and starters
  mvnw  # generated: Maven Wrapper, with mvnw.cmd and .mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties
  src/
    main/
      java/com/pso/catalog/
        Application.java  # generated
        application/
          rest/  # generated: @RestController classes
          service/  # generated: @Service classes, the transaction boundaries
          dto/
            request/  # generated: request records with Jakarta Validation
            response/  # generated: response records
          mapper/  # generated: request to entity to response
        infrastructure/
          entity/  # generated: JPA entities
          persistence/  # generated: Spring Data repositories and specifications
          config/  # generated: @Configuration classes
          security/  # generated: security integration beyond the starter
          filter/  # generated: servlet filters
        shared/
          exception/  # generated: RFC 9457 problems (PsoProblemException subclasses)
          constant/  # generated: constants
          validation/  # generated: reusable validation helpers
      resources/
        application.yml  # generated, plus application-<profile>.yml
        db/migration/  # generated: Flyway migrations V<n>__<name>.sql
    test/java/com/pso/catalog/  # generated: tests with real JWTs and an embedded PostgreSQL
```

Empty packages hold a `.gitkeep`. `infrastructure/client/` appears when `pso make:client` writes the first outbound client. The
package prefix (`com.pso.catalog`, or `--package com.example.catalog` at creation) is free; the layer is the package path below it.

A Java service has **no `providers`, `modules`, `.app` or `app` package**: those are orchestrator conventions. A Java service calls
other services through `PsoHttpClient` (`infrastructure/client/`); its layers are packages, not modules.

## Where each class goes

| Kind | Directory | File |
|---|---|---|
| controller | `<package>/application/rest/` | `*Controller.java` |
| service | `<package>/application/service/` | `*Service.java` |
| request | `<package>/application/dto/request/` | `*Request.java` |
| response | `<package>/application/dto/response/` | `*Response.java` |
| mapper | `<package>/application/mapper/` | `*Mapper.java` |
| repository | `<package>/infrastructure/persistence/` | `*Repository.java` |
| entity | `<package>/infrastructure/entity/` | `*Entity.java` |
| config | `<package>/infrastructure/config/`, `<package>/infrastructure/security/` | `*Config.java` |
| filter | `<package>/infrastructure/filter/` | `*Filter.java` |
| client | `<package>/infrastructure/client/` | `*Client.java` |
| exception | `<package>/shared/exception/` | `*Exception.java` |
| event | `<package>/application/event/` | `*Event.java` |
| listener | `<package>/application/event/` | `*Listener.java` |

`make:event`, `make:listener`, `make:dispatch-event` and `make:dispatch-handler` write their classes to `application/event/`.

Plain helper classes without one of these suffixes are allowed in any package of the service and are ignored by discovery. A class with
a known suffix in the wrong package is `PSO_MISPLACED_RESOURCE`; a badly named one is `PSO_BAD_NAME`.

## The generators

Names are given in kebab-case and become PascalCase classes with the right suffix, in the right layer. Real output (verified):

```text evidence="verified"
$ pso make:request create-customer --service catalog
created    src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/dto/request/CreateCustomerRequest.java
$ pso make:response customer --service catalog
created    src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/dto/response/CustomerResponse.java
$ pso make:service pricing --service catalog
created    src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/service/PricingService.java
$ pso make:mapper customer --service catalog
created    src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/mapper/CustomerMapper.java
$ pso make:entity customer --service catalog
created    src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/infrastructure/entity/CustomerEntity.java
$ pso make:repository customer --service catalog
created    src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/infrastructure/persistence/CustomerRepository.java
```

The generated request is a record with a validation starting point; make it yours:

```java title="src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/dto/request/CreateCustomerRequest.java"
package com.pso.catalog.application.dto.request;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Size;

public record CreateCustomerRequest(@NotBlank @Size(max = 120) String name) {
}
```

For a complete resource (entity, the next Flyway migration, repository, records, mapper, transactional service, controller, tests, and
optionally the orchestrator module) use one command: `pso make:crud <resource> --service <svc> [--orchestrator]`
([Generators](architecture/generators.md)). An entity or a repository needs a database: in a service without one the generators refuse
and name `pso database:enable postgresql --service <svc>`.

## Where does this code go?

| You are writing | Put it in | Why |
|---|---|---|
| an HTTP endpoint | `application/rest/` (`@RestController`) | translates HTTP to a call; validates and authorizes |
| the rule behind it | `application/service/` (`@Service`, `@Transactional`) | the transaction boundary, reusable |
| a request or response shape | `application/dto/request/`, `application/dto/response/` (records) | the public contract; never an entity |
| converting between shapes | `application/mapper/` | one visible place for field mapping |
| a table | `infrastructure/entity/` and a Flyway migration | Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate only validates it |
| queries | `infrastructure/persistence/` (Spring Data, `Specification`) | filters, sorting and pagination run in the database |
| a call to another service | `infrastructure/client/` (`PsoHttpClient`) | named services, never URLs |
| technical configuration, security integration, servlet filters | `infrastructure/config/`, `security/`, `filter/` | how it is done, not what |
| an application error, a constant, a validation helper | `shared/exception/`, `shared/constant/`, `shared/validation/` | genuinely reusable, no business logic |
| an event | `application/event/` (local) or [Dispatch](dispatch/events-and-consumers.md) (distributed) | |

## Common mistakes

- Returning a JPA entity from a controller: map it to a response record.
- Business logic in a controller or a repository: it belongs in `application/service/`.
- A `providers` or `modules` package "to match the orchestrator": the two runtimes follow their own ecosystems on purpose.
- An entity without its migration: the service refuses to start (`Schema-validation: missing table`).
- Configuration classes that duplicate what the PSO starters already configure (security, problems, correlation ids).

## 0.1 services (compatibility)

Services created before 0.2 use a simplified hexagonal layout (`routes/`, `application/`, `ports/`, `adapters/`, `persistence/`,
`events/`, `contracts/`, `configs/`, `security/`). They keep working, and the generators write into their layout (`make:port` and
`make:adapter` exist only there). Never add layered packages to such a service: a service with both is refused
(`PSO_STRUCTURE_MIXED`). [Structure migration](architecture/structure-migration.md) plans the move with `pso structure:inspect`;
[Hexagonal architecture](microservices/hexagonal-architecture.md) describes the 0.1 layout.

## Next steps

- [Java microservice structure](architecture/java-microservice.md): the layers, persistence, validation, errors, tests.
- [The reference CRUD](architecture/reference-crud.md), file by file.
- [PostgreSQL CRUD](spring/postgresql-crud.md)

# Service contracts

> Versioned JSON contracts mirrored into each service and checked for drift - what is generated, what is validated, how to change one safely, and what contracts deliberately do not cover.

`pso make:resource customer --service catalog --route /customers` creates the contract in two places:

```text evidence="verified"
created    gateway/src/.app/contracts/customer.contract.json
created    catalog/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/dto/response/CustomerResponse.java
created    catalog/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/rest/CustomerController.java
created    catalog/src/main/resources/contracts/customer.contract.json
created    catalog/src/test/java/com/pso/catalog/application/rest/CustomerControllerTests.java
created    docs/api/customer.md
created    gateway/src/modules/customer/MODULE.pso.ts
created    gateway/src/modules/customer/controllers/customer.controller.ts
created    gateway/src/modules/customer/routes/ROUTES.pso.ts
```

The two contract files (`gateway/src/.app/contracts/` and `catalog/src/main/resources/contracts/`) are identical copies; the rest of the output is the Spring controller and response record (in the layered packages), its test, an API note and the orchestrator module that go with them. A JSON contract is the shared, versioned description of a forwarding resource; a module that calls its service through `UpstreamClient` (the reference CRUD, `make:crud`) types that API in `modules/<module>/contracts/<name>.contract.ts` instead.

```json title="customer.contract.json (generated)"
{
  "name": "customer",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "service": "catalog",
  "operations": [{ "id": "customerList", "method": "GET", "path": "/customers" }]
}
```

## Validation

`pso validate` checks that the contract is valid JSON of the expected shape, has a semantic version, unique operation ids and a `service` that is declared in the workspace, and that the two copies are byte-identical (`PSO_CONTRACT_DRIFT` otherwise). Reproduced here by changing `version` in the gateway copy only: changing `version` in the gateway copy only makes `pso validate` print

```text evidence="verified"
ERROR   PSO_CONTRACT_DRIFT gateway/src/.app/contracts/customer.contract.json: Contract "customer" differs from its copy in service "catalog"
        hint: Update both copies together (pso make:resource --force regenerates them)
gateway: 5 resource(s), digest 90d8f1f4cc8a
catalog: 6 resource(s), digest 986a7750032c
FAILED
```

and exit with code 1. Regenerating with `--force` rewrites the copy you changed (`overwritten gateway/src/.app/contracts/customer.contract.json`; the other files are reported `unchanged`) and `pso validate` is `OK` again.

## Changing a contract: step by step

1. Decide whether the change is observable by callers (add an operation, rename a path) or not (documentation).
2. Edit **both** copies, or regenerate: `pso make:resource customer --service catalog --route /customers --force` (review the diff before committing; `--force` overwrites what the generator owns).
3. Bump `version`: minor for additions, major for removals or renames, patch for metadata.
4. Run `pso validate`: it must print `OK`.
5. Change the Spring controller and the gateway route in the same commit, so the three agree.

## Variations

| Need | Contract change |
|---|---|
| a new read endpoint | add an operation with a new `id`, bump minor |
| two services expose the same resource name | give each its own contract file; `name` and `service` identify the pair |
| a deprecated operation | keep it for a release, mark the replacement; remove with a major bump |

## What contracts do not cover

Contracts describe **operations**, not payload schemas. Payloads are defined by the Spring DTOs (with Jakarta Validation) and, when the gateway answers a request itself, by `@Dto` classes ([DTO validation](orchestrator/dto-validation.md)). The two are not cross-checked against the contract in this version, so a payload change needs its own review.

## Common mistakes

- Editing one copy.
- Reusing an operation id for a different method or path.
- Treating a green `validate` as proof that the payloads match.

## Next steps

- [Contracts (concept)](concepts/contracts.md)
- [First endpoint](getting-started/first-endpoint.md)

# Service registration

> How services are declared, registered and found, in development and production - the commands, their real output, the validation that runs before anything is saved, and what registration does not grant.

Services are **declared**, never discovered by scanning ports.

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Declare an existing project | `pso services:register billing --port 8083 --runtime spring-boot --depends-on catalog` |
| Remove a declaration | `pso services:unregister billing` (refused while others depend on it; files are never deleted) |
| List | `pso services:list` |
| Inspect one | `pso services:inspect catalog` (declaration, resources, live health) |
| Probe live | `pso services:health` |
| Dependency graph and order | `pso services:graph`, `pso graph` |

## What the commands print

Expected output from a workspace with a gateway and a service that is **not running**:

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso services:list
catalog              service       spring-boot  :8081  deps=[]
gateway              orchestrator  node         :3000  deps=[]

$ pso services:inspect catalog
catalog (service, spring-boot) :8081  health: DOWN
depends on: -   used by: -
  controller  ProductController          src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/rest/ProductController.java
  entity      ProductEntity              src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/infrastructure/entity/ProductEntity.java
  ...

$ pso services:health
DOWN  catalog            http://127.0.0.1:8081/actuator/health
DOWN  gateway            http://127.0.0.1:3000/health/ready
[exit 1]

$ pso graph
startup order: catalog -> gateway
gateway routes GET /products -> catalog
```

`services:health` exits 1 if any service is down, which makes it usable as a CI gate after starting the stack.

## Validation before saving

Registration is validated before it is saved: unique name and port, an existing path inside the workspace, known dependencies, no cycles. Verified refusals:

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso services:register billing --port 8083 --runtime spring-boot --depends-on catalog
error: Path "billing" does not exist in the workspace

$ pso services:unregister catalog        (while gateway declares dependsOn: ["catalog"])
error: Cannot unregister "catalog": required by gateway
hint: Remove those dependencies first
[exit 1]
```

The first refusal is because the folder `billing` had not been created: register an *existing* project, and use `pso create service` to make a new one. Without a dependent, `pso services:unregister catalog` prints `unregistered catalog (project files untouched)`.

## Runtime registry in development

`pso dev` writes `.pso/registry.json` with each service's lifecycle state, process id and last health result, updates it every 5 seconds and mirrors logs to `.pso/logs/`. Studio and `pso services:health` show the same facts.

## Production

The orchestrator reads `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>=host:port`, which is what `pso docker:init` sets in the generated Compose file. DNS-based resolution comes from your platform; PSO does not implement other registries. The service name becomes the variable name (`users-service` becomes `PSO_UPSTREAM_USERS_SERVICE`).

## Variations

| Situation | Do |
|---|---|
| adopt several existing projects at once | `pso init` in the folder that contains them |
| change a port | edit `pso.workspace.json` and `pso validate`; update Compose/ingress too |
| a service that is not a Spring/Node project PSO can start | not supported by `pso dev`; declare it for routing only if the orchestrator forwards to it |

Registration grants **no authorization**: a registered service is only reachable through routes whose guards pass, and it validates tokens itself.

## Common mistakes

- Registering a service and expecting its routes to appear: routes come from `ROUTES.pso.ts`.
- Forgetting `--depends-on`, so `pso dev` starts the gateway before the service it forwards to (it still works, but readiness is reported late).

## Next steps

- [Upstream clients](orchestrator/upstream-clients.md)
- [Development environment](devops/development-environment.md)

# Security integration in services

> How each Spring Boot service validates tokens and scopes on its own, through the PSO security starter - the settings, what a missing setting does, the generated checks, and how to test and troubleshoot it.

Every generated service is its own security boundary. It does not trust the orchestrator to have checked anything. The enforcement lives in `pso-security-spring-boot-starter`; the service only declares settings ([details](spring/security-and-cors.md)).

| Setting | Environment variable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pso.security.jwt.jwks-uri` | `PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI` | where signing keys are fetched |
| `pso.security.jwt.issuer` | `PSO_JWT_ISSUER` | required `iss` |
| `pso.security.jwt.audience` | `PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE` | required `aud` |
| `pso.security.jwt.algorithms` | `PSO_JWT_ALGORITHMS` | allow-list, default `ES256,RS256`; only RS/PS/ES families accepted |

The starter builds a Nimbus decoder with the algorithm allow-list and validators for issuer, audience, timestamps and subject. **If jwks-uri, issuer and audience are all missing, every token is rejected; if only some are missing the service refuses to start; in `staging` and `prod` missing settings are a start-up error.**

On the `local` profile with nothing configured, the service says so when it starts (Expected output):

```text evidence="expected"
WARN [orders,,] ... c.p.s.s.PsoSecurityAutoConfiguration : JWT validation is not configured (pso.security.jwt.*): every bearer token ...
```

and a request without a token is `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` (expected).

## Scopes

Scopes in the token become `SCOPE_*` authorities. `make:resource` generates controllers annotated like:

```java
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_customers:read')")
@GetMapping
public List<CustomerDto> list() { return List.of(); }
```

and tests for authorized, forbidden and anonymous callers. Only `/actuator/health` is public. `pso security:check` flags explicit `PUBLIC` rules for review, `pso.security.enabled: false` without a chain of your own as critical, and a legacy hand-written chain that ends in `permitAll()`.

The service sees the same `Authorization` header the orchestrator forwarded (guarded routes only). Spoofed `x-pso-*` identity headers are ignored; the service trusts the verified token, nothing else.

## How it is tested

The generated tests sign real tokens with a throwaway key and verify them against a real loopback JWKS endpoint (class `PsoTestJwt`). In a new service (verified from the generated test classes) `ApplicationTests` asserts that health is public, that everything else is denied without a token, that a forged bearer token is rejected and that the service prefix matches the workspace declaration; `ProductControllerTests` asserts, for the generated Product API, that a token with the scope succeeds, a token without it is `403`, no token is `401`, and invalid bodies are `400` with the fields at fault. Add the same shape of test to every controller you write.

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| a route open to any authenticated caller | `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")`, or an `AUTHENTICATED` rule in `pso.security.rules` |
| a role instead of a scope | map the roles claim (`roles-claim`) and use `hasRole` |
| a public route (rarely) | an explicit `PUBLIC` rule in `pso.security.rules`; `pso security:check` will flag it for review |
| service-to-service calls | give the caller its own credentials ([service identity](security/service-identity.md)) |

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `401` for every token in local | JWT settings are empty: set `PSO_JWT_*` (the warning above is printed at start-up) |
| service refuses to start in `prod` | a required `PSO_JWT_*` setting is missing; the message names it |
| `401` only for tokens from one issuer | issuer or audience differ: compare the token's `iss`/`aud` with the settings |
| `403` for a valid token | the scope is not in the token (`scope` or `scp` claim): check the identity provider's grant |
| unauthenticated health works, everything else `401` | that is the default: only `/actuator/health` is public |

## Common mistakes

- Copying a development key into a production configuration.
- Adding `permitAll()` to a custom chain to "debug" and leaving it.
- Testing a controller without a test for the anonymous and the forbidden cases.

## Next steps

- [Spring security and CORS](spring/security-and-cors.md)
- [Authorization](security/authorization.md)

# Persistence: PostgreSQL and Flyway

> A service that owns its database, migrations tested against a real PostgreSQL, and the template's outbox table - what --db postgres adds, what you run, what you see, and where to go for a full CRUD example.

```bash
pso create service orders --db postgres
pso make:migration add-orders-table --service orders
```

For a complete, tested example with entity, repository, DTOs, transactions and tests, read [PostgreSQL CRUD in a Spring service](spring/postgresql-crud.md). This page covers what the generator adds and the rules around ownership and migrations.

## What `--db postgres` adds

| Addition | Detail |
|---|---|
| Dependencies | `pso-data-spring-boot-starter` (JPA, `flyway-core`, `flyway-database-postgresql`, `postgresql` runtime) and the embedded PostgreSQL for tests |
| `application.yml` | `pso.database.provider: postgresql`; `DB_URL`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD` read from the environment; no credentials in the file |
| Migrations | an empty `src/main/resources/db/migration/`: the service ships no table of its own. Add the first one with `pso make:migration` |
| Tests | `TestDatabaseConfig` starts an **embedded native PostgreSQL** (no Docker); `DatabaseMigrationTests` checks that the data source answers and that every migration was applied |
| Workspace | `"db": "postgres"` on the service |

Verified file list for `pso create service catalog --db postgres` (database-related files): `src/main/resources/db/migration/.gitkeep`, `src/test/java/com/pso/catalog/DatabaseMigrationTests.java`, `src/test/java/com/pso/catalog/TestDatabaseConfig.java`.

Each service owns its data. **Databases are never shared between services by default.** An existing service can opt in later with `pso database:enable postgresql`; without a chosen provider no database starts ([Database selection and H2](spring/database-and-h2.md)).

## Migrations

`pso make:migration add-orders-table --service orders` creates the next `V<n>__add_orders_table.sql` in `src/main/resources/db/migration/`. Migrations are immutable once applied: add a new version instead of editing one (Flyway refuses to start if an applied migration changed).

When the service starts against a database, Flyway applies the pending versions in order (Expected output from the CRUD example against PostgreSQL 16):

```text evidence="expected"
INFO ... org.flywaydb.core.FlywayExecutor         : Database: jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:55432/docs_catalog (PostgreSQL 16.15)
INFO ... o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate      : Migrating schema "public" to version "1 - create products"
INFO ... o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate      : Successfully applied 1 migration to schema "public", now at version v1
```

and the history is queryable (`SELECT version, description, success FROM flyway_schema_history`): `1 create products t`.

## Services created before 2026-11-14: the `outbox_event` table

Earlier versions of the PostgreSQL service template shipped a first migration, `V1__outbox.sql`, that created a table named `outbox_event`. Nothing in PSO reads or writes it: the transactional outbox of PSO Dispatch is the `pso_outbox` table that `pso dispatch:outbox` adds ([Outbox](dispatch/outbox.md)). New services no longer get that migration, so a generated service contains only tables you or a PSO command asked for.

In a service that already has it:

- **Keep the file.** It was applied, and Flyway refuses to start when an applied migration is changed or removed.
- **PSO never drops a table.** `pso migrate` only reports that the table is there.
- If your own code does not use it, remove it with a migration of your own:

```bash
pso make:migration drop-outbox-event --service orders
```

```sql title="the new migration"
DROP TABLE outbox_event;
```

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| a database in an existing service | `pso database:enable postgresql --service orders` |
| H2 for quick local work | `pso database:enable h2` (local profile only; refused in staging/prod) |
| run against a real PostgreSQL locally | start one (the CRUD page shows a Docker command), set `DB_URL`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD` |
| events with your data in one transaction | `pso dispatch:outbox` ([decision](decisions/outbox-or-direct-publish.md)) |

## Common mistakes

- Editing an applied migration (`FlywayValidateException`, checksum mismatch).
- Sharing one database between services "just for now".
- Putting credentials in `application.yml`.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Check | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| every request fails with `500` `PSO_INTERNAL_ERROR` while the database is down | nothing can open a transaction | the service log under the response's `correlationId`: `CannotCreateTransactionException`, "Connection ... refused" | restore the database; the client never sees the cause (verified) |
| a client that loses a concurrent update sees `500` | `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException` is not mapped by PSO | the service log | add a `@RestControllerAdvice` that answers `409` (not part of the example) |
| `409` on create with a sku that "does not exist" | a row exists that you did not expect (a failed earlier test, another environment) | `select sku from products` | remove it, or use another sku |
| Hibernate validation error at start (†) | an entity and the schema disagree: ddl-auto is `validate` | the start-up log | add a migration; never edit an applied one |
| Flyway refuses to start with a checksum error (†) | an applied migration was edited | `flyway_schema_history` | restore the file, add `V<next>__...` |

(†) marks a standard message of the underlying library, or documented behaviour, that was not reproduced for this page. The first two rows are reproduced with their exact responses in [Build a CRUD API](tutorials/crud-api.md) ("When the database is down", "Optimistic locking").

## Next steps

- [PostgreSQL CRUD](spring/postgresql-crud.md)
- [JPA or JDBC?](decisions/jpa-or-jdbc.md)
- [Database selection and H2](spring/database-and-h2.md)

# Maven dependencies and SNAPSHOTs

> The Maven Wrapper, the PSO BOM, reproducible builds, the release script that produces a file repository and an SBOM, and what PSO does about SNAPSHOT dependencies.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

## Supported

For the installed `0.2.0-rc.3` distribution, generated services request `com.pso:*:0.2.0-rc.3` through the BOM; its portable package carries matching Maven artifacts for `pso java:install`. A CLI run from this framework checkout instead reads `pso-java/pom.xml` and uses `0.1.0-SNAPSHOT`. See [Maven BOM and Java versions](spring/maven-bom.md). The `0.1.0` release run below is an illustrative older fixed-version example, not the installed rc.3 artifact set.

- **Maven Wrapper.** Every service has `mvnw`, `mvnw.cmd` and `.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties` pinned to Maven 3.9.9 with `distributionSha256Sum`. Builds do not depend on a global Maven.
- **One BOM.** Generated POMs import `com.pso:pso-bom`, so every PSO starter shares one version (`pso.version`) and Spring Boot's versions stay managed by the parent. See [Maven BOM and SNAPSHOTs](spring/maven-bom.md).
- **A local development workflow.** `pso java:install` builds the PSO artifacts and installs them into `~/.m2`; nothing is copied by hand.
- **A guard against mutable artifacts.** `pso security:audit` reports `SNAPSHOT` and version-range dependencies in POMs, and `pso deploy` **refuses to deploy a SNAPSHOT build**. Production releases must be immutable.
- **A release preparation script.** `node scripts/release-maven.mjs` (in the framework repository) sets a fixed version on a temporary copy, deploys every module with sources to a **local file repository**, writes SHA-256 sums and a CycloneDX SBOM, and builds a freshly generated service against that repository with an isolated local Maven repository. It never publishes. See [Distribution](devops/distribution-and-installation.md).

## What a release run looks like

Expected output of the stages (abridged):

```text evidence="expected"
PASSED   set release version      - 0.1.0 in every module (temporary copy; the repository is unchanged)
PASSED   deploy to file repository - N jars (+ sources jars and poms), no SNAPSHOT
PASSED   no SNAPSHOT artifacts    - none
PASSED   checksums                - SHA-256 of 54 files
PASSED   SBOM (CycloneDX)         - 156 components; licences: Apache-2.0=121, EPL-2.0=10, BSD-3-Clause=10, MIT=5, ...
NOT RUN  signing                  - no key supplied; artifacts are UNSIGNED (also no GPG signatures)
PASSED   consumer build           - generated service built against the release repository with an isolated local repository
```

## Not implemented

- Publishing the PSO artifacts to a public repository (the `com.pso` group is local until a namespace is owned and registered). Docker builds that resolve them need a repository the build can reach: point the service at your own repository (file, internal Nexus/Artifactory) or vendor the artifacts.
- GPG signing of Maven artifacts (needs your key) and CVE scanning of Maven dependencies (`security:audit` states that Maven CVE scanning is **not** performed). The SBOM inventories the dependencies; it does not assess them.
- Dependency locking beyond what Maven provides.

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| to build a service on your machine | `pso java:install` once, then `mvnw package` |
| to build in CI or a container | publish the BOM and starters to a repository your build reaches, set it in the project's `pom.xml` or `settings.xml` |
| a fixed version for a release | `pso.version` set to a release version; never `-SNAPSHOT` for production |
| to check for mutable versions | `pso security:audit` |

## Common mistakes

- Building a Docker image whose Maven cannot resolve `com.pso` artifacts (they are not on Central).
- Leaving `-SNAPSHOT` in `pso.version` for a deployment (the deploy command refuses it).
- Treating the SBOM as a vulnerability report.

## Next steps

- [Maven BOM](spring/maven-bom.md)
- [Build and deploy](devops/build-and-deploy.md)

# Service-to-service communication

> What PSO provides for calls between services - the gateway path, the Spring HTTP client with TLS and mTLS, events - and what you decide yourself, with the safety rules each path enforces.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

There are three ways for work to cross a service boundary. They have different guarantees; choosing among them is a design decision ([HTTP or Dispatch?](decisions/http-or-dispatch.md)).

| Path | Direction | Use for | Guarantees |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gateway forward** | client to orchestrator to service | requests that start at a user | route policy, JWT checked at the gateway and again in the service, rate limits, correlation id |
| **Spring `PsoHttpClient`** | service to service, synchronous | a service needs another service's answer | declared destinations only, strict URL rules, no redirects, optional TLS/mTLS, bounded retries, correlation propagation |
| **Dispatch events** | service to any number of services, asynchronous | announcing facts | at-least-once delivery, retries, dead letters, optional transactional outbox ([Dispatch](dispatch/overview.md)) |

**Distributed communication.** One public entry point. Services are declared, never discovered by scanning, and discovery never grants authorization.

1. **Client** (browser, app, API consumer): Talks only to the orchestrator. Services are not published outside the private network.
2. **PSO orchestrator** (Node.js + TypeScript): Validates tokens, applies route policy, then forwards the request with hygienic headers (spoofed x-pso-* headers dropped, Authorization forwarded only on guarded routes, timeouts and body limits).
3. **Users service** (Spring Boot): Example service. It validates the JWT itself, so bypassing the orchestrator gains nothing, and enforces scopes with method security.
4. **Orders service** (Spring Boot): Example service with its own database; services never share a database by default. Declared in pso.workspace.json with a port and dependencies.
5. **Notifications service** (Spring Boot): Example consumer. Event-driven delivery between services is part of the optional dispatch subsystem (Redis Streams, RabbitMQ or Kafka), installed with `pso dispatch:install`.
## 1. Through the orchestrator

The orchestrator forwards a request with a verified bearer token (only on guarded routes, and only under the upstream's policy); the service validates it again. This is the default path for anything that originates from a user request, because route policy and token validation apply. [Upstream clients](orchestrator/upstream-clients.md) explains the forwarding rules, including what is stripped (`x-pso-*`, `x-forwarded-for`, a client-supplied `x-correlation-id`).

## 2. Direct calls from a Spring service

Use `PsoHttpClient` (starter `pso-http-spring-boot-starter`):

```java
return http.get("customers", "/customers/{id}", CustomerDto.class, id);
```

The first argument must be a service declared under `pso.http.client.services`; anything else is refused before any network I/O. Redirects are never followed; plain `http` to a non-loopback host is refused unless explicitly allowed; the caller's bearer token is forwarded only to services configured with `forward-bearer: true`, and only when the audience matches. Full reference: [Spring HTTP client](spring/http-client.md).

For back-channel calls that are not on behalf of a user, give the caller its **own** credentials (a service identity: a client certificate with mTLS, or its own token with a dedicated audience and scopes) and let the callee validate it like any other. Do not rely on network location for trust ([service identity](security/service-identity.md)).

## 3. Events

When the caller does not need an answer, publish an event. The consumer is invisible to the publisher, and the broker absorbs downtime. The cost is at-least-once delivery: consumers must be idempotent.

## Making the dependency visible

A call between services is a dependency; record it:

- `pso services:register ... --depends-on` (or `dependsOn` in `pso.workspace.json`) records start-up order.
- Describe the operation in a [service contract](microservices/service-contracts.md).
- Declare event types with their producers and consumers ([event declarations](dispatch/contracts.md)); `pso dispatch:graph` shows the topology.

## What is not provided

- A generated client for another service's API (you write the DTOs and call `PsoHttpClient`).
- A circuit breaker. The client has timeouts and bounded retries (idempotent methods only by default), not a breaker.
- A service mesh. TLS and mTLS between services are available as configuration; certificate issuance and distribution are yours.

## Common mistakes

- Calling a service by a hard-coded URL instead of a declared one.
- Forwarding the user's token everywhere. Forward only where the callee should act as the user, and bind it to an audience.
- Chaining many synchronous calls in a request path: availability multiplies down.
- Using events for something that needs an answer.

## Next steps

- [Spring HTTP client](spring/http-client.md)
- [Service identity and mTLS](security/service-identity.md)
- [Event dispatch](dispatch/overview.md)

# 0.1 hexagonal layout (compatibility)

> The simplified ports-and-adapters layout of 0.1 Java services, kept for existing projects - what each layer owns, a worked port-and-adapter example, and how it maps to the mandatory layered structure of new services.

> [!NOTE]
> This page describes the **0.1 legacy Java structure**, which existing projects retain. New services use the [official layered structure](architecture/java-microservice.md) (`application/`, `infrastructure/`, `shared/`); `make:port` and `make:adapter` are legacy generators and are refused in a layered service.

The legacy service uses a **simplified** hexagonal layout: only the directories that have an architectural purpose exist.

| Layer | Directory | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Inbound adapter | `routes/` | HTTP controllers: translate requests to application calls |
| Application | `application/` | use cases and domain services |
| Ports | `ports/` | interfaces the application needs from the outside |
| Outbound adapters | `adapters/`, `persistence/` | implement ports: databases, remote clients, mappers |
| Events | `events/` | domain events and listeners |
| Contracts | `contracts/` | DTOs shared with callers: never domain entities |

Dependencies point inward: controllers call services, services depend on ports, adapters implement ports. Domain models are not shared between services; they exchange DTOs defined by versioned contracts ([Service contracts](microservices/service-contracts.md)).

PSO does not enforce import direction at compile time; it enforces **where classes live and what they are called**, which keeps the layering visible in code review.

## A worked example: taking payments

The service must charge a card. The provider is a remote API today and may change.

```bash
pso make:port payment-gateway --service orders       # ports/PaymentGatewayPort.java
pso make:adapter payment-gateway --service orders    # adapters/PaymentGatewayAdapter.java
```

```java
// ports/PaymentGatewayPort.java : what the application needs, in the application's words
public interface PaymentGatewayPort { PaymentResult charge(Money amount, String token); }

// application/OrderService.java : knows only the port
@Service @RequiredArgsConstructor
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGatewayPort payments;
    @Transactional public OrderResponse place(OrderRequest r) { /* ... */ payments.charge(total, r.paymentToken()); /* ... */ }
}

// adapters/PaymentGatewayAdapter.java : the remote API lives here, through PsoHttpClient
@Component @RequiredArgsConstructor
class PaymentGatewayAdapter implements PaymentGatewayPort {
    private final PsoHttpClient http;
    public PaymentResult charge(Money amount, String token) { return http.post("payments", "/charges", new ChargeRequest(amount, token), PaymentResult.class); }
}
```

What this buys you: `OrderService` is tested with a fake port and no network; replacing the provider changes one class; the secure-client rules (declared destinations, no redirects) live in one adapter ([Spring HTTP client](spring/http-client.md)).

## When not to add a port

| Situation | Do instead |
|---|---|
| one implementation and no boundary (an in-process helper) | a plain `@Service` |
| a Spring Data repository | the repository interface already is the port; inject it into the service |
| the "adapter" would only forward to one method | skip the layer |

Generated services start with controllers, configuration and DTOs only. Add `ports/` and `adapters/` when a boundary appears, not before.

## Testing consequences

| Layer | Test with |
|---|---|
| controller | MockMvc with real JWT validation (the generated tests) |
| service | a unit test with fake ports |
| adapter | a test against a local fake server |
| persistence | the embedded PostgreSQL ([PostgreSQL CRUD](spring/postgresql-crud.md)) |

## Common mistakes

- Returning entities from controllers.
- Letting adapters call services (the arrow points the wrong way).
- Interfaces for everything "for testability" when a constructor-injected fake of a concrete class would do.

## Next steps

- [Java project structure](microservices/project-structure.md)
- [Controller or service?](decisions/controller-or-service.md)

# Spring Boot starters

> The first-party Maven artifacts behind every generated Spring Boot service, what each one provides and what is not implemented yet.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

A generated service contains your code and a short `application.yml`. Security, request limits, correlation, the outbound HTTP client and database selection come from reusable artifacts in the `pso-java/` project of the framework (group `com.pso`).

| Artifact | Purpose | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `pso-channels-spring-boot-starter` | `PsoChannelPublisher` and `@ChannelPublish`: typed real-time events to browsers over Dispatch ([Channels](orchestrator/channels.md)) | implemented; tested with Dispatch's in-memory adapter, not a broker |
| `pso-storage-spring-boot-starter` | provider-independent file storage (local, S3, Azure Blob): [Storage](spring/storage.md) | implemented; cloud adapters verified against mocks only |
| `pso-bom` | compatible versions of every artifact below | implemented |
| `pso-spring-boot-autoconfigure` | typed and validated `pso.*` configuration, [service prefix](spring/service-prefix.md), [request limits](spring/limits.md), correlation id, database and dispatch selection | implemented |
| `pso-spring-boot-starter` | the artifact services depend on: autoconfigure + web + actuator + validation | implemented |
| `pso-security-spring-boot-starter` | [JWT resource server, authorization rules, CORS, security headers](spring/security-and-cors.md) | implemented |
| `pso-http-spring-boot-starter` | [`PsoHttpClient`](spring/http-client.md): secure outbound HTTP to named services | implemented |
| `pso-data-spring-boot-starter` | [persistence](spring/database-and-h2.md): JPA, Flyway, PostgreSQL driver (never H2) | implemented |
| `pso-dispatch-api` | provider-independent event contracts, runtime and `@PsoEventHandler` ([dispatch](spring/dispatch.md)) | implemented |
| `pso-test` | a local JWKS endpoint and token signer so tests run real JWT validation | implemented |
| `pso-dispatch-redis-starter`, `-rabbitmq-starter`, `-kafka-starter` | independent broker providers, installed with `pso dispatch:install` | implemented (verified against real brokers) |
| `pso-observability-starter` | Micrometer tracing and OTLP metrics/traces export, a Dispatch metrics binder, an observed `PsoHttpClient`; off unless an OTLP endpoint is set ([observability](devops/observability.md)) | implemented (verified against a local OTLP receiver) |
| `pso-ratelimit-redis-starter` | a Redis-backed shared rate limiter for several instances ([rate limiting](security/rate-limiting.md)) | implemented (verified against a real Redis) |

## What the starters do for you

- **Typed configuration:** everything is under `pso.*` and bound to validated classes. An unknown key is a start-up error: a misspelled security property is never silently ignored.
- **One endpoint prefix**, applied once, derived from the service name (`users-service` becomes `/users`).
- **Deny by default:** only `/actuator/health` is public; everything else needs a valid token.
- **Back-off rules:** every bean is `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`. Define your own `SecurityFilterChain`, `JwtDecoder`, `RateLimiter` or `PsoHttpClient` and the starter steps aside. Nothing scans your packages.
- **No unused infrastructure:** no database, broker or consumer starts unless you choose it.

## Lombok and conventions

Generated services include Lombok with explicit annotation processing. See [Lombok conventions](spring/lombok.md).

## Development workflow

The artifacts are not published to Maven Central. Install them once into your local Maven repository with `pso java:install`: the installed rc.3 distribution copies its bundled `com.pso:*:0.2.0-rc.3` repository, a framework checkout builds `com.pso:*:0.1.0-SNAPSHOT` (see [Maven BOM and Java versions](spring/maven-bom.md)).

## Not implemented

- Delayed redelivery and exactly-once delivery ([limits](dispatch/local-and-production.md)).
- Service discovery beyond the named services you declare in YAML.
- Service-to-service identities (token exchange, client credentials) and mutual TLS **to** the service. The HTTP client supports mTLS **from** the service to a remote.
- A rate limiter other than the in-memory and Redis ones (the `RateLimiter` interface is the extension point).
- Published artifacts: the group id `com.pso` is local to this repository until an owned namespace is chosen.

## Common mistakes

- Replacing a starter bean without keeping what it provided (for example a hand-written security chain that ends in `permitAll()`; `pso security:check` flags it).
- Expecting a starter to start infrastructure you did not choose.
- Adding the observability starter and expecting data without an OTLP endpoint (it is off unless one is configured).

## Next steps

- [Spring Boot integration](microservices/spring-boot-integration.md)
- [Configuration](spring/configuration.md)
