# Maven BOM and Java versions

> How the distributed and source-checkout CLIs select matching PSO Java artifacts, and how Maven builds resolve them.

Generated services import one bill of materials and then declare starters without individual versions. The **installed `0.2.0-rc.3` CLI** sets `pso.version` to `0.2.0-rc.3`; the **framework checkout** reads the current `pso-java/pom.xml`, which is `0.1.0-SNAPSHOT` in this checkout. The CLI selects a matching Java version instead of adopting whichever artifacts happen to be on the machine:

```xml
<properties>
  <pso.version>0.2.0-rc.3</pso.version>
</properties>
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.pso</groupId>
      <artifactId>pso-bom</artifactId>
      <version>${pso.version}</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

The `pso.version` property is the only place a PSO version appears. Spring Boot itself stays managed by `spring-boot-starter-parent` 3.5.6 (Java 21 target).

## Install the matching artifacts

```bash
pso java:install        # installed rc.3: copies its bundled com.pso:*:0.2.0-rc.3 repository into ~/.m2
pso create service catalog
```

No JAR is copied by hand. The rc.3 portable distribution includes a Maven file repository next to the CLI. If your authorized package ships it separately, run `pso java:install --from <maven-repository-dir>`. `pso create service` reports when matching artifacts are missing. In a **framework checkout**, `pso java:install` builds `pso-java/` and installs `0.1.0-SNAPSHOT`; after changing the starters there, run it again. Do not substitute the checkout's SNAPSHOT for a distributed rc.3 service.

The group id `com.pso` is **not** an owned Maven Central namespace: the artifacts are never published from this repository. Choose and register a namespace before publishing.

## Releases

Production builds must use an immutable version: set `pso.version` to a release, never a `-SNAPSHOT`. `pso security:audit` reports SNAPSHOT dependencies and `pso deploy` refuses to deploy a SNAPSHOT build.

## Containers

`docker:init` builds a Spring service inside a Docker build, where your local `~/.m2` is not visible. Use `pso docker:init --vendor` to copy the matching artifacts into the service for its image build, or provide a Maven repository the build can reach. Container builds with vendored artifacts are covered by the [Docker workflow](devops/docker.md); the PSO artifacts are not on Maven Central.

## Common mistakes

- Overriding a Spring Boot-managed version next to the PSO BOM.
- Building in a container without a repository that has the `com.pso` artifacts ([Maven dependencies](microservices/maven-dependencies.md)).
- Deploying a `-SNAPSHOT` `pso.version` (refused by `pso deploy`).

## Next steps

- [Maven dependencies](microservices/maven-dependencies.md)
- [Build and deploy](devops/build-and-deploy.md)

# Spring configuration reference

> Every pso.* key with defaults and environment overrides, the profiles and how misspelled keys are handled.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

Every generated service has a complete `application.yml`. The values below are the defaults; `${VAR:default}` shows which environment variable overrides them. Binding uses `@ConfigurationProperties` with Jakarta Bean Validation, and **unknown `pso.*` keys stop start-up**. Environment variables are free-form, so `PSO_JWT_ISSUER` works without being a property.

```bash
pso validate               # includes the typed pso.* checks as PSO_SPRING_SPR* errors
pso security:validate      # focuses on JWT, CORS, rules, prefix, database and dispatch
```

## Groups

| Key | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `pso.service.name` | service name | kebab-case |
| `pso.service.prefix` | `${PSO_SERVICE_PREFIX:/<name>}` | [authoritative prefix](spring/service-prefix.md); `/` disables it |
| `pso.security.enabled` | `true` | `false` removes the starter's chain (you must provide your own) |
| `pso.security.jwt.jwks-uri` / `issuer` / `audience` | `${PSO_JWT_*}` | all three or none |
| `pso.security.jwt.algorithms` | `ES256,RS256` | asymmetric only |
| `pso.security.jwt.clock-skew` | `30s` | 0 to 5 minutes |
| `pso.security.jwt.roles-claim` | `roles` | dotted path allowed |
| `pso.security.cors.*` | disabled | [CORS](spring/security-and-cors.md) |
| `pso.security.rules[]` | empty | explicit authorization rules |
| `pso.security.headers.*`, `pso.security.actuator.health-public` | on, `true` | |
| `pso.http.client.services.<name>.*` | none | [HTTP client](spring/http-client.md) |
| `pso.limits.requests.enabled` / `per-minute` | `true` / `${PSO_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE:600}` | [limits](spring/limits.md) |
| `pso.limits.body.max-size` | `2MB` | |
| `pso.limits.multipart.enabled` / `max-file-size` / `max-request-size` | `false` / `5MB` / `10MB` | |
| `pso.limits.header.max-size` | `16KB` | |
| `pso.limits.timeouts.connection` / `async-request` | `10s` / `30s` | |
| `pso.limits.concurrency.max-requests` | `0` (unlimited) | |
| `pso.dispatch.enabled` / `provider` | `false` / `none` | [dispatch](spring/dispatch.md) |
| `pso.database.provider` | `none` | `none`, `h2`, `postgresql` ([database](spring/database-and-h2.md)) |
| `pso.channels.enabled` / `dispatch-event` / `max-payload` | `false` / `channels.publish` / `32KB` | publishing to [Channels](orchestrator/channels.md) over Dispatch |
| `pso.storage.provider` | unset (storage off) | `local`, `s3`, `azure`; the whole `pso.storage.*` group is on [Storage](spring/storage.md) |
| `pso.observability.correlation.enabled` / `header` | `true` / `X-Correlation-ID` | |

## Profiles

`local`, `dev`, `test`, `staging`, `prod` and `h2`. **There is no default profile**: the `local` profile is never an implicit fallback. `pso dev` activates `local` for the services it starts; Docker images set `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`.

| Profile | What it changes |
|---|---|
| `local` | debug logging, CORS for `http://localhost:3000` and `http://127.0.0.1:3000`, a high rate limit |
| `dev` | shared development environment; values come from the environment |
| `test` | no rate limiting, quiet logs (generated tests use it) |
| `staging`, `prod` | JWT settings are **required** (start-up fails without them) and H2 is refused |
| `h2` | `pso.database.provider: h2` |

Credentials never belong in YAML: use environment variables (`DB_URL`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`, `PSO_JWT_*`). `pso security:check` reports literal secrets (`SEC010`, `SPR011`).

## IDE metadata

The autoconfigure artifact runs Spring Boot's configuration processor, so IDEs offer completion and documentation for every `pso.*` key.

## Validation codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| SPR001 | a YAML file cannot be read |
| SPR002 | unknown `pso.*` key |
| SPR003 | non-asymmetric JWT algorithm |
| SPR004 | JWKS over plain http for a non-loopback host |
| SPR005 | CORS: missing, wildcard or malformed origins, credentials with patterns |
| SPR006 | a `PUBLIC` rule (medium: confirm it is intended) |
| SPR007 | dispatch enabled without a provider |
| SPR008 | unknown database provider |
| SPR009 | H2 in the base, staging or prod configuration |
| SPR010 / SPR011 | HTTP client: plain http, literal TLS password |
| SPR013 | `pso.service.prefix` differs from `pso.workspace.json` |

## What a misspelled key looks like (expected)

Starting a generated service with `--pso.securty.enabled=true` (a typo for `security`) refuses to start:

```text evidence="expected"
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
Description:
Binding to target [... PsoProperties ...] failed:
    Property: pso.securty.enabled
    Origin: "pso.securty.enabled" from property source "commandLineArgs"
    Reason: The elements [pso.securty.enabled] were left unbound.
```

An unknown `pso.*` key is a start-up error, so a security setting cannot be silently ignored. The same goes for a few combinations that are checked at start-up: for instance a `server.servlet.context-path` together with a service prefix stops the service (the prefix would be applied twice).

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| a value for one environment | `application-<profile>.yml` and activate the profile explicitly |
| an override from the platform | the documented `PSO_*` placeholder in `application.yml` (for example `PSO_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`), or Spring's relaxed binding of the property name (dots become underscores, dashes are removed: `pso.limits.requests.per-minute` is `PSO_LIMITS_REQUESTS_PERMINUTE`) |
| to see what is configured | your IDE's completion (configuration metadata ships with the starter) and `pso config:show --service <name>` for the PSO-level view |
| to run with a profile | `./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=local` |

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `APPLICATION FAILED TO START ... left unbound` | a misspelled `pso.*` key: fix the spelling (the Property line names it) |
| staging/prod refuses to start | required `PSO_JWT_*` settings are missing |
| H2 refused | H2 is allowed in the `local` and `h2` profiles only (`SPR009` in `pso security:check`) |
| the service uses defaults you did not expect | no profile is active (there is no default profile): choose one |

## Common mistakes

- Relying on an implicit profile.
- Copying `application-local.yml` values into `prod`.
- Writing credentials in YAML (`SEC010`, `SPR011`).

## Next steps

- [Development or production configuration?](decisions/dev-or-production-config.md)
- [Environment variables](reference/environment-variables.md)

# Service prefix

> The one authoritative prefixing strategy between the orchestrator and Spring services, and how duplicates are prevented.

A request to `GET /customers` on the orchestrator reaches the service as `GET /users/customers`. The prefix is added in exactly **one place on each side** and nowhere else:

| Layer | What happens |
|---|---|
| Orchestrator | the route is declared as `/customers` in `ROUTES.pso.ts`; `Upstream` prepends the service's prefix from `pso.workspace.json` when forwarding |
| Spring service | the starter adds `pso.service.prefix` to every `@RestController`; controllers map `/customers`, **without** the prefix |

## Derivation

`pso create service <name>` derives the prefix and writes it to both `pso.workspace.json` (`"prefix": "/users"`) and `application.yml`:

| Service name | Prefix |
|---|---|
| `users-service` | `/users` |
| `orders-service` | `/orders` |
| `notification-service` | `/notification` |
| `billing` | `/billing` |

Override it with `pso create service orders-service --prefix /purchases`; `--prefix /` means no prefix. Values are normalized (`api//v1/` becomes `/api/v1`) and rejected when they contain upper case, spaces, dot segments or other unsafe characters.

## Duplicate prevention

The service refuses to start when the prefix would be applied twice:

- `server.servlet.context-path` is set together with a prefix (keep the context path empty).
- a controller mapping already starts with the prefix (it would be served at `/users/users/...`).

`pso validate` reports `SPR013` when `pso.service.prefix` and `pso.workspace.json` disagree, because the orchestrator would then forward to the wrong path. Health and other actuator endpoints are **not** prefixed. A controller annotated `@Unprefixed` opts out.

## Migrating an existing service

A service created before prefixes existed serves its paths at the root. Declare `"prefix": "/"` for it in `pso.workspace.json` and set `pso.service.prefix: /` to keep the old behavior.

## Seeing it (verified)

A `catalog` service's workspace entry carries `"prefix": "/catalog"`, and its controllers map paths **without** it; a call goes to `/catalog/ping`. The unprefixed path does not exist (the generated tests assert `404` for `/ping`).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| the gateway forwards but the service answers `404` | `pso.service.prefix` and `pso.workspace.json` disagree (`SPR013` in `pso validate`) |
| `/users/users/...` | a controller mapping already starts with the prefix; remove it or annotate `@Unprefixed` |
| the service refuses to start | a context path is configured together with a prefix |

## A controller named like the service: `@RepeatsServicePrefix`

The prefix is applied once, by PSO, so a controller mapped to `/orders` in the service whose prefix is `/orders` is served at `/orders/orders`. That path is legitimate (the resource is simply named like the service), but a mapping that begins with the prefix is far more often a mistake: a controller that wrote the prefix by hand and would be served at `/orders/orders/...` by accident. The starter therefore **refuses to start** when a mapping begins with the service prefix, unless the controller says the repetition is intended:

```java title="src/main/java/com/pso/orders/application/rest/OrdersController.java"
package com.pso.orders.application.rest;

import com.pso.spring.autoconfigure.RepeatsServicePrefix;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

// Served at /orders/orders: the service prefix /orders plus this mapping.
@RestController
@RepeatsServicePrefix
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrdersController {

    @GetMapping
    public List<String> list() {
        return List.of();
    }
}
```

The generators write it for you, with the same rule: `pso make:controller orders --service orders` and `pso make:resource orders --service orders` add the annotation (and a comment that says why), and so does an explicit path below the prefix such as `--route /orders/archive`. A path that merely looks similar (`/orders-export`) is another segment and is not annotated. Nothing is ever removed from a path.

| Annotation | Import | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `@RepeatsServicePrefix` | `com.pso.spring.autoconfigure.RepeatsServicePrefix` | the controller's path starts with the service prefix **on purpose**; the prefix is still applied, so the public path contains it twice |
| `@Unprefixed` | `com.pso.spring.autoconfigure.Unprefixed` | the controller must be served **without** the service prefix, at exactly its own mapping (an endpoint that is not part of the service's API surface behind the orchestrator, such as a callback path dictated by a third party) |

They are opposites: `@RepeatsServicePrefix` keeps the prefix and accepts the repetition; `@Unprefixed` removes the prefix for that controller. Reach for `@Unprefixed` rarely: the orchestrator forwards to `<prefix><path>`, so an unprefixed controller is not reachable through an ordinary forwarded route.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the prefix inside controller mappings.
- Changing the prefix in one place only.

## Next steps

- [Spring configuration](spring/configuration.md)
- [Routing](orchestrator/routes.md)

# Spring security and CORS

> YAML-driven JWT validation, authorization rules, CORS and security headers, all deny-by-default.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

`pso-security-spring-boot-starter` configures Spring Security from `pso.security.*`. It uses Spring Security and Nimbus for all token handling: **no custom cryptography**.

## JWT

```yaml
pso:
  security:
    jwt:
      jwks-uri: ${PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI:}
      issuer: ${PSO_JWT_ISSUER:}
      audience: ${PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE:}
      algorithms: ${PSO_JWT_ALGORITHMS:ES256,RS256}
```

Validated: signature (asymmetric algorithms only), issuer, audience, expiry and not-before with the configured clock skew, and a non-empty `sub`. `alg: none` and symmetric tokens are rejected. Scopes (`scope` or `scp`) become `SCOPE_*` authorities and the roles claim becomes `ROLE_*`.

- All three settings missing: every token is rejected (a warning is logged). That keeps a fresh service safe in development.
- Some missing, or an invalid value (symmetric algorithm, plain-http non-loopback JWKS, credentials in the URL): the service **does not start**.
- In the `staging` and `prod` profiles missing JWT settings are a start-up error.

## Authorization

Only `/actuator/health` (and its probes) is public. Everything else needs a valid token. Add requirements with method security, or declaratively; paths are relative to the [service prefix](spring/service-prefix.md):

```yaml
pso:
  security:
    rules:
      - path: /customers/**
        methods: [GET]
        access: SCOPES        # PUBLIC | AUTHENTICATED | SCOPES
        scopes: [customers:read]
      - path: /customers/**
        methods: [POST]
        access: SCOPES
        scopes: [customers:write]
        roles: [editor, admin]   # at least one role, and all scopes
```

Rules apply in order; an invalid rule stops start-up. A `PUBLIC` rule is explicit and reported by `pso security:check` for review. Missing identity is `401`; an authenticated caller without the scope or role is `403`.

## CORS

```yaml
pso:
  security:
    cors:
      enabled: true
      allowed-origins: [http://localhost:3000, http://127.0.0.1:3000]
      allowed-methods: [GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS]
      allowed-headers: [Authorization, Content-Type, X-Correlation-ID]
      allow-credentials: false
      max-age: 30m
```

It becomes a real Spring Security CORS policy, applied before authentication so preflight requests need no token. The rules are strict:

- origins are exact (`scheme://host[:port]`, no path, no trailing slash); `*` is rejected;
- `allowed-origin-patterns` accepts only a wildcard subdomain such as `https://*.example.com`, and never together with credentials;
- enabling CORS without any origin is an error: it never defaults to allowing everything;
- headers and methods are listed explicitly.

CORS is a browser rule. It is **not** authentication, and two services on the same host are not trusted because of it. Local origins are in the `local` profile; configure production origins intentionally through `PSO_CORS_ENABLED` and `PSO_CORS_ORIGINS`.

## Headers, errors and replacing the chain

Responses carry the Spring Security defaults (`X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, `Cache-Control: no-store`) plus `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. Error pages for permitted paths stay reachable (a `404` on a public path is not turned into `401`). CSRF protection is disabled because the API is stateless and uses bearer tokens only.

To take full control, define your own `SecurityFilterChain` bean (the starter backs off) or set `pso.security.enabled: false`. `pso security:check` flags a service that has neither the starter nor a chain.

## Not implemented

Service-to-service authentication (token exchange, client credentials), token revocation and introspection.

## What you see (expected)

A generated service with no JWT settings on the local profile warns at start-up, and answers `401` to a request without a token:

```text evidence="expected"
WARN [orders,,] ... c.p.s.s.PsoSecurityAutoConfiguration : JWT validation is not configured (pso.security.jwt.*): every bearer token ...
HTTP/1.1 401   WWW-Authenticate: Bearer   X-Correlation-ID: bfb268c4-8017-4269-bda7-d083bc332384
```

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| a browser call fails with a CORS error | CORS is off by default: enable it with explicit origins (`PSO_CORS_ENABLED`, `PSO_CORS_ORIGINS`); never `*` |
| `401` from a valid token | issuer/audience/algorithm mismatch ([security integration](microservices/security-integration.md)) |
| `403` | the scope is not in the token |

## Common mistakes

- Enabling CORS for every origin to make a demo work.
- Treating CORS as authentication (it is a browser rule).
- Adding `permitAll()` for debugging.

## Next steps

- [Security integration](microservices/security-integration.md)
- [Authentication](security/authentication.md)

# Request and upload limits

> Declarative body, multipart, header, timeout, rate and concurrency limits and exactly where each one is enforced.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

```yaml
pso:
  limits:
    requests: { enabled: true, per-minute: 600 }
    body: { max-size: 2MB }
    multipart: { enabled: false, max-file-size: 5MB, max-request-size: 10MB }
    header: { max-size: 16KB }
    timeouts: { connection: 10s, async-request: 30s }
    concurrency: { max-requests: 0 }
```

| Limit | Enforced by | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `body.max-size` | a servlet filter that counts the bytes **actually read** (so chunked bodies and a lying `Content-Length` cannot bypass it) and answers a declared oversize body before reading it | `413` |
| `multipart.*` (uploads through [PSO Storage](spring/storage.md) need `enabled: true` and sizes at least as large as `pso.storage.upload.max-size`) | `multipart.enabled=false` rejects `multipart/form-data` before any controller; when enabled the container's multipart limits apply (per file and per request, mapped to `spring.servlet.multipart.*`) | `415` / `413` |
| `header.max-size` | the servlet container (`server.max-http-request-header-size`) | `431` or `400` |
| `timeouts.connection` | the container (`server.tomcat.connection-timeout`): slow-client protection | connection closed |
| `timeouts.async-request` | `spring.mvc.async.request-timeout` | `503` |
| `requests.*` | token-bucket rate limiting per client address, per authenticated principal and per route; in-process by default, shared through Redis with the optional `pso-ratelimit-redis-starter` | `429` + `Retry-After` as a [problem](reference/error-standard.md) |
| `concurrency.max-requests` | a semaphore: requests beyond the limit are rejected immediately | `503` + `Retry-After` |

The declarative limits are translated into the real Spring Boot properties at the **lowest precedence**: an explicit `server.*` or `spring.*` property still wins. Health probes are exempt from the rate and concurrency limits.

## What the rate limiter is not

- It is not DDoS protection: it protects one process from one noisy client. Put a gateway, WAF or load balancer in front for volumetric attacks.
- The key is the socket's remote address. `X-Forwarded-For` is read **only** when the peer is listed in `requests.trusted-proxies` (IPs or CIDR), and then from the right, so a client cannot choose its identity.
- The default provider is per instance. For one budget shared across instances add `com.pso:pso-ratelimit-redis-starter` and set `requests.provider: redis`; see [Rate limiting](security/rate-limiting.md) for the full model, the failure policy and the settings. A custom `RateLimiter` bean from earlier versions still replaces the client stage unchanged.

## Inbound and outbound

These limits apply to **inbound** HTTP to this service. Outbound calls have their own limits (timeouts, retries and response size) in [PsoHttpClient](spring/http-client.md).

## Common mistakes

- Raising the body limit globally for one upload endpoint.
- Leaving `per-minute` at the local value in production (`6000` locally, `300` default in `prod`).
- Counting on in-memory rate limiting with several instances: use the Redis provider ([decision](decisions/local-or-distributed-rate-limit.md)).
- Naming a route policy with the service prefix: route policies name the route **without** it.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `413` on a legitimate upload | `pso.limits.body.max-size` (default 2 MB); multipart is disabled unless enabled |
| `431` or `400` | header size above `pso.limits.header.max-size` (the servlet container decides which) |
| `429` for everyone behind a proxy | configure `trusted-proxies` |
| `503` from the limiter | the Redis backend failed with `on-failure: closed` |

## Next steps

- [Rate limiting](security/rate-limiting.md)
- [Spring configuration](spring/configuration.md)

# PsoHttpClient

> Secure outbound HTTP to named services: destination policy, timeouts, size limits, TLS and mTLS, retries, bearer forwarding and error mapping.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

```java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class CustomerService {

    private final PsoHttpClient http;

    public CustomerDto findCustomer(String id) {
        return http.get("customers", "/customers/{id}", CustomerDto.class, id);
    }
}
```

```yaml
pso:
  http:
    client:
      services:
        customers:
          base-url: https://customers.internal:8443
          connect-timeout: 2s
          read-timeout: 5s
          max-response-size: 2MB
          forward-bearer: false
          audience: users-api                       # with forward-bearer: only forward tokens whose audience includes this
          retry: { max-attempts: 2, backoff: 100ms, retry-non-idempotent: false }
          tls:
            trust-store: /etc/pso/trust.p12
            trust-store-password: ${TRUST_STORE_PASSWORD}
            key-store: /etc/pso/client.p12          # setting a key store enables mutual TLS
            key-store-password: ${CLIENT_KEY_PASSWORD}
            server-name: users.internal             # extra identity pin: the server certificate must also carry this name
```

The client is built on Spring's `RestClient` and the JDK `HttpClient`; there is no custom transport.

## API

`get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete` and `exchange(PsoRequest, Class)` (headers, `idempotencyKey`). `exchangeAsync` and `getAsync` return a `Future`; `cancel(true)` interrupts the call (best effort: the remote may still process it). Use `Void.class` for responses without a body.

## Destination policy

- The first argument must be a service declared under `pso.http.client.services`; otherwise `PsoHttpException` with kind `POLICY` is thrown **before any network I/O**.
- Paths are relative to the service's base URL. Absolute URLs, `//host`, backslashes, line breaks, dot segments and encoded separators are refused.
- URI variables are encoded, so a value cannot change the path.
- Redirects are **never followed**, so a remote cannot steer a call to another host.
- Plain `http` is refused for non-loopback hosts unless `allow-insecure-http: true`; credentials, query strings and fragments in `base-url` are refused. Invalid configuration stops start-up.

## Credentials and correlation

The caller's bearer token is forwarded only to services configured with `forward-bearer: true`, and it is taken from the **verified** authentication of the current request (never from a raw header). Without an authenticated caller nothing is forwarded. The correlation id of the current request is propagated, also through async calls.

## Retries

| Request | Retried on connection failure, timeout, 502/503/504 |
|---|---|
| GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS | yes, up to `max-attempts` with backoff and jitter |
| POST, PATCH | only with `retry-non-idempotent: true` **and** an `Idempotency-Key` header |
| any 4xx, TLS failures, policy and size errors | never |

## TLS

Certificate and host name validation are never disabled. A `trust-store` adds private CAs (the JVM trust store is used otherwise). A `key-store` enables mTLS. A failed handshake is reported as kind `TLS`; unreadable material stops start-up with a message that never contains passwords.

## Errors

`PsoHttpException` carries the service name, a kind (`POLICY`, `CONNECT`, `TIMEOUT`, `TLS`, `RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE`, `REMOTE_CLIENT_ERROR`, `REMOTE_SERVER_ERROR`, `CANCELLED`, `INVALID_RESPONSE`) and the remote status. Messages never contain the URL, query string, headers or the remote body. Responses over `max-response-size` fail while being read, with or without a `Content-Length`.

## Rotation, identity and audience

- **Rotation without restart.** The trust store and key store files are checked (at most once per second); when one changes the HTTP client is rebuilt and new connections use the new material. A corrupt or half-written replacement is ignored and the previous material keeps serving (a warning is logged).
- **`tls.server-name`.** The normal host name check always runs. When this is set the server certificate must **also** carry that name as a DNS or IP subject alternative name. It can only make verification stricter. (The Node orchestrator's `serverName` replaces the name used for verification instead; see [Service identity](security/service-identity.md).)
- **`audience`.** With `forward-bearer: true` the caller's token is forwarded only if its `aud` claim includes the value; a token without audience is not forwarded. Whatever the settings, a token is never sent over plain `http` to a non-loopback host.

## Not implemented

Service discovery beyond the declared services (an environment-specific `base-url` is the supported way), circuit breakers and client-credentials token acquisition.

## What the failures look like

| Cause | Result |
|---|---|
| a service name not declared under `pso.http.client.services` | `PsoHttpException` of kind `POLICY`, thrown before any network I/O |
| an absolute URL, `//host`, dot segments or encoded separators in the path | refused by the destination policy |
| the remote answers with a redirect | not followed: the response is returned as is |
| plain `http` to a non-loopback host | refused unless `allow-insecure-http: true` |
| the remote's certificate does not verify | the call fails; verification cannot be disabled |
| a non-idempotent call (POST) that fails | not retried unless `retry-non-idempotent: true` |

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `POLICY` exception for a service you configured | the key under `services` differs from the name you pass (names are exact) |
| the remote returns `401` | the caller's token is forwarded only with `forward-bearer: true` **and** a matching `audience`, and only when the current request has a verified user |
| calls fail only in production | TLS settings differ (trust store, `server-name`); check the remote's certificate names |
| duplicated side effects after a retry | enable retries only for idempotent calls, or send an `idempotencyKey` |

## TLS with PEM files (the same files the orchestrator uses)

A service that calls another service over HTTPS trusts its certificate authority with a PEM file: the very file the orchestrator uses as `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>_TLS_CA_FILE`, that `pso.security.jwt.ca-file` uses for the identity provider and that `pso tls:init --dev` writes as `tls/ca.crt`. No conversion to a key store is needed.

```yaml title="application.yml"
pso:
  http:
    client:
      services:
        customers:
          base-url: https://customers:8082
          tls:
            ca-file: /run/pso/tls/ca.crt            # PEM: one or more authorities
            cert-file: /run/pso/tls/tls.crt         # optional, with key-file: mutual TLS
            key-file: /run/pso/tls/tls.key
            key-password: ${CUSTOMERS_TLS_KEY_PASSWORD:}   # only for an encrypted key
```

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tls.ca-file` | PEM file with the trusted authorities. Without it (and without `trust-store`) the JVM trust store is used |
| `tls.cert-file`, `tls.key-file` | the client certificate (with its chain) and its private key (RSA or EC, PEM): mutual TLS. Both or neither |
| `tls.key-password` | password of an encrypted `key-file`; a secret, from the environment |
| `tls.trust-store`, `tls.key-store` (+ `-type`, `-password`) | the same two things as PKCS12 or JKS key stores. Still supported; use one form per purpose, not both |
| `tls.server-name` | the service identity the certificate must also carry |

Verification is never disabled, whatever the form: a certificate from an authority that is not trusted, a certificate for another host name and a missing client certificate all fail with `PsoHttpException.Kind.TLS`. The files are checked at start-up, and the message names the file and the reason, never a password or key content: `tls.ca-file not found`, `contains no certificate`, `the certificate authority in ... expired on 2026-01-31`, `tls.ca-file and tls.trust-store both name the trusted authorities`. `pso security:validate` reports the contradictory combinations before the service starts (`SPR014`).

## What the caller of your service sees when a remote call fails

A `PsoHttpException` you do not handle becomes a problem that never contains the remote service's body:

| The remote service | Problem |
|---|---|
| answered 404 | `404 PSO_UPSTREAM_NOT_FOUND` |
| answered 409 | `409 PSO_UPSTREAM_CONFLICT` |
| answered another 4xx | `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_REJECTED` (your service made a request the remote refused: that is not the caller's 400, 401 or 403) |
| answered 5xx, or something unreadable | `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_BAD_GATEWAY` |
| did not answer | `504 PSO_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT`, `503 PSO_UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE`, `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_TLS` |

Earlier versions answered `502 PSO_UPSTREAM_BAD_GATEWAY` ("an upstream service returned an invalid response") for a remote 404 as well, which described a failure that had not happened. When a remote answer has a meaning in your domain, translate it on purpose:

```java title="src/main/java/com/pso/orders/application/service/CustomerLookup.java"
package com.pso.orders.application.service;

import com.pso.spring.http.PsoHttpClient;
import com.pso.spring.http.PsoHttpException;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

@Service
public class CustomerLookup {

    public record Customer(String id, String name) {
    }

    private final PsoHttpClient http;

    public CustomerLookup(PsoHttpClient http) {
        this.http = http;
    }

    public Customer require(String customerId) {
        try {
            return http.get("customers", "/customers/{id}", Customer.class, customerId);
        } catch (PsoHttpException e) {
            if (e.isStatus(404)) {
                throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, "unknown customer");
            }
            throw e;
        }
    }
}
```

## Common mistakes

- Building URLs by string concatenation instead of path templates (`/customers/{id}`): variables are encoded for you.
- Forwarding the user's token to every service.
- Disabling TLS checks to "make it work".

## Next steps

- [Service-to-service communication](microservices/service-to-service.md)
- [Service identity and mTLS](security/service-identity.md)

# Database selection and H2

> pso.database.provider, database-free start-up, the opt-in H2 profile and PostgreSQL with Flyway.

```yaml
pso:
  database:
    provider: none      # none | h2 | postgresql
```

## `none` (the default)

The service starts with **no JDBC URL, driver, JPA or Flyway**, even if those libraries are on the classpath: the starter removes database auto-configuration when the provider is `none`. The generated tests assert that no `DataSource` bean exists until a provider is chosen.

## H2: available, never default

H2 is for local development and tests only.

```bash
./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=h2            # adds H2 to the run classpath
./mvnw -Ph2 spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=local,h2  # together with other profiles
```

The `h2` Maven profile adds the persistence starter and H2 to the run classpath only when you ask for it. The `h2` Spring profile sets `pso.database.provider: h2`, which configures an **in-memory** database (`jdbc:h2:mem`): no file is ever created and the H2 console stays disabled. The service **refuses to start** when H2 is combined with the `prod` or `staging` profile, and `pso validate` reports H2 in the base, staging or prod files (`SPR009`).

`pso database:enable h2` makes it permanent for the **local** profile (adds the dependencies and `pso.database.provider: h2` to `application-local.yml`); the base provider stays `none`.

## PostgreSQL

```bash
pso database:enable postgresql --service users-service        # or: pso create service orders --db postgres
```

It adds `pso-data-spring-boot-starter` (JPA, Flyway, driver), sets the provider, adds `spring.datasource` settings read from `DB_URL`, `DB_USER` and `DB_PASSWORD`, creates the Flyway migration directory, records `"db": "postgres"` in the workspace and adds an embedded PostgreSQL test configuration so the service's own tests never need a server. The command is idempotent, supports `--dry-run` and edits only the files it recognizes (it stops with instructions otherwise).

Tests against the embedded PostgreSQL run real Flyway migrations. A connection to a separately running PostgreSQL server was **not** exercised in the framework's own test run.

See [Persistence](microservices/persistence.md) for migrations and the outbox table.

## What you see with PostgreSQL

The real start-up of a service with PostgreSQL (Hikari, Flyway, JPA) and the resulting tables are on [PostgreSQL CRUD](spring/postgresql-crud.md). The decision between ORM and SQL is [JPA or JDBC?](decisions/jpa-or-jdbc.md).

## Common mistakes

- Using H2 as "production light": it is refused outside the local/h2 profiles.
- Credentials in `application.yml`: use `DB_URL`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`.
- Enabling the database starter without a provider and wondering why nothing connects: `pso.database.provider` says what the service uses.

## Next steps

- [PostgreSQL CRUD](spring/postgresql-crud.md)
- [Persistence](microservices/persistence.md)

# Storage

> PSO Storage for Spring Boot services - one API over the local filesystem, Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage, with opaque identifiers, ownership, upload validation, safe downloads and audit events.

## What it is

`pso-storage-spring-boot-starter` gives a service one API to store, read, copy, move, delete, list and sign files, whatever backs it:

| Provider | `pso.storage.provider` | For | Verified |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local filesystem | `local` | development, tests, self-hosted | real filesystem tests (symbolic-link tests need a platform that can create links: skipped on Windows without developer mode) |
| Amazon S3 | `s3` | cloud | adapter tests against a **mocked** S3 client; not run against Amazon S3 or an emulator |
| Azure Blob Storage | `azure` | cloud | adapter tests against **mocked** Azure clients; not run against Azure or Azurite |

The framework owns the infrastructure (streaming, validation, keys, providers, safe downloads, audit). **Your service owns business authorization.** Storage is optional: with no `pso.storage.provider`, nothing is configured and no provider SDK is loaded.

## 1. Enable it

```bash
pso storage:enable local --service hr-service                     # development, self-hosted
pso storage:enable s3 --service hr-service --bucket acme-hr-documents --region eu-west-1
pso storage:enable azure --service hr-service                     # endpoint and container from the environment
pso storage:validate --service hr-service
```

It adds `pso-storage-spring-boot-starter` (and the S3 or Azure SDK; versions come from `pso-bom`), writes the `pso.storage` block, enables multipart, and gives the **local** and **test** profiles a local provider so development and tests never need a cloud account. It writes no secrets: S3 uses the AWS default credential chain, Azure uses `DefaultAzureCredential` (managed identity). Running it again changes nothing.

```yaml
pso:
  storage:
    provider: s3
    s3:
      bucket: acme-hr-documents
      region: eu-west-1
      prefix: hr/
    upload:
      max-size: 5MB          # keep <= pso.limits.multipart.max-file-size
      allowed-content-types: [application/pdf]
  limits:
    multipart: { enabled: true, max-file-size: 5MB, max-request-size: 10MB }
```

| Key | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `provider` | unset | `local`, `s3`, `azure` |
| `local.root` | required for `local` | created with owner-only permissions; keep it outside any served directory |
| `s3.bucket` / `region` / `prefix` / `endpoint` / `path-style-access` | `bucket` required | `endpoint` and path style for MinIO or LocalStack; objects are always private |
| `azure.endpoint` / `container` / `prefix` / `copy-timeout` | `container` required | `endpoint` with a managed identity |
| `azure.connection-string` | none | Azurite and local work only; refused in `prod` and `staging` |
| `upload.max-size` | `10MB` | enforced while streaming |
| `upload.allowed-content-types` / `allowed-extensions` | any | known formats are verified by signature regardless |
| `upload.allow-unverified-types` | `false` | trust the declared type for types without a signature check |
| `download.inline-content-types` | png, jpeg, gif, webp | everything else is an attachment |
| `signed-url.enabled` / `default-ttl` / `max-ttl` | `false` / `1m` / `5m` | S3 and Azure only |
| `scan.required` | `false` | `true` refuses to start without a `ContentScanner` bean |
| `metadata.store` | `provider` | `provider` or `memory` (tests); a `FileMetadataStore` bean replaces both |

## 2. Use it

```bash
pso make:files documents --service hr-service --mime application/pdf --ext .pdf --max-size 5MB
```

writes a controller (upload, download, metadata, list, move, delete, each with a scope check) and a test that exercises real multipart through MockMvc. The part that matters:

```java
@PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_documents:write')")
public ResponseEntity<StoredFile.FileView> upload(@RequestParam("document") MultipartFile file) {
    StorageAccess.Caller caller = storage.currentCaller();
    StoredFile stored = storage.store(caller, UploadedFiles.request(file)
        .ownerRef(caller.subject()).namespace("files/documents").policy(POLICY).build());
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(stored.view());
}

@GetMapping("/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_documents:read')")
public ResponseEntity<InputStreamResource> download(@PathVariable String id) {
    PsoStorageService.FileContent content = storage.open(storage.currentCaller(), id);
    return FileDownloads.response(content, props.getStorage().getDownload().getInlineContentTypes());
}
```

`PsoStorageService` operations (each takes the caller and asks the access policy first):

| Method | Result |
|---|---|
| `store(caller, StorageRequest)` | `StoredFile` with an opaque id (`f_...`), sanitized filename, size, SHA-256, owner, context |
| `open(caller, id)` | `FileContent` (close it) streaming from the provider |
| `metadata(caller, id)`, `list(caller, ListQuery)` | records; `list` is paginated (cursor, at most 200, may return fewer than `limit` when records are hidden from the caller) |
| `copy(caller, id, namespace, ownerRef)`, `move(caller, id, namespace)`, `delete(caller, id)` | copy gives a new id; move keeps the id and changes the key |
| `signedUrl(caller, id, ttl)` | a short-lived provider URL, only when enabled and supported (local returns empty: no URL is invented) |

`StoredFile.view()` is what an API may return; `key` and `provider` stay internal. The Java types: `StorageProvider` (SPI), `FileMetadataStore`, `StorageAccess.Policy`, `StorageAccess.CallerResolver`, `UploadPolicy`, `ContentScanner`, `StorageAuditEvent`.

## 3. Authorization is yours

The default policy is strict: an authenticated caller may store, and may read, move, copy, delete or sign only files they uploaded or that carry their own subject as `ownerRef`. Replace it with a bean:

```java
@Bean
StorageAccess.Policy employeeDocumentsPolicy() {
    return (op, caller, file) -> {
        if (caller == null || caller.subject() == null) return false;
        if (caller.has("ROLE_HR")) return true;                                   // HR manages everything
        return op == StorageAccess.Operation.READ && file != null
            && ("employee:" + caller.subject()).equals(file.ownerRef());           // an employee reads their own
    };
}
```

A policy that throws denies. A denial is `403`; the caller\'s `uploadedBy` and the business owner (`ownerRef`) are separate on purpose: storage identity is not ownership. Check the id belongs to the resource in the URL (`/employees/42/documents/{id}`) as the example in `StorageEndToEndTests` does.

The caller comes from the Spring Security context (the PSO JWT subject and authorities); without Spring Security provide a `StorageAccess.CallerResolver` bean or pass a `Caller` explicitly.

## 4. Security controls

| Control | How |
|---|---|
| size | counted while streaming; a lying length is irrelevant; nothing is stored when exceeded; the per-call `UploadPolicy` can only narrow the limit |
| type | declared type checked against the allow-list **and** the file signature; a PDF declared as text, an executable named `.pdf` and a zip posing as a PDF are refused |
| names | `SafeFileNames.sanitize`: no directories, control or bidirectional characters, no reserved names; never part of a key |
| keys | generated: `<validated namespace>/<random id>`; `..`, absolute paths, empty or dot segments and the reserved `_pso` namespace are refused at the service and again by every provider |
| local provider | each path segment must be a plain file or directory exactly where the key says (symbolic links and junctions refused), temporary file in the same filesystem then rename without replacing, `fsync`, owner-only permissions, stale temp sweep at start-up, no absolute path in any response |
| private by default | no ACLs, no public buckets or containers; S3 `If-None-Match: *` and Azure `If-None-Match: *` refuse overwrites |
| downloads | `FileDownloads` sends `application/octet-stream` for HTML, SVG, XML and script types, `attachment` unless the type is on the inline allow-list, `nosniff`, `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox; default-src 'none'`, `Cache-Control: private, no-store` |
| signed URLs | opt in, authorized per call, capped TTL (default 1 minute, max 5), Azure user-delegation SAS with a managed identity; treat the URL as a credential |
| errors | `StorageProblemAdvice` answers with fixed catalog texts; provider messages (buckets, accounts, paths) stay in the server log |
| audit | a `StorageAuditEvent` for every operation, allowed or denied: operation, file id, subject, outcome, reason; never content, names or paths. Listen with `@EventListener` |
| malware | **no scanning engine is included.** Register a `ContentScanner` bean to scan after the write and before the file becomes addressable (infected or undecidable uploads are deleted, fail closed); `scan.required: true` refuses to start without one |
| rate limiting | uploads pass through the same per-address, per-principal and per-route limits as every request ([limits](spring/limits.md)) |

## 5. What the providers guarantee

- `put`, `copy`, `move` never overwrite; a failed `put` leaves no visible object; `delete` is idempotent.
- S3 and Azure have no cross-object transactions. `move` is copy, save the record, then delete the old object: a crash leaves an orphaned object, never a record pointing at nothing. S3 copy is limited to 5 GB per object; Azure copy is asynchronous and the adapter waits for it (`copy-timeout`), deleting a failed destination.
- Without a known content length, S3 and Azure uploads spool to a temporary file first (both need the length), bounded by the upload limit. `MultipartFile` uploads always have a length.
- Metadata defaults to a small JSON record next to each file (`_pso/files/<id>.json`): no shared database. Listing through it reads one record per file: use a `FileMetadataStore` backed by the service\'s own database for large collections.
- A file whose record was never saved (crash between the two writes) is an unreachable orphan object; there is no automatic sweeper yet.

## 6. Failures

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `415 PSO_HTTP_MULTIPART_DISABLED` | multipart is off | `pso.limits.multipart.enabled: true` (`storage:enable` does it) |
| `413` for a file below `upload.max-size` | `pso.limits.multipart.max-file-size` is smaller | raise both consistently (`storage:validate` reports it as `STO010`) |
| start-up error naming `pso.storage.s3.bucket` (or another key) | required value missing | set it; the message names the property |
| start-up error "needs the AWS SDK" / "Azure SDK" | provider selected without its dependency | add it (`storage:enable` does) |
| `503 PSO_STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE` | the backend failed (credentials, network, disk) | check the server log and `/actuator/health` (`psoStorage` component) |
| `403` everywhere | the default owner-only policy | declare your `StorageAccess.Policy` bean |
| `400` "content does not match its declared type" | the bytes are not what the client claimed | working as designed |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| returning `StoredFile` from a controller | return `stored.view()`: `key` and `provider` are internal |
| letting the client choose `ownerRef` | derive it from the authenticated caller or the resource path |
| using a client filename in a path | never: keys are generated |
| enabling `signed-url` to avoid writing a download route | prefer the authenticated route; signed URLs are bearer credentials |
| assuming uploads are scanned | register a `ContentScanner`; none is included |
| using `local` in production behind several replicas | use `s3` or `azure`, or a shared persistent volume on purpose (`STO005`) |

## Next steps

- [File uploads and downloads in the orchestrator](orchestrator/file-uploads.md)
- [Spring configuration reference](spring/configuration.md) and [request limits](spring/limits.md)

# Dispatch configuration

> The pso.dispatch.* settings, the provider starters and the Spring Boot API for events.

Every generated service carries the dispatch settings, **disabled**:

```yaml
pso:
  dispatch:
    enabled: false
    provider: none
```

With these defaults no broker is contacted, no consumer starts, no topic is created and `PsoDispatch` is a `Disabled` bean that fails clearly if used. Activate with `pso dispatch:install <redis|rabbitmq|kafka>` and `enabled: true` ([Installation](dispatch/installation.md)).

## Settings

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pso.dispatch.enabled` | `false` | master switch |
| `pso.dispatch.provider` | `none` | `redis`, `rabbitmq` or `kafka`; must match the installed starter |
| `pso.dispatch.max-message-size` | `1MB` | upper bound for one envelope |
| `consumer.concurrency` / `consumer.batch-size` | `1` / `10` | parallel handlers and read batch |
| `retry.enabled`, `max-attempts`, `initial-delay`, `max-delay`, `multiplier` | `true`, `3`, `1s`, `30s`, `2.0` | in-process retry with backoff |
| `dead-letter.enabled` | `true` | exhausted and poison messages go to `<channel>.dlq` |
| `idempotency.retention` | `24h` | how long processed ids are remembered |
| `outbox.enabled` and `outbox.*` | `false` | [transactional outbox](dispatch/outbox.md) |
| `redis.*`, `rabbitmq.*`, `kafka.*` | environment references | the provider block written by the installer |

## Start-up validation

`enabled=true` without a provider, without the matching starter on the classpath, with a different installed provider, or with no declared events stops the service with a message naming the fix (for example `pso dispatch:install redis`). Invalid declarations list every problem and start nothing. In production (the `prod` / `production` profile, or `PSO_ENV=production`) `pso.dispatch.trust.mode=off` also stops the service unless `pso.dispatch.allow-unauthenticated=true` declares the legacy mode ([publisher authentication](dispatch/security-and-observability.md)).

With `enabled=false` (the generated default) nothing connects. `PsoDispatch` and, for code that injects it, `Outbox` are placeholders: the service starts, and publishing or storing an event fails with `PSO_DISPATCH_DISABLED`, so a transaction that tried to store an event rolls back instead of losing it. With dispatch enabled there is no placeholder outbox: code that needs `Outbox` while `pso.dispatch.outbox.enabled` is false fails at start-up.

## API

`pso-dispatch-api` provides `PsoDispatch` (publish, health, metrics), `@PsoEventHandler`, `ConsumeContext` and the shared envelope and schema validator; it has no broker client on its classpath. Events are declared in `src/main/resources/dispatch/*.events.json` ([Declaring events](dispatch/events-and-consumers.md)). The delivery guarantee is at-least-once; exactly-once is not claimed ([Reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)).

## What a Spring consumer does at run time

The same envelope, retry, dead-letter and acknowledgement rules as the TypeScript runtime (the verified transcript is the [walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md), which uses a TypeScript consumer for speed). The Spring side adds the transactional outbox ([outbox](dispatch/outbox.md)) and publishes the same counters as Micrometer meters.

## The tests of a service with Dispatch enabled

`pso dispatch:install` also prepares the service's own tests: it adds `com.pso:pso-dispatch-test` with **test scope** and sets, in `application-test.yml`:

```yaml title="src/main/resources/application-test.yml (added)"
pso:
  dispatch:
    provider: memory   # tests publish and consume in process (com.pso:pso-dispatch-test): no broker is needed
```

So when you switch Dispatch on the documented way (`pso.dispatch.enabled: true` in `application.yml`), every `@SpringBootTest` that uses the `test` profile (the generated tests do) still starts, publishes and runs its `@PsoEventHandler` methods without Redis, RabbitMQ or Kafka. A test can inject `MemoryAdapter` to look at what was published.

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Test only | the adapter exists only where `pso-dispatch-test` is on the classpath; the dependency has test scope, so it is not in the application artifact |
| Never in production | `pso.dispatch.provider=memory` with a production profile stops start-up; `pso security:validate` reports it outside `application-test.yml` (`SPR015`) |
| Not a broker | it proves nothing about delivery, ordering, redelivery after a crash or durability |
| Real broker tests | an integration test that must use the broker selects it itself: `@SpringBootTest(properties = "pso.dispatch.provider=redis")`, with the broker URL from the environment |

The Dispatch classes of a layered service live in `application/event/` (`events/` in the 0.1 layout); a test of them uses the same package.

```java title="src/test/java/com/pso/orders/application/event/OrdersPlacedBrokerTests.java (an integration test against the real broker)"
package com.pso.orders.application.event;

import com.pso.dispatch.PsoDispatch;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.ActiveProfiles;

@SpringBootTest(properties = {"pso.dispatch.enabled=true", "pso.dispatch.provider=redis"})
@ActiveProfiles("test")
class OrdersPlacedBrokerTests {

    @Autowired PsoDispatch dispatch;

    @Test
    void publishesThroughRedis() {
        dispatch.publish("orders.placed", new OrdersPlacedEvent("o-1", "c-1", 12.5));
    }
}
```

## Common mistakes

- A handler that mixes a database write and a broker publish without the outbox ([decision](decisions/outbox-or-direct-publish.md)).
- Declaring the event in YAML but forgetting to install a provider starter.
- Treating `@PsoEventHandler` methods as request handlers: they run on consumer threads, without a request context or an authenticated user.

## Next steps

- [Walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md)
- [Outbox](dispatch/outbox.md)

# PostgreSQL CRUD in a Spring service

> How the generated layered service persists its data - datasource and pool, the Flyway migration, the JPA entity, the repository and database-level filters, transactions and the 409 for duplicates, pagination limits, the tests against a real PostgreSQL - and how to add a table or a resource.

`pso create service catalog` generates a service whose Product CRUD persists in PostgreSQL. This page reads its persistence layer
file by file, with the code exactly as generated. The same pattern is what `pso make:crud` writes for every new resource.

| Layer | File | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| configuration | `src/main/resources/application.yml` | datasource, pool, Flyway, Hibernate validation, UTC |
| schema | `src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_products.sql` | the table, its constraints and indexes; Flyway is the only writer of DDL |
| entity | `infrastructure/entity/ProductEntity.java` | the JPA mapping (`@Version`, UTC timestamps, `BigDecimal`) |
| repository | `infrastructure/persistence/ProductRepository.java`, `ProductSpecifications.java` | Spring Data queries; filters in the database |
| service | `application/service/ProductService.java` | transactions, the duplicate check, the constraint turned into a `409` |
| page requests | `shared/validation/PageRequests.java` | page, size and the allowed sort fields |

## 1. Configuration

The datasource reads the environment; credentials are never in a file. Hibernate validates the mapping against the schema Flyway
created and never changes it:

```yaml title="catalog/src/main/resources/application.yml (excerpt, generated)"
  jackson:
    deserialization:
      fail-on-unknown-properties: true   # a request with a property the contract does not have is a 400, never silently ignored
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/catalog}
    username: ${DB_USER:}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD:}
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:10}
  flyway:
    enabled: true
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false            # no database access while a response is rendered
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate           # Flyway owns the schema (db/migration); Hibernate only checks the entities match it
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc:
          time_zone: UTC
```

| Setting | Why |
|---|---|
| `ddl-auto: validate` | Hibernate checks entities against the schema and **never changes it**; a mismatch stops the start-up |
| `open-in-view: false` | no queries while the response is rendered; a lazy-loading mistake fails in the service instead of leaking a connection |
| `maximum-pool-size` | the database has a connection limit: size it as `limit / number of instances`, minus a margin for tools |
| `time_zone: UTC` | timestamps are written and read in UTC, whatever the server's zone |
| `fail-on-unknown-properties` | the request records are the contract: an extra property is a `400`, not ignored data |

`pso docker:up` provides `DB_URL`, `DB_USER` and `DB_PASSWORD` to the container (the password generated into `.infra/`, mounted as a
file secret). To run the service from the IDE, point the three variables at a PostgreSQL of your own.

## 2. The migration

```sql title="catalog/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_products.sql"
CREATE TABLE products (
    id           UUID             PRIMARY KEY,
    sku          VARCHAR(64)      NOT NULL CHECK (char_length(sku) >= 3),
    name         VARCHAR(120)     NOT NULL CHECK (char_length(name) >= 1),
    description  VARCHAR(2000),
    price        NUMERIC(12, 2)   NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0.00 AND price <= 9999999999.99),
    active       BOOLEAN          NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ      NOT NULL,
    updated_at   TIMESTAMPTZ      NOT NULL,
    version      BIGINT           NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    CONSTRAINT uk_products_sku UNIQUE (sku)
);
```

Uniqueness is a **database constraint**: it holds even when two requests race. Money is an exact `NUMERIC`, never a float. The
migration also indexes what the list endpoint sorts by. Migrations are append-only: `pso make:migration <name> --service catalog`
writes the next version (`V2__<name>.sql`).

## 3. The entity and the repository

```java title="catalog/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/infrastructure/entity/ProductEntity.java (excerpt)"
    @Setter
    @Column(name = "price", nullable = false, precision = 12, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal price;

    /** optimistic locking: a concurrent update of the same row fails instead of silently overwriting the other one */
    @Version
    @Column(name = "version", nullable = false)
    private long version;
```

```java title="catalog/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/infrastructure/persistence/ProductRepository.java"
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<ProductEntity, UUID>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<ProductEntity> {

    boolean existsBySku(String sku);

    boolean existsBySkuAndIdNot(String sku, UUID id);
}
```

Filters are a `Specification`, executed by the database, never a list filtered in memory. The `name` filter is a case-insensitive
contains whose `%` and `_` are escaped:

```java title="catalog/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/infrastructure/persistence/ProductSpecifications.java (excerpt)"
        if (sku != null && !sku.isBlank()) {
            spec = spec.and((root, query, cb) -> cb.equal(root.get("sku"), sku.strip()));
        }
```

## 4. The service: transactions and conflicts

Every public method is a transaction (`readOnly` for reads). A write is flushed at once, so a constraint violation is reported inside
the transaction, by name, as a `409` with a sentence that does not echo the caller's input:

```java title="catalog/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/service/ProductService.java (excerpt)"
    /** writes now (not at commit) so a constraint violation is reported here, as a 409, inside this transaction */
    private ProductEntity saveAndFlush(ProductEntity entity) {
        try {
            return repository.saveAndFlush(entity);
        } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
            throw translate(e);
        } catch (ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
            throw new ConflictException("the product was changed by another request; read it again and retry");
        }
    }
```

The list method builds the page request with `PageRequests.of(page, size, sort, SORTABLE, DEFAULT_SORT, MAX_PAGE_SIZE)`: a sort field
the endpoint does not allow, or a size above 100, is a `400` before any query runs, and ties are broken by `id` so a page never repeats
or skips a row.

## 5. The tests

```bash
./mvnw test
```

The generated tests start the real application context with an **embedded PostgreSQL** (no Docker needed), the real Flyway
migrations and real signed JWTs. `ProductControllerTests` covers the round trip, validation, a duplicate SKU (sequential and ten
concurrent creations: exactly one row), 404 and malformed ids, 401/403, and pagination, sorting and filtering in the database;
`DatabaseMigrationTests` proves the data source is PostgreSQL and every migration ran. A new service runs 16 tests.

## 6. Another table or resource

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| a complete resource like products | `pso make:crud order --service catalog [--orchestrator] --fields "..."` ([Generators](architecture/generators.md)) |
| one entity and its repository | `pso make:entity invoice --service catalog`, `pso make:repository invoice --service catalog`, then the table with `pso make:migration create-invoices --service catalog` |
| a database in a service created with `--template empty` | `pso database:enable postgresql --service billing` (adds the driver, the datasource, Flyway and the schema validation) |
| JDBC instead of JPA | inject `JdbcTemplate` in the service and keep the same transaction structure; write SQL with `?` parameters |

`make:entity` and `make:repository` refuse in a service without a database, naming the command that adds one.

## 7. Publishing an event in the same transaction (outbox)

If other services must learn about a new product, do not publish after the save and hope. Store the event in the same transaction:

```bash
pso dispatch:install redis --service catalog
pso dispatch:outbox --service catalog
```

```java
@Transactional
public ProductResponse create(CreateProductRequest request) {
    ...
    ProductEntity saved = repository.saveAndFlush(mapper.toEntity(request));
    outbox.publish("catalog.product-created", Map.of("productId", saved.getId().toString()));   // rolls back with the product
    return mapper.toResponse(saved);
}
```

Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must tolerate a repeated event. Details: [transactional outbox](dispatch/outbox.md).

## Production considerations

- **Credentials**: environment variables or your secret manager only. The `prod` profile refuses H2.
- **Pool**: set `DB_POOL_SIZE` from the database limit and the instance count; watch pool wait time in [metrics](devops/observability.md).
- **Migrations**: run on start-up for a single instance; for many instances prefer a one-off migration job before the rollout. Never use `ddl-auto: update`.
- **Backups and restore tests** are yours; PSO provisions the development database, it does not operate production databases.
- **Timeouts**: a slow query holds a pooled connection. Add statement timeouts at the database role (`ALTER ROLE catalog_app SET statement_timeout = '5s'`).
- **Least privilege**: the application role needs DML on its tables; use a separate, more privileged role for migrations if your policy requires it.

## Anti-patterns

| Do not | Do instead |
|---|---|
| return the entity from a controller | return a response record (`application/dto/response`) |
| concatenate request data into SQL | derived queries, `Specification`, `@Query` with named parameters, `JdbcTemplate` with `?` |
| `ddl-auto: update` or `create` | Flyway migrations and `validate` |
| edit an applied migration | add a new version |
| put `@Transactional` on controllers or repositories | on service methods |
| check uniqueness only in code | a database constraint, translated into a `409` |
| read `DB_PASSWORD` into a file or image | inject it at run time |

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `FlywayValidateException: Validate failed ... checksum mismatch` | an applied migration was edited; restore it and add a new version |
| `Schema-validation: missing table [...]` | an entity without its migration, or the migration did not run (`flyway.enabled`, wrong `DB_URL`) |
| `Connection to ... refused` at start | the database is not reachable at `DB_URL`; with `pso docker:up`, check `pso docker:ps` |
| `HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out` | the pool is exhausted: slow queries, a transaction left open, or too small a pool |
| `403` on a call that worked yesterday | the token no longer carries `products:write`; check scopes, not the database |
| `PSO_VALIDATION_FAILED` | read the `errors` list; each entry names the field |

## Next steps

- [The reference CRUD](architecture/reference-crud.md) and [Build a CRUD API](tutorials/crud-api.md)
- [Database selection and H2](spring/database-and-h2.md)
- [Transactional outbox](dispatch/outbox.md)
- Projects that keep the 0.1 layout: [a CRUD by hand in the 0.1 layout](architecture/manual-crud-0-1.md)

# Lombok conventions

> How Lombok is configured in generated services and which annotations belong where.

Every generated Spring service includes Lombok. The version is the one Spring Boot manages, compiled with `release 21`. The `pom.xml` declares the dependency as `provided`, configures the annotation processor path explicitly and excludes Lombok from the packaged jar; `lombok.config` marks generated code so tools can skip it.

| Use | Annotation |
|---|---|
| services and controllers (constructor injection) | `@RequiredArgsConstructor` on a class whose dependencies are `final` fields |
| JPA entities | `@Getter`, `@Setter` on the fields that may change, `@NoArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PROTECTED)` (see the generated `ProductEntity`) |
| request and response DTOs | a Java **record**; no Lombok needed (see `CreateProductRequest`, `ProductResponse`) |
| mutable beans a framework binds | `@Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor @AllArgsConstructor @Builder` |

## Rules

- **Never `@Data` on a JPA entity.** Its generated `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` use mutable state and relationships.
- Avoid `@ToString` on anything that holds secrets or entity relationships: it can leak values or recurse.
- Avoid `@EqualsAndHashCode` on mutable entities unless you define identity semantics explicitly (for example by id only).
- Prefer records for DTOs; reserve Lombok for beans that frameworks need to mutate.
- Use constructor injection for services. `pso make:service` generates a `@Service @RequiredArgsConstructor` class.

The generated tests check that the template follows these rules (no `@Data` or `@ToString` defaults).

## What it looks like

`pso make:service pricing --service catalog` prints and creates:

```text evidence="verified"
created    src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/service/PricingService.java
```

```java title="catalog/src/main/java/com/pso/catalog/application/service/PricingService.java (generated)"
package com.pso.catalog.application.service;

import lombok.RequiredArgsConstructor;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

/** Dependencies are final fields: Lombok generates the constructor and Spring injects through it. */
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PricingService {
}
```

Add your dependencies as `private final` fields and the generated constructor injects them. The generated request and response DTOs are records.

## Common mistakes

- `@Data` on a JPA entity.
- `@ToString` on a class that holds a token or an entity relationship.
- Lombok on records (not needed).

## Next steps

- [Java project structure](microservices/project-structure.md)
- [PostgreSQL CRUD](spring/postgresql-crud.md) (entities written by hand, no `@Data`)
