# Event contracts and versioning

> The canonical envelope, the closed schema subset, compatibility policies and the contract lock file.

## The envelope

Every event on every provider is the same UTF-8 JSON document, serialized canonically (fixed field order, payload keys sorted). The TypeScript and Java implementations are tested against shared contract data and produce identical bytes.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `envelopeVersion` | Version of the envelope itself (`1`) |
| `id` | Unique event id. It is the idempotency key |
| `type` | Event name, a dotted lower-case name such as `users.created` |
| `version` | Schema version of the payload |
| `source` | The publishing service |
| `occurredAt` | UTC timestamp |
| `correlationId` | Carried across services; generated when absent |
| `causationId` | Optional: the event that caused this one |
| `trace` | Optional trace context field. It is carried, not exported (no OpenTelemetry integration) |
| `contentType` | `application/json` |
| `payload` | The event data |

Unknown fields are rejected. Limits: 1 MiB per envelope (configurable down with `pso.dispatch.max-message-size`), 256 characters per metadata value, nesting depth 32. A message that violates them is treated as poison on consume ([Reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)). No arbitrary deserialization happens: payloads are parsed as plain JSON data.

## Schemas

Payload schemas use a **closed JSON-Schema subset** with identical semantics in both languages: `type`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `enum`, `minimum`, `maximum`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `minItems`, `maxItems`, `pattern`, plus `title` and `description`. Anything outside the subset is a validation error at `pso dispatch:validate`, not a silently ignored keyword. Publishing validates the payload; consuming validates it again before the handler runs.

## Compatibility

Each event declares `compatibility`: `backward`, `forward`, `full` (default) or `none`. When you add a new `version` of an event, `pso dispatch:validate` checks the new schema against the highest lower version recorded in the lock file. `none` is the explicit, reviewable way to declare a deliberate breaking change. A consumer lists versions it still understands with `accepts: [1]`; an event with any other version is dead-lettered as `PSO_DISPATCH_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION`.

## The lock file

`pso dispatch:lock` writes `pso.dispatch.lock.json` with the schema of every declared event version. Afterwards the same name and version can never change its schema (`pso dispatch:validate` fails); change means a new version. The file is meant to be committed.

```bash
pso dispatch:validate    # declarations, schemas, lock, compatibility (exit 1 on errors)
pso dispatch:lock        # record the current contracts
```

## What locking does

`pso dispatch:lock` records each event's channel, schema and a hash in `pso.dispatch.lock.json`. Expected output:

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso dispatch:lock
locked: orders.placed@1
```

```json
{
  "comment": "Locked event contracts. Managed by `pso dispatch:lock`; commit it.",
  "contracts": {
    "orders.placed": {
      "1": { "channel": "orders.events", "hash": "6fa7cff47ed3e8cd", "schema": { "type": "object", "required": ["orderId"], ... } }
    }
  }
}
```

Until it exists, `pso dispatch:validate` reports `INFO PSO_DISPATCH_UNLOCKED ... orders.placed v1 is not locked yet` (an informational finding, not an error). After locking, changing the schema of `orders.placed` version 1 is rejected: publish version 2 and state the compatibility.

## Variations

| Change | What to do |
|---|---|
| add an optional field | new version with compatibility declared; lock again |
| rename or remove a field | a new major event version; keep consuming the old one until producers move |
| a deliberate incompatible change | `compatibility: none` as the explicit escape hatch, reviewed |

## Common mistakes

- Editing a schema under the same name and version.
- Not committing the lock file.
- Treating the schema as the only guard: consumers should still be tolerant.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Check | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PSO_DISPATCH_SCHEMA_CHANGED` | a schema changed after `pso dispatch:lock` while still declared as the same version | `git diff` of the schema | declare `version: 2`, then `pso dispatch:lock` |
| `PSO_DISPATCH_004` | the `schema` path in `EVENTS.pso.ts` does not exist | the path in the error | correct it (it also trips the lock check, so two errors appear) |
| `PSO_DISPATCH_UNLOCKED` (`INFO`) | a new event version has no recorded contract | `pso dispatch:validate` | run `pso dispatch:lock` and commit `pso.dispatch.lock.json` |

All three were reproduced; the output is in [Checking Dispatch and what its errors mean](dispatch/diagnostics.md).

## Next steps

- [Events and consumers](dispatch/events-and-consumers.md)
- [Walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md)

# Walkthrough: publish, consume, retry, dead-letter

> A real run of Dispatch over Redis Streams - install, declare, validate, start, a successful event, a handler that fails three times, a poison message - with the commands, the broker's contents, the logs and the metrics, and what each means.

Everything below was captured from one run on a Windows machine against a real Redis 7 container, with a generated orchestrator as the consumer. The consumer reacts to `orders.placed` and publishes `orders.confirmed`. Event ids, channel names (they contain a per-run suffix) and timings belong to that run.

> [!NOTE]
> The orchestrator acts as the consumer here because it is the quickest way to run a real consumer without a Java build. The same envelope, retry and dead-letter behavior applies to Spring services.

## 1. Install and declare

```bash
pso dispatch:install redis --service gw
```

```text evidence="verified"
package.json: + @pso/dispatch
package.json: + ioredis
pso.config.json: dispatch.provider = redis (enabled stays false; secrets are ${env:...} references)
src/dispatch/: modules go here, each with an EVENTS.pso.ts
infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml: a local development broker (not started by PSO)
Next: declare your events, then set pso.dispatch.enabled=true (and the broker URL) to activate. See /docs/dispatch/overview.
```

Dispatch stays **disabled** until you enable it, and PSO never starts the broker: `infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml` is a file for you to run (`docker compose -f infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml up -d`).

The contract and the consumer, in `src/dispatch/orders/`:

```typescript title="EVENTS.pso.ts"
export default defineEvents({
  events: [
    { name: "orders.placed",    version: 1, channel: "orders.demo62984",           schema: "schemas/order-placed.schema.ts", publish: false },
    { name: "orders.confirmed", version: 1, channel: "orders.confirmed.demo62984", key: "orderId" },
  ],
  consumers: [OrderPlacedConsumer],
});
```

```typescript title="orders.consumer.ts"
@DispatchConsumer("orders.placed")
export class OrderPlacedConsumer {
  constructor(private readonly dispatch: Dispatch) {}
  async handle(payload: { orderId: string; fail?: boolean }) {
    if (payload.fail) throw new Error("payment provider unavailable");
    await this.dispatch.publish("orders.confirmed", { orderId: payload.orderId });
  }
}
```

`publish: false` says this service only consumes `orders.placed`; `key` makes events with the same `orderId` ordered together.

## 2. Check what you declared (no broker, no code run)

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso dispatch:validate
INFO    PSO_DISPATCH_UNLOCKED gw (src/dispatch/orders/EVENTS.pso.ts)
        orders.placed v1 is not locked yet
        fix: Run `pso dispatch:lock` to record its contract
...
valid. Static validation only: event delivery is verified by running the service against a broker.

$ pso dispatch:events
orders.placed@1  channel orders.demo62984  gw consumes  schema yes  consumers: gw
orders.confirmed@1  channel orders.confirmed.demo62984  gw publishes  schema none  consumers: -

$ pso dispatch:consumers
orders.placed                gw  OrderPlacedConsumer  group gw  (src/dispatch/orders/orders.consumer.ts)

$ pso dispatch:graph
gw --orders.confirmed--> channel:orders.confirmed.demo62984
channel:orders.demo62984 --orders.placed--> gw
```

The `INFO ... not locked yet` lines are not errors: `pso dispatch:lock` records the contracts so later schema changes are checked for compatibility. Run it once the contracts are agreed.

## 3. Start with Dispatch enabled

The service was started with `PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true`, the broker URL in the environment, and short retry delays so the demo is quick:

```text evidence="expected"
dispatch.retry.maxAttempts = 3, initialDelay = 200ms, maxDelay = 400ms   (defaults: 3, 1s, 30s)
```

## 4. A successful event

Another service publishes `orders.placed` (here written directly to the stream with the canonical envelope). The consumer runs, publishes `orders.confirmed` and the message is acknowledged.

What `orders.confirmed` contains afterwards (the stream entry, decoded):

```json evidence="expected"
{"id":"0ad97c56-f9e6-4959-b7c3-230ba8e740a1","type":"orders.confirmed","source":"gw","correlationId":"6d5c6049-83e9-403f-a6d0-0f8bf41ef200","payload":{"orderId":"o-100"}}
```

> [!NOTE]
> In this run the incoming event carried `correlationId: "corr-evt-ok-1"`, but the event the handler published got a **new** correlation id and no `causationId`. If you need a chain from one event to the next, set those fields yourself when you publish (the TypeScript `publish(type, payload, { correlationId, causationId })` accepts them); do not assume they are copied.

## 5. A handler that fails

A second event asks the handler to fail. The consumer retries in-process with backoff while the message stays **unacknowledged**, then gives up and moves the message to the dead-letter channel. The orchestrator terminal (verified):

```text evidence="verified"
2026-11-08 15:26:07.488 WARN  consumer failed  event=orders.placed id=evt-bad-1 attempt=1 error=Error
2026-11-08 15:26:07.701 WARN  consumer failed  event=orders.placed id=evt-bad-1 attempt=2 error=Error
2026-11-08 15:26:08.102 WARN  consumer failed  event=orders.placed id=evt-bad-1 attempt=3 error=Error
```

Notice the gaps (about 213 ms, then 401 ms): the backoff doubles from `initialDelay` up to `maxDelay`. The log names the event type, the event id and the attempt; the error is the class name, not the message (messages can contain secrets).

## 6. The dead-letter channel

After the third attempt the original bytes were published to `<channel>.dlq` with headers that say why, and only then acknowledged (expected):

```json evidence="expected"
{"envelope":"{\"envelopeVersion\":1,\"id\":\"evt-bad-1\",\"type\":\"orders.placed\", ...","h:x-pso-reason":"handler-failed:Error","h:x-pso-attempts":"3","h:x-pso-group":"gw","h:x-pso-original-channel":"orders.demo62984","h:x-pso-dead-letter-id":"8a0378a8-4798-4469-b1d2-2c02e1b52f55"}
```

## 7. A poison message

A third entry was invalid (its payload does not match the schema). Poison messages are not retried (`attempts` is `0`) and go straight to the dead-letter channel:

```json evidence="expected"
{"envelope":"{...\"id\":\"evt-poison-1\"...","h:x-pso-reason":"PSO_DISPATCH_ENVELOPE_INVALID","h:x-pso-attempts":"0","h:x-pso-group":"gw","h:x-pso-original-channel":"orders.demo62984","h:x-pso-dead-letter-id":"8034eb48-8968-4773-a797-64acdff257a4"}
```

## 8. What the broker and the metrics say afterwards

The consumer group had nothing pending and no lag: every message, including the failed ones, was acknowledged after being handled or dead-lettered (expected):

```text evidence="expected"
name gw  consumers 1  pending 0  last-delivered-id 1794151571002-0  entries-read 3  lag 0
```

The diagnostics endpoint (`/_pso/telemetry`, enabled with `PSO_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN`) reports what really happened, and the adapter's own health probe:

```json evidence="expected"
{"metrics":{"published":1,"publishFailed":0,"consumed":1,"failed":3,"retried":2,"deadLettered":2,"dropped":0,"duplicates":0,"poison":1,
 "byType":{"orders.placed":{"published":0,"consumed":1,"failed":3},"orders.confirmed":{"published":1,"consumed":0,"failed":0}}},
 "health":{"status":"up","detail":"PING answered"}}
```

Read it: one event published (`orders.confirmed`), one successfully consumed, three handler failures (the three attempts), two retries, two dead letters (the failing event and the poison one), one poison message.

## What this does not show

- Exactly-once delivery: not provided. A crash between the handler and the acknowledgement redelivers the message (tested separately with a killed consumer process); consumers must be idempotent.
- Replaying dead letters: there is no automatic replay. Inspect the `.dlq` channel with broker tooling and republish deliberately.
- Lag and dead-letter *depth* in Studio: the counters above are exported; depth and lag are not.

## Try it yourself

1. Start Redis (`docker compose -f infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml up -d`).
2. Declare events as above, `pso dispatch:validate`.
3. Run the orchestrator with `PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true`, `REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6379` (your URL, kept in the environment) and a diagnostics token.
4. Add entries with `redis-cli XADD <channel> '*' envelope '<json>'`, watch the terminal, then inspect `<channel>.dlq` and `/_pso/telemetry`.

## Next steps

- [Reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)
- [Events and consumers](dispatch/events-and-consumers.md)
- [Redis Streams, RabbitMQ or Kafka?](decisions/redis-rabbitmq-or-kafka.md)

## Common mistakes

- Reading `published: 1` as "the work is done": it counts accepted publishes.
- Looking for the failed message in the original stream: after exhausted retries it is acknowledged and lives in `<channel>.dlq`.
- Setting a very large `maxAttempts` with long delays on an ordered channel: the retried message holds back the ones behind it.

# Declaring, publishing and consuming events

> EVENTS.pso.ts and @DispatchConsumer in TypeScript, dispatch/*.events.json and @PsoEventHandler in Java.

Nothing is inferred and nothing is discovered by running your code: events and consumers are declared, and `pso dispatch:validate` reads the declarations statically.

## TypeScript (orchestrator)

Each module that uses events has an `EVENTS.pso.ts`. It lists the events and the consumer classes that are active:

```ts title="src/dispatch/users/EVENTS.pso.ts"
import { defineEvents } from "@pso/dispatch";
import { UserCreatedConsumer } from "./users.consumer";

export default defineEvents({
  events: [{ name: "users.created", version: 1, channel: "users.events", key: "userId", schema: "schemas/user-created.schema.ts" }],
  consumers: [UserCreatedConsumer],
});
```

```ts title="src/dispatch/users/users.consumer.ts"
import { DispatchConsumer, type ConsumeContext } from "@pso/dispatch";

@DispatchConsumer("users.created", { group: "billing" })
export class UserCreatedConsumer {
  async handle(payload: { userId: string }, ctx: ConsumeContext): Promise<void> {
    // idempotent work; ctx.attempt is 1 on the first try
  }
}
```

A decorated class that is not listed in `consumers` is never registered; `pso dispatch:validate` reports it (`PSO_DISPATCH_008`). Publish through the injected abstract `Dispatch`:

`Dispatch` is built in like `Upstream`: inject it by constructor type in any provider or controller of the module, without listing it in `providers`.

```ts
import { Dispatch } from "@pso/dispatch";

export class UsersService {
  constructor(private readonly dispatch: Dispatch) {}
  async create(userId: string) {
    await this.dispatch.publish("users.created", { userId }, { correlationId: "…" });
  }
}
```

`publish` resolves when the provider acknowledged the event; the result states what that acknowledgement means for the provider. It never means "consumed". With dispatch disabled, `Dispatch.publish` fails with `PSO_DISPATCH_DISABLED`.

## Java (Spring Boot)

Declarations are JSON files on the classpath, `src/main/resources/dispatch/*.events.json`:

```json
{ "events": [ { "name": "users.created", "version": 1, "channel": "users.events", "key": "userId", "compatibility": "full",
                "schema": { "type": "object", "required": ["userId"], "properties": { "userId": { "type": "string" } } } } ] }
```

```java
@Component
class UserHandlers {
    record UserCreated(String userId) {}

    @PsoEventHandler("users.created")
    void on(UserCreated event, ConsumeContext ctx) { /* idempotent work */ }
}

@Service
class Users {
    private final PsoDispatch dispatch;
    Users(PsoDispatch dispatch) { this.dispatch = dispatch; }
    void create(String id) { dispatch.publish("users.created", java.util.Map.of("userId", id)); }
}
```

A service that only consumes an event sets `"publish": false` on it; publishing it then fails with `PSO_DISPATCH_NOT_PUBLISHER`. Several services may consume the same channel in separate groups (the group defaults to the service name); a message whose type belongs to another consumer on the same channel is acknowledged and skipped.

## Generators, and the difference between a local event and a Dispatch event

Two mechanisms carry the word "event". They are not interchangeable and each has its own generators:

| | Local application event | PSO Dispatch event |
|---|---|---|
| Reach | the same process | every service that declares it, through the broker |
| Delivery | synchronous, in the publisher's thread; lost with the process | at least once; retries and dead letters |
| Contract | a Java class | a versioned declaration with a schema, checked by `pso dispatch:validate` |
| Generators | `pso make:event`, `pso make:listener` (Spring) | `pso make:dispatch-event`, `pso make:dispatch-handler` (Spring and orchestrator) |
| API | `ApplicationEventPublisher`, `@EventListener` | `PsoDispatch` / `Dispatch`, `@PsoEventHandler` / `@DispatchConsumer` |

```bash
pso dispatch:install redis --service orders
pso make:dispatch-event orders.placed --service orders --fields "orderId:string,customerId:string,total:number" --key orderId
pso make:dispatch-event orders.placed --service billing --consume-only --fields "orderId:string,customerId:string,total:number"
pso make:dispatch-handler orders.placed --service billing
pso dispatch:validate
```

In a layered service the payload record and the handler are written to `application/event/` (package `<base>.application.event`);
in a service with the 0.1 layout they go to `events/`.

The publisher gets the declaration and the payload record; a consumer declares the same event with `--consume-only` (`"publish": false`) and gets a handler:

```java title="orders: src/main/java/com/pso/orders/application/event/OrdersPlacedEvent.java (generated)"
package com.pso.orders.application.event;

public record OrdersPlacedEvent(String orderId, String customerId, double total) {
}
```

```java title="billing: src/main/java/com/pso/billing/application/event/OrdersPlacedHandler.java (generated)"
package com.pso.billing.application.event;

import com.pso.dispatch.ConsumeContext;
import com.pso.dispatch.PsoEventHandler;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class OrdersPlacedHandler {

    @PsoEventHandler("orders.placed")
    public void on(OrdersPlacedEvent event, ConsumeContext ctx) {
        // idempotent work; ctx.attempt() is 1 on the first try
    }
}
```

```java title="orders: publishing (your code)"
package com.pso.orders.application.service;

import com.pso.dispatch.PsoDispatch;
import com.pso.orders.application.event.OrdersPlacedEvent;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class OrderEvents {

    private final PsoDispatch dispatch;

    public OrderEvents(PsoDispatch dispatch) {
        this.dispatch = dispatch;
    }

    public void placed(String orderId, String customerId, double total) {
        dispatch.publish("orders.placed", new OrdersPlacedEvent(orderId, customerId, total));
    }
}
```

In the orchestrator the same two commands write `src/dispatch/<module>/EVENTS.pso.ts`, the schema under `schemas/` and a `@DispatchConsumer` class listed in `consumers`. A published version is never edited: declare the next `--version`. Inside a transaction that also changes data, publish through the transactional outbox ([Outbox](dispatch/outbox.md)).

A local event, for comparison (it never leaves the service):

```bash
pso make:event order-placed --service orders
pso make:listener order-placed --service orders
```

## Rules

- Declare the event first; publishing an undeclared type fails.
- Channel names and event names are validated (lower-case, dotted or dashed).
- Handlers must be idempotent: delivery is at-least-once ([Reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)).
- Do not construct broker clients in application code; use the API above.

## What it looks like when it runs

A real consumer, its retries, the dead-letter entry and the counters are in the [walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md). The static views of the same declarations (expected):

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso dispatch:consumers
orders.placed                gw  OrderPlacedConsumer  group gw  (src/dispatch/orders/orders.consumer.ts)

$ pso dispatch:events
orders.placed@1  channel orders.demo62984  gw consumes  schema yes  consumers: gw
orders.confirmed@1  channel orders.confirmed.demo62984  gw publishes  schema none  consumers: -
```

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| a consumer that republishes | inject `Dispatch` in the consumer constructor and call `publish` ([walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md)) |
| ordered processing per entity | declare `key` on the event (for example `orderId`) |
| a consume-only event | `publish: false` on its declaration |
| to chain correlation | pass `{ correlationId, causationId }` to `publish`; they are not copied automatically |

## Common mistakes

- A handler that is not idempotent.
- Letting a failing handler retry forever: set `retry.max-attempts` and watch the dead letters.
- Publishing an event this service declared `publish: false` (`PSO_DISPATCH_NOT_PUBLISHER`).
- Publishing an undeclared type (`PSO_DISPATCH_UNKNOWN_EVENT`).

## Next steps

- [Reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)
- [Contracts](dispatch/contracts.md)

# Redis Streams, RabbitMQ and Kafka

> The three independent provider adapters, their capabilities, and how to migrate between them.

Each provider is a separate adapter implementing one stable contract (`DispatchAdapter`) that also reports **capabilities**, so documentation, `pso dispatch:providers` and Studio state what each transport really guarantees. A service installs one provider (`pso dispatch:install`). The core packages contain no broker client.

| | Redis Streams | RabbitMQ | Kafka / Redpanda |
|---|---|---|---|
| TypeScript library | `ioredis` | `amqplib` | `kafkajs` |
| Java dependency | `pso-dispatch-redis-starter` | `pso-dispatch-rabbitmq-starter` | `pso-dispatch-kafka-starter` |
| Channel maps to | stream | durable topic exchange + queue per group | topic |
| Publish acknowledgement | `XADD` answered (in memory unless the server persists) | persistent + mandatory publish with confirms; unroutable is refused | `acks=all`, idempotent producer |
| Ordering | per key (single stream) | per queue | per key within a partition |
| Consumer groups | yes | queue per group | yes |
| Acknowledge | `XACK` after the handler | manual ack after the handler | manual offset commit after the handler |
| Crashed consumer | `XAUTOCLAIM` of stale pending entries | broker requeues unacked | uncommitted offset is re-read |
| Topology creation | `streamCreation: auto \| require` | exchanges and queues created on subscribe | `topicCreation: auto \| require` |

Run `pso dispatch:providers` for the capability metadata of each adapter.

## Provider notes

- **Redis Streams** (never Pub/Sub): `XADD MAXLEN ~` retention, groups created from the start (`0`), a dedicated reader connection, stale entries reclaimed after `min-idle`.
- **RabbitMQ**: publishing to a channel that has no bound queue yet is refused rather than silently dropped. Create the consumer first or use a channel with an existing group.
- **Kafka**: SASL requires TLS; the adapter refuses SASL over plaintext. `partitions` and `replication-factor` apply only when topics are auto-created.

## Configuration

Spring `application.yml` (`pso.dispatch.<provider>.*`) and the orchestrator's `pso.config.json` (`dispatch.<provider>.*`) use the same keys. Secrets are environment references, for example `${env:REDIS_URL}` or `${REDIS_URL:}`; the CLI never writes a credential into a file and never prints one.

## Migrating between providers

Event declarations, handlers and the envelope do not change. Plan the cut-over as a data migration: drain or dual-publish, because streams, queues and topics do not share offsets.

1. `pso dispatch:remove --service <name>` (declarations and handlers are kept).
2. `pso dispatch:install <new-provider> --service <name>` and set the new broker's environment variables.
3. Run `pso dispatch:doctor` against the new broker.
4. Enable. Consumers of the old transport must be drained first; messages already in the old broker are not copied.

## What the CLI says about each provider

`pso dispatch:providers` prints the capability metadata the adapters themselves report. Expected output (abridged):

```text evidence="expected"
redis
  publish ack: XADD acknowledged by Redis: in memory, durable only if the server persists (AOF) or replicates
  ordering:    per stream (single consumer per group member); not partitioned
  redelivery:  pending entries are reclaimed (XAUTOCLAIM) after pso.dispatch.redis.min-idle
  dead letter: <channel>.dlq stream
  lag:         observable
rabbitmq
  publish ack: publisher confirm for a persistent message routed to a durable queue
  ordering:    none guaranteed with concurrency > 1
  dead letter: <channel>.dlq exchange and queue
  lag:         not available
kafka
  publish ack: acks=all: acknowledged by all in-sync replicas (durability depends on min.insync.replicas)
  ordering:    per partition (events with the same key); never global
  note:        A message being retried blocks later messages of its partition. Exactly-once processing is NOT provided.
```

Choosing between them: [Redis Streams, RabbitMQ or Kafka?](decisions/redis-rabbitmq-or-kafka.md).

## Common mistakes

- Choosing by name recognition rather than operations capacity.
- Assuming RabbitMQ publishes to a channel that has no consumer yet (it is refused).
- Running Kafka without pre-creating topics in production.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Check | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `NOT-CONFIGURED` | dispatch is disabled or the broker variable is unset (`REDIS_URL`, `RABBITMQ_URL`, `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`) | `pso dispatch:inspect` | enable it and set the variable |
| `DOWN` | nothing answers at that address; Kafka reports a timeout after 8 s | the address and the broker | start the broker |
| RabbitMQ refuses to publish | no consumer group has declared the queue yet (unroutable) | the provider's note in `pso dispatch:providers` | start a consumer first |
| a Kafka partition stops advancing | the message being retried blocks later ones of its partition | the dead-letter topic `<channel>.dlq` | fix the handler |

Verified outputs for the connection checks of all three providers are in [Checking Dispatch and what its errors mean](dispatch/diagnostics.md).

## Next steps

- [Reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)
- [Local and production](dispatch/local-and-production.md)

# Installing and removing dispatch

> pso dispatch:install, dispatch:outbox and dispatch:remove, what they change and what they never touch.

Dispatch is installed per service, on request. Generated projects never include a broker adapter.

```bash
pso dispatch:install redis --service users-service   # or rabbitmq | kafka
pso dispatch:inspect                                  # what is declared (no broker is contacted)
pso dispatch:doctor                                   # connects to the configured broker and reports honestly
```

## What `dispatch:install` changes

| Service type | Changes |
|---|---|
| Spring Boot | adds `pso-dispatch-<provider>-starter` to `pom.xml`, sets `pso.dispatch.provider`, adds the provider block with environment references, creates an empty `dispatch/<service>.events.json` |
| Orchestrator | adds `@pso/dispatch` and the client library (`ioredis`, `amqplib` or `kafkajs`) to `package.json`, writes `dispatch.*` in `pso.config.json`, creates `src/dispatch/` |
| Workspace | `infra/dispatch/<provider>.compose.yml`, a local development broker that PSO does not start |

`enabled` stays `false`. Activation is a separate, explicit step: set `pso.dispatch.enabled=true` and the broker environment variable (`REDIS_URL`, `RABBITMQ_URL` or `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`). The commands are idempotent, support `--dry-run` and `--json`, never overwrite your declarations, handlers or unrelated configuration, and one service holds one provider (installing a second fails and names `dispatch:remove`).

## Enabling

When `enabled=true` the service validates everything before it listens: provider selected, adapter present, events declared, broker reachable. Any problem stops start-up with a message that names the fix and never contains a broker URL or credential.

## Removing

`pso dispatch:remove --service <name>` removes the adapter dependency and the provider block and sets `enabled: false`, `provider: none`. Event declarations and handlers are kept and stay valid but inactive.

## Optional outbox

`pso dispatch:outbox --service <name>` (Spring services with PostgreSQL and an installed provider) adds the `pso_outbox` Flyway migration once and sets `pso.dispatch.outbox.enabled=true`. See [Outbox](dispatch/outbox.md).

## Command overview

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `dispatch:providers` | capabilities of each provider and where it is installed |
| `dispatch:install` / `dispatch:remove` / `dispatch:outbox` | change a service |
| `dispatch:inspect` | declared setup per service, secrets redacted |
| `dispatch:validate` | static checks of declarations, schemas, lock file, provider consistency |
| `dispatch:lock` | write `pso.dispatch.lock.json` |
| `dispatch:events` / `dispatch:consumers` | what is declared and who consumes it |
| `dispatch:graph` | topology (`--mermaid`) |
| `dispatch:doctor` | connect to the configured broker (the only command that does) |

All accept `--json`. Discovery is structural: `EVENTS.pso.ts` and `*.events.json` are read as data and your code is never executed.

## What the commands print

Expected output of installing Redis into an orchestrator (the install leaves dispatch **disabled**):

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso dispatch:install redis --service gw
package.json: + @pso/dispatch
package.json: + ioredis
pso.config.json: dispatch.provider = redis (enabled stays false; secrets are ${env:...} references)
src/dispatch/: modules go here, each with an EVENTS.pso.ts
infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml: a local development broker (not started by PSO)
Next: declare your events, then set pso.dispatch.enabled=true (and the broker URL) to activate. See /docs/dispatch/overview.

$ pso dispatch:inspect --service gw
gw (node)  provider: redis  adapter: redis  disabled
  events:    orders.placed@1 -> orders.events
  consumers: -

Declared configuration only: use `pso dispatch:doctor` to test the broker connection.

$ pso dispatch:remove --service gw --dry-run
[dry-run] package.json: - ioredis (@pso/dispatch stays: declarations still use it)
[dry-run] pso.config.json: dispatch disabled, provider none
[dry-run] kept: 1 event declaration(s) and 0 consumer(s) (they stay valid and are inactive)
```

## Is the broker reachable? `dispatch:doctor`

The only command that connects (expected):

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso dispatch:doctor --service gw        # URL set, Redis running
static validation: no findings
UP             gw (redis): PING answered [44 ms]            (exit 0)

$ pso dispatch:doctor --service gw        # URL points at a port nobody listens on
static validation: no findings
DOWN           gw (redis): cannot connect to Redis (Error)  (exit 1)

$ pso dispatch:doctor --service gw        # no broker URL in the environment
static validation: no findings
NOT-CONFIGURED gw (redis): invalid dispatch configuration:  (exit 0)
```

`UP` proves the connection and the adapter's own probe; it does not prove events flow. `NOT-CONFIGURED` exits 0 on purpose (nothing is wrong yet); `DOWN` exits 1, so it can gate a deployment.

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| to try it locally | `docker compose -f infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml up -d`, export the URL, set `enabled: true` |
| to switch provider | `pso dispatch:remove` then `pso dispatch:install <other>` ([migration](dispatch/providers.md)) |
| to undo it | `pso dispatch:remove`: declarations and handlers are never deleted |

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| publishing says dispatch is disabled | set `enabled` and install a provider (`PSO_DISPATCH_DISABLED`) |
| `DOWN ... cannot connect` | URL, network, credentials (they are redacted in output); is the container running? |
| `install` says another provider is installed | a service uses one provider: `dispatch:remove` first |

## Next steps

- [Walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md)
- [Contracts](dispatch/contracts.md)

# Delivery guarantees, retries, dead letters and idempotency

> What at-least-once means in PSO Dispatch and exactly what the runtime does on success, failure and poison messages.

**Guarantee: at-least-once.** A published event is delivered one or more times; handlers must be idempotent. PSO does not claim exactly-once, because a broker and a database cannot be committed atomically.

## What the consumer runtime does

1. Parse and validate the envelope, the version (`version` or `accepts`) and the payload schema.
2. If the event id was already processed by this group, acknowledge and skip (duplicate).
3. Run the handler. On success: record the id in the idempotency store, then **acknowledge** (acknowledgement is always after the handler).
4. On failure: retry in-process with exponential backoff (`retry.max-attempts`, `initial-delay`, `max-delay`, `multiplier`). The message stays unacknowledged during retries.
5. When attempts are exhausted: publish the original bytes to `<channel>.dlq` with headers `x-pso-reason`, `x-pso-attempts`, `x-pso-group`, `x-pso-original-channel`, `x-pso-dead-letter-id`, and only then acknowledge.
6. If publishing to the dead-letter channel fails, the message is **not** acknowledged and the transport redelivers it. With `dead-letter.enabled=false` an exhausted message is dropped and counted.

**Poison messages** (invalid envelope, unsupported version, schema violation) skip retries and go straight to the dead-letter channel. Publishing validates the same rules, so poison only comes from other producers or older contracts.

## Idempotency

The key is `group:eventId`. The store is a stated choice, logged at every start (`dispatch idempotency store`). `dispatch.idempotency.store` is `auto` by default: the provider's own Redis when the provider is `redis`, otherwise this process's memory (`retention` 24h by default). The in-memory store does not survive restarts or span instances: after a restart, or on another instance, a redelivered event runs its handler again (production logs a warning about it). Set `dispatch.idempotency.store: "redis"` with `dispatch.idempotency.redisUrl: "${env:NAME}"` to give RabbitMQ and Kafka consumers the durable, shared store too. For durable, shared deduplication use the Redis store (TypeScript `RedisIdempotencyStore`; Java Redis starter store) or make the handler itself idempotent, for example with a unique constraint. Treat the store as an optimization; correctness belongs in the handler.

### Concurrent consumers: the claim

An event id is **claimed atomically before the handler runs** (one Lua step in Redis; in memory inside one process), so two instances that receive the same event at the same moment do not both run it. The first one takes a lease on `group:eventId`; the others wait for it and then acknowledge the event as a duplicate. The runtime renews the lease while the handler runs and turns it into the completion record afterwards. Both runtimes write the same keys and values, so Node and Java consumers of one group share them.

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| the same event reaches several instances at once | one runs the handler; the others wait, see the completion and acknowledge (`duplicates`) |
| the handler fails (retries exhausted) | the claim is released and the event is dead-lettered; a replay or redelivery is handled, not treated as a duplicate |
| the consumer dies after claiming | nobody renews the lease; after `dispatch.idempotency.lease` (default `30s`; Spring `pso.dispatch.idempotency.lease`) another consumer may claim the event |
| another consumer still holds the claim after one lease period | the delivery is given back to the broker (`contended`) and redelivered |
| the store cannot be reached | the handler does **not** run; the message is given back to the broker and an error is logged. Unreachable never means "not seen" |
| completion cannot be recorded after the handler ran | the message is acknowledged and an error is logged: a later redelivery of that id runs the handler again |
| a renewal finds the lease gone (a consumer cut off from the store for longer than the lease) | the handler keeps running, another consumer may run it too; counted as `leaseLost` and logged |

**The guarantee is at-least-once, not exactly-once.** The claim removes the concurrent-duplicate window while the store is reachable and leases are renewed; it cannot undo an effect outside the store. A handler that charges a card, sends an e-mail or calls another service must carry its own idempotency key (the event id is a good one) or a unique constraint, because a crash between the effect and the completion record, a lost lease, or a redelivery after `retention` runs it again. A custom `IdempotencyStore` that implements only `has`/`add` keeps working, with the earlier non-atomic check.

## Limits you should know

- Retries are in-process: a failing message blocks its consumer slot (and, per partition or stream, the messages behind it) for the duration of the backoff. There is no delayed redelivery.
- If a consumer crashes, the transport redelivers (Redis `XAUTOCLAIM`, RabbitMQ requeue, Kafka uncommitted offset). Duplicates are expected after crashes.
- A delivery that finds another consumer working on the same event id occupies its consumer slot while it waits (at most one lease period).
- Ordering is only per key within a partition or queue (see [Providers](dispatch/providers.md)).
- Dead letters are not replayed automatically. Inspect the `.dlq` channel with your broker tooling and republish deliberately.

## The numbers from a real run

A consumer whose handler always fails, with `max-attempts 3`: three `WARN consumer failed ... attempt=N` lines with a growing delay, the original message in `<channel>.dlq` with `x-pso-reason: handler-failed:Error` and `x-pso-attempts: 3`, nothing left pending in the consumer group, and the counters `failed 3, retried 2, deadLettered 2` (the second dead letter was a poison message, counted also as `poison 1`). The full transcript is in the [walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md).

## Common mistakes

- Assuming dead letters are replayed: they are not.
- A handler that cannot tolerate a repeat.
- Large `retry.max-attempts` with long delays on an ordered channel: the retried message blocks the ones behind it.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Check | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| duplicates | all providers are at-least-once | the handler | make it idempotent; deduplicate on the event `id` |
| messages in `<channel>.dlq` | the retry budget ended | the consumer logs under the message's correlation id | fix the cause, then replay deliberately |
| events lost when a service crashes between saving and publishing | publishing after the database commit is not atomic | the code path | use the transactional outbox ([tutorial](tutorials/transactional-outbox.md)) |
| Redis loses entries | trimming (`MAXLEN`) is approximate and persistence is the server's | the server's AOF setting and the stream length | size retention above the slowest consumer; enable AOF or replication |

Provider guarantees as printed by `pso dispatch:providers` are in [Checking Dispatch and what its errors mean](dispatch/diagnostics.md).

## Next steps

- [Walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md)
- [Outbox](dispatch/outbox.md)

# Transactional outbox

> Store the event in the same database transaction as your data and relay it afterwards (Spring Boot + PostgreSQL).

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> Implemented for **Spring Boot with a JDBC database** and verified against a real PostgreSQL and Redis. There is **no TypeScript outbox**.

Without an outbox, "save the order, then publish `orders.created`" can lose the event if the process dies in between. The outbox closes that gap: the event is inserted into `pso_outbox` through your `JdbcTemplate` inside the same transaction as the business change, and a relay publishes it afterwards.

```bash
pso database:enable postgresql --service orders-service
pso dispatch:install redis --service orders-service
pso dispatch:outbox --service orders-service     # migration V<n>__pso_outbox.sql + pso.dispatch.outbox.enabled=true
```

In a layered service the event is published from the transactional service in `application/service/`, with its payload record
from `application/event/` (`pso make:dispatch-event orders.created --fields "orderId:string"`):

```java title="orders-service/src/main/java/com/pso/orders/application/service/OrderService.java"
package com.pso.orders.application.service;

import com.pso.orders.application.dto.request.CreateOrderRequest;
import com.pso.orders.application.dto.response.OrderResponse;
import com.pso.orders.application.event.OrdersCreatedEvent;
import com.pso.orders.application.mapper.OrderMapper;
import com.pso.orders.infrastructure.persistence.OrderRepository;
import com.pso.spring.autoconfigure.dispatch.Outbox;
import lombok.RequiredArgsConstructor;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final OrderMapper mapper;
    private final Outbox outbox;

    @Transactional
    public OrderResponse create(CreateOrderRequest request) {
        OrderResponse created = mapper.toResponse(repository.saveAndFlush(mapper.toEntity(request)));
        outbox.publish("orders.created", new OrdersCreatedEvent(created.id().toString()));   // rolls back with the order
        return created;
    }
}
```

The outbox stores events only while Dispatch is enabled (`pso.dispatch.enabled: true`, also in the test profile): otherwise
`Outbox.publish` throws `PSO_DISPATCH_DISABLED` and the transaction is not completed. [The outbox tutorial](tutorials/transactional-outbox.md)
does this on a generated CRUD service and runs its tests.

`Outbox.publish` applies the same checks as `PsoDispatch.publish` (declared, publishable, schema, size) at insert time, so an invalid event fails in your transaction, not later.

## Relay behavior

- Rows are read with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so several instances can run relays at once without sending a row twice concurrently.
- A row is marked published only **after** the broker acknowledged it. A crash between the acknowledgement and the update republishes the row with the **same event id**: still at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate on the id.
- A broker failure records `attempts`, `last_error` (the error class, never a message with credentials) and a backoff; after `max-attempts` the row gets `failed_at` and is left for you to inspect. It is never deleted automatically.
- Published rows older than `retention` are deleted; pending and failed rows are never deleted.

Settings: `pso.dispatch.outbox.{enabled, poll-interval, batch-size, max-attempts, retry-backoff, retention}`. Enabling the outbox without a database, or without dispatch, stops start-up with the command to run.

Services created before 2026-11-14 may contain an `outbox_event` table from an earlier service template; it is unrelated, not used by the relay and no longer generated ([what to do with it](microservices/persistence.md)).

## Verify failure recovery

In a test environment, publish an event inside a transaction that you deliberately roll back: neither the business row nor the `pso_outbox` row should remain. Then commit with the broker unavailable. The row should remain pending while relay attempts fail; after broker recovery, the relay can publish it. Observe the event id in the consumer and apply a unique constraint or equivalent idempotent business operation so a repeated publication has no second effect.

If rows accumulate, check `pso.dispatch.enabled`, broker connectivity with `pso dispatch:doctor`, and the outbox attempt and error-class columns. A row marked failed is retained for an operator to investigate; there is no documented automatic replay command. The [step-by-step outbox tutorial](tutorials/transactional-outbox.md) follows this recovery path.

## What to look at when it misbehaves

| Symptom | Look at | Resolve |
|---|---|---|
| events are not published after a commit | `pso_outbox` rows: `published_at` is null and `attempts` is growing | restore the broker; the relay retries with backoff and records the error class in `last_error` |
| a row has `failed_at` set | the row reached `pso.dispatch.outbox.max-attempts` | inspect the error; fix the cause; it is kept for you, never deleted automatically |
| the same event arrives twice | a crash between the broker acknowledgement and the row update | consumers deduplicate on the event id (at-least-once) |
| `outbox.publish` throws in your transaction | the event is undeclared, consume-only, violates its schema or is too large | fix the declaration or payload; the transaction rolls back, as intended |
| the table keeps growing | `retention` removes **published** rows only | pending and failed rows stay until handled |

A step-by-step exercise (commit while the broker is down, then restore it) is in [Make an event follow a database commit](tutorials/transactional-outbox.md); the decision of whether you need it is [outbox or direct publish?](decisions/outbox-or-direct-publish.md).

## Next steps

- [Transactional outbox tutorial](tutorials/transactional-outbox.md)
- [Reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)

# Dispatch security and observability

> Transport security, secret handling, what is logged, metrics and health, and what observability is not implemented.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

## Security

- **Secrets never live in files the CLI writes.** Broker URLs and credentials are environment references (`${env:RABBITMQ_URL}` / `${RABBITMQ_URL:}`). `dispatch:inspect`, Studio and the AI context redact them; `dispatch:doctor` masks credentials in any error it prints.
- **Errors are sanitized.** Connection failures report the error class and the fix, not the URL. Log lines carry event type, id, attempt and error class, never payloads or metadata values.
- **Transport:** use `rediss://`, `amqps://` or Kafka `ssl` for anything that leaves your machine. Kafka SASL is refused over plaintext. Authentication is whatever the broker supports through the URL or the SASL block; PSO adds no custom crypto.
- **No arbitrary deserialization.** Payloads are parsed as JSON data and validated against the declared schema; classes are never instantiated from message content. Java handlers bind the validated JSON to the handler parameter type with Jackson.
- **Size and shape limits** (1 MiB, depth 32, metadata length) are enforced before a handler runs.

Authorization of who may publish or consume a channel is a broker concern (ACLs, vhost permissions, Redis ACL users). PSO does not model it.

### Publisher authentication

The envelope's `source` is a field the producer writes: on its own it proves nothing. A service with a signing key adds a transport header to every event it publishes (the envelope format does not change, so a consumer that does not verify ignores it):

```text evidence="illustrative"
x-pso-signature: v1=base64url( HMAC-SHA256( key, channel + "\n" + the exact envelope bytes ) )
```

A consumer looks the key up by the source the envelope claims, so a service holding only its own key cannot sign as another one, and neither the content nor the channel can change without invalidating the signature. Both runtimes produce identical signatures (checked against shared contract data).

| Setting | Node | Spring |
|---|---|---|
| this service's key (32+ characters, environment only) | `PSO_DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY` | `pso.dispatch.signing-key` (the same variable binds to it) |
| a publisher's key on the consumer | `PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_KEY_<SERVICE>` | the same variables, or `pso.dispatch.trust.keys.<service>` |
| mode | `dispatch.trust.mode` | `pso.dispatch.trust.mode` |

| Mode | Unsigned event | Wrong signature | Valid signature |
|---|---|---|---|
| `off` (default) | handled | handled (not checked) | handled |
| `permissive` | handled and counted (`unverified`) | dead-lettered | handled, `verifiedSource` set |
| `required` | dead-lettered | dead-lettered | handled, `verifiedSource` set |

A refused event is never handled or retried; it goes to `<channel>.dlq` with the reason `PSO_DISPATCH_UNTRUSTED:unsigned`, `:unknown-source` or `:invalid`. Handlers read the authenticated publisher from `ctx.verifiedSource` (Java: `ctx.verifiedSource()`); use it, not `envelope.source`, for authorization. To migrate: give every publisher its key, run consumers in `permissive` until `unverified` stays at zero, then switch to `required`. Several comma separated keys per service allow rotation.

#### Production policy and privileged consumers

Trust mode `off` is a development default, not a production one. With `PSO_ENV=production` (or `NODE_ENV=production`; Spring: the `prod` / `production` profile, which the generated image sets) a service whose Dispatch is enabled **does not start** with mode `off`: the error names `dispatch.trust.mode` and the keys to set. `required` without any key is refused everywhere.

| You want | Set | Result |
|---|---|---|
| secure production | `dispatch.trust.mode: required`, `PSO_DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY`, `PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_KEY_<SERVICE>` | only signed events of known services are handled |
| to migrate without dropping traffic | mode `permissive` with the keys | unsigned events still handled and counted (`unverified`); wrong signatures refused |
| to keep a legacy installation running as it is | `PSO_DISPATCH_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED=true` (exactly `true`) | starts with mode `off`; an `INSECURE legacy mode` warning at every start |

The legacy switch is never equivalent to a verified publisher. A consumer that **acts on who published** an event declares it, and then never runs on a claim in any mode:

```ts title="a privileged consumer (Node)"
@DispatchConsumer("billing.invoice-paid", { requireVerified: true })
export class GrantCredit { handle(payload: InvoicePaid, ctx: ConsumeContext) { /* ctx.verifiedSource is always set here */ } }
```

An unsigned, forged or unknown publisher is dead-lettered for that consumer (`PSO_DISPATCH_UNTRUSTED:...`) while ordinary consumers of the same event keep the behaviour of the mode; a service with such a consumer and no verification key refuses to start (`PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_KEYS`). In Java call `ctx.requireVerifiedSource()`: it returns the verified publisher or throws, so the message fails instead of being authorized on the envelope's claim. The Channels bridge is such a consumer: see [Channels](orchestrator/channels.md).

Limits: keys are symmetric, so a consumer able to verify a service could also sign as it (give each key only to its service and its verifiers). A captured, validly signed event can be replayed by someone who can write to the broker; the idempotency store suppresses replays inside its retention, and broker authentication and ACLs remain the first line of defence. A broker connection being authenticated does not, by itself, authenticate the `source` of a message.

## Observability

Implemented:

- Counters in both runtimes: published, publish failures, consumed, handler failures, retries, dead-lettered, dropped, duplicates, poison, processing count/total/max time.
- `Dispatch.health()` / `PsoDispatch.health()`: the adapter's own probe (`PING`, channel open, metadata request).
- `correlationId` is generated or propagated in the envelope and appears in structured log fields.
- `pso dispatch:doctor` for a live connection test.

In an orchestrator the dispatch counters and broker health are part of the [runtime telemetry](devops/observability.md) (diagnostics endpoint and, with an OTLP endpoint, the `pso.dispatch.*` metrics; Spring services publish the same counters plus `pso.outbox.*` as Micrometer meters). **Not implemented:** trace context carried in the event envelope end to end (the envelope only has a `trace` field), consumer lag display in Studio, a `dispatch:health` command, alert rules. Redis exposes lag and pending counts through the adapter (`groupInfo`) for your own diagnostics.

## What the telemetry says (expected)

With `PSO_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN` set, `GET /_pso/telemetry` returns the dispatch counters and the adapter's own health. From the walkthrough run:

```json evidence="expected"
{"metrics":{"published":1,"publishFailed":0,"consumed":1,"failed":3,"retried":2,"deadLettered":2,"dropped":0,"duplicates":0,"poison":1,
 "byType":{"orders.placed":{"published":0,"consumed":1,"failed":3},"orders.confirmed":{"published":1,"consumed":0,"failed":0}}},
 "health":{"status":"up","detail":"PING answered"}}
```

and the log says what failed without exposing it: `WARN consumer failed event=orders.placed id=evt-bad-1 attempt=1 error=Error` (the error class, never the message). Broker URLs and credentials do not appear in logs (asserted by tests).

## Common mistakes

- Logging payloads in handlers (they may contain personal data).
- Putting the broker URL with credentials in a file instead of the environment.
- Alerting on the counters only: also watch the `.dlq` channels in the broker.

## Next steps

- [Runtime telemetry](devops/observability.md)
- [Walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md)

# Dispatch graph, inspect and Studio

> How to see the declared topology and the live connection status, and what the views never fabricate.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

Everything shown comes from two honest sources and the views say which:

- **Declared**: read statically from `EVENTS.pso.ts`, `*.events.json` and the configuration. No code runs and no broker is contacted.
- **Live**: an explicit, opt-in connection probe (`pso dispatch:doctor`, or the probe button in Studio) that connects with the configured environment variables, reads the adapter health and disconnects.

```bash
pso dispatch:graph            # services, events, channels, producers and consumers
pso dispatch:graph --mermaid  # the same as a Mermaid diagram
pso dispatch:events           # declared events with version, channel, schema yes/no
pso dispatch:consumers        # who consumes what, in which group
```

Studio's **Dispatch** view lists each service's provider, enabled state, declared events and consumers, the validation findings and, on request, the probe result. It is read-only (Studio never publishes, consumes or edits). When a running service exposes the diagnostics endpoint, the view also shows the **measured** counters (published, consumed, failed, retried, dead-lettered, poison, duplicates) and the adapter's own health; consumer **lag** and dead-letter **depth** are shown as unavailable because they are not exported. Studio does not invent numbers: a service that is not running or not instrumented says so.

## What the commands print

Expected output for the walkthrough's service (one consumed event, one published event):

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso dispatch:graph
gw --orders.confirmed--> channel:orders.confirmed.demo62984
channel:orders.demo62984 --orders.placed--> gw

$ pso dispatch:events
orders.placed@1  channel orders.demo62984  gw consumes  schema yes  consumers: gw
orders.confirmed@1  channel orders.confirmed.demo62984  gw publishes  schema none  consumers: -

$ pso dispatch:consumers
orders.placed                gw  OrderPlacedConsumer  group gw  (src/dispatch/orders/orders.consumer.ts)
```

Read `dispatch:graph` as arrows: a publisher points at the channel it writes, a channel points at the consumers of each event type. With several services the graph shows who talks to whom without reading any code.

```bash
pso dispatch:graph --mermaid     # paste into any Mermaid renderer (documentation, pull requests)
pso dispatch:doctor              # opt-in live probe: connects, reads adapter health, disconnects
```

The live counters for a real run, and what each means, are in the [walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md).

## Common mistakes

- Reading the graph as live state: it is the *declared* topology.
- Treating a green `dispatch:doctor` as proof that events flow: it proves the connection only.
- Expecting lag or dead-letter depth in Studio: use your broker's tooling for those.

- [Walkthrough: publish, consume, retry, dead-letter](dispatch/walkthrough.md)

# Local development, production and verification

> Running a local broker, production checklist, what was verified against real brokers and what remains unverified.

## Local development

`pso dispatch:install` writes `infra/dispatch/<provider>.compose.yml` (Redis, RabbitMQ, or Redpanda-compatible Kafka). PSO never starts it; run it with `docker compose -f infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml up -d`, export the environment variable it documents, set `enabled: true`, and run `pso dispatch:doctor`. For unit tests use the in-memory adapter (`@pso/dispatch/testing`, `pso-dispatch-test`), which implements the same contract without a broker.

## Production checklist

- TLS and authentication on the broker connection; credentials from a secret store, not files.
- Persistence on the broker (Redis AOF or replicas, RabbitMQ durable queues are used, Kafka replication factor greater than 1).
- Monitor the `.dlq` channels and alert on non-empty ones.
- A durable idempotency store or idempotent handlers.
- `retry.max-attempts` and delays sized so backoff does not stall a partition longer than you can afford.
- Pre-create topics/streams and use `require` topology mode where the service account may not create them.
- Run `pso dispatch:validate` and `pso dispatch:lock` in CI.

## What was verified

Against real brokers (Docker: Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka) and a real PostgreSQL:

- TypeScript core runtime and provider suites; Java runtime and Spring Boot integration suites.
- TypeScript to Java and Java to TypeScript event exchange on all three providers.
- Retry, dead-letter, poison handling, duplicate suppression, consumer crash recovery (a killed consumer process), broker outage and recovery.
- CLI install/remove/outbox on generated Spring and orchestrator projects, built with real Maven and run against the brokers.
- The outbox: commit/rollback atomicity, relay, broker failure and recovery, max attempts, concurrent relays, retention, Spring auto-configuration.

Tests that need a broker skip with an explicit reason when none is available (`node scripts/dispatch-brokers.mjs up` starts them); a skipped run is not a verified run.

## Known limits

In-process retries and no delayed redelivery; no exactly-once; no TypeScript outbox; no OpenTelemetry or lag in Studio; numeric values such as `1.0` may serialize differently between TypeScript and Java (use integers or strings for identifiers); RabbitMQ refuses publishing to a channel without a bound queue; the Redis group starts at the beginning of the stream; Docker builds of Spring services need the `com.pso` artifacts to be published or installed.

## A local session, end to end

```bash
pso dispatch:install redis --service gw
docker compose -f infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml up -d
export REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6379            # PowerShell: $env:REDIS_URL = "redis://127.0.0.1:6379"
pso dispatch:doctor --service gw                   # UP gw (redis): PING answered
# set enabled: true, start the service, publish, watch the log
```

The outputs of each step are on [Installation](dispatch/installation.md) and in the [walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md).

## Common mistakes

- Treating the local compose file as a production broker.
- Skipping the production checklist items on TLS, persistence and `.dlq` alerts.
- Running broker tests without a broker and reading the skipped result as a pass.

## Next steps

- [Providers](dispatch/providers.md)
- [Observability and security](dispatch/security-and-observability.md)

# Checking Dispatch and what its errors mean

> How to prove a broker is reachable, lock event contracts, and read the errors Dispatch gives for Redis Streams, RabbitMQ and Kafka - each one reproduced on a real workspace and real brokers.

Dispatch moves events between services through a broker. Three questions come up before any event flows, and PSO answers each with a command that **does not trust configuration**:

| Question | Command | What it really does |
|---|---|---|
| Is my declaration consistent? | `pso dispatch:validate` | reads sources and schemas; contacts no broker |
| Can I change a contract safely? | `pso dispatch:lock` and then `validate` | records the contract; later changes are compared with it |
| Is the broker there? | `pso dispatch:doctor` | validates, then **connects** to each configured broker |

Everything below was run on a generated workspace with one orchestrator (`gw`), against real brokers (Redis 7, RabbitMQ 3.13 and Kafka 3.8 in local containers). Output is as printed; the broker addresses are the ones of the verification run.

## Install a provider

```bash
pso dispatch:install redis --service gw
```

```text evidence="verified"
package.json: + @pso/dispatch
package.json: + ioredis
pso.config.json: dispatch.provider = redis (enabled stays false; secrets are ${env:...} references)
src/dispatch/: modules go here, each with an EVENTS.pso.ts
infra/dispatch/redis.compose.yml: a local development broker (not started by PSO)
Next: declare your events, then set pso.dispatch.enabled=true (and the broker URL) to activate. See /docs/dispatch/overview.
```

```json title="gw/pso.config.json (written by the command)"
{
  "dispatch": {
    "enabled": false,
    "provider": "redis",
    "redis": { "url": "${env:REDIS_URL}" }
  }
}
```

Dispatch stays **disabled** until you enable it; the broker address is an environment reference, never a literal. `rabbitmq` and `kafka` work the same way (`amqplib` and `kafkajs` are added instead of `ioredis`, and the address comes from `RABBITMQ_URL` or `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`). One provider is installed per service at a time: removing one is a command of its own.

```bash
pso dispatch:remove --service gw
```

```text evidence="verified"
package.json: - ioredis (@pso/dispatch stays: declarations still use it)
pso.config.json: dispatch disabled, provider none
```

Your event declarations and handlers are never deleted.

## What each provider guarantees

`pso dispatch:providers` prints the delivery contract of each adapter. Read it before you choose: the guarantees differ, and they are the contract your handlers must be written against.

```bash
pso dispatch:providers
```

```text evidence="verified"
redis
  publish ack: XADD acknowledged by Redis: in memory, durable only if the server persists (AOF) or replicates
  ordering:    per stream (single consumer per group member); not partitioned
  redelivery:  pending entries are reclaimed (XAUTOCLAIM) after pso.dispatch.redis.min-idle
  dead letter: <channel>.dlq stream
  lag:         observable
  note:        Redis Streams, never Pub/Sub. Retention is approximate MAXLEN trimming: size it above your slowest consumer.

rabbitmq
  publish ack: publisher confirm for a persistent message routed to a durable queue
  ordering:    none guaranteed with concurrency > 1
  redelivery:  unacknowledged messages are requeued on connection loss; nack requeues after a pause
  dead letter: <channel>.dlq exchange and queue
  lag:         not available
  note:        Publishing before any consumer group declared its queue is refused (unroutable), never silently dropped.

kafka
  publish ack: acks=all: acknowledged by all in-sync replicas (durability depends on min.insync.replicas)
  ordering:    per partition (events with the same key); never global
  redelivery:  offsets are committed only after processing; a failed message is redelivered from its offset
  dead letter: <channel>.dlq topic
  lag:         observable
  note:        A message being retried blocks later messages of its partition. Redpanda works the same way. Exactly-once processing is NOT provided.
```

All three give **at-least-once** delivery: a handler can receive the same event twice, so handlers must be idempotent ([reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)). Choosing between them is a design decision: see [Redis, RabbitMQ or Kafka?](decisions/redis-rabbitmq-or-kafka.md).

## Is the broker there? `pso dispatch:doctor`

`dispatch:doctor` has three possible answers, and it never reports a connection it did not make:

| Answer | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `UP` | it connected and the broker answered |
| `DOWN` | it tried and failed (exit code 1) |
| `NOT-CONFIGURED` | dispatch is disabled or the broker address is missing: nothing was attempted |

With nothing set, it says so:

```bash
pso dispatch:doctor
```

```text evidence="verified"
static validation: no findings

NOT-CONFIGURED gw (redis): invalid dispatch configuration:
```

Turn dispatch on and give the address through the environment, then ask again. One run per provider, against its real broker:

```bash
REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:56379 PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true pso dispatch:doctor
```

```text evidence="verified"
static validation: no findings

UP             gw (redis): PING answered [42 ms]
```

```bash
RABBITMQ_URL=amqp://guest:guest@127.0.0.1:56672 PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true pso dispatch:doctor
```

```text evidence="verified"
static validation: no findings

UP             gw (rabbitmq): connection open [107 ms]
```

```bash
KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS=127.0.0.1:59092 PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true pso dispatch:doctor
```

```text evidence="verified"
static validation: no findings

UP             gw (kafka): metadata request answered [193 ms]
```

Each `UP` line says what was actually proven: `PING answered`, `connection open`, `metadata request answered`. That is **reachability**, not delivery. A broker can be up while a topic, queue or permission is wrong; only publishing and consuming prove that ([walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md)).

Now point each at a port where nothing listens:

```text evidence="verified"
DOWN           gw (redis): cannot connect to Redis (Error)
DOWN           gw (rabbitmq): cannot connect to RabbitMQ (Error)
DOWN           gw (kafka): connection timed out after 8 s
```

Kafka takes 8 seconds to give up, the others fail at once: do not set a CI timeout below 10 s for `dispatch:doctor`. All three exit with code 1.

## Declare events, then validate

An event is declared in an `EVENTS.pso.ts`, with a JSON schema file and a consumer class:

```tree title="What the walkthrough below creates (workspace root: lab/)"
lab/
  pso.dispatch.lock.json  # generated: written by pso dispatch:lock at the workspace root, commit it
  gw/src/dispatch/orders/
    EVENTS.pso.ts  # manual: declares the events and lists the consumers
    schemas/order-placed.schema.ts  # manual: the payload contract of orders.placed
    orders.consumer.ts  # manual: the handler of orders.placed
```

```typescript title="gw/src/dispatch/orders/EVENTS.pso.ts"
import { defineEvents } from "@pso/dispatch";
import { OrderPlacedConsumer } from "./orders.consumer";
export default defineEvents({
  events: [
    { name: "orders.placed", version: 1, channel: "orders.events", schema: "schemas/order-placed.schema.ts", publish: false },
  ],
  consumers: [OrderPlacedConsumer],
});
```

```typescript title="gw/src/dispatch/orders/schemas/order-placed.schema.ts"
export default { type: "object", required: ["orderId"], properties: { orderId: { type: "string" } } };
```

```typescript title="gw/src/dispatch/orders/orders.consumer.ts"
import { Dispatch, DispatchConsumer } from "@pso/dispatch";

@DispatchConsumer("orders.placed")
export class OrderPlacedConsumer {
  constructor(private readonly dispatch: Dispatch) {}
  async handle(payload: { orderId: string }) { void payload; }
}
```

`publish: false` means this service consumes the event but does not own it: it never publishes it. Validate:

```bash
pso dispatch:validate
```

```text evidence="verified"
INFO    PSO_DISPATCH_UNLOCKED gw (src/dispatch/orders/EVENTS.pso.ts)
        orders.placed v1 is not locked yet
        fix: Run `pso dispatch:lock` to record its contract
valid. Static validation only: event delivery is verified by running the service against a broker.
```

`INFO` does not fail validation; it tells you the contract is not protected yet. See what PSO understood:

```bash
pso dispatch:events
pso dispatch:consumers
```

```text evidence="verified"
orders.placed@1  channel orders.events  gw consumes  schema yes  consumers: gw
```

```text evidence="verified"
orders.placed                gw  OrderPlacedConsumer  group gw  (src/dispatch/orders/orders.consumer.ts)
```

## Lock the contract

```bash
pso dispatch:lock
pso dispatch:validate
```

```text evidence="verified"
locked: orders.placed@1
```

```text evidence="verified"
no findings
valid. Static validation only: event delivery is verified by running the service against a broker.
```

The lock file records each event version's schema. From now on a change to that schema is compared with the record. This is what protects consumers you do not control: a producer cannot quietly add a required field to a version that is already in the wild.

## What goes wrong, and what you see

### A schema file that does not exist (`PSO_DISPATCH_004`)

```text evidence="verified"
ERROR   PSO_DISPATCH_004 gw (src/dispatch/orders/EVENTS.pso.ts)
        schema file schemas/missing.schema.ts of "orders.placed" does not exist
ERROR   PSO_DISPATCH_SCHEMA_CHANGED gw (src/dispatch/orders/schemas/missing.schema.ts)
        the schema of orders.placed v1 changed after it was locked: published events of that version would no longer match
        fix: Declare version 2 (with a compatible schema or compatibility: "none"), then run `pso dispatch:lock`
2 error(s). Static validation only: event delivery is verified by running the service against a broker.
```

Two errors come from one cause: the locked schema is no longer found. Correct the path.

### A breaking change to a locked version (`PSO_DISPATCH_SCHEMA_CHANGED`)

The schema gained a new required field (`total`) while still declared as version 1:

```text evidence="verified"
ERROR   PSO_DISPATCH_SCHEMA_CHANGED gw (src/dispatch/orders/schemas/order-placed.schema.ts)
        the schema of orders.placed v1 changed after it was locked: published events of that version would no longer match
        fix: Declare version 2 (with a compatible schema or compatibility: "none"), then run `pso dispatch:lock`
1 error(s). Static validation only: event delivery is verified by running the service against a broker.
```

The error names its own fix: a changed contract is a **new version**. Declare `version: 2`, keep serving version 1 while consumers migrate, then lock. See [contracts](dispatch/contracts.md) for compatibility modes.

### A consumer of an event nobody declares (`PSO_DISPATCH_007`)

```text evidence="verified"
ERROR   PSO_DISPATCH_007 gw (src/dispatch/orders/orders.consumer.ts)
        consumer OrderPlacedConsumer handles "orders.shipped", which src/dispatch/orders/EVENTS.pso.ts does not declare
1 error(s). Static validation only: event delivery is verified by running the service against a broker.
```

A typo in an event name would otherwise create a consumer that never receives anything and fails silently. Validation turns it into an error.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Check | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `NOT-CONFIGURED` from `dispatch:doctor` | dispatch is disabled or the broker variable is unset | `pso dispatch:inspect` shows `disabled`; the environment | set `PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true` and `REDIS_URL`, `RABBITMQ_URL` or `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS` |
| `DOWN` | nothing answers at that address | the address; a firewall; the container | start the broker; `docker ps` for a local one |
| `UP` but no event arrives | reachability is not delivery: the channel, queue or topic differs, or the consumer group is new | `pso dispatch:events` for the channel; the broker's own tooling | align the channel name on both sides; see the [walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md) |
| `PSO_DISPATCH_SCHEMA_CHANGED` | a locked schema changed | `git diff` of the schema file | add a version, then `pso dispatch:lock` |
| `PSO_DISPATCH_007` | the consumer's event name is not declared | the name in `@DispatchConsumer` and in `EVENTS.pso.ts` | make them identical |
| publishing to RabbitMQ before any consumer started is refused | the queue is declared by the consumer group, and an unroutable message is refused, not dropped | the provider's `note` | start (or deploy) a consumer first, or declare the queue ahead |
| a Kafka consumer stops advancing | a failing message blocks its partition while it is retried | the consumer logs and the `<channel>.dlq` topic | fix the handler or let the retry budget end in the dead-letter topic |
| duplicates in your data | at-least-once delivery | whether the handler is idempotent | deduplicate on the event `id` |

## Production considerations

- Make `dispatch:validate` and `dispatch:doctor` part of your pipeline: `validate` before the build (no broker needed), `doctor` after deploy against the real broker.
- Commit `pso.dispatch.lock.json`: it is the memory of what consumers rely on.
- Size retention above your slowest consumer (Redis trims approximately, Kafka and RabbitMQ per their own policies).
- Watch dead-letter channels (`<channel>.dlq`): messages there are failures that need a person.
- Secrets stay `${env:...}` references. `dispatch:inspect` redacts them in its output.

## Common mistakes

- Treating `UP` as proof that events flow.
- Changing a locked schema in place instead of declaring a new version.
- Assuming exactly-once: none of the three providers offers it.
- Publishing from a service that does not own the event (`publish: false` consumers).
- Installing a second provider and expecting both to work in one service.

## Next steps

- [Dispatch walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md): publish and consume against real Redis
- [Providers](dispatch/providers.md)
- [Contracts](dispatch/contracts.md)
- [Reliability](dispatch/reliability.md)
