# Distributed frontend: FEI and MEI

> How PSO Web structures a browser application as one application shell (FEI) and independent business-domain microfrontends (MEI), why the pieces are split this way, and what each one owns.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** with unit tests and real-browser runs (Chrome) against a multi-service sample application: a local Compose backend, and a cloud workload on a remote VM reached through an authenticated SSH tunnel. Frontends are deployed by PSO's own cloud engine as static resources (see "Deploying a shell and microfrontends with the cloud engine"), or published to a site root by `pso frontend:publish`; both use the same release functions. **Not done:** a deployment of the frontends to the remote VM.

PSO Web already describes a backend declaratively: an orchestrator, services, routes, contracts. The distributed frontend applies the same idea to the browser. A workspace gets **one application shell** and **one microfrontend per business domain**, each a normal React and TypeScript project, and the framework manages everything structural between them.

```architecture title="Where each piece runs"
Browser (client)
  FEI, the application shell (shell) # layout, sign-in, session, navigation, middleware, notifications, the one orchestrator connection
    MEI customers (microfrontend) # /customers/* | its own pages, hooks, state, tests and release
    MEI catalog (microfrontend) # /catalog/* | its own pages, hooks, state, tests and release
    MEI orders (microfrontend) # /orders/* | its own pages, hooks, state, tests and release
  PSO API client (library) # native fetch
    PSO orchestrator (orchestrator) # calls |
      services (service) # forwards to |
```

## Who owns what

| Concern | FEI (shell) | MEI (microfrontend) |
|---|---|---|
| Browser URL and history | owns the one router | uses `<Routes>` below its mount path; never creates a router |
| Sign-in, session, token | owns them; the token never leaves it | receives `usePsoContext()` (user, scopes, `api`, `channels`) |
| Layout and navigation chrome | owns them | renders only its own pages inside the shell |
| Middleware | owns the mandatory pipeline | may add domain middleware that runs after it and cannot weaken it |
| Business logic, state, components | none | all of it |
| Build and release | own project, own release | own project, own release |

## Why this split

A shell that every team edits becomes the bottleneck the split exists to avoid. A shell that does nothing becomes N applications that each reinvent sign-in. PSO takes the middle path: the shell is small and generic, and **everything a user should experience once** (identity, session, error handling, the connection to the backend) lives in it. A team that works on customers changes `mei-customers` and nothing else.

Two rules make the independence safe rather than accidental. A MEI **cannot import the FEI's source** and the FEI **cannot import a MEI's source**: they meet only through a versioned contract (the shared context, 1.0) and a manifest. And **no frontend talks to a microservice**: every request goes to the orchestrator, which is where tokens are verified and scopes enforced.

## What you write and what PSO manages

You write `FEI.pso.ts`, `MEI.pso.ts` and `ROUTES.pso.ts` (data, read without being executed), pages and components, and optional middleware. PSO manages Module Federation, the route table, the runtime configuration, shared React singletons, hashed assets and the release manifest. A generated `rspack.config.ts` is one line.

## Stack

React 18.3, TypeScript (strict), Tailwind CSS 4, React Icons, React Router 7, native `fetch` and `WebSocket`, Rspack 2.3 with Module Federation 2.9. These exact versions were built together and are pinned in the generated projects. Vite and Axios are not used.

## Limits and what this is not

- **Module Federation is not a sandbox.** A loaded microfrontend runs in the same JavaScript realm as the shell. PSO reduces mistakes (no token in the context, no direct URLs, manifests with hashes and signatures) but cannot contain malicious code. Treat every MEI as code with the same release standards as the shell.
- Browser checks (guards, scope-based navigation, middleware) shape the interface. They are **not** an authorization boundary; the orchestrator enforces access.
- PSO does not replace React. It adds structure around it.
- The shell loads microfrontends from approved manifests. A new MEI release that is compatible needs no shell rebuild; an incompatible one is refused before it runs.
- Real-time updates use the Channels connection the shell owns. A backend without Channels still works: the Orders page falls back to bounded polling.

---

# Create a shell and microfrontends

> The developer workflow end to end: generate the FEI and three MEIs with the CLI, register them, develop one MEI alone, run the whole ecosystem, validate, build and publish independently.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified.** This exact sequence was run with the public CLI against a scratch workspace (install, typecheck, tests, builds all passing) and against the Commerce fixture. Timings on a development machine: `npm install` about 10 to 20 s per project, a production build 2 to 5 s per project.

You need a workspace with an orchestrator, because a frontend talks only to it.

```bash
pso create workspace shop
cd shop
pso create orchestrator shop-gateway
pso create fei shop --install
pso create mei customers --register --install
pso create mei catalog --register --install
pso frontend:graph
```

`create fei` and `create mei` generate a complete project under `frontend/`, register it in `pso.workspace.json` (name, kind, path, development port), vendor the framework packages next to it (so it builds without access to the framework checkout) and, with `--install`, run `npm install`. Ports are 4200 for the shell and 9000, 9001, ... for microfrontends; `--port` overrides.

`--register` also lists the new MEI in the FEI. Without it, `pso frontend:validate` reports `PSO_MEI_NOT_REGISTERED` with the exact command to run (`pso fei:register customers`). Registration adds an entry to `FEI.pso.ts` (mount path `/customers`, entry scopes `customers:read`) and checks the relationship in both directions.

## Develop one microfrontend alone

```bash
pso frontend:dev --standalone customers
```

The MEI starts on its own port with the **development host adapter**: a stand-in for the shell that provides the same context contract (user, scopes, `api`, `channels`, `notifications`, `navigate`) and a form to paste a development token (`pso idp:dev token --scopes customers:read`). The adapter exists only in the standalone entry and refuses to run in a production build. Requests go to your orchestrator through a dev-server proxy at `/api`.

## Run everything together

```bash
pso frontend:dev
```

Starts the shell and every registered MEI on their declared ports, wires the shell's development runtime configuration to the MEI dev servers, and proxies `/api` to the orchestrator (`PSO_ORCHESTRATOR_URL`, default the workspace orchestrator's port). A port that is already in use stops the start with the name of the project and the port.

## The loop

1. Change `src/pages` in one MEI. Hot updates apply without touching the others.
2. `pso frontend:validate` checks declarations, relationships, route ownership, conflicts, contract compatibility and the architecture rules (no router in a MEI, no absolute URL in `fetch`).
3. `npm test` inside the project runs its own tests.
4. `pso frontend:build customers --base-path /app/` builds that one project; a MEI also gets its release manifest.
5. `pso frontend:publish customers --site <dir>` publishes it without rebuilding the shell (see Releases).

## Common mistakes

- Running `npm install` before the vendored packages exist. Generate projects with the CLI; do not copy a project by hand.
- Updating the framework and rebuilding only some projects. The vendored copy is part of each build: after a framework update run `pso frontend:install` and rebuild.
- Expecting `/api` to exist in `pso frontend:dev --standalone` without a running orchestrator. The page shows a gateway-timeout error with a correlation id, which is the intended failure mode.
- On Git Bash for Windows, arguments such as `/shop/` are rewritten to Windows paths. Set `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` for the command.

---

# FEI.pso.ts, MEI.pso.ts and ROUTES.pso.ts

> The declarative contracts of the frontend ecosystem: what each field means, how they are read without being executed, and which validation errors name which configuration.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** (`contracts.test.ts`, `workspace-frontends.test.ts`, and the generated projects' own tests).

Like every PSO declaration, these files are **data**. `defineFEI`, `defineMEI`, `defineFrontendRoutes` and `defineMiddleware` only give the editor types. The CLI and Studio read the files without executing them: an object literal with literals only. A function call, a variable or `process.env` inside a declaration is reported as an error, because importing project code would run it before trust exists.

## FEI.pso.ts

```typescript
import { defineFEI } from "@pso/frontend";

export default defineFEI({
  name: "fei-commerce",                              // fei-<name>, kebab-case
  server: { port: 4200 },
  orchestrator: { service: "gateway", basePath: "/api" },
  security: { authentication: "jwt", session: "centralized", loginPath: "/login" },
  middlewares: ["authentication", "authorization", "session", "context", "telemetry"],
  locale: { default: "en", supported: ["en"] },
  microfrontends: [
    { name: "mei-customers", path: "/customers", scopes: ["customers:read"], loading: "lazy", title: "Customers", icon: "customers" },
  ],
});
```

- `orchestrator.service` must be the workspace's orchestrator. `basePath` is a same-origin path; the API client never accepts an absolute URL.
- `middlewares` is the navigation pipeline in order. `authentication` and `authorization` are mandatory while authentication is `jwt`, `authentication` must run before `authorization`, and nothing may run before `authentication` (a custom middleware must not see an unauthenticated navigation).
- Each microfrontend has a **mount path** it owns exclusively. Paths cannot be parameterized, nested inside another mount, or start with `/api`, `/_mei`, `/_pso`, `/_fei`, `/health` or `/channels`: those belong to the API, the remote artifacts and PSO itself.
- `scopes` are what the user needs to **enter** the MEI. They hide navigation and block loading the MEI; they are a user-experience mechanism.

## MEI.pso.ts

```typescript
export default defineMEI({
  name: "mei-customers", host: "fei-commerce", server: { port: 9000 },
  orchestrator: { service: "gateway" },
  expose: { module: "./src/module.tsx" },
  security: { inheritFromHost: true, scopes: ["customers:read", "customers:write"] },
});
```

`inheritFromHost: false` is refused: a MEI never has its own authentication lifecycle. `middlewares` may list domain middleware but never a mandatory FEI middleware. `contract.context` is the shared-context version the MEI was built for (default `1.0`).

## ROUTES.pso.ts

```typescript
export default defineFrontendRoutes({
  routes: [
    { path: "/", page: "./src/pages/Customers.tsx", title: "Customers" },
    { path: "/new", page: "./src/pages/CreateCustomer.tsx", scopes: ["customers:write"] },
    { path: "/:id", page: "./src/pages/CustomerDetails.tsx" },
  ],
});
```

Paths are relative to the mount, so these become `/customers`, `/customers/new` and `/customers/:id`. A route has a `page`, a `redirect` or `children`, never both a page and a redirect. Files are project-relative and cannot contain `..`. PSO generates the lazy route table from this file (`.pso/generated/`, never edited).

## What `pso frontend:validate` checks

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PSO_FEI_ROUTE_CONFLICT` | two mounts overlap; names both entries by index |
| `PSO_FEI_ROUTE_RESERVED` | a mount under `/api`, `/_mei` and the like |
| `PSO_MEI_NOT_REGISTERED` / `PSO_MEI_HOST_MISMATCH` | the MEI names a host that does not list it |
| `PSO_MEI_SCOPE_MISMATCH` | the FEI requires a scope the MEI does not declare |
| `PSO_MEI_CONTRACT_INCOMPATIBLE` | the MEI needs a newer or different major shared-context version |
| `PSO_ROUTE_CONFLICT` | the same effective path is declared twice (parameter names do not make routes different) |
| `PSO_MEI_OWN_ROUTER` | a MEI source uses `BrowserRouter`, `HashRouter` and the like |
| `PSO_MEI_DIRECT_URL` | a MEI calls `fetch("https://...")` |
| `PSO_FRONTEND_CONTRACT_STALE` | generated orchestrator types are older than the orchestrator |

## Limits and common mistakes

- A computed declaration (`name: process.env.NAME`) is rejected; use a literal and configure the environment through the runtime configuration.
- Route precedence is deterministic: static segments beat `:param` beats `*`. Two routes of the same shape are an error, not a coin flip.
- Declaring a scope in the FEI does not secure anything on the server. Every scope the MEI needs must also be enforced by the orchestrator.

---

# Routing, middleware and the shared context

> How the shell resolves and authorizes a destination before loading a microfrontend, how the navigation middleware pipeline works, and exactly what a MEI receives from usePsoContext().

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified**: pipeline and routing logic by unit tests; the behavior (redirect with `returnTo`, hidden navigation, access denied before loading, back and forward, refresh on nested routes, MEI to MEI without reloading the shell) by real-browser runs.

## One router, owned by the shell

The shell creates the only history instance. A MEI renders `<Routes>` below its mount path, so `/customers/42` is resolved by the shell (`/customers/*` belongs to `mei-customers`) and then by the MEI (`/:id`). React Router is used as is: nested routes, parameters, query parameters, lazy loading, redirects. A MEI that creates its own `BrowserRouter` would fight the shell over the URL, so `pso frontend:validate` rejects it, and the generated module refuses to render outside a router.

Routes carry `title`, `scopes` and free `meta`; the shell derives breadcrumbs from them and sets the document title. A path nothing owns shows the shell's not-found page, a missing scope shows access denied, and a MEI that cannot be loaded shows a "module unavailable" page with a retry. In each case the rest of the application keeps working.

## The navigation pipeline

Every navigation runs the shell's middlewares in the order `FEI.pso.ts` lists them, **before** the MEI is loaded:

```text evidence="illustrative"
Navigation requested
 authentication  not signed in: redirect to /login?returnTo=<this path>
 authorization   a required scope is missing: access denied (403 page)
 session         about to expire: one shared refresh, or sign out and redirect
 context         locale, tenant check, correlation id
 telemetry       measures the navigation
 microfrontend resolution: load the approved release (only if all of the above continued)
 MEI domain middleware (optional), then rendering
```

```typescript
import { defineMiddleware } from "@pso/frontend";

export default defineMiddleware({
  name: "application-context",
  async execute(context, next) {
    context.set("locale", "pt-BR");
    return next();
  },
});
```

A middleware returns the result of `next()`, or `context.redirect(path)` or `context.deny(status, reason)` to stop. It can be asynchronous and is cancelled when the user navigates again. A redirect to anything that is not an absolute path inside the application (`//host`, `https://...`, backslashes) is refused. An exception is reported as a pipeline error that names the middleware.

A MEI may add domain middleware (`middlewares` in `MEI.pso.ts`). It runs only after the shell's pipeline continued, can write only keys under `mei.<name>.`, can deny, and can redirect only inside its own mount. It cannot replace, reorder or skip the mandatory middleware.

## What a MEI receives

```typescript
const { user, permissions, hasScope, locale, tenant, theme, navigate, api, channels, notifications, get, correlationId } = usePsoContext();
```

The context is a frozen snapshot with a version (`contractVersion`, currently 1.0). It contains **no access token, no refresh function and no setter** for session, tenant or permissions. `api` is the orchestrator client (the token is attached inside it), `channels` subscribes through the shell's single connection, `navigate` accepts only paths inside the application, and `get(key)` reads what a shell middleware published. A MEI built for contract 1.x runs in a host that offers 1.y with y at least x; a different major version is refused when the release is published and again when it is loaded.

## The lifecycle, in practice

The pipeline runs when the location, the session status or the session's scopes change, never during an ordinary re-render, and it is the shell's. The order is the declared order of `middlewares` in `FEI.pso.ts`; each middleware may be asynchronous, call `next()` once (a second call is an error) or end the navigation with `redirect`, `deny` or by throwing (reported as the failing middleware's name). A new navigation aborts the signal of the previous one, so a slow earlier run can never overwrite the newer result. A microfrontend may add domain middleware, which runs only after the shell's middleware allowed the navigation and cannot write the keys the shell owns (`user`, `tenant`, `permissions` and the like) or weaken a decision: it can deny more, not allow what the shell denied. An unauthorized navigation to a microfrontend's route is decided before its code is loaded. Redirects must be paths inside the application. The browser's middleware is user experience: **the orchestrator enforces every scope and tenant rule**, whatever the interface shows (verified: a user without permissions, a read-only user and forged tokens are refused by the orchestrator directly).

```typescript evidence="illustrative"
export default defineMiddleware({
  name: "maintenance-window",
  async execute(context, next) {
    if (context.to.path.startsWith("/orders/new") && (await isFrozen())) return context.deny(503, "Orders are frozen");
    return next();
  },
});
```

Routes whose identifiers contain dots work in the browser; on the server, routes whose last segment ends in a real file extension need to be declared for nginx (see native deployment).

## Limits and common mistakes

- **Middleware is not security.** Anything it denies is reachable from the browser's developer tools. The orchestrator enforces every scope, tenant rule and business rule.
- Do not use the shared context as a global store. Each MEI keeps its own state; the context is for identity, navigation and capabilities.
- `scopes` on a route hide and block in the interface; a MEI route with `scopes: ["customers:write"]` shows "Access denied" without a request being sent, but the same endpoint called by other means is checked by the orchestrator.
- Query parameters are available in the middleware target and through React Router in the page; passing a customer to the Orders MEI works with `navigate("/orders/new?customerId=...")`.

---

# Authentication, the API client, typed contracts and Channels

> How the shell signs users in and keeps the session, how every request reaches only the orchestrator through a native-fetch client, how typed contracts are generated from the orchestrator, and how real-time events reach microfrontends.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> **Partially verified.** The API client, session handling, PKCE flow (against a fake identity provider in unit tests), contract generation and the Channels manager are verified by unit tests; the client, a pasted development token, orchestrator requests and a real `order.updated` Channels event were verified in a real browser. **Authorization Code with PKCE has not been run against a real identity provider**: this repository has none (the development identity provider publishes keys only). Orchestrator-backed cookie sessions are **not implemented**: the orchestrator has no session endpoint.

## Sign-in and session

The shell owns sign-in. The runtime configuration (a file the deployment publishes, never built into the bundle) selects the provider:

- `oidc`: Authorization Code with PKCE (S256), `state` and `nonce`. The code verifier is single use and held only for the redirect. Redirect targets after sign-in (`returnTo`) must be paths inside the application.
- `dev-token`: a pasted token, for development. It works in development builds, or in a production build made with `pso frontend:build --allow-dev-token`, which shows a permanent warning banner. It is refused otherwise.

The access token lives in the memory of the shell's session manager. It is not in React state, not in the shared context and not in `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` (development builds keep a pasted token in `sessionStorage` so a reload does not ask again; production does not). A reload therefore signs the user out and, after signing in, returns them to the page they asked for. Token claims are decoded for display only; the orchestrator verifies the signature, issuer, audience, scopes and tenant.

**What the shell checks at sign-in** (tested against a real Keycloak in Chrome): the provider's endpoints must be https (plain http only for localhost); the callback must carry the `state` this browser created; an ID token must have the configured issuer, this client as audience (and as authorized party when there are several audiences), be unexpired and carry **this sign-in's nonce** (a missing nonce is a mismatch); an access token from another issuer is refused. The ID token's signature is not verified in the browser (it came straight from the token endpoint over TLS, which OIDC Core allows); the orchestrator verifies the access token on every request. A callback page that mounts twice redeems the single-use code once. **Logout** ends the provider's session (RP-initiated, with the ID token as hint and a post-logout redirect inside the application). **Session restoration:** the token is memory-only, so after a reload the shell asks the provider silently (`prompt=none`) if a flag in `sessionStorage` says this tab had a session; `login_required` is not an error and drops the flag, so there is no loop; `restoreSession: false` switches it off. **Scopes** are read from the configured claim and from `scp` together, because providers differ (Keycloak and Azure AD keep OIDC scopes in `scope` and permissions in `scp`). The orchestrator reads both too.

## Session strategies

Supported: **bearer tokens with PKCE** (above). Not provided: cookie sessions. The orchestrator-backed HttpOnly-cookie session was evaluated and not added: a PKCE flow whose token lives in memory and whose renewal is shared satisfies the requirements without a server-side session store, CSRF tokens and rotation that would need their own review. If you add cookie sessions yourself, keep them additive next to bearer tokens, `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite`, with CSRF protection on unsafe methods (the client already sends a CSRF header when configured for cookies). Limits: a token cannot be revoked before it expires (keep access-token lifetimes short; Keycloak's server-side logout stops the next renewal, which was verified); a refresh token held in memory is lost on reload and restored through the provider session, not stored.

Sessions expire: a timer refreshes shortly before expiry when the provider issued a refresh token, **one refresh at a time for the whole application** however many microfrontends have requests in flight, and otherwise ends the session. Sign-out is broadcast to other tabs.

## The API client

```typescript
const { api } = usePsoContext();
const customers = await api.get<Customer[]>("/customers");
const created = await api.post<Customer>("/customers", { name, email });
```

Built on native `fetch`: a configured same-origin base path plus a validated relative path (an absolute URL, `//host`, backslashes, `..` and control characters are refused before a request exists), JSON, query parameters, cancellation, timeouts, a correlation id on every request, and RFC 9457 Problem Details turned into `PsoApiError` (`status`, `problem`, `fieldErrors`, `correlationId`). Failures are classified: problem, http, network, timeout, cancelled, invalid response, refused.

**Retries are conservative.** GET (and other idempotent methods) may be retried after a network error or 502, 503 or 504; a POST is **never** retried automatically unless the caller supplied an idempotency key. After a 401 the client performs one shared refresh and repeats only idempotent requests. `dedupe: true` lets concurrent identical GETs share one call.

## Typed contracts

```bash
pso frontend:contracts
pso frontend:contracts --check
```

Generates `src/models/contract.generated.ts` in every frontend project from the orchestrator's real route metadata and the DTO classes its controllers validate. It contains the request DTO types, a table of operations (method, path, scopes, authentication) and `ORCHESTRATOR_CONTRACT_VERSION`. **Response types exist only where the orchestrator declares them.** A route may publish an optional `responses` block in its `ROUTES.pso.ts` entry; nothing is inferred from a running service or from samples, and a route without the block keeps working and stays untyped (`unknown`). `pso frontend:validate` warns when a project's copy is older than the orchestrator and `--check` fails in CI.

```typescript evidence="illustrative"
{
  method: "GET", path: "/customers/:id", controller: CustomersController, action: "findById",
  security: { guard: "jwt", scopes: ["customers:read"] },
  metadata: { service: "customers" },
  responses: { 200: "CustomerResponse", 401: "problem", 403: "problem", 404: "problem" }
}
```

Values name a `@Dto()` class of the orchestrator (`"CustomerResponse"`, `"CustomerResponse[]"`, `"CustomerResponse | null"`), `"void"` for no body or `"problem"` for an RFC 9457 body. A response-only DTO is complete unless a field is declared with `?`. Pagination is a DTO you declare (`CustomerPage { items: CustomerResponse[]; total: number }`): PSO does not invent an envelope. The orchestrator does not validate what the service answers, so keep the DTO in step with the service; the `responses` block is metadata for typed frontends, not enforcement.

**Why responses are not validated at runtime.** Checking every response in the orchestrator was evaluated and is not on by default. The orchestrator forwards the service's body; validating it means buffering and parsing every response (it would break streaming and large downloads and add latency and memory to the one component all traffic crosses), and a mismatch has no good production answer (a 500 turns a harmless extra field into an outage, passing it through makes the check decorative). The service owns its response, so the check belongs where the answer is produced: contract tests of the service against the declared `responses`, run in CI, and the breaking-change report above. If an opt-in check is added later it should be per route, off in production, and report instead of failing.

The generated file also exports `createOperations(api)`, typed calls over the host's `api` (authentication, correlation, cancellation and error classification unchanged):

```typescript evidence="illustrative"
const ops = createOperations(usePsoContext().api);
const customers = await ops.call("GET /customers");                              // CustomerResponse[]
const one = await ops.call("GET /customers/:id", { params: { id } });             // CustomerResponse
const created = await ops.call("POST /customers", { body: { name, email } });    // body checked against the DTO
```

The compiler rejects an operation that is not in the contract, a missing body, a body of the wrong type and a wrong use of the response. Path parameters are URL-encoded and can never add a segment or a query. When the orchestrator changes, `pso frontend:contracts` compares the new contract with the previous one and lists **breaking** changes (an operation, a response status or a field removed or retyped, a response field made optional, a request field made required, more scopes needed) apart from **additive** ones; `--fail-on-breaking` makes the command exit 1. Event payloads are not part of this contract yet.

## Channels

The shell owns one WebSocket connection. `channels.subscribe("order.<id>", handler)` shares one server-side subscription per channel across all listeners, closes it when the last listener leaves (so navigation leaves nothing behind), re-authenticates after a session change and reconnects within bounded attempts. A MEI never opens a socket, and Dispatch brokers are never exposed to the browser. Event delivery is at least once: handlers should re-read state (the Orders page treats an event as "it changed" and asks the orchestrator what it is).

## Keycloak as the provider, and moving a running workload to it

Keycloak is only an example of a standards-compliant provider; PSO needs an issuer, its keys, an audience and permissions in `scope` or `scp`. A deployment of it must not be a development one: a pinned, supported version, the production `start` mode with a real database, hostname and proxy settings that match the public address, HTTP only on the loopback behind managed HTTPS, a private management interface, a dedicated realm, a public client with Authorization Code and PKCE, explicit redirect URIs and secrets that never leave the server's secret store.

```architecture title="Target topology of the Azure validation server (proposed, not deployed)"
browser (client)
  shared nginx server on 443 (proxy) # HTTPS |
    gateway (orchestrator) # / | the only backend of the browser; validates tokens
      customers, catalog and orders (service) # forwards |
    Commerce frontend (shell) # /commerce/ | static files served from the site root
    Keycloak (security) # /idp/ | loopback only; management port private; its own database
```

The gateway and the services accept **one issuer each** (TypeScript and Java alike): there is no multi-issuer mode, and an unrestricted one would be unsafe, so none is offered. Moving a running workload from the test-token provider to Keycloak is therefore a controlled migration: deploy the four applications with the new issuer, JWKS location and audience as ordinary blue-green releases in a planned window (tokens of the old provider stop working as each one switches, so business requests fail briefly until all four are active), verify, and keep each previous release as the rollback. Nothing is left as an uncontrolled fallback: the development-token sign-in stays a build-time option that shows a warning banner and is not part of a production build.

## Channels, in more detail

Tested against the real Channels server on real sockets: one connection and one server-side subscription per channel however many microfrontends listen; one microfrontend leaving never removes another's subscription; a faulty listener never stops the others; sixty rapid mount and unmount cycles leave no connection, subscription or listener; a gateway restart is followed by reconnection with backoff, a fresh token and re-subscription; a rejected token ends in `closed` after the bounded number of attempts and the error carries no token; `close()` (logout) releases everything and nothing reconnects. Three defects were found and fixed: a subscription cancelled while its subscribe request was in flight stayed on the server, the retry budget was reset by any open socket so a rejected token retried forever, and the server refused rate-limited `unsubscribe` frames (it no longer charges them). In the local Commerce stack the order is decided immediately and no Channels server runs, so a live event is only demonstrated on a stack that has one.

## Limits and common mistakes

- Do not put the token in a MEI's own storage or request it from the shell: there is no API for it by design.
- A JavaScript wrapper cannot stop other code in the page from calling `fetch`. The boundary is the deployment: same-origin routing, `connect-src 'self'` and private service networks.
- A channel the user may not read answers with an authorization error from the server; the interface cannot grant it.
- Without Channels on the backend the Orders page polls every few seconds for a bounded number of times; it does not poll forever.

# Styling, isolation and performance

> How Tailwind CSS, shared design tokens and cascade layers keep independently built microfrontends visually coherent without style collisions, and the performance measures PSO takes and reports.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and measured** on one development machine over loopback (Chrome, one run each). The numbers below are **measurements of the Commerce fixture**, not guarantees: compression, network latency and cache state of your deployment differ.

## One reset, shared tokens, layers

Tailwind 4 ships a CSS reset (Preflight). If every microfrontend loaded it, each would restyle the shell. PSO's strategy:

- The **shell** loads Preflight once and sets the values of the design tokens (`--pso-bg`, `--pso-surface`, `--pso-fg`, `--pso-brand`, radii, font) for light and dark themes (`data-theme` on the document).
- A **microfrontend** imports `@pso/frontend-react/tokens.css` (the token names only, mapped to Tailwind colors such as `bg-surface`, `text-muted`, `border-line`) and the Tailwind **utilities** layer. It never loads a reset and never selects bare elements.
- Everything sits in cascade layers (`theme`, `base`, `components`, `utilities`) so utilities always win over base styles and order does not depend on which bundle loaded first.
- Domain-specific CSS goes in CSS Modules or under `[data-pso-mei="<name>"]`, an attribute the generated module puts on its root.

Utilities are idempotent (`flex` means the same thing in every bundle), so duplicated utility rules across microfrontends are harmless. Tailwind **prefixes** were considered and not used by default: they make markup noisy and are unnecessary once the reset is single and selectors are limited to utilities; a team that needs one can add it in its own stylesheet. Teams share the **tokens**, not a component library: each MEI owns its components, and the fixture's three MEIs deliberately carry their own small copy of a UI kit.

## Accessibility defaults

The generated shell has a skip link, landmarks, keyboard-operable navigation with visible focus, `aria-live` notifications, loading states with `role="status"`, and errors with `role="alert"`; it honors `prefers-reduced-motion` and `prefers-color-scheme`. The Studio view of the frontend was checked with axe (WCAG 2 A and AA) with no violations; the generated shell was exercised in a real browser but has not been through a full accessibility audit.

## Performance measures

| Measure | How it is done |
|---|---|
| Lazy loading | each microfrontend loads on first navigation; `loading: "eager"` is opt-in; nothing is preloaded at start |
| Code splitting | page chunks per route; the MEI's `React` is shared, not downloaded again |
| Hashed, immutable assets | `[contenthash]` file names; `Cache-Control: immutable` for versioned files, `no-store` for pointers and the runtime configuration |
| Prefetch | hovering or focusing a navigation entry prefetches that microfrontend only if the user may open it, and not when `Save-Data` is on or the connection is 2G |
| Request deduplication | opt-in per GET (`dedupe: true`) |
| Subscriptions | one connection, reference-counted channels, released on navigation |
| Budgets | `budgets: { shellKb }` in `FEI.pso.ts` fails `pso frontend:build` when the gzip size is exceeded |

## Measurements (Commerce fixture, production build, loopback, one run)

| What | Result |
|---|---|
| FEI build output, gzip (all JS and CSS) | 171 KB |
| First load of the shell (JS and CSS, 7 requests, served uncompressed) | 560 KB |
| First navigation to a microfrontend (7 requests, uncompressed) | 141 KB, 147 ms to render |
| Second microfrontend | 167 ms |
| Repeat visit | 3 of 3 JS and CSS files from the browser cache |
| Cold load to the sign-in page | 336 ms |
| Create a customer / place an order through the SSH tunnel to Azure | 168 ms / 170 ms |
| Order confirmed after placement (asynchronous, observed in the page) | about 2.5 s |

A MEI's build output (about 210 KB gzip) is larger than what a browser downloads, because it includes a fallback copy of React that is fetched only if the shell does not provide a compatible one. These figures were taken without compression and without a CDN. No claim is made that this is faster than another architecture: it was not compared.

## Measured on the deployed Commerce frontend (real nginx with gzip, real Keycloak login, Chrome, loopback, one run)

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| Cold load to the sign-in page | 7 requests (2 JavaScript, 1 CSS), 179 KB transferred, about 145 ms |
| First microfrontend after sign-in (callback, token exchange, microfrontend, cold) | 15 requests, 52 KB, about 360 ms including the provider round trip |
| Second and third microfrontend, cold | about 110 ms, 9 requests, 50 KB |
| Navigation between microfrontends already loaded | median 28 ms, p95 38 ms over 120 navigations, no JavaScript request |
| Repeated navigation, resources | DOM nodes 244 to 246, JS event listeners 172 to 170, heap +0.5 MB after 120 navigations |
| Warm reload | 20 requests, 10 KB transferred, 4 served from the browser cache |
| React DOM | in one script (the shell's); no microfrontend carries its own copy |
| Layout shift, long tasks | 0.001, none |
| Build output, gzip | shell 168.5 KB JS + 4.2 KB CSS; microfrontends about 212 KB JS + 2 KB CSS each (a fallback React copy that the browser does not download) |

Methodology: Chrome DevTools Protocol counters after a forced garbage collection. An earlier run seemed to show DOM nodes and listeners growing with every navigation; the cause was the measuring tool (Playwright element handles from `waitForSelector` keep elements alive), not the application, and disappeared with `locator().waitFor()`. No comparison with another architecture was made, so no improvement is claimed.

## CSS isolation, checked in a browser

Preflight (the global reset) is present once, in the shell's stylesheet. Microfrontend stylesheets (6 to 7 KB each) declare no global element selectors (`body`, `html`, `*`, `h1`, `a`, `button`). Loading all three microfrontends leaves the shell's computed styles unchanged. Headings are identical across microfrontends. Switching the theme in the shell changes the shell and the microfrontend content through shared custom properties and survives a reload. axe-core (WCAG 2 A and AA) found no violations on Customers, Catalog and Orders in light and dark themes, there is no horizontal overflow at 390, 768 and 1280 px, and the interface uses SVG icons and no emoji. Limits: CSS is not sandboxed. A microfrontend that ships a global rule would affect everything, which is why the generated CSS is checked for global selectors in the evidence run; utility class names are shared by design, and a microfrontend that adds its own unscoped class can still collide with another.

## Limits and common mistakes

- Importing `tailwindcss` (the full bundle) in a MEI re-introduces the reset; import `tailwind/theme` and `utilities` as the template does.
- A global selector in a MEI (`button { ... }`) affects the whole page; the framework cannot prevent it, only the template's conventions and review do.
- The shell reload is not triggered by a MEI release: a browser that already loaded the old release keeps it until the page reloads.
