# Deploying a shell and microfrontends with the cloud engine

> How a FEI and its MEIs are deployed as static resources by the same plan, approval, signature, lock, history, atomic activation and rollback as a backend service, how nginx is managed for them, and how independent releases stay safe.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** with the engine run inside the Linux image of the cloud end-to-end tests, against a **real nginx** (`static-engine-nginx.test.ts`, `static-nginx.test.ts`), with in-process engine tests (`static-deploy.test.ts`), and in Chrome against the Commerce frontend deployed that way (26 of 26 navigation and workflow checks, 13 of 13 independent-lifecycle checks). **Not done:** a deployment of the frontend to the Azure VM, and an interrupted deployment with a real killed worker (recovery was verified with a simulated interruption).

A frontend is deployed with the engine you already use. There is no second deployment tool: `pso frontend:declare` writes a declaration, and `pso release:plan`, `release:approve`, `release:deploy`, `release:status`, `release:history` and `release:rollback` work on it as on any service.

```bash
pso frontend:build fei-commerce --base-path /commerce/
pso frontend:declare fei-commerce --connection azure --base-path /commerce/ --api-port 3000 --probe-port 8080
pso release:plan commerce-fei
pso release:deploy commerce-fei --approve --yes
pso frontend:build customers --sign-key release.pem --key-id release-1
pso frontend:declare customers --connection azure --probe-port 8080
pso release:deploy commerce-customers --approve --yes
pso release:rollback commerce-customers --yes
```

## What is different from a service

The declaration has a service with `runtime: "static"` and the strategy `static`. Nothing is started, so there is no port, no process, no drain. The build output (the `dist` directory) travels as the usual checksummed artifact; the plan, the signature and trust checks, the approval, the deployment lock, the state machine, the audit log and the history are the engine's own. Activation calls the **same functions** as `pso frontend:publish` (`@pso/frontend/release`, bundled into the agent), so the CLI and the engine cannot disagree about what a release is.

On the server everything lives in one **site root** per domain (`<agent home>/sites/<site>`), shared by the shell and its microfrontends:

```tree title="Site root of one domain on the server"
sites/commerce/
  fei/
    <version>/ # immutable shell releases (index.html, pso-fei.json)
    assets/ # one content-addressed pool of every shell release's hashed assets
    current.json # the active shell (and a `current` symlink)
  _mei/
    <name>/
      v/
        <version>/ # immutable microfrontend releases
      active.json # the active pointer, written atomically
      history.json # every activation
  pso-runtime-config.json # remotes, trusted signing keys, sign-in provider
```

## Who touches nginx

Only a **shell** release can change the web-server configuration. The managed file `pso-<app>.conf` is generated from one function shared with `pso frontend:nginx`, written through the adapter's usual transaction: back up, write, `nginx -t`, graceful reload, restore on failure. A shell release whose generated file is identical to the one in place changes nothing and reloads nothing. A **microfrontend** deployment never touches nginx at all (its declaration is refused if it asks for it): the shell's file already serves `/_mei/` for every microfrontend, so a compatible update is one pointer write and the nginx worker processes stay the same (verified by comparing their process ids).

The generated configuration serves the shell under its base path with the entry page as the fallback for every path that is not a file: a path is a file only when its extension is a known static-asset one (`js`, `css`, `json`, `png`, `svg`, `woff2`, `map`, `html`, `pdf` and the like), so an application identifier such as `/customers/acme.corp` or `/orders/ORD-1.2.3` is a route. A missing script or stylesheet is a **404** and never the entry page. Versioned remote files are `immutable`; the pointer, the history and the runtime configuration are `no-store`; text is compressed; every location repeats the security headers (nginx drops inherited `add_header` as soon as a location sets its own) with a policy of `script-src 'self'` and `connect-src 'self'`; the orchestrator is proxied under one prefix with WebSocket upgrades, and `/channels`. Nothing else under the site root, such as the lock directory or the release directories, is reachable.

## The lifecycle, and what keeps it safe

1. The candidate is verified against its manifest (hashes, files, signature policy of the site) and for **compatibility with the active shell** (shared-context contract, React major) before anything is copied into the site. An incompatible or tampered candidate fails the deployment and is not even staged.
2. It is copied into its own versioned directory, then activated with one atomic write. The previous version's files stay, so a browser tab that loaded them keeps working until it reloads.
3. The engine verifies the result **through nginx**: for a shell, that the entry page answers with this release and that a missing asset is a 404; for a microfrontend, that the pointer, the manifest (against the hash the pointer records) and the entry file served are the ones just published. A failure puts the previous release back.
4. A shell's hashed assets go into the shared pool, so a tab still running the previous shell resolves its lazy chunks after a new shell is activated, and one URL can never resolve to two contents.
5. Registry writes (pointers, history) happen under a site lock that is taken over from a dead process, so concurrent publishes cannot interleave.
6. Retention (`static.retain`, default 5) never removes the active version, the one it replaced, or fewer than two versions; the engine keeps its own release directories under the usual retention.
7. `release:rollback` points one resource back to its previous release after the same checks, so a microfrontend that no longer fits a newer shell cannot be rolled back to by accident.

## Recovery

An interrupted static deployment is reconciled from what exists, not by replaying steps. `release:recover` sweeps leftover staging directories and temporary files, checks every pointer against its manifest hash and files, and then either completes the deployment forward (the new version was already active and consistent) or closes it without touching the active release. If nginx already serves a configuration for a shell release that was never activated, the previous configuration is restored from its backup; if that cannot be done, the deployment is marked as needing an operator.

## Sharing the server of an existing application (one address, one certificate)

A shell normally owns a virtual host. When the application's public address and certificate already belong to another PSO application (typically the orchestrator on port 443), the frontend can **join that server** instead of competing for it:

- The **host** declares `nginx.attachPoint: true`. Its managed file then includes `<managed directory>/attach/<host>/*.conf` in its public server and in its loopback servers. That is the only change to the host, made by one ordinary deployment of it (blue-green, `nginx -t` first, rollback as always). The directory is a subdirectory, so the http-level include of the managed directory never loads a fragment by mistake.
- The **shell** declares `nginx.attachTo: "<host>"` (`pso frontend:declare ... --attach-to <host>`). It gets no server: the engine writes only its locations (`pso-<shell>.conf`, with the same ownership marker, transaction, `nginx -t`, graceful reload and restore as any managed file) into the host's directory, serves them under its base path, and verifies the release through the host's loopback listener (`--probe-port`). An attached shell declares no `api`: it reaches the orchestrator through the host's own routes, and its runtime configuration says so (`--orchestrator-path /`).
- Releases stay independent. Updating a microfrontend never touches nginx. Updating the shell rewrites only its fragment (the host's file is byte-identical afterwards). Deploying the host again keeps the include, so the attached frontend keeps being served. Frontend assets are never packaged in the host's release, and a frontend update never needs a host deployment or a restart.
- `location` rules decide by specificity, so the host's `/` keeps every route that is not under the shell's base path; the shell's own rules (`/commerce/...`, `/_mei/`, the asset pool) are more specific.

The shell's **runtime configuration** (`pso-runtime-config.json`: where the orchestrator is, how users sign in, which release signers are trusted) is declared too, so it is deployed and rolled back with the shell instead of being written by hand: `--orchestrator-path`, `--channels-path`, `--auth none|dev-token|oidc` with the `--oidc-*` options, `--require-signature` and `--trust-key <keyId>=<public key>`. It holds no secret.

The server's deployment policy decides which strategies it accepts; a server provisioned before frontends existed does not list `static` in `allowedStrategies`, and the plan says so (`BLOCKED: the server policy does not allow the "static" strategy`). Only the server's administrator changes that (`pso environment:policy <application> --set allowedStrategies=...`); no declaration can.

## What was tested for interruption and TLS

A real detached deployment worker was killed with SIGKILL at several moments after it reported `SWITCHING_TRAFFIC` (inside a Linux container with a real nginx), for shells and for microfrontends, and `release:recover` was run each time. The outcomes were: completed forward (the new version was already active and consistent), rolled back (nginx already served the new shell configuration but the shell was not active, so the backup was restored) or closed without touching the active release. In every case the lock was free afterwards, no staging file was left, the registry, the files and what nginx served agreed, and the next deployment worked. Two defects were found this way and fixed: recovery could not find the nginx backup when the worker died before recording its id (it now finds it by deployment name), and an activation killed between the pointer write and the history write is now completed by writing the missing history entry.

HTTPS was tested with a real nginx and a private certificate chain that the client verified strictly (no verification was disabled): the shell over TLS, the plain port redirecting with the path kept, HSTS and the security headers, routes and missing files as above, and a client that does not trust the chain refused. TLS 1.1 was refused by the client's own minimum, so that last check does not prove the server's protocol list on its own. A certificate from a public authority was not used.

If the browser must call an identity provider's token endpoint from another origin, declare it with `--connect-src https://idp.example.com`: it is added to the Content-Security-Policy `connect-src` (https only, plain http only for localhost). Nothing else is opened.

## Limits and common mistakes

- **One service per static deployment.** A shell and each microfrontend are separate deployments, which is what allows them to be released independently.
- The shell's nginx file needs `--api-port`, the loopback port that always reaches the orchestrator's active release; it is the orchestrator's `internalPort`. Without a managed orchestrator, the shell cannot reach its backend.
- When the shell uses TLS, the public port only redirects; declare `--probe-port` so the engine can verify the release through a loopback listener it adds to the same file.
- Without `--probe-port` a microfrontend is verified on the site root only (a warning is logged), not through nginx.
- Shell asset file names must be content-hashed (the production build produces them); a name that already exists in the pool with other bytes refuses the release.
- An identifier whose last segment ends in a real file extension (`/catalog/sku/acme.json`) still looks like a file. Declare such routes on the shell (`pso frontend:declare ... --route "/catalog/sku/:id"`, or `static.routes` in the declaration): a declared route is given the entry page before the file rules apply. `:name` matches one segment, a trailing `/*` anything below. Everything else that looks like a file and is missing stays a 404, and the API prefix, `/_mei/` and the asset pool never fall back to the entry page.
- An operator edit of the managed shell file through the file editor is refused by the existing lint because the file uses `root` and `alias`; change the declaration and deploy instead.

---

# Module Federation, releases and rollback

> How a MEI is loaded from an approved release manifest, how releases are published, activated and rolled back independently on a site root, what is verified before a release runs, and how the native cloud deployment reuses all of it.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> **Partially implemented.** Verified in real-browser runs on a local site root served like the generated nginx layout (31 of 31 checks): independent update, rollback, tampering, a missing release, an untrusted signer, strict Content-Security-Policy. The same functions run inside the cloud engine (see the page on native deployment, verified against a real nginx). **Not implemented:** signing with the credential-store signers of the signer commands (this uses an Ed25519 PEM key file). **Not done:** a deployment of the frontend to the Azure VM; the Commerce frontend was validated against the Azure backend through the SSH tunnel, served from a local site root.

## How the shell loads a microfrontend

The shell never loads a script URL it was handed. Its **runtime configuration** (published by the deployment next to the shell, never built into it) lists each approved MEI and where its release pointer is. Loading `mei-customers` does:

1. read `/_mei/mei-customers/active.json`, a tiny never-cached pointer to the active version and the SHA-256 of its manifest;
2. fetch the manifest `v/<version>/pso-manifest.json` and check that it matches that hash;
3. validate it: name, host, shared-context contract, shared dependency versions (React is a singleton: same major, and the shell not older than the MEI);
4. verify the Ed25519 signature when the site requires one (`requireSignature`) or when a signature and trusted keys are both present;
5. load the entry with a Subresource Integrity hash taken from the manifest, and every chunk with hashes embedded at build time;
6. check that the module is a PSO microfrontend of the expected name and compatible contract.

Locations must be same-origin under `/_mei/`, or an origin the configuration lists over HTTPS. A failure at any step shows a "module unavailable" page for that MEI and nothing else; configuration, trust, compatibility and signature failures are not retried, network failures are retried a bounded number of times.

## Releases on a site root

```bash
pso frontend:config --site ./site --auth oidc --oidc-issuer https://idp.example --oidc-authorize https://idp.example/authorize --oidc-token https://idp.example/token --oidc-client commerce-web --require-signature --trust-key release.pem --key-id release-1
pso frontend:build --base-path /commerce/ --sign-key release.pem --key-id release-1
pso frontend:publish fei-commerce --site ./site --base-path /commerce/
pso frontend:publish customers --site ./site
pso frontend:releases --site ./site
pso frontend:rollback customers --site ./site
pso frontend:nginx --site /srv/pso/sites/commerce --base-path /commerce/
```

A published version is **immutable**: publishing the same version with different bytes is refused, and nothing is ever deleted by publishing. Activation is one atomic write of the pointer, so a browser that already holds the previous version's files keeps working (they stay on disk and are served as immutable) while new page loads get the new one. Before activation PSO verifies the files against the manifest, the compatibility with the active shell (a release built for another React major or contract is refused and **not even copied**), and the signature policy. `frontend:rollback` points one MEI back to its previous (or a chosen) version after the same checks, so a MEI that is no longer compatible with a newer shell cannot be rolled back to by accident. Every activation is appended to `history.json`. The other microfrontends, the shell and the runtime configuration are not touched: in the verified scenario their files were byte-identical before and after an update.

`pso frontend:nginx` prints a same-origin configuration (`/commerce/` the shell, `/_mei/` the remotes, `/api/` the orchestrator, immutable caching for versioned files, `no-store` for pointers, and a Content-Security-Policy of `script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'`). It is printed for review; the managed nginx adapter of the cloud engine generates the same locations from the same function when a shell is deployed natively.

## When a reload is needed

A compatible MEI release needs no shell rebuild and does not interrupt other MEIs. A user who already loaded a MEI keeps that version until the page reloads; PSO does not force a reload and makes no claim of zero-downtime deployment. A shell release that changes the shared-context major version requires publishing compatible MEIs first or refusing the shell.

## Limits and common mistakes

- Publishing a MEI before the shell fails: it is checked against the host it will run in.
- Changing files inside a published version directory by hand breaks the hashes; the browser then refuses them.
- Signing protects the release you publish, not the machine that holds the key: keep the key off shared servers.
- Rolling back the pointer re-enables an older signed release; protect write access to `active.json` like any deployment credential.

---

# FEI and MEI security model

> The frontend trust model stated plainly: what the shell protects, what the browser cannot protect, how remote code, tokens, redirects, CSRF and content policy are handled, and which claims PSO deliberately does not make.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** by unit tests and real-browser negative scenarios (tampered chunk and entry refused by integrity, untrusted signer refused, missing release, unauthorized route, strict CSP with no violations). Items marked "not provided" are limits, not oversights.

## The trust model in four sentences

The **orchestrator and the services** are the security boundary: they verify tokens (JWT/JWKS), scopes, tenants and business rules on every request. The **browser is not trusted**: every check in a guard, a middleware or a hidden button is a user-experience decision that anyone with developer tools can bypass. **Module Federation runs trusted remote code in the same JavaScript context as the shell**: it is not a sandbox, and PSO does not claim client-side code can contain a malicious microfrontend. So **every MEI is held to the same release standard as the shell**.

## What PSO does about it

| Risk | Control |
|---|---|
| Wrong or swapped remote code | locations come from the runtime configuration; manifests are hashed and optionally Ed25519-signed; scripts load with Subresource Integrity; same-origin or listed HTTPS origins only |
| Tampered file on the server | SRI makes the browser refuse it (verified for an entry and a chunk) |
| Incompatible release reaching users | contract and shared-dependency checks at publish time, again at load time |
| Token theft by another MEI | the token is held inside the session manager; the shared context has no token, refresh or setter; the `api` client attaches it |
| Credentials in bundles | none are generated; `PSO_ALLOW_DEV_TOKEN` is the only credential-related build switch and shows a banner |
| Open redirect | `returnTo`, `navigate()` and middleware redirects accept only absolute paths inside the application |
| Arbitrary backend URLs | the API client refuses absolute URLs, `//host`, `..` and backslashes before a request exists |
| Direct broker access | Channels only; Dispatch brokers are never browser-facing |
| Path traversal | route files, manifest paths and release paths must stay inside their directory |
| XSS | React escapes by default; the templates use no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`; the generated nginx policy forbids inline and remote scripts |
| Conflicting session refreshes | one shared, in-flight refresh for the whole application |
| Credential leakage in logs | `redact` removes bearer tokens, JWTs and secret-looking fields |

The generated Content-Security-Policy is `default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'`. The whole Commerce workflow was run under it with no violations.

## CSRF and cookies

The default is bearer tokens in memory, sent in the `Authorization` header: no ambient credentials, so no CSRF. The client can send an `X-CSRF-Token` and use same-origin credentials for a cookie-based session, but **orchestrator-backed sessions are not implemented**, so that path exists in the client and is not exercised.

## Not provided

- Containment of a malicious microfrontend. Use review, signing and restricted publish rights.
- Verification of a token signature in the browser. It would add nothing: the server does it.
- A real identity provider. Authorization Code with PKCE is implemented and unit-tested against a fake provider; run it against yours before relying on it.
- Protection against someone who can write the site root: they can publish a release signed with a key you trust only if they hold that key, but they can re-point `active.json` to an older signed release.

## What was checked against a real deployment

- **Orchestrator-only.** The production bundles of the Commerce shell and the three microfrontends contain no backend host, port, private address or credential. In Chrome the page talked only to its own origin and to the identity provider, every business call went through the orchestrator's prefix with a bearer token, and the identity provider's token endpoint was the only cross-origin call (declared in `connect-src`). Module Federation is not a sandbox and a JavaScript wrapper cannot stop arbitrary browser requests: the Content-Security-Policy (`default-src 'none'`, `script-src 'self'`, `connect-src` limited to the site and the declared provider, `frame-ancestors 'none'`) and private backend networking are what do that.
- **The orchestrator does not trust the interface.** Directly, without the frontend: no token gave 401; a token with a tampered payload and an `alg: none` token gave 401; a user with no commerce scopes got 403; a read-only user could read and got 403 on a write; the refusal body is RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`. A user the shell denies is also denied by the orchestrator.
- **A Java service reads `scope` and `scp` together** (the framework's starter used to read only the first, which dropped the permissions of a Keycloak token). Services were rebuilt with the fix.
- **Release trust.** A microfrontend is loaded only from an approved release whose manifest hashes verify; when the site requires signatures the manifest's ed25519 signature must verify against a key listed in the runtime configuration, and a valid checksum on unsigned or unauthorized metadata is not trusted. Integrity is never silently disabled.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a hidden button as authorization. Add the scope to the route in the orchestrator.
- Building production with `--allow-dev-token`. It is for validation environments; it prints a banner on purpose.
- Allowing `unsafe-inline` or a CDN origin in the content policy to make something work. Fix the cause.
- Putting an API key into `FEI.pso.ts`: declarations are literals that end up in the source tree, and the runtime configuration holds no secret by design.

---

# The Frontend view in PSO Studio

> What the Frontend section of PSO Studio shows for the FEI and MEIs of a workspace (read-only by default) and the opt-in operations (validate, build, development servers, local publish and rollback) behind pso studio --frontend-ops.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> **Partially implemented, verified in a real browser** (14 of 14 checks including an axe scan with no WCAG 2 A/AA violations). The view is **read-only**: it shows and re-validates; starting, stopping, building and publishing are CLI commands. Deployments of a shell or a microfrontend made by the cloud engine are listed by the release commands (`pso release:status`, `pso release:history`); Studio's Cloud section reads the same engine state, but it was **not exercised** with a static resource, and the Frontend view itself does not show release versions.

Open Studio from the workspace (`pso studio`) and choose **Frontend**. Studio keeps its existing boundaries: it listens on loopback only, requires its access token, and the local workspace is read-only. The Frontend view uses the same analysis as `pso validate` and `pso frontend:validate`, so it cannot disagree with them, and it does not contain a second implementation of any command.

## What it shows

- **Relationships**: the FEI, each registered MEI with its mount path, development port and entry scopes, and the orchestrator they all reach through. A MEI that names a host but is not registered is marked.
- **Development servers**: whether something answers on each declared port right now (a short TCP probe; it says nothing about the health of what answers).
- **Status**: validation result, number of microfrontends and effective routes, the middleware order, the authentication mode, and whether each project's generated orchestrator contract matches the orchestrator.
- **Route ownership**: every effective browser route, which project owns it, its page or redirect and the scopes it needs.
- **Diagnostics**: the findings of `pso frontend:validate` with the exact file and a fix.
- **Operate from the CLI**: the commands for dev, build, publish, rollback and releases.

**Re-validate** re-reads the declarations and shows the new result; it changes nothing.

## Why there are no start and stop buttons

## Operations (opt-in)

By default the view is read-only, like the rest of local Studio. Start Studio with `pso studio --frontend-ops` and the view gains an **Operations** panel: **Validate**, **Build** (one project or all, with a base path), **Start dev servers**, **Stop**, **Restart**, **Publish to local site** and **Roll back on local site**, with the output of the last operation, the development-server log and a table of the releases that are active on the local site root.

Nothing in Studio implements these actions. Each one runs the same command a developer would type (`pso frontend:validate`, `pso frontend:build`, `pso frontend:dev`, `pso frontend:publish`, `pso frontend:rollback`) in the workspace, so the same validation, build, signature, compatibility and rollback code applies, and the same output is shown.

Boundaries that stay in force:

- Studio listens on loopback only and needs the access cookie from the URL it printed. A state-changing request must also come from the same origin with the `x-pso-studio` header and a JSON body, exactly like the Cloud operations.
- A project argument can only be a project of this workspace. Base paths are checked against the same grammar as the CLI. Nothing the browser sends is used as a command line or a path.
- **Publish** and **Roll back** write only into `.pso/studio-site` inside the workspace and require a typed confirmation (`publish mei-customers`, `rollback mei-customers`): the action and the project. A wrong or missing confirmation changes nothing.
- One operation runs at a time (a second request gets a 409). Output is bounded and scrubbed of anything that looks like a secret. Development servers started from Studio are stopped when Studio closes.
- Deploying to a server and rolling back there are not done from this panel: a frontend declared with `pso frontend:declare` is an ordinary deployment, so its plan, approval, deploy, active release and history are in the **Cloud** section (and `pso release:status`, `pso release:history`, `pso release:rollback`), with that section's roles and confirmations. Studio keeps no credentials of its own.

## Limits and troubleshooting

- A port shown as "not running" may be a different tool's port: the probe checks reachability only.
- Contract state is "orchestrator not analyzable" when the orchestrator's own routes do not validate; fix `pso validate` first.
- The view reads project files; after changing a declaration press **Re-validate**.
- Release versions per environment appear in `pso frontend:releases --site <dir>`, not in Studio.

---

# Frontend troubleshooting

> Symptoms you will see while developing and operating a FEI and its microfrontends, what causes each, and what to do, including errors that name the exact configuration responsible.

> [!STATUS]
> **Verified**: every entry below was observed, or is produced by a tested check. Messages are quoted as printed; ids and paths in them are illustrative.

## Symptoms

| You see | Cause | Do this |
|---|---|---|
| `PSO_FEI_ROUTE_CONFLICT ... microfrontends[2]: "mei-b" mounts "/orders/new", which overlaps "mei-a"` | two mounts overlap | give each MEI its own, non-nested prefix in `FEI.pso.ts` |
| `PSO_MEI_NOT_REGISTERED` | the MEI names a host that does not list it | `pso fei:register <name>` |
| `PSO_MEI_SCOPE_MISMATCH ... requires scope "x" to enter mei-y, but mei-y does not declare it` | the FEI gates entry on a scope the MEI does not know | add it to `security.scopes` of the MEI or remove it from the FEI entry |
| `PSO_MEI_CONTRACT_INCOMPATIBLE ... major versions differ` | the MEI was built for another shared-context major | rebuild the MEI against the shell's framework version |
| `PSO_MEI_OWN_ROUTER` | the MEI creates its own router | use `<Routes>`, `useNavigate` and `useParams` only |
| `Port 4200 (fei-shop) is already in use` | another process on the port | stop it or change the port in `pso.workspace.json` and the declaration |
| `<name> has no installed dependencies` | `npm install` was not run | `pso frontend:install` |
| Page shows "<name> is unavailable" with "the release information could not be fetched" | no active release (nothing published, or the pointer is missing) | `pso frontend:releases --site <dir>`, then publish |
| "... was refused: the manifest is not signed" / "does not match" / "not trusted" | the site requires signatures | publish a release signed with a key listed in the runtime configuration |
| "Failed to find a valid digest in the 'integrity' attribute" in the console | a served file differs from what the build recorded | republish the release; check that nothing rewrites JS on the way (minifying proxies, injected scripts) |
| `mei-customers 0.2.0 was not activated` with `shared dependency "react": the MEI needs ^19.0.0 but the host provides 18.3.1` | the release needs another React than the shell | align versions; the previous release stays active |
| `mei-customers 1.1.0 is already published with different content` | published versions are immutable | increase the version |
| Sign-in page appears again after a reload | production keeps the token in memory only | expected; you return to the page you asked for |
| `a production build refuses a development runtime configuration` | the site's configuration says `mode: development` | regenerate it with `pso frontend:config` |
| A framework update changed nothing in a project | the vendored tarball has the same name and version, so npm kept the old install | delete `node_modules/@pso` and `package-lock.json`, then `pso frontend:install` |
| On Windows Git Bash, `Invalid --base-path "C:/Program Files/Git/shop/"` | the shell rewrote an argument starting with `/` | set `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` |

## A microfrontend is blank in the shell but works standalone

The usual causes are a second copy of React or React Router (the shared singletons are declared for you; do not override them in `rspack.config.ts`), a global CSS selector colliding with the shell, or a router created inside the MEI. `pso frontend:validate` finds the last one. Open the console: a version mismatch is reported by Module Federation with both versions.

## More symptoms seen while hardening

- **After sign-in the page shows "Access denied: missing scope".** The token has the permissions in a claim the shell did not read. The shell reads the configured claim and `scp`; check the provider's mapper (Keycloak: a realm-role mapper to `scp`) and that the access token (not only the ID token) carries them.
- **"Sign-in failed: there is no sign-in in progress" right after a successful login.** The callback was processed twice. Current builds redeem the code once; an older build needs rebuilding with the current `@pso/frontend-react`.
- **The token request is blocked by the browser.** The Content-Security-Policy `connect-src` does not list the provider: redeploy the shell with `--connect-src https://your-idp`, and add the application's origin to the provider's web origins.
- **A route with a dot in its last segment returns 404 from nginx.** Its ending looks like a real file extension. Declare it on the shell: `--route "/catalog/sku/:id"`.
- **Studio shows no Operations panel.** Start it with `pso studio --frontend-ops`; without the option it is read-only by design.
- **Tests that use React fail with "Invalid hook call" or `useContext` of null on Windows.** Run them from the upper-case drive spelling (`D:/...`); the lower-case one loads the framework twice.

## Collect this before asking for help

`pso frontend:validate --json`, `pso frontend:inspect`, the browser console, the correlation id shown on an error (it appears in the orchestrator's logs), and `pso frontend:releases --site <dir>` for release problems.

## Limits

- Studio shows the same findings (Frontend view) but cannot repair them.
- Dev servers use `localhost`; on machines where it resolves to IPv6 only, probes written for `127.0.0.1` will report a server as down.

---

# Several shells (FEIs) in one workspace

> How 0.2.0 runs several independent application shells side by side, what each one owns, how collisions are detected, and how public and authenticated routes are declared per shell.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** in real Chrome with the reference workspace: `fei-shop` (public home and catalog, protected cart) and `fei-admin` (fully authenticated, permission-protected users) on their own hosts, their own OIDC clients, their own runtime configurations and sites.

0.1 allowed one FEI per workspace. In 0.2.0 a workspace may have several, each an **independent application** with its own:

| | per shell |
|---|---|
| identity and port | `fei-shop` on 4200, `fei-admin` on 4201 (collisions are errors) |
| host and base path | `shop.<domain>/`, `admin.<domain>/` (or one host with distinct, non-nested base paths) |
| authentication | `security.authentication` in its own `FEI.pso.ts` |
| OIDC client and redirect URIs | one client per shell in the generated realm |
| microfrontends | each MEI belongs to one shell (`host` in its `MEI.pso.ts`) |
| runtime configuration, build output, version | its own site under `.infra/sites/<env>/<fei>` |
| publication lifecycle | `pso frontend:publish <fei|mei> --env <env>` targets the right site |

```bash
pso create fei shop
pso create fei admin
pso create mei catalog --host shop
pso create mei users --host admin
pso fei:register catalog --public
pso fei:register users --scopes users:admin   # also added to mei-users' security.scopes
```

With several shells, a command that acts on one of them is told which one (`--host`, `--fei`), or infers it from the MEI's own `host`; it never guesses. A MEI registered in a shell it is not built for is an error (`PSO_MEI_HOST_MISMATCH`), as is a MEI whose `host` is not a FEI of the workspace (`PSO_MEI_HOST_UNKNOWN`). Route conflicts are checked inside each application: two shells may both have a public `/`.

## Public and authenticated routes per shell

Public pages are declared by the shell that owns them, never by a microfrontend:

```ts
// fei-shop/ROUTES.pso.ts: the home page is public
{ path: "/", page: "./src/pages/Home.tsx", title: "Home", public: true }

// fei-shop/FEI.pso.ts
microfrontends: [
  { name: "mei-catalog", path: "/catalog", public: true },          // every catalog route is public
  { name: "mei-cart", path: "/cart", scopes: ["cart:write"] },     // needs a session and the scope
]
```

`fei-admin` declares no public route: every page asks for a session. Contradictions are refused at validation time: a public route with scopes (`PSO_ROUTE_PUBLIC_SCOPES`), `public` and `meta.public` disagreeing (`PSO_ROUTE_PUBLIC_AMBIGUOUS`), a microfrontend making its own route public (`PSO_ROUTE_PUBLIC_MEI`), scopes in a shell without authentication (`PSO_FEI_AUTH_CONTRADICTION`), a public path the microfrontend does not route (warning `PSO_FEI_PUBLIC_PATH_UNROUTED`). Sign-in redirects stay inside the origin (`returnTo` is a same-origin path), and `/auth/callback` is served by the shell itself.

A public page does not make any backend endpoint public: the orchestrator and each service keep authenticating every request. An endpoint is public only when its route says so (`security: { public: true }`) and the service that serves it declares the same rule (`pso make:resource --public` writes both). In the reference workspace the shop's public catalog reads `GET /catalog/products` (declared public on both tiers), while `/api/accounts/users` still answers 401 to a visitor on the shop's own origin.

## What goes wrong
- `This workspace has 2 FEIs: pass --fei <name>`: commands never guess the shell.
- A MEI built for one shell and registered in another: `PSO_MEI_HOST_MISMATCH`.
- A public page that calls a protected endpoint gets 401 for visitors: declare the endpoint public on both tiers, or show the data only after sign-in.

---

# The infrastructure engine (0.2.0)

> Why PSO 0.2.0 resolves infrastructure from declarations, what the engine does in each step, and where its responsibilities stop.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified (0.2.0).** Unit and CLI tests with real files, the real Docker Compose parser and the real nginx; a reference workspace (`fixtures/pso-reference`: one orchestrator, two Spring services, two shells, three microfrontends, Keycloak, TLS and mutual TLS) provisioned, started in containers, validated through the edge, used in real Chrome and deployed with an automatic rollback. **Not done:** a deployment to a remote production host (PSO produces a reviewable bundle for it), DNS record creation at a provider.

In 0.1 a developer described the application declaratively (services, routes, contracts, frontends) but still wrote the infrastructure by hand: certificates, the identity provider's clients and redirect URIs, nginx server blocks, compose files, environment variables in each service, and the same host names repeated in all of them. Every new frontend or service meant editing five files consistently. 0.2.0 removes that work: **the developer declares what the application needs, PSO resolves how it is configured and run.**

## What you declare, and what PSO derives

| Source of truth | Declares |
|---|---|
| `pso.workspace.json` | services, ports, roles, dependencies, databases, frontends |
| `ROUTES.pso.ts`, `FEI.pso.ts`, `MEI.pso.ts` | routes, public and protected pages, scopes, microfrontend mounts |
| `pso.infra.json` (new, optional) | environments (local, staging, production), host names, where TLS material and secrets come from, the identity provider, which hops use mutual TLS, container limits |

Nothing in `pso.infra.json` repeats the workspace: it only says what the application code cannot know. Without it, PSO derives a single local development environment. `pso infra:init` writes a starting contract.

From these three sources the engine derives every resource of an environment: a development certificate authority and one certificate per container (with exactly the names its clients verify), the mutual-TLS client identity of the orchestrator, generated development secrets, the Keycloak realm (one OIDC client per shell, its redirect URIs and web origins computed from the hosts), the edge gateway's nginx configuration (one server per host), the static server of each shell, each shell's runtime configuration, the container topology, the proposed hosts entries and the environment of each service when it runs as a local process.

## The pipeline

1. **Discover.** The workspace file, the frontend declarations and the contract are read as data.
2. **Build a dependency graph.** Resources depend on each other (a certificate on its authority, a runtime configuration on its site directory); the graph also gives the container startup order.
3. **Identify missing or invalid resources.** Each resource is inspected against the disk without changing anything: `pso infra:plan`.
4. **Generate what is authorized.** In a development environment PSO generates development material. In staging and production it never generates certificates, keys or secrets: those are supplied by the operator, and PSO only verifies them.
5. **Configure references.** Generated configuration refers to certificates by mount path and to secrets by name (`secret://db-catalog`), never by value.
6. **Validate connectivity and security.** `pso infra:validate --probe` checks the running environment for real, through the edge, with certificate verification.
7. **Reconcile.** When a service, a shell or a microfrontend registration changes, the affected resources are updated automatically (development) or reported (other environments).
8. **Report actionable errors.** Every refusal names the declaration responsible and the command that fixes it.

## Why it is built this way

- **Idempotency is the safety property.** Running `pso infra:apply` twice changes nothing the second time; a valid certificate, key or secret is never regenerated because a command ran again. Regeneration happens only when something is missing, invalid (wrong authority, missing host name, mismatching key, expired) or when you ask for it (`pso infra:rotate`).
- **Ownership is explicit.** A resource is either PSO's (`owner: pso`) or the operator's (`owner: external`). PSO writes only its own resources, and only files whose content it can prove it wrote (their hash is in `.infra/state.json`). A hand edit is *drift*: reported, never overwritten silently.
- **The engine composes existing PSO pieces.** The edge and shell servers use the same nginx renderer as `pso frontend:nginx` and the runtime agent; shells are published with the same release engine as `pso frontend:publish`; containers run on Docker Engine and Compose. PSO owns the topology, the order of operations and the verification, not the container runtime.
- **Production never runs on untrusted material.** A production environment that names the development authority is a contract error, local secret storage is refused outside development, and `dev-token` sign-in is refused in production.

## Where to go next

- [The infrastructure contract and the `.infra` directory](infrastructure/contract.md)
- [Resource lifecycle: ownership, drift, repair, recovery](infrastructure/resource-lifecycle.md)
- [Security model, certificates and secrets](infrastructure/security-and-certificates.md)
- [Hosts and environments](infrastructure/hosts-and-environments.md)
- [The container engine](infrastructure/containers.md)
- [Local development](infrastructure/local-development.md)
- [Deployment](infrastructure/deployment.md)
- [Studio infrastructure console and API Client](infrastructure/studio-api-client.md)
- [Migrating a 0.1 workspace](infrastructure/migration.md)
- [Troubleshooting](infrastructure/troubleshooting.md)

## Limits of 0.2.0
- Remote deployment is a reviewable bundle (or the 0.1 cloud engine); `pso deploy --env` starts containers only on a Docker Engine this machine reaches.
- DNS records are never created; certificates for staging and production are never generated; system trust stores are never changed.
- Keycloak changes after the first import of a staging or production realm are applied through its administration API, not by PSO.
- The engine reads FEIs statically: a FEI declaration with errors is skipped until `pso frontend:validate` passes.
