# The infrastructure contract and the .infra directory

> Every member of pso.infra.json, the defaults PSO derives, the validation rules, and the layout and ownership of the managed .infra directory.

`pso.infra.json` sits next to `pso.workspace.json`. It is optional: without it PSO uses one local development environment (`local`, domain `pso.localhost`, runtime `process`, development TLS and local secrets). `pso infra:init` writes a starting contract derived from the workspace.

## A complete example

This is the contract of the reference workspace (`fixtures/pso-reference`), validated by the tests:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "defaultEnvironment": "local",
  "environments": {
    "local": { "kind": "development", "domain": "pso.localhost", "runtime": "docker", "httpsPort": 8443,
               "tls": { "source": "pso-dev-ca" }, "secrets": { "provider": "local" }, "dns": { "provider": "none" } },
    "staging": { "kind": "staging", "domain": "staging.pso.localhost", "runtime": "docker", "httpsPort": 9443,
                 "tls": { "source": "external", "dir": "./ops/staging/tls" },
                 "secrets": { "provider": "file", "dir": "/run/pso-staging-secrets" },
                 "dns": { "provider": "external" }, "deploy": { "target": "bundle" } }
  },
  "identity": { "provider": "keycloak", "realm": "pso-reference",
                "users": [ { "username": "ana", "scopes": ["catalog:read", "cart:write", "users:admin", "accounts:read"] },
                           { "username": "bob", "scopes": ["catalog:read", "cart:write"] } ] },
  "services": { "accounts": { "mtls": true } }
}
```

## Members

| Member | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `schemaVersion` | always `1` | required |
| `defaultEnvironment` | the environment used when `--env` and `PSO_INFRA_ENV` are absent | the only one declared |
| `environments.<name>.kind` | `development`, `staging` or `production`: decides what PSO may generate | required |
| `environments.<name>.domain` | DNS suffix: a host label `shop` becomes `shop.<domain>` | required |
| `environments.<name>.runtime` | `process` (`pso dev`) or `docker` | `process` |
| `environments.<name>.hosts` | explicit fully-qualified names for a FEI (by its name), `api` or `identity` | derived |
| `environments.<name>.httpsPort` | public HTTPS port of the edge gateway | `8443` (development), `443` |
| `environments.<name>.publishServices` | development only: also publish every service container on `127.0.0.1:<port>` | `false` |
| `environments.<name>.tls` | `{ "source": "pso-dev-ca" }` or `{ "source": "external", "dir": "<directory in the PSO layout>" }` | development: `pso-dev-ca`; otherwise `external` |
| `environments.<name>.secrets` | `{ "provider": "local" \| "env" \| "file", "dir": "/run/secrets" }` | development: `local`; otherwise `env` |
| `environments.<name>.dns` | `{ "provider": "none" \| "hosts-file" \| "external" }`: PSO never creates DNS records | `none` |
| `environments.<name>.identity` | for an external provider: `issuer`, `jwksUri`, `authorizationEndpoint`, `tokenEndpoint`, `logoutEndpoint` (https) | - |
| `environments.<name>.deploy` | `{ "target": "docker" \| "bundle", "dockerContext": "<context>" }` | development: `docker`; otherwise `bundle` |
| `identity.provider` | `keycloak` (a container PSO configures), `pso-dev` (offline development tokens), `external`, `none` | `none` |
| `identity.realm`, `.host`, `.audience` | realm name, host label, the audience every token carries | workspace name, `auth`, `pso-api` |
| `identity.users` | development users (`username`, `scopes`): their passwords are generated secrets, never written here | - |
| `api.host` | host label of the API (the orchestrator through the edge) | `api` |
| `frontends.<fei>` | `host` label, `basePath` (`/admin/`), runtime sign-in `auth` (`oidc`, `dev-token`, `none`), OIDC `clientId` | `<fei without fei->`, `/`, `oidc` when an identity provider exists, the FEI name |
| `services.<name>` | `mtls: true` (the orchestrator must present a client certificate), `resources` (`memory`, `cpus`), `secrets` (declared secret names mounted as files) | - |
| `secrets.<name>` | declared application secrets: `description`, `generate: "random"` (development only) | - |
| `docker` | Compose `project` name, `logs` (`maxSize`, `maxFile`), default `resources`, `images` (`nginx`, `postgres`, `keycloak`) | `<workspace>-<env>`, `10m`/3 |

## Rules the contract enforces

They are errors, not warnings, because each one would produce an environment that is insecure or cannot work:

- `PSO_INFRA_TLS_PRODUCTION`: production cannot use the development authority. `PSO_INFRA_SECRETS_LOCAL`: staging and production cannot keep secrets in PSO's local store.
- `PSO_INFRA_SECRET_IN_CONTRACT`: a member named like a value (`value`, `password`, `secret`, `key`) under `secrets`, or a credential on a development user. The contract is committed; values are not.
- `PSO_INFRA_IDENTITY_DEV`: the `pso-dev` identity cannot serve a production environment. `PSO_INFRA_DEV_TOKEN_PRODUCTION`: `dev-token` sign-in is refused in production.
- `PSO_INFRA_HOST_CONFLICT`: two shells on one host with overlapping base paths (a shell at `/` would swallow `/admin/`), or a shell on the API's or the identity provider's host.
- `PSO_INFRA_UNKNOWN_SERVICE`, `PSO_INFRA_UNKNOWN_FRONTEND`, `PSO_INFRA_UNKNOWN_SECRET`: the contract names something the workspace does not declare.
- `PSO_INFRA_RESERVED_NAME`: a service named `edge`, `idp`, `*-db` or `*-client` would collide with the generated topology.

## The `.infra` directory

`.infra/` is managed by PSO and excluded from version control (`pso infra:apply` adds `.infra/` to `.gitignore` and writes `.infra/.gitignore`). Everything in it can be regenerated from the declarations, except development key material and secrets, which are reused on purpose.

| Path | Content | Sensitive |
|---|---|---|
| `ca/<env>/ca.crt`, `ca.key` | development certificate authority | key: yes |
| `certs/<env>/<name>/tls.crt`, `tls.key`, `ca.crt` | one certificate per container (`edge`, the orchestrator and its `-client` identity, each service, `idp`) | key: yes |
| `secrets/<env>/<name>` | development secrets (database passwords, Keycloak administrator, development users, API client) | yes |
| `identity/<env>/realm.json`, `signing-key.pem`, `jwks.json` | Keycloak realm (passwords are placeholders) or the pso-dev signing key and public keys | key: yes |
| `nginx/<env>/edge.conf`, `<fei>.conf` | edge gateway and shell static servers | no |
| `sites/<env>/<fei>/` | each shell's site root: published shell and microfrontend releases, `pso-runtime-config.json` | no |
| `docker/<env>/compose.yml`, `compose.deps.yml` | container topology; dependencies for local processes | no |
| `hosts/<env>.hosts` | proposed hosts entries | no |
| `env/<env>/<service>.env` | environment of a service as a local process (`secret://` references) | no |
| `state.json` | ownership, file hashes, facts (fingerprints, expiry), last provisioning | no secret |
| `journal/`, `state.lock` | interrupted-write records, the provisioning lock | no |
| `logs/infra.log` | operational log (redacted) | no secret |
| `backups/<tx>/` | hand-edited files replaced by `pso infra:repair` | as the original |
| `deploy/<env>/` | release records and bundles (configuration only) | no |

Key and secret files are readable by their owner only: mode `0600` on POSIX; on Windows the inherited access list is removed and only the current user and SYSTEM keep access. Docker Desktop reads such files through its file sharing (verified with the real nginx reading a restricted key).

## What goes wrong most often
- Putting a value in `secrets` or a password on a development user: refused (`PSO_INFRA_SECRET_IN_CONTRACT`). Values belong to the environment's provider.
- Declaring a staging environment with `tls.source: "external"` but a `tls.dir` that does not exist on the deployment host: the resources stay `external-unverified` locally and are listed as prerequisites by `pso deploy --env staging --dry-run`.
- Naming a service in `services` that the workspace does not declare (`PSO_INFRA_UNKNOWN_SERVICE`): the contract never creates a service.

---

# Resource lifecycle: ownership, drift, repair and recovery

> How PSO decides what to create, update or leave alone, how it detects hand edits, how an interrupted run is completed, and how rotation works.

Every resource has a **status** (what the disk says now) and a planned **action** (what applying would do). `pso infra:plan` shows both and changes nothing.

| Status | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `ok` | present and valid | none |
| `missing` | not there yet | `create` (if PSO may generate it), otherwise `supply` |
| `invalid` | there but unusable: wrong authority, missing host name, mismatching key, expired, unreadable | `replace` (PSO-owned) or `supply` |
| `outdated` | configuration PSO wrote, and the declarations changed since | `update` |
| `drifted` | configuration whose content PSO did not write (edited by hand, or never PSO's) | `repair`, only with `pso infra:repair --yes` |
| `exposed` | a key or secret readable by others | `protect` (restrict the permissions; nothing is regenerated) |
| `external-ok` / `external-missing` | an operator-supplied resource, verified / absent or invalid | none / `supply` |
| `external-unverified` | supplied on the deployment host, not visible from this machine (a secret variable, a remote directory) | listed as a deployment prerequisite |

## Idempotency

A second `pso infra:apply` reports `nothing to do`. Certificates are compared with what they must be (issuer, names, validity, key), not with when they were made: a certificate is replaced only when it would not work. Secrets are never regenerated once they exist. Rendered configuration is deterministic (no timestamps, stable ordering), so "nothing changed" is detectable byte for byte.

## Reconciliation

`pso create service|fei|mei`, `pso fei:register` and `pso fei:unregister` call the engine after they change a declaration. Development environments are reconciled at once and the command prints what changed and which running containers need a restart. For example, creating a third shell gives:

```text evidence="verified"
reconciled "local" after creating FEI "fei-partners": cert:edge, identity:realm, nginx:edge, site:fei-partners, nginx:fei-partners, runtime-config:fei-partners, docker:compose, hosts
  restart if the stack is running: pso docker:restart edge fei-partners idp --env local
```

The edge certificate is re-issued because it must name the new host, the realm gets the shell's OIDC client with its redirect URIs, the edge routes the new host, and nothing else changes (the other certificates keep their fingerprints). Staging and production environments that were provisioned before only get the list of affected resources and `pso infra:apply --env <name> --yes`.

## Drift and ownership

PSO records the SHA-256 of every file it writes in `.infra/state.json`. On the next run:

- content equal to what PSO would write now: `ok`;
- content equal to what PSO wrote last time, but the declarations changed: `outdated`, updated automatically;
- any other content: `drifted`. Apply skips it and says so; `pso infra:repair` (which needs `--yes` when it would overwrite something) regenerates it and keeps the edited file in `.infra/backups/<run>/`.

The right place for a change is the declaration it derives from; a hand edit of generated configuration is lost on repair by design. Developer-owned files are never managed: a service `Dockerfile` is created once when missing (marked as generated) and never overwritten afterwards; the 0.1 `docker-compose.yml` is never touched.

## Interrupted runs

Every write is atomic (a temporary file in the same directory, then one rename). Before writing a resource the engine records it in `.infra/journal/`; the record is removed when the resource is complete. A certificate is written key first and certificate last, so an interruption leaves a pair that does not match, which the next inspection detects as invalid. The next `pso infra:apply` reports the interrupted resources, removes partial temporary files and completes the work. One lock (`.infra/state.lock`) keeps two provisioning runs apart; a lock left by a process that no longer exists is taken over and reported.

## Rotation

Rotation is explicit: `pso infra:rotate <resource> --env <name> --yes` replaces a valid certificate, authority, signing key or secret. Rotating the authority re-issues every certificate it signed in the same run. Running containers keep the old material until they restart; the command lists them. Operator-supplied material is rotated at its source.

## Recovery and what goes wrong
- An interrupted run: the next `pso infra:apply` reports it and completes it; nothing to do by hand.
- Restoring `.infra/state.json` from another machine makes every generated file look drifted: delete the file and run `pso infra:repair --yes` to record fresh hashes (key material and secrets are kept).
- Deleting `.infra/ca/<env>` replaces the development authority on the next apply and re-issues every certificate of that environment.

---

# Security model, certificates and secrets

> TLS on every hop, mutual TLS, the development certificate authority, operator-supplied certificates, JWT keys and JWKS, the identity provider's clients, secret references and how PSO keeps key material out of files, images, logs and Studio.

## TLS on every hop

In the generated container topology every connection that carries a credential is TLS, verified against the environment's authority and the peer's name:

```architecture title="Hops of the container topology"
Browser (client)
  edge (proxy) # TLS for every public host; unknown hosts are refused (handshake fails or 421)
Edge network
  shell containers (shell) # static, public files only: no credential reaches them
  orchestrator (orchestrator) # inbound TLS (PSO_HTTP_TLS_CERT_FILE), verified by the edge as "gateway"
  identity provider (security) # TLS, verified by the edge as "idp"
Internal network
  services (service) # TLS; mutual TLS when services.<name>.mtls is true
  databases (database) # one per service, password from a secret file
```

The orchestrator terminates TLS itself (0.2.0: `PSO_HTTP_TLS_CERT_FILE`, `PSO_HTTP_TLS_KEY_FILE`, optional `PSO_HTTP_TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE` for inbound mutual TLS), so the hop behind the edge is encrypted too. With `"mtls": true` a service requires a client certificate issued by the environment's authority; the orchestrator presents its own client identity (`cert:<orchestrator>-client`). The reference workspace verifies it for real: a client without a certificate gets `tlsv13 alert certificate required` from `accounts`.

## Certificates

- **Development** (`tls.source: "pso-dev-ca"`): PSO creates one authority per environment and one certificate per container, ECDSA P-256, with exactly the names its clients verify (the container name, `localhost` for its own health check, and the public hosts for the edge). The authority exists only on this machine; PSO never installs it in a system trust store. A browser trusts it only if you install it yourself (the validation scenarios pin the edge certificate's public key instead).
- **Staging and production** (`tls.source: "external"`): the operator supplies the files in the same layout (`ca.crt`, `<name>/tls.crt`, `<name>/tls.key`). PSO verifies them where they are (chain, key, names, validity) and mounts them read-only; it never writes them and never generates production certificates.
- **Expiry**: certificates closer than 30 days to expiry are warnings in `pso infra:plan`, `infra:status`, `infra:validate` and Studio. Nothing is replaced silently; `pso infra:rotate` replaces on purpose.

## Identity provider, JWT and JWKS

- `keycloak`: PSO generates the realm: one role per scope found in the declarations, one public OIDC client per shell (Authorization Code with PKCE S256, redirect URIs and web origins computed from the shell's host, base path and development server), an audience mapper (`pso-api`) and a role-to-`scp` mapper. Development users get generated passwords (placeholders in the realm, resolved from secret files when Keycloak starts). A development-only confidential client (`pso-api-client`) serves request tools such as the Studio API Client.
- The `iss` claim is the address the browser uses (`https://auth.<domain>:<port>/realms/<realm>`); services fetch the keys from the provider's internal name. That binding is declared explicitly (`PSO_JWT_JWKS_TRUSTED_HOSTS`, `PSO_JWT_JWKS_PRIVATE_HOSTS`, the authority in `PSO_JWT_JWKS_CA_FILE`): the orchestrator refuses a key host that is not bound to the issuer.
- `pso-dev`: an ES256 signing key in `.infra/identity/<env>/signing-key.pem`, public keys served by the edge; `pso infra:token --user <name>` signs development tokens. Refused in production.
- `external`: PSO only configures issuer, audience and JWKS from the contract.

## Secrets

Generated configuration contains **references**, never values. A service receives a secret as a file under `/run/secrets` (Compose secrets); Spring reads it as a configuration property through `configtree`, Postgres through `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE`, Keycloak through a start script that reads the file. No value appears in the compose file, the environment section, an image or a log. One provider per environment:

| Provider | Value lives in | Allowed in |
|---|---|---|
| `local` | `.infra/secrets/<env>/<name>`, owner-only | development |
| `env` | `PSO_SECRET_<NAME>` injected by the platform | all |
| `file` | `<secrets.dir>/<name>`, a mounted secret file | all |

For local processes, `.infra/env/<env>/<service>.env` holds `DB_PASSWORD=secret://db-catalog`; `pso dev` resolves the reference into the child's environment at start.

## What PSO never does

- install an authority or change a system trust store, edit the system hosts file without `--apply --yes`, or create DNS records;
- generate certificates, keys or secrets for staging or production;
- print key material or secret values: `pso infra:inspect` and Studio show fingerprints, names, dates, sources and lengths; every log line and `docker:logs` output is redacted (private keys, JWTs, `password=`/`token=` values, bearer tokens and every secret value PSO has seen);
- commit or bake secrets: `.infra/` is ignored, `pso infra:validate` fails when a secret value appears in a generated file, in `.env` or in the 0.1 compose file, or when `.infra/secrets` is tracked by git.

## Limits
- The development authority is not a PKI: no revocation, no hardware key protection, no audit trail. It exists so that development runs with real verification.
- Response bodies in the Studio API Client are masked only for values PSO knows are secret; a service that returns another credential in its body shows it to the developer who sent the request.

---

# Hosts and environments

> How PSO resolves host names, origins, OIDC redirect URIs, web origins and the addresses each component uses, in development, staging and production, and what it never does with DNS.

## Host names

Each environment has a `domain`. A shell `fei-shop` is served on `shop.<domain>` (its host label is the name without `fei-`, overridable with `frontends.<fei>.host`), the API on `api.<domain>`, the identity provider on `auth.<domain>`. `environments.<env>.hosts` can name any of them explicitly. Every name derived here is used consistently in the edge configuration, the edge certificate, the realm's redirect URIs and web origins, each shell's runtime configuration and the hosts entries; there is no second place to edit.

The development default domain is `pso.localhost`: Chrome, Edge and Firefox resolve every `*.localhost` name to this machine, so no hosts file is needed for a browser. Other clients (curl, Node) need either the hosts block (`pso infra:hosts --apply --yes`, which needs administrator rights for the system file and only changes PSO's marked block) or an explicit mapping; PSO's own probes and the Studio API Client map the environment's hosts to loopback themselves.

## Origins and OIDC addresses

For a shell at `https://shop.pso.localhost:8443/` PSO derives:

| Value | Example | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| origin | `https://shop.pso.localhost:8443` | edge server, realm web origins (CORS of the token endpoint) |
| redirect URIs | `https://shop.pso.localhost:8443/auth/callback`, plus `http://localhost:4200/auth/callback` in development | realm client |
| post-logout URIs | `https://shop.pso.localhost:8443/`, plus the development server | realm client |
| runtime configuration | issuer, endpoints, client id `fei-shop` | `/pso-runtime-config.json` of that shell |

The API is same-origin for every shell (`/api` on the shell's host goes to the orchestrator), so no CORS is needed between a shell and the API.

## Addresses: host versus container

A container never reaches another one through `localhost`: inside a container, `localhost` is the container itself. PSO resolves every address for the place it is used from:

| Caller | Reaches `catalog` at | Reaches the identity provider's keys at |
|---|---|---|
| a container | `https://catalog:8081` | `https://idp:8443/...` |
| a local process (`pso dev`) | `http://127.0.0.1:8081` | `https://127.0.0.1:8443/...` |
| a browser | through the edge only | through `https://auth.<domain>:<port>` |

`pso infra:inspect` prints both columns; Studio's Hosts page shows them.

## Development, staging and production

| | development | staging | production |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS | PSO development authority | operator's (development authority allowed with a warning) | operator's only |
| secrets | `local` (generated) | `env` or `file` | `env` or `file` |
| edge port | loopback only | all interfaces | all interfaces |
| internal network | reachable for debugging | isolated from the host | isolated from the host |
| sign-in | OIDC, dev-token allowed | OIDC | OIDC only |
| Keycloak (when used) | `start-dev`, realm re-imported on each start | `start`; production database is a prerequisite | `start`; production database is a prerequisite |
| deployment target | `docker` (this machine) | `bundle` | `bundle` |

## DNS

PSO never pretends to have created a record. `dns.provider: "external"` means the records are yours to create; `pso deploy --env <name> --dry-run` lists every host that must resolve to the deployment host as a prerequisite. `hosts-file` is a development tool and is refused for staging and production.

## What goes wrong
- A non-browser client cannot resolve `*.pso.localhost`: add the hosts block (`pso infra:hosts --apply --yes`) or map the names yourself.
- Two shells on one host with base paths `/` and `/admin/`: refused, the shell at `/` would receive every request. Use two hosts or two distinct base paths.
- Calling another container through `localhost` in hand-written configuration: it reaches the caller itself. Use the service name.

---

# Identity provider reconciliation (Keycloak)

> How PSO keeps an already running Keycloak realm in line with the declarations through its administration API, what it owns, what it never touches, and which changes need authorization.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** against the running Keycloak of the reference workspace: drift created through the real administration API was detected, refused without authorization, corrected with it; an unmanaged client was left alone; users, credentials and the confidential client's secret survived; Keycloak was not restarted. A third FEI added after startup got its OIDC client live and a real browser signed in to it.

The generated realm file is imported only when a realm does not exist yet. After that, the realm lives in Keycloak, and PSO reconciles it through the **administration API**:

```bash
pso infra:identity                     # drift report, changes nothing
pso infra:identity --apply             # routine changes (create what is missing)
pso infra:identity --apply --yes       # also sensitive changes (change existing managed clients)
pso infra:identity --apply --prune --yes   # also remove managed clients whose frontend was removed
```

## What PSO owns

Every client and role PSO creates carries the attribute `pso.managed=true`. Only those are compared and changed:

| Resource | Desired state from |
|---|---|
| one public OIDC client per FEI | its host, base path and development server: redirect URIs, web origins, post-logout URIs, PKCE S256, audience and scope mappers |
| the development API client | development environments only (Studio API Client) |
| one realm role per scope | the scopes used by the FEI, MEI and route declarations and by development users |
| development users | `identity.users` (development only): missing users are created with the password from their secret; missing roles are added |

A client with the same clientId **without** the marker belongs to someone else: it is reported and never modified.

## Change classes

| Change | Class |
|---|---|
| create a missing client, role, protocol mapper, development user; add a missing role to a development user | routine: `--apply` |
| change redirect URIs, web origins, flows or mappers of an existing managed client | **sensitive**: `--apply --yes` (exit 3 without it) |
| remove a managed client that no declaration needs anymore | **sensitive**: `--apply --prune --yes` |

Never changed: users and their credentials, sessions, client secrets (they are never sent, so never reset), realm settings outside the managed objects, objects without the marker. The realm is never recreated.

## Automatic reconciliation in development

When `pso create fei`, `pso fei:register` or any change regenerates the realm in a development environment, PSO applies the routine changes to the **running** Keycloak at once, so a new shell can sign in without restarting Keycloak or opening its console:

```text evidence="illustrative"
reconciled "local" after creating FEI "fei-partners": cert:edge, identity:realm, nginx:edge, ...
  identity provider updated live: create-client fei-partners
```

Sensitive changes are never applied automatically; the command names the one to run.

## What goes wrong

- `the identity provider refused the administrator sign-in`: the `idp-admin` secret is not the one Keycloak was started with.
- `not reachable`: the stack is not running; the next start imports the realm file if the realm does not exist, otherwise run `pso infra:identity --apply` once it runs.
- A client owned by someone else with the FEI's clientId: rename the FEI's `clientId` in `pso.infra.json`, or add the marker in Keycloak to hand it over deliberately.

---

# The container engine

> The container topology PSO generates (edge, shells, orchestrator, services, databases, identity provider), dependency order, health checks, networks, volumes, secrets, limits, selective operations and safe cleanup.

PSO runs containers with **Docker Engine and Compose v2**; it does not reimplement a runtime. What PSO owns is the topology (generated from the declarations into `.infra/docker/<env>/compose.yml`), dependency resolution, the order of operations, health verification and safe defaults.

## The generated topology

| Container | Image | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `edge` | `nginx:1.27-alpine`, user 101, read-only | TLS termination, one server per public host, `/api` and `/channels` to the orchestrator, `/` to the shell, identity host to Keycloak; the only published port |
| `fei-<name>` | `nginx:1.27-alpine`, user 101, read-only | one static server per shell; its site root (`.infra/sites/<env>/<fei>`) is mounted read-only and the active release follows `fei/current.json` |
| orchestrator | built from `./<path>` | inbound TLS, upstream TLS (and mutual TLS), JWT configuration |
| each service | built from `./<path>` | TLS with its own certificate; mutual TLS when declared |
| `<service>-db` | `postgres:17-alpine` | one database per service that owns one; data in the named volume `<service>-db-data` |
| `idp` | `quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.0` | the realm generated from the declarations |

Every container gets a health check, `restart: unless-stopped`, `no-new-privileges`, all capabilities dropped (except where an image needs its own user switch), log rotation (`json-file`, `max-size`/`max-file` from the contract) and resource limits (defaults per kind, overridable per service). Two networks: `edge` (gateway, shells, orchestrator, identity provider) and `internal` (orchestrator, services, databases, identity provider; isolated from the host outside development).

Publishing a new shell or microfrontend release (`pso frontend:publish <project> --env <env>`) changes what is served without restarting any container: the release engine writes immutable versions and one pointer, and the shell container follows the pointer. On Windows hosts, where the release engine cannot create its POSIX `fei/current` symlink, the container maintains that view itself, so behaviour is identical on every host.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `pso docker:plan --env <env>` | startup order, images (built or pulled), published ports, networks, volumes, secrets (names), limits; pending infrastructure changes. Needs no Docker |
| `pso docker:build --env <env> [--service <name>] [--vendor]` | creates missing Dockerfiles (never overwrites one), vendors the framework packages with `--vendor`, builds the service images |
| `pso docker:up --env <env> [--service a,b] [--no-deps] [--build]` | development: provisions missing infrastructure and builds missing images first; checks every published host port; starts in dependency order and waits until every container is healthy |
| `pso docker:restart <name...> --env <env> [--recreate]` | restarts only those containers; `--recreate` picks up changed environment, mounts or images |
| `pso docker:ps`, `docker:logs <name>`, `docker:inspect [<name>]` | state and health, redacted logs, the effective definition as Compose resolves it |
| `pso docker:down --env <env>` | stops and removes containers and networks; **keeps volumes**. `--volumes` deletes the data too and needs `--yes` |

`--service catalog` starts `catalog` and everything it depends on (its database, the identity provider, the services it depends on); `--no-deps` starts only that container. In the reference workspace a rebuild of one service is `pso docker:up --service catalog --no-deps --build`: one image is rebuilt, one container recreated, the rest keeps running.

A running container whose mounted generated configuration changed after it started (for example the edge's nginx configuration and certificate after `pso create fei` added a host) is re-created by the next `pso docker:up`, which names it and the changed files. The identity provider is not re-created for a changed realm file: the running realm is updated through its administration API (see [identity reconciliation](infrastructure/identity-reconciliation.md)).

## Ports

In Docker mode only the edge is published (`127.0.0.1:8443` in development). Service containers are not published unless `publishServices: true`, so a container stack and local `pso dev` processes (or other applications) do not fight over ports. Before anything starts, `pso docker:up` checks that every port it will publish is free and names the container and the declaration to change; it does not discover the conflict halfway through.

## Dockerfiles and portability

Service images are built from each service's directory. A missing `Dockerfile` is generated once (marked as generated) and is yours afterwards. Framework packages that resolve to a path on this machine cannot be installed inside an image build: `pso docker:build --vendor` copies the `@pso/*` tarballs (Node) and the `com.pso` artifacts (Maven) into the service, as `pso docker:init --vendor` did in 0.1.

## Limits and what goes wrong
- A port held by another process is reported before anything starts; PSO never stops a process it did not start.
- `pso docker:down --volumes` deletes database data and needs `--yes`; Studio does not offer it.
- Images are built on this machine; a registry for remote hosts is a production prerequisite.
- Keycloak in development is re-imported on every start (realm changes apply after `pso docker:restart idp`); its users and sessions do not survive a restart.

---

# Local development

> The ways to run a workspace locally in 0.2.0, local processes with or without containerized dependencies, the full container stack, one service or one shell, and how secrets reach local processes.

| You want | Command |
|---|---|
| every service as a local process (0.1 behaviour) | `pso dev` |
| one service and what it depends on, with its database and the identity provider in containers | `pso dev --service catalog --with-dependencies` |
| the same plus the development servers of one shell | `pso dev --service gateway --with-dependencies --fei shop` |
| the whole environment in containers, followed until Ctrl+C | `pso dev --docker` |
| one environment other than the default | `pso dev --env <name> ...` |

`--with-dependencies` uses `.infra/docker/<env>/compose.deps.yml`: databases published on `127.0.0.1:5432`, `5433`, ... and Keycloak on the environment's HTTPS port, so the issuer is identical to the one the container stack uses. The services start as processes with their usual environment plus what the engine prepared in `.infra/env/<env>/<service>.env` (identity provider, database address); `secret://` references are resolved into the child process only. Verified in the reference workspace:

```text evidence="verified"
starting infrastructure dependencies: catalog-db, idp ...
[pso] catalog: infrastructure environment "local" (.infra/env/local/catalog.env): 12 variable(s), secrets resolved for DB_PASSWORD (values not shown)
Ready:
  catalog            http://127.0.0.1:8091      READY/UP
```

`pso dev --docker` is `pso docker:up` followed by waiting for Ctrl+C, which stops the containers and keeps the data volumes. `--service` and `--with-dependencies` without a contract are refused with the hint to run `pso infra:init`: a 0.1 workspace keeps behaving as before.

The development servers of shells (`pso frontend:dev`, or `--fei` above) use `dev-token` sign-in by default; the container stack uses real OpenID Connect through the environment's identity provider. `pso frontend:dev --fei <name>` starts one shell and the microfrontends it mounts.

## What goes wrong
- `--with-dependencies` publishes the identity provider on the environment's HTTPS port: a running container stack holds the same port. Stop it first (`pso docker:down`); the conflict is reported before anything starts.
- A service port held by another program: `pso dev` refuses to start that service and names the port.
- A secret that was never provisioned: the service is not started and the message names it (`pso infra:apply`).

---

# Deployment of an environment

> pso deploy --env, release records, verification through the edge, automatic rollback, the bundle target for remote hosts, and the prerequisites PSO cannot satisfy for you.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** against the local Docker Engine with the reference workspace: a verified release, then a failing release rolled back automatically. The `bundle` target is verified by the CLI tests. **Not done:** deploying to a remote host directly; for that, use the bundle, or the 0.1 cloud engine (`pso release:plan`, `pso release:deploy`).

`pso deploy --env <name> --dry-run` shows the plan: infrastructure changes, images to build, the target, prerequisites the operator must satisfy on the target (DNS records, supplied certificates and secrets), and blockers (a drifted file, an unpublished shell, a supplied resource that is missing). Nothing is deployed without `--yes`.

## What a release is

A release of an environment is the set of service images plus the generated configuration the containers mount (compose, nginx, realm, runtime configurations). It is recorded under `.infra/deploy/<env>/releases/<id>/`: image ids, copies of the configuration and their checksums. Key material and secrets are never copied: they stay with the environment's providers.

## Target `docker`

The default for development environments: the Docker Engine this machine talks to.

1. apply pending infrastructure changes (configuration only outside development);
2. build the service images; record the release; tag the images with the release id;
3. start in dependency order and wait for health;
4. verify through the edge with certificate verification: every shell and its runtime configuration, the API's readiness (directly and through a shell's same-origin path), the identity provider's discovery document (its issuer must equal what services expect), and that an unknown host is refused;
5. if starting or verification fails and a previous release exists: restore its configuration and images and start it again; the failed release stays recorded for inspection.

```text evidence="verified"
verification failed (containers did not become healthy (exit 1)): rolling back to 20261124092415-9040c90d ...
error: release 20261124092507-d3715585 failed verification and was rolled back to 20261124092415-9040c90d
```

`pso rollback --env <name> [--to <release>] --yes` restores a recorded release on purpose.

## Target `bundle`

The default for staging and production: a directory under `.infra/deploy/<env>/bundles/<release>/` with the configuration, `MANIFEST.json` (checksums and image list) and `DEPLOY.md` (prerequisites and the command to start it). It contains no key and no secret value. It is what an operator reviews and runs on the target host.

## Production prerequisites

PSO does not, and cannot, do these for you:

- DNS records for every public host (listed by `--dry-run`);
- certificates from a trusted authority in the PSO layout, on the host (`tls.dir`);
- secrets through the platform (`PSO_SECRET_<NAME>` variables, or files under `secrets.dir`);
- for Keycloak: a production database and administrator procedures (the generated realm is imported once; later realm changes are applied through the administration API);
- an image registry the target can pull from, or a build on the target;
- backups of the database volumes.

## What goes wrong
- A drifted generated file blocks the deployment: a release must be reproducible from the declarations (`pso infra:repair`).
- A shell without a published release blocks it: publish first (`pso frontend:publish <fei> --env <env>`).
- The first release of an environment has nothing to roll back to: a failed first release is left running for inspection.

---

# Remote hosts and SSH deployment

> Registering a Linux host, what PSO checks on it, the remote deployment lifecycle over SSH, status, logs, rollback and its limits, and how credentials stay out of the workspace.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** against an isolated, disposable Linux host reached over SSH (a Docker-in-Docker container with sshd, key-only login, an unprivileged deploy user): registration with a pinned host key, inspection, prerequisite checks with the operator's own certificates and secret files, a verified deployment, status and logs from the host, an automatic rollback of a failing release, an explicit rollback, the deployment lock, and the same operations from Studio. **Not done:** a deployment to a real production server (by design during framework development); installing Docker or opening firewall ports (PSO never does that).

An environment whose `deploy.target` is `ssh` is deployed to a Linux host that PSO reaches over SSH. Nothing about the host is provider-specific: any machine with Docker Engine, Compose v2 and an SSH server works.

```json
"staging": {
  "kind": "staging", "domain": "staging.example.com", "runtime": "docker", "httpsPort": 443,
  "tls": { "source": "external", "dir": "/etc/pso/staging/tls" },
  "secrets": { "provider": "file", "dir": "/etc/pso/staging/secrets" },
  "deploy": { "target": "ssh", "connection": "staging-host", "root": "/srv/pso" }
}
```

`tls.dir` and `secrets.dir` are paths **on the host**: the operator places the certificates (PSO layout) and the secret files there. They never travel from your machine.

## Registering a host

A host is a connection, registered once on each machine that deploys:

```bash
pso connection:add staging-host --host staging.example.com --user deploy --auth agent --accept-host-key SHA256:...
```

- The SSH host key is **pinned** after you approve its fingerprint (obtain it out of band); a different key later is a refusal, never a prompt. Host-key verification cannot be disabled.
- Credentials: the SSH agent (`--auth agent`), a key file that stays where it is (`--auth key --key <file>`: only its path is recorded), or a password/passphrase kept in PSO's protected credential store (`--password-stdin`, `--passphrase-stdin`). Nothing is written to the workspace or to `pso.infra.json`.
- A jump host (`--jump user@bastion:22`) is checked with the same strict options.

## What PSO checks on the host

`pso host:inspect <connection>` reads the operating system and architecture, Docker and Compose versions usable by the deploy user, free disk under the root, listening ports, existing PSO deployments and whether the host can resolve Docker Hub. `pso host:check --env <name>` turns that into the prerequisites of one environment:

| Check | Blocks the deployment when |
|---|---|
| docker / compose | missing, stopped, or the deploy user is not in the docker group |
| root | the deployment root (or its nearest existing parent) is not writable |
| disk | less than 1 GB free (warning under 4 GB) |
| ports | the edge port is used by something that is not this environment |
| tls | `ca.crt` or a `tls.crt` is missing, not issued by the authority, expired, or lacks a required name; a key is missing or unreadable (keys are only tested, never read) |
| secrets | a secret file is missing or empty (never read) |

PSO never installs packages, changes the firewall or creates users. Every check prints what the administrator must do.

## The deployment lifecycle

`pso deploy --env staging --dry-run` checks the host and prints the plan. `pso deploy --env staging --yes`:

1. resolves the environment and applies pending configuration (never generating keys or secrets outside development);
2. validates the host prerequisites (above); nothing changes on the host when one fails;
3. takes the environment's lock on the host (`<root>/<project>/.deploy-lock`, an atomic directory) and locally: concurrent deployments of the same environment are refused;
4. builds the service images here and assembles the release: generated configuration and published sites with a `MANIFEST.sha256` (no key, no secret);
5. transfers the release over SSH and verifies **every checksum on the host** before going on;
6. transfers only the images the host does not already have (compared by layer identity; `docker save | docker load`, no registry needed);
7. starts the release in dependency order and waits until every container is healthy. Containers run as the owner of the operator's certificates and secret files (written to the release's `.env` as `PSO_CONTAINER_USER`); root is refused;
8. verifies through an SSH tunnel to the host's edge, with the operator's authority: shells, runtime configurations, API readiness, the identity provider's discovery (issuer and endpoints), refusal of unknown hosts;
9. activates the release (`current` symlink, `history.json`), or
10. if starting or verification fails and a previous release exists, starts the previous release again.

## Status, logs, rollback

```bash
pso deploy:status --env staging          # active release, releases on the host, containers and health, lock
pso deploy:logs gateway --env staging --tail 200
pso rollback --env staging --yes         # the release before the active one; --to <release> for another
pso deploy:unlock --env staging --yes    # a lock an interrupted deployment left (refused if it cannot be removed)
```

## Rollback limitations

- Named volumes (databases) belong to the Compose project and are kept across releases and rollbacks.
- **Database migrations are not reverted.** Flyway migrations are forward-only: a rollback starts the previous application against the current schema. Keep migrations backward compatible (expand, then contract in a later release).
- The first release of an environment has nothing to roll back to: a failing first release is left running for inspection.
- Keycloak realm changes in staging/production are not part of a release: reconcile them with `pso infra:identity --env <name>` (see [identity reconciliation](infrastructure/identity-reconciliation.md)).

## Production prerequisites

Before the first deployment of a `production` environment, the operator provides, on the host:

- Docker Engine and Compose v2, an unprivileged deploy user in the `docker` group, SSH key or agent login (password login disabled), and the host's key fingerprint obtained out of band;
- the edge port reachable from the users (firewall and DNS are the operator's: `dns.provider: "external"`);
- certificates from the organisation's authority in the PSO layout under `tls.dir` (`ca.crt`, one `tls.crt`/`tls.key` per container with the names `pso host:check` lists), owned by the deploy user, keys readable by that user only;
- every secret file under `secrets.dir` (`pso host:check` lists the expected names; contents are never read or copied by PSO);
- backups of the database volumes: PSO keeps volumes across releases but does not back them up;
- the people: outside development the generated realm carries clients and roles but **no users**; Keycloak imports it on its first start only when the realm does not exist yet, and users, credentials and identity federation remain the organisation's. Later client changes: `pso infra:identity --env production`.

Then: `pso host:check --env production` (all green), `pso deploy --env production --dry-run`, review, `pso deploy --env production --yes`.

## What goes wrong

- `Host key verification failed` (from OpenSSH): the host presents another key than the one you approved; find out why before re-registering it.
- `... belongs to root`: give the certificates and secret files to an unprivileged user, readable by that user only.
- `another deployment of "staging" is running`: wait; `pso deploy:unlock` only after you made sure it is not.
- A port in use on the host: stop what holds it or change `httpsPort`; nothing was changed.

---

# Studio infrastructure console and API Client

> The 0.2.0 areas of PSO Studio (infrastructure, containers, hosts, certificates, deployment, two shells) and the API Client, with its execution boundary and what it never exposes.

`pso studio` adds these areas in 0.2.0; each one reads the same engine as the CLI, so Studio and the `infra:` commands cannot disagree.

| Area | Shows | Operations (`pso studio --ops`) |
|---|---|---|
| Infrastructure | environment, resources by module with owner, status and next action, validation and live probes | apply, repair |
| Containers | topology in dependency order, state and health, logs (redacted) | start all / one, restart one, stop one, stop all (volumes are kept) |
| Hosts | public hosts, addresses as containers and as processes, the hosts block | - |
| Certificates | authorities and certificates (names, expiry, fingerprint), secrets (source and length only) | rotate (development) |
| Deployment | the deployment plan, blockers, prerequisites, frontend publication, releases | - (deployments run from the CLI) |
| Frontend | every shell with its own microfrontends, public mounts | (as before, `--frontend-ops`) |
| API Client | endpoints, request builder, responses, saved requests, history | sends requests |

Without `--ops` these pages are read-only. With it, every operation needs a typed confirmation (`restart fei-admin`, `apply local`) that the server checks again, plus the same CSRF defence as every mutating Studio endpoint (same-origin `Origin`, a custom header, JSON only). A non-development environment must additionally be acknowledged by name. Deleting data volumes is a CLI-only action.

## API Client

Endpoints are discovered from the orchestrator's `ROUTES.pso.ts` (method, path, access) and the services' operation contracts. A request is built from a **target**, a method, a path, path parameters, query parameters, headers, a body (JSON, raw with a content type, form fields, or form-data with file uploads), authentication, variables and a timeout. Every method is available: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS.

Authentication:

- **Development user**: the server obtains a real token for a declared development user from the environment's Keycloak (password grant through the development-only client) or signs one with the pso-dev identity. The token never reaches the page.
- **Bearer**: a token you paste.

The response shows status, time, size, whether TLS was verified, headers and the body (JSON formatted). Requests can be cancelled; the timeout is enforced by the server.

### The execution boundary

The API Client runs requests on the Studio server so it can verify TLS against the environment's authority and resolve local host names. It is **not a proxy**:

- a request names a target (`edge:api`, `edge:<fei>`, `service:<name>` when services are published, `process:<name>`), never a URL; the server builds the URL and refuses it if the origin changed;
- paths with a scheme, a host, `//` or dot segments, forged `Host`/`Content-Length`/`Transfer-Encoding` headers, header injection and bodies on GET/HEAD are refused;
- redirects are returned, never followed; request bodies are limited to 10 MB, responses to 5 MB;
- a service that requires mutual TLS is not offered as a direct target (call it through the orchestrator);
- requests to a staging or production environment need `pso studio --ops`.

### History and collections

The last 100 requests are kept in `.pso/studio/api-history.json`, readable by its owner only: method, path, masked query values and headers (`Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED]`, cookies, API keys, anything named like a token or secret), status and time; **no bodies**. Saved requests (`.pso/studio/api-collections.json`) store sensitive header values as `{{name}}` references, and variables whose name looks sensitive are kept in memory only. Response bodies are shown as received, except values PSO knows are secret (environment secrets, issued tokens, tokens typed into the client), which are masked.

### Reference requests

A CRUD module generated by `pso create orchestrator` or `pso make:crud` ships a version-controlled collection,
`<orchestrator>/docs/api/<resource>.collection.json`. Studio lists it under **Reference requests**: options (public), create, list with
page, size and sort, filter, find, update, delete, and the expected failures (invalid body `400`, duplicate `409`, missing `404`,
unauthorized `401`, forbidden `403`). Loading one fills the builder; it is sent with a development user, never with a stored token: the
file holds **no credential**, only `"auth": { "kind": "dev-user" }`, and is safe to commit.

Requests target the orchestrator (`edge:api`), which is how clients use the API. The collection also carries one request **directly to
the microservice** (for example `process:catalog`, labelled "bypasses the orchestrator"): it is for diagnosing the service, which then
authorizes the token itself.

## Limits
- Direct requests to services need `publishServices: true` in Docker mode, or the services running as local processes.
- A service that requires mutual TLS is reached through the orchestrator only.
- WebSocket channels are not exercised by the API Client.

---

# Migrating a 0.1 workspace to 0.2.0

> What changes, what does not, the migration command with its inspection and its adoption of existing certificates and keys, and the behaviour changes to review.

A 0.1 workspace keeps working with the 0.2.0 CLI without any change: `pso dev`, `pso validate`, `pso docker:init`, `pso docker:build` (with the root `docker-compose.yml`), `pso deploy --target native|compose` and the cloud commands behave as before. The infrastructure engine is adopted explicitly.

## Upgrading the CLI first

Download the `0.2.0-rc.3` portable ZIP ([Downloads](downloads/index.md)), or update an installed distribution that trusts the same key with `pso update install --package <extracted-zip>\.pso-install\packages\0.2.0-rc.3.psopkg`. The rc.3 Windows installer is unsigned and unvalidated end to end, so it is not an upgrade path. See [Installation](getting-started/installation.md) and [release integrity and Windows installation](infrastructure/release-integrity-and-signing.md). Workspaces live outside the installation and are not touched by an update, rollback (`pso update rollback`) or removal of the portable folder.

## Preparing to migrate an application

Before running `--apply` on a real application workspace:

1. **Use the installed CLI**, not a framework checkout: `Get-Command pso -All` (PowerShell) or `type -a pso` (Git Bash) must resolve to the installation's `bin` ([installed and development CLI](devops/installed-and-development-cli.md)), and `pso --version` must print 0.2.0.
2. **Commit or back up the workspace** (a clean `git status`), so every change the migration makes is a reviewable diff.
3. **Run the inspection** (`pso workspace:migrate`) and read every finding. `conflict`, `ambiguous`, `unmapped` and `exposed-extra` are decisions for you; only `add` is applied.
4. **Check the prerequisites of the environments you will use**: Docker Desktop running for `runtime: "docker"`, free edge port (8443 by default), and for staging or production the operator-supplied certificates and secret files on the host (`pso host:check --env <name>`).
5. **Apply**, then verify: `pso infra:plan` (no changes), `pso validate`, `pso docker:up --env local`, `pso infra:validate --probe`, and the application's own tests.
6. **Keep the backup** under `.infra/backups/migrate-<time>/` until the migrated application has been verified; reverting is restoring those files (or `git checkout`).

## The migration command

```bash
pso workspace:migrate              # inspection: nothing is written
pso workspace:migrate --apply      # migration
```

It **adds** and **adopts**; it never rewrites application code, declarations, DTOs, routes, dispatch contracts, data or the 0.1 generated files. The only edit to an existing file is the narrow, backed-up Spring security addition of step 5:

1. creates `pso.infra.json` (one local development environment; identity `keycloak` when a `keycloak/` directory exists, `pso-dev` when `pso idp:dev init` was used, otherwise `none`; `--identity` overrides it);
2. adopts a valid development TLS directory (`tls/` from `pso tls:init --dev`): the authority and every certificate it issued for a declared service are copied into `.infra/` and recorded as PSO-owned, so they are **reused, not regenerated** (`tls/` itself stays: the 0.1 compose file mounts it);
3. adopts the development identity key of `pso idp:dev` when the identity is `pso-dev`;
4. excludes `.infra/` from version control and provisions the local environment: only what is still missing is generated;
5. **Spring security**: for each Spring service, compares `pso.security.rules` in `application.yml` with the routes the orchestrator declares public. A declared public route that no rule makes public was answered with 401 by the service in 0.1 (secure by default); the migration appends only the missing `PUBLIC` rule at the end of the list, marked `# added by pso workspace:migrate (0.2.0)`, after a backup to `.infra/backups/migrate-<time>/`. Existing and custom rules are kept as they are and nothing is ever made public that no declaration asks for. Cases it cannot decide are reported, not changed:

   | Finding | Meaning | Action |
   |---|---|---|
   | `covered` | an existing rule already makes the route public | none |
   | `add` | the rule is missing | added by `--apply` |
   | `conflict` | an explicit rule gives the path another access | the developer's rule is kept; decide which side is right |
   | `ambiguous` | no `application.yml`, or a `pso.security.rules` block that cannot be read with certainty (flow style, unknown keys) | add the rule by hand (the message gives it) |
   | `exposed-extra` | a service rule makes `PUBLIC` a path the orchestrator protects | review; never removed automatically |
   | `unmapped` | no controller of the service maps the route (it may be forwarded elsewhere) | add the rule by hand if the service does serve it |

6. writes `.infra/migration-0.2.0.json` with what was reused, provisioned and added.

A workspace that already has `pso.infra.json` skips steps 1–4 and still runs step 5, so it can be re-run safely after an upgrade; a second run reports `Nothing to migrate.` Verified on the reference workspace with real HTTP: before, the declared public route answered 401; after, 200 without a token while the protected routes of the same service still required one.

It refuses to run when the frontend declarations have errors. It was verified on a copy of the 0.1 Commerce workspace: no application file changed, and the environment was complete afterwards (`pso infra:plan`: 0 changes).

## Behaviour changes to review

| Change | Why | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| A workspace may have several FEIs | independent shells | commands that act on one shell take `--fei` when there are several (`fei:register`, `fei:unregister`, `frontend:dev`, `frontend:config`) |
| `security.authentication: "none"` with microfrontends that need scopes is an error (`PSO_FEI_AUTH_CONTRADICTION`) | nobody could ever enter them | enable authentication or remove the scopes |
| A public route with scopes, or `public` contradicting `meta.public`, is an error | one route, one access decision | keep one spelling; public routes need no scopes |
| `pso fei:register --scopes` also adds the scopes to the MEI's `security.scopes` | the two lists are one decision | review the MEI declaration diff |
| `pso make:resource --public` declares the rule in the Spring service too | the service is secure by default and kept answering 401 | services generated before 0.2.0: `pso workspace:migrate --apply` adds the missing rules (step 5) |
| `pso docker:build` uses the 0.2 topology once `pso.infra.json` exists | one source of truth | the root `docker-compose.yml` keeps working with `pso deploy --target compose` |

New runtime options (all opt-in): orchestrator inbound TLS (`PSO_HTTP_TLS_CERT_FILE`, `PSO_HTTP_TLS_KEY_FILE`, `PSO_HTTP_TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE`).

## What goes wrong
- `note: pso.infra.json exists`: the infrastructure steps were done before; only the Spring step runs.
- A Spring `conflict`: the migration never weakens or rewrites an existing rule; decide which side is right and edit it yourself.
- A `tls/` authority without its key, expired, or certificates it did not issue are not adopted: the migration says so and the local environment gets new development material.
- Frontend declarations with errors block the migration: fix them with `pso frontend:validate` first.

---

# Infrastructure troubleshooting

> The infrastructure problems you will actually meet, what each message means and the fix.

## Troubleshooting table

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `host port(s) already in use: 8443 (published by edge)` | another process (a local `pso dev`, another stack) listens there | stop it, or change `environments.<env>.httpsPort`; nothing was started |
| `drift: ... edited by hand since PSO generated it` | a generated file was changed | move the change into the declarations, then `pso infra:repair --env <env> --yes` (the edited copy is kept in `.infra/backups/`) |
| `cert:<name>: does not name <host>` | a host was added or renamed | `pso infra:apply` re-issues it (development); supply a new certificate (operator) |
| gateway restarts with `PSO_SEC_JWKS_HOST` | the JWKS host is not bound to the issuer | generated configurations declare `PSO_JWT_JWKS_TRUSTED_HOSTS`; for a hand-written one, add the key host there |
| a public endpoint answers 401 | the service is secure by default and has no PUBLIC rule | `pso make:resource --public` declares it; for older services add the `pso.security.rules` entry |
| a shell answers 404 | no release published in its site | `pso frontend:build <fei> --env <env>` then `pso frontend:publish <fei> --env <env>` |
| `the infrastructure of "<env>" is not up to date` (staging/production) | pending changes are never applied implicitly outside development | `pso infra:plan --env <env>`, then `pso infra:apply --env <env> --yes` |
| `needs resources that only the operator can supply` | a supplied certificate or secret is missing or invalid | `pso infra:validate --env <env>` names each one |
| `the identity provider refused the token request` | the stack is not running or the realm predates the last change | `pso docker:ps`; `pso docker:restart idp` re-imports the realm (development) |
| `cannot restrict access to <file>` (Windows) | `icacls` failed | check the permissions of the workspace directory; nothing was written |
| `another PSO process (pid ...) is changing this workspace's infrastructure` | two runs at once | wait; a lock of a process that no longer exists is taken over automatically |
| `an earlier provisioning was interrupted` | a run was killed mid-write | nothing to do: the next apply completes it |
| `--env, --with-dependencies ... use the infrastructure contract` | 0.1 workspace | `pso infra:init` or `pso workspace:migrate` |

---

# Release integrity, signing and Windows installation

> The three different guarantees a PSO distribution can carry (package integrity, cryptographic release signing, Windows code signing), what 0.2.0 has, how to install and upgrade on Windows, and what is required before an official release.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> **Partial by necessity.** Package integrity (checksums, per-file hashes, SBOM, reproducible tarballs) is implemented and verified. Cryptographic release signing works with any Ed25519 key, but no official release identity exists yet. Windows code signing (Authenticode) is prepared but not done: no trusted code-signing certificate is available.

## Three different guarantees

| Guarantee | Answers | 0.2.0 release candidate |
|---|---|---|
| **Package integrity** | Is this exactly the file that was built? | `SHA256SUMS`, per-file hashes in the signed inventory of a `.psopkg`, CycloneDX SBOM, reproducible npm tarballs (two independent packs, identical integrity) |
| **Cryptographic release signing** | Did the release owner produce it? | the npm artifacts are **unsigned**; the Windows package is signed with the project's **development** key (integrity only: the key travels with the files, so it does not authenticate a publisher) |
| **Windows code signing (Authenticode)** | Has Windows verified the publisher? | **not signed**: Smart App Control, SmartScreen or enterprise policy may refuse to start the installer |

A checksum published next to the file proves integrity only as far as that page can be trusted. PSO never generates a throwaway signing identity and presents it as an official one.

## Installing on Windows

- **Portable ZIP** (recommended while the installer is unsigned): extract to a folder you can write to, run `.\pso.cmd --version`. A private Node.js runtime is bundled; nothing on the machine is changed.
- **Installer** (`PSO-Web-<version>-win-x64.exe`, Inno Setup): published with rc.3 as an **experimental** asset. It is unsigned, its real installation flow has not been validated end to end, and it is not a supported installation method for rc.3.

Maintenance of an installation (both forms):

```bash
pso integrity check --full                 # every file against the signed inventory (read-only)
pso repair --full                          # restore damaged files from the authenticated package
pso update install --package <file.psopkg> # side by side, verified, atomically activated
pso update rollback                        # back to the previous version
pso uninstall --root <dir> --yes           # standard: keeps configuration, cache and logs; your projects are never inside it
```

Upgrading from 0.1.x keeps every workspace untouched: workspaces live outside the installation. After upgrading, run `pso workspace:migrate` in each workspace (inspection first).

### Portable installation, step by step

1. Verify before extracting (PowerShell): `(Get-FileHash .\PSO-Web-<version>-win-x64-portable.zip -Algorithm SHA256).Hash` must equal the ZIP's line in `SHA256SUMS`, and `SHA256SUMS.sig` must verify with `release-signing-key.public.pem` (Ed25519). In a release candidate that key is the development key: the check proves integrity, not who published it.
2. Extract into a folder you can write to that is not `Program Files`, for example `%LOCALAPPDATA%\PSO`.
3. Run `<folder>\pso.cmd --version` and `<folder>\pso.cmd integrity check --full`.
4. Add `<folder>\bin` to your **user** PATH, open a new terminal, and confirm with `Get-Command pso -All` that it resolves to that folder (see [installed and development CLI](devops/installed-and-development-cli.md) when an npm-linked checkout answers instead).

### Windows installer limitations

The installer of `0.2.0-rc.3` is published as an experimental asset; it is not Authenticode-signed and not a supported installation method. A prior rc.1 unsigned build was refused by Smart App Control on the validation machine ("An Application Control policy blocked this file", Code Integrity event 3077), showing that acceptance of one unsigned file does not predict acceptance of another. PSO never asks you to switch Smart App Control, SmartScreen or Defender off. Use the **portable ZIP** ([Downloads](downloads/index.md)) until the installer is signed and its installation flow validated. Both rc.3 files, their checksums and the Ed25519 signature of `SHA256SUMS` (development key `7ebced00…`) are on the private release `v0.2.0-rc.3`.

## The permanent PSO release signing identity

Three keys or certificates are involved, and none replaces another:

| | Purpose | Kind | Where it is verified |
|---|---|---|---|
| Artifact checksums (`SHA256SUMS`) | the file is the one that was built | SHA-256, no key | by hand, by `pso update`, by the portable validation |
| PSO release signature | the release owner produced the package and the checksums | **Ed25519** key pair | `.psopkg` signature, `SHA256SUMS.sig`, the installation's trust store (updates signed by another key are refused) |
| Windows Authenticode | Windows knows the publisher | X.509 code-signing certificate from a public CA | Smart App Control, SmartScreen, `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` |

The development key used for release candidates (`~/.pso-psd/keys/release.private.pem`) is **not** the release identity and must not become it: it has lived on a development machine.

### Establishing it (only with the release owner's authorization)

1. **A clean, dedicated machine**, preferably offline, with full-disk encryption, no development tools beyond Node.js 24 and the released `pso`.
2. **Generate** onto encrypted removable media (for example a BitLocker To Go drive), never into a repository or a synchronised folder:

   ```powershell
   pso dist keygen --kind signing --out E:\pso-release-identity --name pso-release-2027
   ```

   The command never prints the private key and never overwrites an existing one. The private PEM is **not passphrase-protected**: its protection is the encrypted medium and the file's ACL (the owner only).
3. **Back it up**: a second encrypted medium kept in another physical place. Losing every copy means future releases cannot update existing installations.
4. **Publish the public key** `pso-release-2027.public.pem` and its fingerprint (printed by keygen) through channels users already trust (the repository's release page and a second independent channel). Record the fingerprint in the release notes of every release.
5. **Sign releases** by mounting the medium only for the build and pointing the build at it:

   ```powershell
   $env:PSO_RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY_FILE = "E:\pso-release-identity\pso-release-2027.private.pem"
   node scripts/release.mjs npm --out release-out/<version>/npm
   node scripts/psd/build-release.mjs --label <version> --dev-alpha --signing-key $env:PSO_RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY_FILE --runtime <node.exe> --runtime-license <file>
   Remove-Item Env:PSO_RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY_FILE   # then eject the medium
   ```

   The Windows pipeline has two modes today: the public development distribution (`--dev-alpha`: unencrypted, bundled Node.js) and an encrypted private preview for named recipients (`--recipients`). A public release signed with the official identity uses the first one, but its release notes and portable notice still call it an "Unsigned Developer Alpha"; that designation must be changed before the first official release.

6. **Moving installations to the official key**: an installation trusts exactly the key it was installed with, and its trust store is integrity-protected, so a package signed by the official key is refused by an installation that trusts the development key. Install the first officially signed release fresh (a new portable folder or the signed installer); workspaces are outside the installation and are not affected.
7. **Compromise**: stop signing, publish a revocation notice with the fingerprint through the same channels, generate a new identity, and ask users to install fresh.

### Windows code signing

A production release is Authenticode-signed during its build; there is no step that signs an installer afterwards, because the
uninstaller is embedded in the installer and both must be signed before any checksum is computed.

| What | How it is handled |
|---|---|
| the installer `PSO-Web-<version>-win-x64.exe` and its uninstaller `unins000.exe` | signed by the PSO publisher while Inno Setup compiles, together with the temporary copies Setup runs from TEMP (Windows SDK SignTool, SHA-256, RFC 3161 timestamp), each signature verified as Windows verifies it. Signing only the finished file would leave those copies unsigned, and Smart App Control blocks them |
| the bundled `node.exe` | keeps the OpenJS Foundation's signature, which is verified; PSO never re-signs a third-party file |
| `pso.cmd`, generated `mvnw.cmd` | scripts cannot carry Authenticode signatures: they are covered by the package's per-file integrity (`pso integrity check --full`) |
| `.psopkg`, `SHA256SUMS` | unchanged Ed25519 signatures; `SHA256SUMS` is computed after signing and records the signed installer |

The certificate is a publicly trusted code-signing certificate bought and held by the release owner (PSO provides none). Its key lives in
hardware: a token, an HSM or a cloud signing service such as Azure Artifact Signing. The build reads the signing identity from the environment
and never stores keys, passwords or tokens in the repository. A **release gate** stops the build when a required executable is unsigned,
untrusted, untimestamped or signed by another publisher. An unsigned build exists only as an explicitly labelled development build.

**Status:** the signing pipeline and the release gate are implemented and tested without a certificate. No certificate has been
provisioned yet, so no PSO release is Authenticode-signed: `0.2.0-rc.3` is unsigned, and Smart App Control can block its installer.
Acceptance of a signed release under Smart App Control is validated on an isolated Windows 11 machine before it is published.

## Before an official release

1. The permanent release identity (above), authorized by the release owner.
2. A trusted code-signing certificate, a production build that passes the Authenticode release gate, and its validation under Smart App Control on an isolated Windows 11 machine.
3. Explicit approval to publish.

## What goes wrong

- Windows refuses to start the installer: it is not Authenticode-signed; use the portable ZIP, or ask your administrator to allow it by SHA-256.
- `pso update install` refuses a package: it is signed by another key than the installation trusts; that is the protection working.

---

# CLI overview

> Every implemented pso command, with usage, flags, examples and failure cases.

The `pso` CLI is how you create, validate, run, secure, build and document a PSO workspace. This reference is generated from the command registry of the installed CLI, so every command listed here exists and nothing else does.

Start with [the CLI workflow](cli/workflow.md) to see which commands write files, which inspect declarations, and which contact running processes. Return to a command page for its exact usage and failure cases.

> [!TIP]
> Every command supports `--help`. Most support `--json` for machine output, and every command that writes files supports `--dry-run`.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | The command ran and failed: validation errors, conflicts, a refused unsafe request |
| 2 | Unknown command, or a command from the specification that is not implemented |
| 3 | Explicit authorization required (`--yes`) for `deploy` or `rollback` |
| 70 | Internal error |

## Commands

| Command | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`pso agent:enroll`](cli/agent-enroll.md) | Enroll this machine with a single-use token an administrator created (the token is read from standard input or a hidden prompt, never from an argument) |
| [`pso agent:install`](cli/agent-install.md) | Install the runtime agent over SSH, provision it (server identity, policy, a single-use administrator enrollment) and enroll this machine as its first superadministrator. Remote management stays disabled unless you choose a mode |
| [`pso agent:releases`](cli/agent-releases.md) | List the agent releases kept on the server: the active and the previous one, each build's version, build id, checksum, installation time and installer, and the history of activations and rollbacks |
| [`pso agent:rollback`](cli/agent-rollback.md) | Return the server's agent to an earlier release (the previous one, or a named one from agent:releases): the release's checksum is verified again and it must start before the link is switched atomically. Server identity, roles, policy and deployments are untouched |
| [`pso agent:status`](cli/agent-status.md) | Show the agent's version, mode and who is enrolled |
| [`pso agent:uninstall`](cli/agent-uninstall.md) | Remove the management agent from the server. Applications, their data and processes stay unless --purge-applications is given (refused while services run) |

These exist in the specification but exit with code 2 in this version: `pso dispatch:health`. See [Event dispatch](dispatch/overview.md).
