# pso release:sign

> Sign the release manifest (application, immutable commit or artifact checksum, strictly increasing sequence) with a local signer. The server verifies it against its own trust store and refuses replays and downgrades

Sign the release manifest (application, immutable commit or artifact checksum, strictly increasing sequence) with a local signer. The server verifies it against its own trust store and refuses replays and downgrades.

## Usage

```text
pso release:sign <environment> --signer <name> --sequence <n> [--path <checkout>] [--artifact <file>] [--out <file>] [--json]
```

## Flags

`--signer`, `--sequence`, `--path`, `--artifact`, `--out`, `--json`.

## Examples

```bash
pso release:sign production --signer release-bot --sequence 12
pso release:sign production --signer release-bot --sequence 13 --path ../app-checkout --out signed/prod-13.json
```

## What it changes

- Writes a signed release manifest: application, immutable commit (or artifact checksum), sequence and time, signed over a domain-separated Ed25519 signature.

## Failure cases

- A checkout with uncommitted changes is refused: the server deploys the commit, not the working tree.
- A sequence not greater than the last signed release deployed is later refused by the server as a replay or downgrade.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

# pso release:url

> Where the deployed application can be reached, from the deployment metadata and the REAL nginx file; --verify measures each layer independently (process, local health, proxy, this machine, TLS, optional SSH tunnel). COMPLETED is not proof of public access

Where the deployed application can be reached, from the deployment metadata and the REAL nginx file; --verify measures each layer independently (process, local health, proxy, this machine, TLS, optional SSH tunnel). COMPLETED is not proof of public access.

## Usage

```text
pso release:url <application> [--verify] [--tunnel] [--ca-file <pem>] [--save-ca] [--json]
```

## Flags

`--verify`, `--tunnel`, `--ca-file`, `--save-ca`, `--json`.

## Examples

```bash
pso release:url shop-gateway
pso release:url shop-gateway --verify
pso release:url shop-gateway --verify --tunnel --ca-file ./ca.pem --save-ca
```

## What it changes

- Reads the nginx file PSO manages on the server and lists every URL of the application (public, redirect, private loopback). With --verify it measures process, local health, proxy, reachability from this machine, TLS and optionally an authenticated SSH tunnel, each on its own.

## Failure cases

- A COMPLETED deployment is not proof of public access: a silent timeout from this machine with a healthy server is reported as a hypothesis (filtering on the path), never as a named cause.
- A private-CA certificate needs --ca-file; verification is never disabled.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

# pso security:check

> Examine real configuration and sources for security problems, for one environment and with the configuration sources the application runs with in it (exit 1 on high/critical; --strict also medium)

Examine real configuration and sources for security problems, for one environment and with the configuration sources the application runs with in it (exit 1 on high/critical; --strict also medium).

## Usage

```text
pso security:check [--env development|test|staging|production] [--strict] [--json]
```

## Flags

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--env` | The environment to evaluate: development, test, staging or production. |
| `--strict` | Treat medium findings as failures as well as high and critical findings. |
| `--json` | Print findings for tools without exposing secret values. |

## Examples

```bash
pso security:check
pso security:check --env production --strict
pso security:check --json
```

## What it changes

- Reads route policies, keys, Spring configuration and the security configuration of ONE environment (`--env`, else PSO_ENV, else development) from the sources the application itself reads in it: for development that includes the project's `.env` files, for production only the process environment.
- The output names the environment and where each project's configuration came from. It does not issue a JWT or send an HTTP request.

## Verify the result

- Use the reported resource and finding id to correct the declaration.
- A clean development result says nothing about production: run `pso security:check --env production` where the production variables are set (a pipeline, the platform).
- After a clean report, test a protected route with no token, a token missing scope and a correctly scoped token.

## Failure cases

- Exit code 1 on high or critical findings (`--strict` also medium). Findings never include secrets.
- `SEC005 ... is not configured for "development"`: put the `PSO_JWT_*` variables in the orchestrator's `.env`, or declare `security.authentication.*` in `pso.config.json`.
- `SEC013`: the development identity provider (`pso idp:dev`) is configured for production.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

## See also

- [security/auditing](security/auditing.md)

# pso services:health

> Probe every declared service live (exit 1 if any is DOWN)

Probe every declared service live (exit 1 if any is DOWN).

```text
pso services:health [--json]
```

## Flags

`--json`.

## Examples

```bash
pso services:health
pso services:health --json
```

## What it changes

- Probes each declared health endpoint; it changes no configuration.

## Illustrative output

This sample shows the shape of the result. Names, ports, digests and timings may differ in your workspace.

```text evidence="illustrative"
UP    gateway    http://127.0.0.1:3000/health/ready  4ms
DOWN  catalog    http://127.0.0.1:8081/actuator/health
```

## Verify the result

- A DOWN row names the URL to inspect in that service's log.
- All UP rows establish reachability, not correctness of a protected business endpoint.

## Failure cases

- Exit code 1 when any declared service is DOWN. It probes live; it never trusts the registry file.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

# pso signer:generate

> Create an Ed25519 release-signing key on THIS machine. The private key goes to the protected credential store (never to a file, a project or a server); the public key is what an environment is told to trust

Create an Ed25519 release-signing key on THIS machine. The private key goes to the protected credential store (never to a file, a project or a server); the public key is what an environment is told to trust.

## Usage

```text
pso signer:generate <name> [--json]
```

## Flags

`--json`.

## Examples

```bash
pso signer:generate release-bot
```

## What it changes

- Creates an Ed25519 key pair. The private key goes to the protected credential store of THIS machine; nothing is written to the project or to a server.

## Failure cases

- Fails when no protected credential store is available (PSO never falls back to a plain-text file).
- A name that already exists is refused: rotation means a new key, never an overwrite.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

# pso storage:enable

> Opt a Spring service into PSO Storage: adds the storage starter (and the S3 or Azure SDK), the pso.storage settings and multipart uploads; S3/Azure services use the local provider in the local and test profiles

Opt a Spring service into PSO Storage: adds the storage starter (and the S3 or Azure SDK), the pso.storage settings and multipart uploads; S3/Azure services use the local provider in the local and test profiles.

## Usage

```text
pso storage:enable <local|s3|azure> [--service <name>] [--root ./storage] [--bucket <b>] [--region <r>] [--container <c>] [--endpoint <url>] [--max-size 5MB] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

## Flags

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--service` | Choose the Spring service. |
| `--root` | Relative local storage root (default ./storage). |
| `--bucket` | S3 bucket name. |
| `--region` | AWS region. |
| `--container` | Azure container name. |
| `--endpoint` | Azure blob endpoint or an S3-compatible emulator. |
| `--max-size` | pso.storage.upload.max-size (default 5MB). |
| `--dry-run` | Preview the changes. |
| `--json` | Print machine-readable results. |

## Examples

```bash
pso storage:enable local --service hr-service
pso storage:enable s3 --service hr-service --bucket acme-hr-documents --region eu-west-1 --dry-run
pso storage:enable azure --service hr-service
```

## What it changes

- Adds `pso-storage-spring-boot-starter` (and the S3 or Azure SDK, versioned by `pso-bom`), writes the `pso.storage` block and enables multipart uploads.
- S3 and Azure services get a local provider in the local and test profiles; no credential is ever written.

## Verify the result

- Run `pso storage:validate --service <name>`; start the service and read the `psoStorage` health component.

## Failure cases

- Only Spring services are supported. A root outside the service, an invalid bucket or container name and a non-HTTPS endpoint are refused before anything is written; running it again changes nothing.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

## See also

- [spring/storage](spring/storage.md)

# pso types

> Write src/pso-types.d.ts in the orchestrator: the registered service names and the guard names as TypeScript types, so the compiler checks them wherever they are named (--check: exit 1 when the file is missing or out of date)

Write src/pso-types.d.ts in the orchestrator: the registered service names and the guard names as TypeScript types, so the compiler checks them wherever they are named (--check: exit 1 when the file is missing or out of date).

## Usage

```text
pso types [--check] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

## Flags

`--check`, `--dry-run`, `--json`.

## Examples

```bash
pso types
pso types --check
pso types --dry-run
```

## What it changes

- Writes `src/pso-types.d.ts` in the orchestrator: the services registered in `pso.workspace.json` and the guards of the project as TypeScript types.
- From then on the compiler refuses a service or guard name that does not exist in `ROUTES.pso.ts`, `Upstream.forward` and `UpstreamClient`. Without the file every string is accepted, as before.

## Illustrative output

This sample shows the shape of the result. Names, ports, digests and timings may differ in your workspace.

```text evidence="illustrative"
created    gateway/src/pso-types.d.ts
services: catalog, customers, orders
guards:   jwt
```

## Verify the result

- `npm run typecheck` in the orchestrator.
- `pso types --check` exits 1 when the file is missing or out of date (for a pipeline).

## Failure cases

- Run it again after `pso create service`, `pso services:register` or `pso make:guard`: the file is generated, never edited by hand.
- The run-time checks do not depend on it: `pso validate` and start-up refuse an unknown service or guard either way.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

## See also

- [orchestrator/routes](orchestrator/routes.md)

```text
pso update check --catalog <file|https url> [--channel <stable|beta|dev>] [--root <dir>] [--trust <public.pem>] | install [--catalog <file|https url> | --package <file.psopkg>] [--channel <stable|beta|dev>] [--key <recipient-private.pem>] [--allow-downgrade] [--root <dir>] [--trust <public.pem>] | rollback [--root <dir>] [--json]

```

## Failure cases

- Catalogs must be signed, unexpired and newer than the last one seen (replay protection). Package size and SHA-256 are checked, the new version is verified before activation, and the previous version is kept for rollback.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

# pso validate

> Validate workspace structure, conventions and contracts (exit 1 on errors)

Validate workspace structure, conventions and contracts (exit 1 on errors).

## Usage

```text
pso validate [--write-manifest [--dry-run]] [--json]
```

## Flags

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--write-manifest` | Persist the deterministic discovery manifest after validation. |
| `--dry-run` | See the usage line and the task guide for this option. |
| `--json` | Return diagnostics in machine-readable form. |

## Examples

```bash
pso validate
pso validate --json
pso validate --write-manifest
```

## What it changes

- Reads workspace structure, declarations and contracts without starting the application.
- Only `--write-manifest` writes a manifest; ordinary validation leaves project files unchanged.

## Illustrative output

This sample shows the shape of the result. Names, ports, digests and timings may differ in your workspace.

```text evidence="illustrative"
gateway: 5 resource(s), digest 618af77aaa00
catalog: 4 resource(s), digest a29b9b85d072
OK
```

## Verify the result

- An `OK` and exit code 0 mean the static checks passed.
- Use `pso services:health` and an HTTP request for runtime evidence.

## Failure cases

- Exit code 1 with diagnostics such as `PSO_ROUTE_004` (method mismatch) or `PSO_PORT_CONFLICT`. Nothing is executed to produce them.
- `No pso.workspace.json found`: run it inside a workspace.

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

# pso workspace:migrate

> Migrate a workspace to 0.2.0: add pso.infra.json, adopt the existing development TLS authority, certificates and identity key (reused, not regenerated), provision the local environment, and add the PUBLIC rules that Spring services generated before 0.2.0 lack for routes the orchestrator declares public (with backups). Without --apply it only reports; application logic, declarations and data are never changed

Migrate a workspace to 0.2.0: add pso.infra.json, adopt the existing development TLS authority, certificates and identity key (reused, not regenerated), provision the local environment, and add the PUBLIC rules that Spring services generated before 0.2.0 lack for routes the orchestrator declares public (with backups). Without --apply it only reports; application logic, declarations and data are never changed.

## Usage

```text
pso workspace:migrate [--apply] [--identity keycloak|pso-dev|none] [--json]
```

## Flags

`--apply`, `--identity`, `--json`.

## Examples

```bash
pso workspace:migrate
pso workspace:migrate --apply
pso workspace:migrate --apply --identity keycloak --json
```

## What it changes

- Inspection without `--apply`. With it: writes pso.infra.json, adopts a valid `tls/` authority and its certificates and the `pso idp:dev` key (reused, not regenerated), excludes .infra/ from git and provisions the local environment. Application code, declarations and data are never changed.
- Spring security: compares each Spring service's `pso.security.rules` with the routes the workspace declares and adds only the missing rules for declared public routes, at the end of the list, marked `# added by pso workspace:migrate (0.2.0)`. Custom rules are kept; a backup goes to `.infra/backups/`; a second run adds nothing.
- A workspace that already has pso.infra.json skips the infrastructure steps and still checks the Spring rules; the result is recorded in `.infra/migration-0.2.0.json`.

## Illustrative output

This sample shows the shape of the result. Names, ports, digests and timings may differ in your workspace.

```text evidence="illustrative"
migration to 0.2.0 of "pso-reference" (inspection: nothing is written)
  note: pso.infra.json exists: the infrastructure steps are done (pso infra:plan); only the remaining steps run
Spring security (routes the orchestrator declares public):
  ok       catalog: GET /catalog/products -> rule at line 71 (/catalog/products) already makes it public

Nothing to migrate.
```

## Failure cases

- `conflict`: an explicit rule gives the public path another access; the developer's rule is kept. Decide which one is right.
- `ambiguous`: no application.yml, or a `pso.security.rules` block that cannot be read with certainty; the message gives the rule to add by hand.
- `exposed-extra`: a service rule makes PUBLIC a path the orchestrator protects; reported, never removed automatically.
- Frontend declarations with errors block the migration (pso frontend:validate).

## Exit codes

`0` on success, `1` when the command ran and failed. See the [exit code table](cli/index.md#exit-codes).

## See also

- [infrastructure/migration](infrastructure/migration.md)

# Development environment

> pso dev, the runtime registry, logs and Studio - what each does, a day-to-day workflow, and how to debug the environment itself.

```bash
pso dev                      # everything
pso dev --only gateway       # a subset
pso dev --install            # run npm install where dependencies are missing
pso dev --smoke              # start, report, stop (useful in CI)
```

`pso dev`:

1. validates the workspace (refuses to start on errors);
2. checks that every port is free;
3. starts services **dependency-first**: Node services with `npm run dev` (compile + run), Spring services with `mvnw spring-boot:run`;
4. waits for each health endpoint, with `--timeout` seconds;
5. writes `.pso/registry.json` and mirrors service output to `.pso/logs/<service>.log`;
6. checks health every 5 seconds and logs `UP` / `DOWN` transitions (`[pso] <name> is now DOWN`);
7. on Ctrl+C stops everything in reverse order and kills the whole process tree.

A service may override its command in `pso.workspace.json`: `"dev": { "command": ["node", "server.js"] }` (an argument list, never a shell string).

Expected terminal output when everything is healthy (the layout is the command's; addresses are those of your workspace):

```text evidence="expected"
Starting 2 service(s)...

Ready:
  catalog            http://127.0.0.1:8081      READY/UP
  gateway            http://127.0.0.1:3000      READY/UP

Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

## A day-to-day workflow

1. Start everything once: `pso dev` in one terminal.
2. Change a controller in the orchestrator: stop only the gateway and restart it (`Ctrl+C`, then `pso dev --only gateway`; the compile step runs again). The Spring service keeps running if you start it separately.
3. Change a Spring class: Spring needs a restart too (`spring-boot:run`); use your IDE's run configuration for fast cycles and keep `pso dev` for integration.
4. Before committing: `pso validate`, `pso security:check`, `pso test`.

Logs of each service are in `.pso/logs/<service>.log`; the orchestrator's are readable text on a terminal (colour only when attached to one) and JSON when redirected, so the file contains JSON lines. Read them with `Get-Content .pso\logs\gateway.log -Tail 20 -Wait`.

## Studio

```bash
pso studio
```

A read-only control center on the loopback interface, protected by a one-time token and a Host check: overview with verified health and service topology, services, routes with policy, module explorer, security, observability (scrubbed logs), diagnostics and environment settings. It reads real files and probes real endpoints. See [PSO Studio](devops/studio.md).

## Other inspection commands

`pso services:health`, `pso services:graph`, `pso graph`, `pso routes:inspect <route id or path>`, `pso inspect --service <name>`. Verified examples are on [Service registration](microservices/service-registration.md) and [Structural discovery](concepts/structural-discovery.md).

## When the environment misbehaves

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| `pso dev` exits immediately | the first line says why: validation failure, port in use, missing dependencies |
| one service never becomes ready | `.pso/logs/<service>.log`; for Spring the active profile and `PSO_JWT_*` |
| a service is `DOWN` after being `UP` | it crashed or its health path stopped answering: the log tells; `pso dev` reports, it does not restart |
| orphan processes after a crash | `pso dev` kills process trees on exit; if the terminal was force-closed, find leftover `java`/`node` processes by their port before starting again (do not kill processes you do not recognise) |
| the registry file is stale | it is rewritten every 5 seconds while `pso dev` runs; delete `.pso/` if it is left over |

## Common mistakes

- Running `pso dev` from outside the workspace (it looks upward for `pso.workspace.json`).
- Expecting hot reload: restart the affected service.
- Committing `.pso/`.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Check | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pso dev` refuses to start | a port is already used, or two services share one | the message before anything starts | free the port or change it in `pso.workspace.json` |
| a Spring service starts and exits | JWT settings are missing | its log: `pso.security.jwt.jwks-uri is required` | set `PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI` for Spring services |
| logs are not coloured | output is redirected, `NO_COLOR` is set, or `CI` is set | `echo $NO_COLOR` | unset them, or set `PSO_LOG_COLOR=always` |
| a service shows `DOWN` in `pso services:health` | it is not running or its health path is wrong | the URL printed | start it or fix `health` |

See [Logging](devops/logging.md) for colour and format controls.

## Next steps

- [Running the environment](getting-started/running.md)
- [Diagnose a local workspace](tutorials/local-debugging.md)

# Native builds and deployment

> Package artifacts with checksums, plan a release, deploy it with health verification and roll back - the native target, the Compose target, and how the cloud descriptors relate.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

## Build

```bash
pso build [--service name]
```

Type-checks and **compiles** Node services (`npm run build`), packs them with `npm pack`, builds Spring services with `mvnw package`, and writes `.pso/artifacts/manifest.json` with each artifact's SHA-256. Validation errors stop the build.

## Test and lint

`pso test` runs each service's own tests (`npm test` / `mvnw test`); services without tests are reported as `no-tests`. `pso lint` runs workspace validation, the security check and the TypeScript check, and reports missing dependencies instead of skipping them.

## Plan, deploy, roll back (native target)

```bash
pso deploy:plan --target native --dir D:\apps\shop --release 1.0.0
pso deploy      --target native --dir D:\apps\shop --release 1.0.0 --yes --health-url http://127.0.0.1:3000/health/ready
pso rollback    --dir D:\apps\shop --yes
```

- `deploy:plan` changes nothing and shows exactly what would happen.
- `deploy` **requires `--yes`** (exit code 3 otherwise).
- Artifacts are checksum-verified before and after copying into `<dir>/releases/<version>+<hash>/`. The release is activated by an atomic switch of `<dir>/current.json`.
- A failing `--health-url` (repeatable) rolls back automatically.
- SNAPSHOT builds are refused.

The result on disk (expected; the layout follows from the command):

```text evidence="expected"
D:\apps\shop\
  current.json                         { "release": "1.0.0+3f9a1c2e", "previous": "0.9.0+ab12cd34" }
  releases\1.0.0+3f9a1c2e\gateway\gateway-0.1.0.tgz
  releases\1.0.0+3f9a1c2e\catalog\catalog-0.1.0.jar
```

The Compose target plans the same way (expected output):

```text evidence="verified"
$ pso deploy:plan --target compose
target:   compose
steps:
  1. docker compose build
  2. docker compose up -d --wait

Nothing has been changed. Run `pso deploy` with the same options and --yes to apply.
```

## A release, step by step (native)

1. `pso validate` and `pso security:check --strict` (CI).
2. `pso build`; archive `.pso/artifacts/manifest.json`.
3. `pso deploy:plan ...` and review it (a person reads it).
4. `pso deploy ... --yes --health-url <url>` from a protected job.
5. Verify: `GET <health-url>` answers; `current.json` names the new release.
6. If something is wrong later: `pso rollback --dir ... --yes` re-activates the previous release atomically.

## Limits

PSO places artifacts and switches the active release; **starting the processes from a release is up to you** (service manager, scripts). The `compose` target runs `docker compose build` and `up -d --wait`; building the images needs the PSO artifacts to be reachable (see [Docker](devops/docker.md)). **Cloud and cluster platforms** are covered by generated, statically validated descriptors only (`pso deploy:init`, `pso deploy:validate`: Kubernetes, ECS, Container Apps, Cloud Run); PSO never applies them ([cloud descriptors](devops/cloud-descriptors.md)).

## Variations

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| a release directory with rollback on a VM | the native target |
| the local stack in containers | `pso docker:init` then the compose target |
| managed platforms | `pso deploy:init --target <platform>` (kubernetes, ecs, container-apps or cloud-run), then your platform's tooling |
| signed, installable packages for other machines | [signed packages and the installer](devops/distribution-and-installation.md) |

## Releases and SNAPSHOT versions

`pso deploy` and `pso deploy:plan` (native target) refuse a Spring service that is not built from fixed versions. Two versions of its `pom.xml` decide that, plus any dependency pinned to a SNAPSHOT:

| Version | Where | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| the service's own | `<project><version>` | the artifact you deploy |
| the PSO artifacts | `<pso.version>` | every `com.pso` dependency; `0.1.0-SNAPSHOT` is a local development build from `pso java:install` |

The version of the Spring Boot parent is not part of the rule. (Earlier versions read exactly that one, so a service on PSO SNAPSHOT artifacts was accepted as a release.)

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso deploy:plan --target native --dir /srv/shop --release 1.0.0
error: Refusing to deploy a SNAPSHOT build:
 - orders: the PSO artifacts are 0.1.0-SNAPSHOT (<pso.version>): a local development build of com.pso:*
hint: A release uses fixed versions: build the PSO artifacts with a release version (node scripts/release-maven.mjs) and set <pso.version> and the service <version> to fixed versions. For a development deployment pass --allow-snapshot
```

| Policy | Command | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Release | `pso deploy --target native --dir <path> --release 1.0.0 --yes` | refused while any of the versions above is a SNAPSHOT |
| Development deployment | add `--allow-snapshot` | accepted; the plan is marked `DEVELOPMENT DEPLOYMENT` and lists the SNAPSHOT versions |
| Production | `PSO_ENV=production` | `--allow-snapshot` itself is refused |

## Common mistakes

- Deploying a SNAPSHOT (refused) or a build whose checksums do not match the manifest (refused).
- Assuming `deploy` starts the processes.
- Skipping `--health-url`: without it a broken release is not detected automatically.

## Next steps

- [CI/CD](devops/ci-cd.md)
- [Production security checklist](security/checklist.md)

# Docker and Docker Compose

> Generated hardened Dockerfiles and a Compose file - what each contains, how to use them, what was verified by running containers and what was not, and the one publishing prerequisite that blocks image builds today.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

```bash
pso docker:init --dry-run
pso docker:init
pso docker:build        # needs a running Docker daemon
```

## What `docker:init` creates

Verified output for a workspace with an orchestrator:

```text evidence="verified"
$ pso docker:init
created    .env.example
created    .github/workflows/ci.yml
created    docker-compose.yml
created    gateway/.dockerignore
created    gateway/Dockerfile
```

| File | Highlights |
|---|---|
| `<service>/Dockerfile` | multi-stage; Node: install, compile, prune, run `dist/main.js` as user `node`; Spring: wrapper build, JRE image as a non-root user (uid 10001); `HEALTHCHECK` on the service's health path |
| `<service>/.dockerignore` | excludes `node_modules`, `target`, `dist`, `.env`, `keys`, `*.pem` |
| `docker-compose.yml` | one published port (the orchestrator, bound to `127.0.0.1`); internal network; `read_only`, `cap_drop: ALL`, `no-new-privileges`; `depends_on` with `service_healthy`; for the orchestrator, per upstream: its address (`PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>`), its endpoint prefix (`_PREFIX`) and its transport, TLS by default (`_TLS`, `_TLS_CA_FILE`) or, with `--transport plaintext`, an explicit `_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT`; for a Spring service with TLS its certificate, key and a health check that verifies them; `stop_grace_period` |
| `.env.example` | the required `PSO_JWT_*` variables, without values you should keep; commented out: shutdown, the private identity provider (`PSO_JWT_JWKS_PRIVATE_HOSTS`, `PSO_JWT_JWKS_CA_FILE`) and `PSO_TLS_DIR` |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | see [CI/CD](devops/ci-cd.md) |

The generated Compose file (verified; one-service workspace):

```yaml
x-pso-env: &pso-env
  PSO_JWT_ISSUER: ${PSO_JWT_ISSUER:?set PSO_JWT_ISSUER}
  PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE: ${PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE:?set PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE}
  PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI: ${PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI:?set PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI}
  PSO_JWT_ALGORITHMS: ${PSO_JWT_ALGORITHMS:-ES256}
  # an identity provider on a private network or with a private certificate authority (empty = not used; see .env.example)
  PSO_JWT_JWKS_PRIVATE_HOSTS: ${PSO_JWT_JWKS_PRIVATE_HOSTS:-}
  PSO_JWT_JWKS_CA_FILE: ${PSO_JWT_JWKS_CA_FILE:-}
  PSO_SECURITY_JWT_CA_FILE: ${PSO_JWT_JWKS_CA_FILE:-}

services:
  gateway:
    build: ./gateway
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *pso-env
      PORT: "3000"
      HOST: "0.0.0.0"
      PSO_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS: "${PSO_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS:-5000}"
    stop_grace_period: "${PSO_STOP_GRACE_PERIOD:-40s}"
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    networks:
      - internal
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"

networks:
  internal:
    driver: bridge
```

Required variables use `${VAR:?message}`: a missing value stops Compose instead of starting an unsecured stack. Verified: with the variables unset, `docker compose config` fails with `required variable PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE is missing a value: set PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE`; with them set, `docker compose config --quiet` exits 0.

## Use it

```bash
pso tls:init --dev            # development only: a local certificate authority and one certificate per service, in ./tls
pso docker:init --vendor      # Dockerfiles and docker-compose.yml (TLS between the orchestrator and the services)
cp .env.example .env          # then edit the values; never commit .env
docker compose config --quiet # validates the file and the variables
docker compose up -d --wait   # builds if needed, starts, waits for health
```

Service-to-service addresses inside Compose are service names (`catalog:8081`). The orchestrator receives each one as `PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG=catalog:8081` together with the service's endpoint prefix (`PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG_PREFIX=/catalog`): the workspace file is not in the image, so the prefix travels with the address.

The values in `.env.example` are placeholders. An orchestrator with at least one guarded route loads the issuer's keys when it starts and does not start without them (`PSO_SEC_INIT`): `PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI` must be the HTTPS address of your identity provider's key set. For an identity provider on a private network, see [the section below](#an-identity-provider-inside-the-stack).

## Transport between the orchestrator and the services

The orchestrator image runs in production mode, where an upstream on another host must use TLS ([service identity](security/service-identity.md)). `docker:init` generates one of two transports; nothing is chosen silently and there is no switch for "all upstreams".

| | `pso docker:init` (default: `--transport tls`) | `pso docker:init --transport plaintext` |
|---|---|---|
| orchestrator to service | HTTPS; the certificate's authority and host name are verified, always | plain HTTP on the private network `internal` |
| generated per upstream | `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>_TLS: "true"`, `_TLS_CA_FILE: /run/pso/tls/ca.crt` | `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT: "${...:-true}"` |
| Spring service | serves HTTPS only (`SERVER_SSL_CERTIFICATE`, `SERVER_SSL_CERTIFICATE_PRIVATE_KEY`); its health check verifies the certificate | serves plain HTTP |
| the caller's bearer token | forwarded to the service, which verifies it again | **not forwarded** (the orchestrator never sends a token over a plaintext hop to another host): a route the service must authenticate answers 401 |
| use it for | production and anything that carries credentials | a local stack without authenticated routes, or an existing deployment while it migrates |

### TLS (the default)

The compose file reads the certificates from `PSO_TLS_DIR` (default `./tls`) and mounts them read-only: each service gets its own directory, the orchestrator gets the authority only.

```text evidence="illustrative"
tls/ca.crt                 the certificate authority the orchestrator trusts for its upstreams
tls/<service>/tls.crt      the service's certificate: it must name the service ("catalog") and "localhost" (the container health check)
tls/<service>/tls.key      the service's private key
tls/<service>/ca.crt       the same authority, next to the service
```

| Where the certificates come from | Do |
|---|---|
| development, tests | `pso tls:init --dev` creates them (ECDSA P-256, 365 days, `--days` to change; `--hosts idp` adds certificates for other containers). The flag is required: without `--dev` nothing is created. The keys are generated on your machine, unprotected, and `tls/` is added to `.gitignore` |
| production | certificates and keys from your own certificate authority, in the same layout, or `PSO_TLS_DIR` pointing at them. PSO does not generate, ship or reuse production keys |
| either | `pso tls:check` verifies the directory: issuing authority, validity dates (a warning under 30 days, an error when expired), that each key belongs to its certificate and that each certificate names its service. No key material is printed |

`docker:init` runs the same check and reports the result when it generates the files. Mutual TLS (the service authenticates the orchestrator by a client certificate) is configured with `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>_TLS_CERT_FILE` and `_TLS_KEY_FILE` ([service identity](security/service-identity.md)); the generated file does not set it up.

### Plain HTTP (explicit)

```bash
pso docker:init --transport plaintext --force
```

```yaml
      PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG: "catalog:8081"
      PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG_PREFIX: "/catalog"
      PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT: "${PSO_UPSTREAM_CATALOG_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT:-true}"
```

The authorization is per upstream: an upstream you add by hand is still refused without TLS, and `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT=false` in `.env` makes the orchestrator refuse to start until that upstream has TLS. Plain HTTP on a private network is not encryption. Each time a token is withheld the orchestrator logs `bearer token not forwarded to upstream` with the reason and the service; at start-up it logs one warning per plaintext upstream.

An upstream whose TLS is already configured in the orchestrator's `pso.config.json` (`http.upstreams.<name>.tls`) keeps that configuration in both modes: nothing is generated for it, and the file is copied into the image.

### Migrating an existing deployment

A `docker-compose.yml` generated earlier is never replaced silently (`docker:init` reports a conflict). To keep plain HTTP, regenerate with `--transport plaintext --force`: the result is what you had, plus the prefix variables. To move to TLS: `pso tls:init --dev` (or your own certificates), `pso tls:check`, `pso docker:init --force`, then start the stack again.

## An identity provider inside the stack

A JWKS address that resolves to a private address is refused: that is the protection against a configuration (or a DNS answer) pointing the orchestrator at internal systems. An identity provider that really is on a private network is approved by naming it, exactly, in `.env`:

```bash title=".env"
PSO_JWT_ISSUER=https://idp:8443
PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI=https://idp:8443/.well-known/jwks.json
PSO_JWT_JWKS_PRIVATE_HOSTS=idp:8443
PSO_JWT_JWKS_CA_FILE=/run/pso/tls/ca.crt
```

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PSO_JWT_JWKS_PRIVATE_HOSTS` | exact `host:port` entries. Only the JWKS URI itself, and only when its host and port match an entry, may resolve to a private-network address (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, fc00::/7). Loopback, link-local and metadata addresses stay refused, HTTPS stays required, redirects stay refused, and no other private destination becomes reachable |
| `PSO_JWT_JWKS_CA_FILE` | PEM file, inside the containers, with the authority that signed the identity provider's certificate. Verification is never disabled; without the file a private certificate is refused (`jwks_tls`) |

The compose file passes both to the orchestrator and to the Spring services (`pso.security.jwt.ca-file`). The path above is where the TLS mode mounts the authority; an identity provider with another authority needs its own mount in `docker-compose.override.yml`. Infrastructure (the identity provider, PostgreSQL, Redis, a broker) and the variables that point the services at it go in that override file: see [the next section](#infrastructure-postgresql-redis-rabbitmq).

## Infrastructure: PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ

`pso docker:init` generates the containers of **your services** and nothing else. It never adds a database or a broker, and a generated service has no address for one: every service reads its infrastructure from environment variables, and the deployment supplies them. There are two supported ways, and they use the same variables.

| The service uses | Variables it reads (already in its generated configuration) | Enabled by |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL (`pso create service <name> --db postgres`) | `DB_URL` (a JDBC URL), `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD` | always; Flyway migrates when the service starts |
| Dispatch over RabbitMQ (`pso dispatch:install rabbitmq`) | `RABBITMQ_URL` | `PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true` |
| Dispatch over Redis (`pso dispatch:install redis`) | `REDIS_URL` | `PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true` |
| the distributed rate limit of the orchestrator | the variable its `pso.config.json` names in `http.rateLimit.redisUrl` ([rate limiting](security/rate-limiting.md)) | `http.rateLimit.provider: "redis"` |
| another PSO service, called with `PsoHttpClient` | the variable you put in `pso.http.client.services.<name>.base-url`, and `tls.ca-file` ([service to service](microservices/service-to-service.md)) | always |

Three rules apply in the generated images, because they run in production mode (`SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` for a Spring service):

- **Dispatch must be authenticated.** A service with Dispatch enabled does not start without `PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_MODE=required`, its own `PSO_DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY`, and on a consumer the key of each publisher it accepts, `PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_KEY_<SERVICE>` ([publisher authentication](dispatch/security-and-observability.md)).
- **Secrets come from the environment**, never from the image and never from a committed file: `.env` next to the Compose files (git-ignored) or the secret store of your platform.
- **A service owns its database.** One PostgreSQL server may hold several databases, but each service gets its own `DB_URL`.

### In the same Compose project: `docker-compose.override.yml`

`docker-compose.yml` belongs to the generator (`pso docker:init --force` rewrites it). Everything the deployment adds goes in `docker-compose.override.yml`, which you write and PSO never touches. Docker Compose merges the two files by itself; with the development identity provider, name all three (`-f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.idp.yml -f docker-compose.override.yml`).

The example is a workspace where `orders` and `catalog` each have a PostgreSQL database, `orders` publishes Dispatch events through RabbitMQ and `catalog` consumes them:

```yaml title="docker-compose.override.yml" evidence="illustrative"
# Infrastructure of this deployment (not generated by PSO). Secrets come from .env.
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment: { POSTGRES_USER: app, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD}" }
    volumes:
      - ./infra/init-databases.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql:ro   # CREATE DATABASE orders; CREATE DATABASE catalog;
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d orders"], interval: 5s, timeout: 3s, retries: 20 }
    networks: [internal]
  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3.13-alpine
    environment: { RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER: app, RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS: "${RABBITMQ_PASSWORD:?set RABBITMQ_PASSWORD}" }
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD-SHELL", "rabbitmq-diagnostics -q check_port_connectivity"], interval: 5s, timeout: 5s, retries: 40, start_period: 20s }
    networks: [internal]
  orders:
    environment:
      DB_URL: "jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/orders"
      DB_USER: app
      DB_PASSWORD: "${DB_PASSWORD:?}"
      PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED: "true"
      RABBITMQ_URL: "amqp://app:${RABBITMQ_PASSWORD:?}@rabbitmq:5672"
      PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_MODE: required
      PSO_DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY: "${ORDERS_DISPATCH_KEY:?}"
    depends_on: { postgres: { condition: service_healthy }, rabbitmq: { condition: service_healthy } }
  catalog:
    environment:
      DB_URL: "jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/catalog"
      DB_USER: app
      DB_PASSWORD: "${DB_PASSWORD:?}"
      PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED: "true"
      RABBITMQ_URL: "amqp://app:${RABBITMQ_PASSWORD:?}@rabbitmq:5672"
      PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_MODE: required
      PSO_DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY: "${CATALOG_DISPATCH_KEY:?}"
      # a consumer also names the key of each publisher it verifies: PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_KEY_<SERVICE>, with the publisher's
      # name in upper case ("orders" here), set to "${ORDERS_DISPATCH_KEY:?}"
    depends_on: { postgres: { condition: service_healthy }, rabbitmq: { condition: service_healthy } }
volumes:
  pgdata:
```

What to keep when you adapt it:

- **`networks: [internal]`** puts the container on the network of the generated services; it is reachable by its service name (`postgres:5432`) and has **no published port**. Publish one only on `127.0.0.1`, and only to inspect it from your machine.
- **A health check and `depends_on` with `service_healthy`**: a Spring service that starts before its database fails its migration and is restarted by `restart: unless-stopped`; with the dependency it starts once, in order.
- **`${VAR:?}`** for every secret, with the value in `.env`. The signing keys are at least 32 characters (for example `openssl rand -hex 32`).
- Redis is added the same way: `image: redis:7-alpine`, a health check with `redis-cli ping`, and `REDIS_URL: "redis://redis:6379"` on the services that use it.
- A Spring service that calls another one receives its address here as well, over TLS with the mounted authority: for a service declared with `base-url: ${CATALOG_URL:...}` and `tls.ca-file: ${SERVICES_CA_FILE:}` (names you choose), set `CATALOG_URL: "https://catalog:8082/catalog"` and `SERVICES_CA_FILE: /run/pso/tls/ca.crt`.
- The generated containers have a read-only root file system; that does not apply to the infrastructure containers you add, which need their data volume.

Then `docker compose config --quiet` and `docker compose up -d --wait` as above.

### External infrastructure (production)

A production deployment normally uses a database and a broker that already exist outside the Compose project: a managed PostgreSQL, a Redis or RabbitMQ service, or servers your organisation operates. Nothing changes in the application or in the generated files: **do not add the containers, set the same variables** to the external addresses.

```yaml title="docker-compose.override.yml" evidence="illustrative"
services:
  orders:
    environment:
      DB_URL: "${ORDERS_DB_URL:?}"          # jdbc:postgresql://db.example.internal:5432/orders?sslmode=verify-full
      DB_USER: "${ORDERS_DB_USER:?}"
      DB_PASSWORD: "${ORDERS_DB_PASSWORD:?}"
      PSO_DISPATCH_ENABLED: "true"
      RABBITMQ_URL: "${RABBITMQ_URL:?}"     # amqps://user:password@broker.example.internal:5671
      PSO_DISPATCH_TRUST_MODE: required
      PSO_DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY: "${ORDERS_DISPATCH_KEY:?}"
```

| Point | Rule |
|---|---|
| transport | encrypted, with verification: `sslmode=verify-full` in the JDBC URL, `amqps://`, `rediss://`. Certificate verification is never switched off |
| credentials | one account per service with the rights that service needs, delivered by the platform's secret store or `.env`; never in the image, in `application.yml` or in the repository |
| network | the containers must be able to reach the address: the generated network `internal` is an ordinary bridge with outbound access. No inbound port is needed for infrastructure |
| migrations | Flyway runs the service's `db/migration` files when it starts, with the account in `DB_USER`; PSO never drops tables or data ([migrations](microservices/persistence.md)) |
| start order | there is no `depends_on` for something outside the project: a service that cannot reach its database fails its health check and is restarted until it can |
| other targets | the same variables apply to the descriptors of `pso deploy:init` and to a native deployment: only the place where they are set changes ([environment configuration](devops/environment-configuration.md)) |

Verified on 2026-11-14 with a consumer application outside the framework (three Spring services with PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ with the transactional outbox, service-to-service HTTPS, the development identity provider): the first form above with that application's names, started with `docker compose up -d --wait`. The external form was not run against a managed service; it differs only in the values of the variables.

## Stopping containers

`docker compose stop` sends `SIGTERM`. The orchestrator stops accepting connections, lets running requests finish within `PSO_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS` (default 5000), releases Channels and Dispatch and exits 0 ([runtime lifecycle](concepts/runtime-lifecycle.md)). Docker kills a container that is still running after `stop_grace_period`; the generated file sets it from `PSO_STOP_GRACE_PERIOD` (default `40s`). Keep it longer than `PSO_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS` + 11 s, or Docker ends the process before its own deadline. A Spring service ends through Spring's graceful shutdown and reports exit code 143 (the JVM's answer to `SIGTERM`).

## What was verified by running containers

| Item | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Spring runtime image options: non-root uid 10001, read-only root file system with a tmpfs `/tmp`, all capabilities dropped, `no-new-privileges` | a service jar was run in `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` with exactly those options; `/actuator/health` answered `200` from the host (the service must listen on `0.0.0.0` inside a container: `HOST=0.0.0.0`, which the Compose file sets) |
| Compose file syntax and required variables | `docker compose config` (above) |
| The generated stack as a whole, authenticated end to end (2026-11-14, `node scripts/validate-generated-deployment.mjs`, also run by `node scripts/release-gate.mjs --release`) | a fresh workspace (one orchestrator, the Spring services catalog and orders, generated resources, `tls:init --dev`, `docker:init --vendor`) plus a test identity provider, PostgreSQL, Redis and RabbitMQ from an override file. Images built, stack started with `docker compose up -d --wait`, every service healthy on its first start. A JWT from the identity provider is verified by the orchestrator, forwarded over verified HTTPS, verified again by the Spring service, and the request reads and writes PostgreSQL with the caller as author. Refused: no token, expired, wrong issuer, wrong audience, invalid signature (401 at the gateway), missing scope (403 at the gateway), missing role (403 at the service). TLS: a certificate from another authority, a wrong name, or no configured authority give 502; without TLS the orchestrator exits 1. Recovery of Redis and of the identity provider, key rotation, restart of single services, a 12 s request completing under a 15 s grace period with exit 0, stop and start of the whole stack |

## What was not verified

- The stack validation is part of the release approval run (`--release`), not of `npm test` or of the regression gate without `--release`: it builds images and takes several minutes. Without `--vendor` the builds cannot succeed from a clean checkout, because they must download the PSO artifacts (`com.pso:*` for Spring, `@pso/*` for Node) from a registry and those are not published.
- Mutual TLS inside Compose (it is verified outside Compose: [service identity](security/service-identity.md)), an expired service certificate inside Compose (verified outside it), a public identity provider, and Kafka as the broker of the stack.
- Any registry push, multi-architecture build or vulnerability scan of the images.

> [!WARNING]
> Until the PSO artifacts are published, build the orchestrator image with the packages vendored or from a private registry (the tarballs from `node scripts/release.mjs npm` can be installed from a file or registry), and build Spring images against a repository your build can reach (the file repository from `node scripts/release-maven.mjs`, or your own). The Dockerfile comments say the same.

## Variations

| Need | Do |
|---|---|
| to inspect without writing files | `pso docker:init --dry-run` |
| an image build that does not need this machine's PSO packages | `pso docker:init --vendor --force`: packs the `@pso/*` packages the service uses into `<service>/vendor/pso/*.tgz`, points `package.json` at them with relative paths and makes the Dockerfile copy `vendor/` before `npm install`. Commit `vendor/`. Without it, `docker:init` prints a `WARNING` naming the dependencies that resolve to a path on this machine |
| the same for a Spring service | the same command copies the `com.pso:*` artifacts of the service's `<pso.version>` from the local Maven repository (`pso java:install` puts them there; `--maven-repo <dir>` names another one) into `<service>/vendor/maven`, and the Dockerfile seeds the build's local repository with them (`COPY vendor/maven /root/.m2/repository`). Third-party dependencies still come from Maven Central or your mirror. Commit `vendor/`. Outside Docker (CI, another checkout) copy `vendor/maven/.` into the local repository before building. Without it, `docker:init` prints a `WARNING` for each Spring service |
| to overwrite after editing | `--force` (a differing file is otherwise a conflict, never overwritten silently) |
| a different registry/tag for deployment | generate cloud descriptors with [deploy:init](devops/cloud-descriptors.md) |
| to expose the orchestrator beyond loopback | put a TLS-terminating proxy in front rather than changing the bind ([TLS](security/tls-and-mtls.md)) |

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `required variable ... is missing a value` | copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill it in |
| `pso docker:build`: the daemon is not running | start Docker Desktop; nothing was built |
| image build fails resolving `com.pso:pso-bom` or `@pso/http` | the artifacts are not published: run `pso docker:init --vendor --force` so the service carries them, or see the warning above |
| `The PSO Java artifacts <version> were not found` from `--vendor` | run `pso java:install` first, or pass `--maven-repo` |
| the vendored version is a `-SNAPSHOT` | fine for development images; for a release build fixed-version artifacts with `node scripts/release-maven.mjs`, set `<pso.version>` to that version and vendor again |
| a Spring service cannot reach `localhost:5432`, or its container restarts with a connection error | no `DB_URL` was given to the container: see [Infrastructure](#infrastructure-postgresql-redis-rabbitmq) |
| a Spring container with Dispatch enabled exits at start in the `prod` profile | production refuses an unauthenticated Dispatch: configure the keys and `pso.dispatch.trust.mode`, see [publisher authentication](dispatch/security-and-observability.md) |
| the container is `unhealthy` | check `docker logs <container>`; the Spring service needs `HOST=0.0.0.0` and the `PSO_JWT_*` variables in `prod` |
| the service cannot write a file | `read_only: true`; write only to `/tmp` or a declared volume |

# Environment configuration

> Separating development, test, staging and production - the files, the selector, a worked example with the values that really differ, and the commands that prove what each environment will use.

Environments are `development`, `test`, `staging` and `production`. Select one with `--env` or `PSO_ENV` (default `development`).

```tree title="Configuration files by layer"
my-platform/
  pso.workspace.json  # generated: layer 2, workspace-wide "config"
  pso.config.production.json  # optional: layer 4, workspace-wide production overrides
  gateway/
    pso.config.json  # optional: layer 3, service settings
    pso.config.production.json  # optional: layer 4, service production overrides
```

Runtime variables (`PSO_CFG_server__port=9000`) and `--set` override files. Secrets are always references (`${env:NAME}`), supplied by the environment: `gateway/.env` locally, your secret manager in production.

## A worked example

Common settings in the service file; only what differs in the production file:

```json title="gateway/pso.config.json" evidence="illustrative"
{ "http": { "limits": { "maxBodyBytes": 1048576 } }, "security": { "authentication": { "algorithms": ["ES256"] } } }
```

```json title="gateway/pso.config.production.json" evidence="illustrative"
{ "logging": { "level": "info" }, "http": { "rateLimit": { "perMinute": 300, "provider": "redis", "redisUrl": "${env:RATE_LIMIT_REDIS_URL}" } } }
```

Now see what each environment will use, and where every value comes from:

```bash
pso config:show --service gateway --env production
pso config:validate --env production
```

Expected output of the first command for one value (from a real run, with `--set logging.level=debug`): `logging.level "debug" <- cli`, and `server.port 8081 <- workspace`; the last column names the layer that won ([Configuration resolution](concepts/configuration.md)). A literal secret in a file is an error you will see in `config:validate`:

```text evidence="expected"
ERROR   PSO_CONFIG_PLAINTEXT_SECRET gateway/pso.config.json: "database.password" looks like a secret stored as plain text
        hint: Reference it instead: "${env:NAME}" or "${secret:NAME}"
FAILED
```
*(expected output)*

## What differs between environments (typical)

| Setting | Development | Production |
|---|---|---|
| log format and level | pretty, `info` or `debug` | JSON, `info` |
| JWT key source | local PEM | JWKS over https from your identity provider |
| rate limit | high | sized for traffic; shared through Redis with several instances |
| upstream transport | plaintext to loopback | TLS (required for non-loopback hosts) |
| ports and addresses | fixed local ports | `PSO_UPSTREAM_<NAME>` from the platform |

## Variations

| You want | Do |
|---|---|
| a value for every environment | `pso.config.json` |
| a production-only value | `pso.config.production.json` or an environment variable |
| a secret | an environment variable referenced as `${env:NAME}` |
| to try a value once | `--set key=value` on the command |
| the Spring equivalent | profiles (`application-prod.yml`) and environment variables ([Spring configuration](spring/configuration.md)) |

## Good practice

Keep production values out of development files, run `pso config:validate --env production` and `pso security:check` in CI, and never commit `.env`. Review `pso config:show --env production` in a pull request that changes configuration, so you review the *effect*, not just the diff.

## One environment per service in development

`pso dev` starts every project of the workspace with its own environment. Lowest to highest priority:

| # | Source | Reaches |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `<workspace>/.env.<environment>` (for example `.env.development`) | every project |
| 2 | `<project>/.env` | that project only |
| 3 | `<project>/.env.<environment>` | that project, that environment |
| 4 | the environment `pso dev` runs in | every project; explicit, so it wins over files |
| 5 | `PORT`, `HOST`, `PSO_WORKSPACE`, `PSO_SERVICE` | set from `pso.workspace.json`; a file cannot change them |

`<environment>` is `PSO_ENV`, `development` when it is not set.

```ini title="customers/.env"
DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/customers
DB_USER=customers_app
DB_PASSWORD=customers-dev
PSO_LOG_LEVEL=debug
```

```ini title="orders/.env"
DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
DB_USER=orders_app
DB_PASSWORD=orders-dev
REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6379
```

```ini title=".env.development (shared by every project)"
PSO_JWT_ISSUER=http://localhost:9443
PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE=pso-api
PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI=http://127.0.0.1:9443/.well-known/jwks.json
```

- A project's files reach that project only: `orders` never sees the database password of `customers`.
- `<workspace>/.env` is **not** read by `pso dev`: that name belongs to Docker Compose (the variables of the containers of the generated deployment).
- When a variable is both in a file and in the shell, the shell wins and `pso dev` says so (`DB_URL comes from the environment of pso dev`). Only names are printed, never values.
- The files are a development mechanism. Never commit them (`.env` and `.env.*` are in the generated `.dockerignore`; add them to `.gitignore`).
- Running the orchestrator alone with `npm run dev` reads `<orchestrator>/.env` only.

Verify: `pso dev` prints one line per service such as `[pso] orders: environment: the process environment, .env.development (3 variables), orders/.env (4 variables)`.

## Static checks read what the application reads

`pso security:check`, `pso security:validate` and `pso lint` evaluate **one environment** (`--env`, else `PSO_ENV`, else `development`) with the sources above, and print which they used:

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso security:check
environment: development (default; choose another with --env or PSO_ENV)
  gateway: configuration from the process environment, gateway/.env (3 variables)
  catalog: configuration from the process environment
OK
This result is about "development". It says nothing about production: run `pso security:check --env production` where the production variables are set (a pipeline, the platform).
```

For `production` no environment file is read, so a developer's `.env` can never make a production check pass. Checks that read files (keys, hard-coded secrets, route policies, Spring configuration, every `pso.config.<environment>.json` that exists) run whatever environment was chosen: a mistake in `pso.config.production.json` is a finding of a development check too. Earlier versions of `pso security:check` evaluated `production` by default and did not read the gateway's `.env`, so a project set up as documented was reported as not configured; a pipeline that relied on that default now passes `--env production` (or sets `PSO_ENV=production`).

## Common mistakes

- Putting a production URL in the base file "for now".
- Forgetting that an environment variable beats the file, and wondering why the file edit has no effect (`config:show` shows the origin).
- Misspelling a key: the warning `Unknown configuration key` lists the valid keys.

## Next steps

- [Configuration resolution](concepts/configuration.md)
- [Development or production configuration?](decisions/dev-or-production-config.md)

# CI/CD

> The generated GitHub Actions workflow, the checks worth running in any CI in the order that fails fastest, and a release pipeline that produces checksummed, signed artifacts.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

`pso docker:init` writes `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with three jobs:

| Job | Steps |
|---|---|
| `orchestrator` | Node 24, `npm install`, TypeScript check, `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` |
| `spring` (matrix over services) | Temurin 21 with Maven cache, `./mvnw -B -ntp verify` |
| `compose` | `cp .env.example .env`, `docker compose config --quiet` |

The workflow is generated and statically checked; it has **not been executed on GitHub** here. It also assumes the PSO artifacts are installable in the runner (see the Docker page's warning).

## Checks to add, in order of cost

If the `pso` CLI is available in your pipeline, run the cheap, dependency-free checks first so a broken change fails in seconds:

| Step | Needs | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| `pso validate` | nothing installed | structure, routes, contracts, module wiring |
| `pso config:validate --env production` | nothing installed | unknown keys (errors in production and with `--strict`), wrong types, plaintext secrets |
| `pso security:check --strict` | nothing installed | missing JWT config, unignored keys, hard-coded credentials, risky public routes |
| `pso lint` | npm dependencies | the three above plus TypeScript type-check |
| `pso test` | npm and Maven | each service's own tests |
| `pso security:audit` | network | npm advisories; SNAPSHOT/range scan of POMs |
| `pso build` | npm and Maven | artifacts with SHA-256 manifest |

then `pso deploy:plan` for review and `pso deploy --yes` from a protected, manually approved job. Deployment never happens implicitly.

```yaml
# an extra job in your own workflow
pso-checks:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with: { node-version: "24" }
    - run: node path/to/pso/packages/cli/bin/pso.js validate
    - run: node path/to/pso/packages/cli/bin/pso.js security:check --strict
```

(Illustrative: how you obtain the CLI in CI depends on how you install it; the packages are not published, see [installation](getting-started/installation.md).)

## A release pipeline

To produce publishable evidence for each release, run the release scripts from the framework repository in a protected job:

```bash
node scripts/release.mjs npm  --out release-out/npm   --sign-key "$SIGNING_KEY_FILE"
node scripts/release-maven.mjs --out release-out/maven --sign-key "$SIGNING_KEY_FILE"
node scripts/verify-release.mjs release-out/npm --trust release-public.pem
```

They pack the artifacts, write SHA-256 sums, a CycloneDX SBOM, a licence inventory and a secret scan, and (with a key supplied from the CI secret store, never from the repository) sign the checksums and a provenance statement. Nothing is published by the scripts. See [Distribution](devops/distribution-and-installation.md) for what each stage proves and what it does not (the provenance is self-asserted, not an attested SLSA build; there is no GPG or Authenticode signing).

## Pipeline hygiene

- Keep secrets in the CI secret store; the scripts refuse a signing key located inside the repository.
- Run the cheap checks on every pull request; the expensive ones on merge.
- Archive `manifest.json`, `SHA256SUMS` and the SBOM with the release.
- Never let a pull request from a fork access deployment credentials.

## Common mistakes

- Deploying from the same job that runs untrusted code.
- Caching `node_modules` across Node major versions.
- Treating `npm audit` as complete: Maven dependencies are not scanned by PSO.

## Next steps

- [Docker](devops/docker.md)
- [Build and deploy](devops/build-and-deploy.md)

# Health checks and observability

> Health endpoints, logs and correlation ids in one place, with what each runtime exposes, what a probe returns, and where the deeper guides are.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

## Health

| Service | Endpoints |
|---|---|
| Orchestrator | `GET /health/live`, `GET /health/ready` (framework module; public; exempt from rate limiting) |
| Spring | `GET /actuator/health` with liveness/readiness probes enabled; details never shown |

`pso dev`, `pso services:health`, Docker `HEALTHCHECK` and the deploy `--health-url` check all use them. Verified answer of the orchestrator's readiness endpoint:

```text evidence="expected"
GET /health/ready  ->  200  {"status":"UP","upstreams":1}
```

That body is unchanged for an orchestrator without dependencies. Readiness answers **503** with `{"status":"DOWN", ...}` and `Retry-After: 5` in three cases: start-up has not finished, shutdown has begun, or a **required dependency** of this instance is unavailable. Dependencies are reported under `checks` (the key appears only when there is something to report):

```text evidence="expected"
GET /health/ready  ->  503  {"status":"DOWN","upstreams":1,"checks":{"dispatch":{"status":"DOWN","required":true,"detail":"probe timed out after 2000 ms"}},"state":"ready"}
```

| Dependency (`checks` key) | Present when | Required by default |
|---|---|---|
| `dispatch` | Dispatch is enabled | yes |
| `channels` | Channels use the Redis bus | yes |
| `rateLimit` | rate limiting uses Redis | only with the failure policy `closed` (with `open` requests are still served) |

Probes run in the background (every 5 seconds, each bounded to 2 seconds; `http.readiness.intervalMs` and `http.readiness.timeoutMs`), so a request to `/health/ready` only reads the last result. A dependency is reported `DOWN` after two consecutive failed probes and `UP` again on the first success. To keep an instance in rotation while a dependency is down, list it in `http.readiness.optional` (`PSO_READINESS_OPTIONAL=dispatch,channels`): it is still reported, with `"required":false`. Upstream services are counted, never probed: one unavailable service must not take every gateway instance out of rotation. Liveness (`/health/live`) never looks at dependencies. Details never contain addresses or credentials.

This is what `pso services:health` prints when nothing is running (exit code 1):

```text evidence="expected"
DOWN  catalog            http://127.0.0.1:8081/actuator/health
DOWN  gateway            http://127.0.0.1:3000/health/ready
```

| Probe | Use it for | Do not use it for |
|---|---|---|
| liveness (`/health/live`) | "restart me if I am stuck" | checking dependencies: a down upstream must not restart the gateway |
| readiness (`/health/ready`) | "send me traffic" | slow checks: it is called often |

## Logs

The orchestrator logs one line per request (timestamp, level, correlation id, trace id, method, path, status, duration) plus start-up and security events, as readable coloured text on a terminal and as JSON elsewhere; Spring services use Spring Boot's console pattern locally and structured JSON in `prod`/`staging`. Tokens, keys and secrets are redacted. See the full guide: [Logging](devops/logging.md).

## Correlation ids

A client-supplied `x-correlation-id` is **accepted when it is well-formed** (8 to 64 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`) and replaced by a generated UUID when it is not. The orchestrator returns it in the response (header and error body) and sends it to the upstream service, so one request can be followed across logs. Spring services apply the same rule and put it in the logging context.

## Metrics and traces

The orchestrator has request and upstream metrics, W3C trace propagation and an opt-in OpenTelemetry export (OTLP over protobuf by default, or JSON) with the official SDK; Spring services get the same through `pso-observability-starter`, which is off unless an OTLP endpoint is configured. Studio shows what was measured and says "not instrumented" or "unavailable" instead of showing zeros. See [Runtime telemetry](devops/observability.md). Dispatch keeps in-process counters and adapter health ([Dispatch observability](dispatch/security-and-observability.md)).

## Not implemented

OTLP logs export and sampling policies beyond the sampling probability setting; consumer lag and dead-letter depth are not exported. `pso dispatch:health` is not implemented (exit code 2); use `pso dispatch:doctor`.

## A minimal production setup

1. Probes: liveness and readiness on the paths above.
2. Logs: `PSO_LOG_FORMAT=json` for the orchestrator, the `prod` profile for Spring, shipped from stdout.
3. Metrics and traces: set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` to your collector.
4. Alerts: `ERROR`/`FATAL` logs, readiness failing, dead-letter channels non-empty.

## Common mistakes

- Pointing a liveness probe at a path that checks the database.
- Alerting on `4xx`: they are mostly client mistakes; alert on `5xx` and on latency.
- Dropping the correlation id in your own HTTP clients.

## Next steps

- [Logging](devops/logging.md)
- [Runtime telemetry](devops/observability.md)
- [Studio](devops/studio.md)

# PSO Studio

> The local developer control center: what each screen shows, where the data comes from and how it is protected.

```bash
pso studio [--port N] [--no-open] [--remote]
```

Studio is a read-only control center (with `--remote` it also gains the **Cloud** section to manage servers: see [Studio Cloud section](cloud/studio-cloud.md)) for the workspace it was started in. Every figure comes from the workspace files, the `pso dev` registry, live health probes or log files. Nothing is simulated: when a source does not exist, the screen says so instead of showing zero.

![PSO Studio overview for a generated workspace before either service has started, showing zero healthy services, one declared route, topology and configuration diagnostics](../../assets/screenshots/studio-overview.png)

*A real Studio capture from a disposable workspace before `pso dev` started. `0/2` healthy means both declared services are stopped; it does not mean the route declaration is missing. The topology shows the gateway-to-catalog route, while Recent activity names missing development JWT settings. Start the services and refresh to compare the live state.*

## Screens

| Screen | Developer question | Data source |
|---|---|---|
| Overview | Is my application running and what needs attention? | live probes, `pso dev` registry, route and module analysis, diagnostics, logs |
| Workspaces | Which workspace is this and what does it declare? | `pso.workspace.json` |
| Services | Which services exist, are they healthy, how are they connected? For Spring services: which starters, prefix, security, HTTP client, database and dispatch settings are in effect, and does the configuration validate? | workspace, live probes, registry, discovered resources, `application*.yml` (read statically, no secret values) |
| Routes | Which endpoints are exposed, who may call them and where do they go? | `ROUTES.pso.ts` registries (static analysis) |
| Modules | How are modules composed and is any declaration broken? | `MODULE.pso.ts` and `ROUTES.pso.ts` (static analysis) |
| Dispatch | Which providers, events, producers and consumers are declared, and (on request) is the broker reachable? | `EVENTS.pso.ts`, `*.events.json`, dispatch configuration (static), opt-in connection probe |
| Security | How is authentication configured and which routes are protected? | `security.*` configuration, route analysis, `security:check` |
| Observability | What did my services log, can I follow one request? | `.pso/logs/*.log` |
| Diagnostics | What is wrong and how do I fix it? | route validation, security checks, security configuration |
| Settings | Where does each setting come from, is it valid per environment? | configuration layers (values masked) |

## Health states

Health is derived from a live probe of the declared health endpoint and the `pso dev` lifecycle. It is never inferred from registration alone.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Healthy | the health endpoint answered `200` in under one second and the lifecycle is `READY` (or the service was not started by `pso dev`) |
| Degraded | it answers, but the lifecycle is not `READY` or the probe was slow (over 1000 ms) |
| Unhealthy | the endpoint answered with a non-`200` status, or `pso dev` reports the service as started or failed but nothing answers |
| Stopped | nothing answers on the declared port and no running process is registered |
| Unknown | the probe could not be run |

## Routes and modules

Only routes declared in a valid `ROUTES.pso.ts` appear as active; a controller decorator alone never implies exposure. The module graph draws `MODULE.pso.ts` imports only. Runtime communication between services is drawn in the Overview topology, never mixed into the module graph. An unresolved import is drawn to a marked placeholder.

## Observability

The log viewer reads structured JSON lines (and classifies plain text lines by keyword). It supports severity, service, correlation id, free text and time range filters, and shows tables in pages of 50 entries; the server returns at most 1000 entries per request. Time ranges only match lines that carry a timestamp. There are no charts other than counts taken from the real log lines and the latest health probe latency.

Runtime telemetry of the orchestrator (requests, errors, latency, rate limiting and, in the API payload, dispatch counters) is shown on the Observability page when the service exposes its authenticated diagnostics endpoint ([Runtime telemetry](devops/observability.md)); every other service is shown as Not instrumented, Not configured, Unavailable or Unknown with the reason, and without numbers. Consumer lag and dead-letter depth are **not available**: the runtime does not export them, and Studio never shows a zero in their place.

## Security of Studio itself

- Binds to `127.0.0.1` only, requires a one-time token (cookie `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`) and checks the `Host` header against DNS-rebinding.
- **Read-only:** every method other than `GET` is rejected, and there are no configuration mutation endpoints. If mutation is ever added it must go through authenticated, authorized and audited framework APIs.
- Content security policy `default-src 'self'` with no inline script or style, no framing, no form posts, no remote origins. The interface renders all data as text; log lines containing HTML are shown literally.
- Secrets are masked on the server: bearer tokens, JWTs, private keys and secret-looking keys (`password`, `token`, `apiKey`, `authorization`, ...) never reach the browser, the API or the copied diagnostic context.
- No CORS headers are sent, so other origins cannot read the API.
- Localhost is not treated as harmless: the token, the host check and the read-only rule apply there too. Remote access is not supported; do not expose the port.

## Documentation and AI context

Screens link to the matching documentation (routes, modules, security, dispatch, error codes and command references). The documentation is built on first use and served by Studio under `/docs/` on the same origin. On Diagnostics, **Copy AI context** copies a sanitized summary (workspace counts, routes and diagnostics) for AI-assisted troubleshooting; it never contains tokens, keys or secret values.

## Interface

Dark and light themes (follows the system preference and remembers your choice), collapsible navigation, global search over services, routes, modules and pages (press `/` or `Ctrl+K`), keyboard-accessible tables, graphs and drawers (`Esc` closes a drawer and returns focus), and responsive layouts down to phone width. Views refresh every five seconds only while visible and only where live data matters (Overview, Services, Observability); refresh pauses while you type or a drawer is open, and requests made obsolete by navigation are cancelled.

## Not implemented

Remote access with authentication, configuration editing, lifecycle actions (start, stop, restart), notifications and consumer lag / dead-letter depth (not exported by the runtime).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| the browser shows "access denied" | the URL carries a one-time token: use the URL printed by the current `pso studio` run (a previous token is invalid) |
| a service shows as unavailable | Studio probes real endpoints: start the service (`pso services:health` says the same) |
| the observability screen is empty | it reads `.pso/logs/*.log`, written by `pso dev`; a service started elsewhere has no log there |
| consumer lag or dead-letter depth is missing | they are not exported; Studio shows "unavailable", not zero |

## Common mistakes

- Sharing the Studio URL (it contains the token).
- Exposing the port beyond loopback: remote access is unsupported.
- Reading "healthy" as "correct": it means the health probe answered.

## Next steps

- [Development environment](devops/development-environment.md)
- [Runtime telemetry](devops/observability.md)
