# Runtime telemetry and OpenTelemetry

> What the orchestrator measures, the authenticated diagnostics endpoint, W3C trace propagation, the opt-in OTLP export and how Studio shows it without inventing numbers.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> Implemented and verified for the **TypeScript orchestrator** (real traffic, real OTLP collector endpoints, real Redis for the dispatch counters, Studio in a real browser) and for **Spring Boot services** through `pso-observability-starter`. Export uses the **official OpenTelemetry SDK / Micrometer exporters**. Consumer lag and dead-letter depth are **not exported** and therefore not shown. OpenTelemetry **logs** are not exported (logs stay structured JSON with the correlation and trace ids).

Everything below is measured from real requests. A value that cannot be measured is reported as unavailable, never as zero.

## What is measured

| Signal | Detail |
|---|---|
| HTTP requests | count by status class, duration histogram per declared route (`http.server.request.duration`, seconds, fixed bounds 5 ms to 10 s), in-flight requests, 401/403/429 counts. Unknown paths are one `unmatched` label; routes are the **declared** templates, never raw URLs |
| Upstream calls | latency histogram and outcome per upstream: `ok`, `timeout`, `unavailable`, `tls`, `bad_gateway`, `response_too_large`, `aborted` |
| Rate limiting | provider and allowed/denied/backend-failure counters (absent when limiting is off) |
| Dispatch | publish/consume/retry/dead-letter counters and the broker health seen by the adapter (absent when dispatch is not installed) |
| Lifecycle | `starting`, `ready`, `draining`, `stopped`; shutdown start and in-flight count; a client that disconnects is recorded as 499, not as a success |

A request is recorded when its connection closes, so every exit path (including aborts) is counted exactly once.

## The diagnostics endpoint

`GET /_pso/telemetry` exists **only** when `PSO_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN` (32 or more characters) is set; otherwise the path does not exist (`404`). With a token it requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (constant-time comparison) and answers `401` otherwise. The token is a secret: set it as a variable or `"${env:NAME}"`; a value written in `pso.config.json` is refused at start-up, and a token shorter than 32 characters stops start-up. The document contains no credentials, payloads, raw paths or client addresses, and the diagnostics calls themselves are not counted.

## Distributed tracing

The orchestrator implements W3C Trace Context. A valid incoming `traceparent` is continued; an invalid or all-zero one starts a new trace. The trace is returned in the response `traceparent`, forwarded to upstream services with a **new child span id** (the caller's own span id is never forwarded), and written as `traceId` in the structured request log. Spring services receive the header; whether they propagate it further depends on their own instrumentation.

## OpenTelemetry export (opt-in)

Nothing leaves the process by default. Setting the standard `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` enables a push of **metrics and spans** over OTLP/HTTP (`/v1/metrics`, `/v1/traces`) with the official `@opentelemetry/sdk-metrics`, `sdk-trace-base` and `exporter-*-otlp-*` packages (optional dependencies of `@pso/http`, loaded only when an endpoint is set; a missing package is a start-up error that names it). Spans carry the same trace and span ids that were put in the `traceparent` headers, so the exported tree matches what crossed the wire: server span, then one client span per upstream call.

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | `http(s)://collector:4318`; no credentials in the URL; in production a remote endpoint must be `https://` |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` | `http/protobuf` (default, per the specification) or `http/json`; gRPC is not supported |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` | `name=value,name2=value2` (for example an API key; never logged) |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | resource `service.name` (default: the service name) |
| `PSO_OTEL_EXPORT_INTERVAL_MS` | export period, 500 to 600000 (default 10000) |
| `PSO_OTEL_TRACES=false` | export metrics only |

Metric names: `http.server.request.duration`, `http.server.active_requests`, `pso.upstream.request.duration`, `pso.upstream.requests`, `pso.auth.failures`, `pso.ratelimit.decisions` (only when rate limiting is configured), and `pso.dispatch.{published,publish_failures,consumed,handler_failures,retries,dead_lettered,duplicates}` (only when dispatch is installed): a subsystem that is not configured exports no data point, never a zero. Span buffering is bounded (1000 spans), shutdown flushes with a 5 s deadline, and export failures never affect requests. Sampling follows the incoming sampled flag; other sampling policies and OTLP logs are not implemented.

## Spring Boot services

Add `com.pso:pso-observability-starter`. It brings Micrometer Tracing with the OpenTelemetry bridge and the official OTLP exporters, and maps the same variables (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME`, `PSO_OTEL_EXPORT_INTERVAL_MS`) onto Spring Boot's `management.otlp.*` properties at the lowest precedence. **Without an endpoint both exporters are switched off** (Boot would otherwise push to `localhost:4318`), while W3C `traceparent` propagation stays on. `PsoHttpClient` calls are observed (client span, `http.client.requests`, `traceparent` to the remote), inbound requests produce server spans and `http.server.requests`, and dispatch/outbox counters (`pso.dispatch.*`, `pso.outbox.*`, `pso.dispatch.broker.up`, `pso.ratelimit.decisions`) are Micrometer meters exported with the rest. The resource carries `service.name` from `pso.service.name`. Studio does not read Spring services' telemetry (only the orchestrator's diagnostics endpoint): use your collector.

## What Studio shows

Studio's **Observability** page has a *Runtime telemetry* panel. For each service it asks the diagnostics endpoint (Studio reads the same `PSO_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN` from its own environment; the token never goes to the browser) and shows one of six states:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Healthy | the service answered, readiness is UP and no degradation rule matched |
| Degraded | the service answered and at least one rule matched (the panel lists which) |
| Unavailable | the service did not answer on its port |
| Not configured | the service runs but its diagnostics endpoint is off |
| Not instrumented | the service has no PSO telemetry (Spring services) |
| Unknown | Studio has no token, or the tokens differ, or the answer was not understood |

Degradation rules: state other than `ready`, readiness not UP, 5xx at 5% or more of at least 20 requests, rate-limit backend failures, a dispatch broker reported down, or an upstream failing in half or more of at least 10 calls (client aborts do not count). Numbers (requests, 5xx, rate limited, average latency) appear only for services that answered; every other row says why there are none. The table also shows, per service that answered, the dispatch counters (published, consumed, retries, dead letters) and the broker health from the adapter's own probe, or "not installed"; the API additionally carries upstream and shutdown details.

## What you see (verified)

With `PSO_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN` set, the telemetry of a gateway that served a few requests includes Dispatch counters when Dispatch is enabled; the verified dispatch section from a real run is on [Walkthrough](dispatch/walkthrough.md). The log side of the same requests is in [Logging](devops/logging.md): one `request` line per request with the status, duration, correlation id and trace id.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `/_pso/telemetry` is `404` | diagnostics are off by default: set `PSO_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN` (32 or more characters) |
| `401` from it | wrong or short token |
| nothing arrives at the collector | export is off unless `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set; check the endpoint is safe and reachable |
| traces do not connect across services | send a W3C `traceparent`; the orchestrator continues and forwards it |

## Common mistakes

- Using the diagnostics token as a general API key.
- Alerting on raw counters without rates.
- Expecting metrics from a service that is not instrumented (Studio says "not instrumented").

## Next steps

- [Logging](devops/logging.md)
- [Health checks and observability](devops/health-and-observability.md)

# Signed packages and installation lifecycle

> Build a signed (optionally encrypted) .psopkg, compile the Windows installer, install, check integrity, repair, update, roll back and uninstall, and produce npm and Maven release evidence - with the real output of each step and the limits that remain.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> Implemented and tested on disposable installation roots: the `.psopkg` format, `setup`, `integrity`, `repair`, `update` (with rollback) and `uninstall`; the Windows installer **builds** with Inno Setup 7, installs an encrypted package for a developer who created their own recipient key, repairs, updates and rolls back correctly. Not verified: a **signed** installer (it is not code-signed), SmartScreen, other Windows versions and corporate application-control policies. Release scripts for npm and Maven prepare checksums, SBOM, licence inventory and signatures with a key you supply; **nothing is published**, and there is no GPG or Authenticode signing.

Output labelled *verified* below was captured from a real run on an isolated temporary installation root; ids, sizes and times belong to that run.

## 1. The package

A `.psopkg` is one file: a JSON header (name, version, platform, components, file list with SHA-256), a payload (zstd-compressed archive, optionally AES-256-GCM encrypted) and an **Ed25519 signature** over the header and payload digests. The signature is verified against keys **you** trust *before* anything is decrypted or decompressed.

```bash
pso dist keygen --kind signing   --out keys --name release     # keep release.private.pem secret
pso dist keygen --kind recipient --out keys --name customer    # only needed for encrypted packages
pso dist build  --out stage                                    # allowlist from dist.config.json; secrets are excluded and reported
pso dist pack   --stage stage --sign-key keys/release.private.pem --out pso.psopkg
pso dist verify pso.psopkg --trust keys/release.public.pem
```

What a package of the framework's own CLI looks like (Expected output; 6958 files, 11.2 MB, built from `dist.config.json` in the repository):

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso dist inspect pso-0.1.0.psopkg --trust release.public.pem
pso 0.1.0 (win32/x64) signed by 08f3c745354b3cc3
components: cli@0.1.0
not encrypted
6958 file(s)

$ pso dist verify pso-0.1.0.psopkg --trust release.public.pem
OK  pso 0.1.0 (win32/x64), 6958 file(s), signed by 08f3c745354b3cc3
every file was decompressed and its SHA-256 checked
```

- Nothing is signed or encrypted unless you pass a key. Private keys are never printed and never overwritten.
- `--encrypt --recipient <public.pem>` wraps a random content key for each recipient (X25519 + HKDF + AES-256-GCM). There is **no universal key**. `verify` of an encrypted package without the recipient key checks only the header and signature and says so.
- Extraction refuses absolute paths, `..`, drive letters, reserved names, case-duplicates and links, enforces size and ratio limits, and is all-or-nothing.
- Encryption protects content in transit and at rest. It does **not** prevent a legitimate recipient from reverse engineering what they receive.
- Keys: keep signing keys outside the repository (the release scripts refuse a key located inside it); distribute only public keys.

## 2. Installation lifecycle

Every command operates on an explicit root: `--root`, else `PSO_HOME`, else the installation the running `pso` was started from (its own launcher says which). PSO never guesses a directory and refuses file system roots, home and system directories and links.

```bash
pso setup     --package pso.psopkg --root C:\Tools\pso --trust release.public.pem
pso integrity check --full --root C:\Tools\pso          # read-only
pso repair    --dry-run --root C:\Tools\pso
pso update    check   --catalog catalog.json --root C:\Tools\pso
pso update    install --catalog catalog.json --root C:\Tools\pso
pso update    rollback --root C:\Tools\pso
pso uninstall --complete --yes --root C:\Tools\pso
```

| Command | Guarantee |
|---|---|
| `setup` | Package fully verified first; side by side under `versions/<v>`; a signed inventory is stored with the trusted public key |
| `integrity` | Never modifies anything. Quick = presence and size; `--full` = SHA-256. Extra files are reported, not deleted |
| `repair` | Restores files of the **installed version only** from an authenticated package; never upgrades; config, cache and logs are untouched; failure rolls back |
| `update` | Signed catalog with expiry and a rising `sequence` (replay protection); channels stable/beta/dev; size and SHA-256 checked; new version verified before an atomic switch; previous version kept; interrupted updates are cleaned up |
| `uninstall` | Removes only files listed in the inventory; links are unlinked, never followed. Standard keeps config/cache/logs; `--complete` removes everything PSO owns; `--purge` also deletes projects you name with `--project <dir> --confirm <same dir>` that carry a PSO marker file |

Exit codes: `0` success, `1` problems found or refusal, `2` blocked by a missing toolchain (installer).

### Install and verify (Expected output)

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso setup --package pso-0.1.0.psopkg --root <root> --trust release.public.pem
installed 0.1.0 (6958 file(s)) into <root>

$ pso setup ...  (again)
error: INSTALL_EXISTS: version 0.1.0 is already installed

$ pso integrity check --full --root <root>
OK  <root>  version 0.1.0  (full check)
  ok   installation state: install.json lists 1 version(s)
  ok   inventory signature: signed by a trusted key; 6958 file(s)
  ok   version: 0.1.0
  ok   file hashes (SHA-256): 6958 of 6958 file(s) intact
  ok   unexpected files: none
  ok   repair source: the authenticated package is cached
  ok   shim bin/pso.cmd: present in the version directory
```

What was installed: under `<root>` there are `versions/0.1.0/` (the files of the package: `bin/pso.cmd`, `node_modules/@pso/...`), `.pso-install/` (`install.json`, the signed `inventory-0.1.0.json`, `packages/0.1.0.psopkg` as the repair source, `trust/*.public.pem`) and the owned user-data directories `config`, `cache`, `logs`.

### Damage, detect, repair (Expected output)

A file was deleted and another corrupted:

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso integrity check --full --root <root>
PROBLEMS  <root>  version 0.1.0  (full check)
  ok   inventory signature: signed by a trusted key; 6958 file(s)
  FAIL file hashes (SHA-256): 2 of 6958 file(s) damaged
  FAIL shim bin/pso.cmd: missing
  damaged: bin/pso.cmd (missing)
  damaged: node_modules/marked/package.json (size-mismatch)
Run `pso repair` to restore damaged files from the authenticated package.
[exit 1]

$ pso repair --dry-run --root <root>
[dry-run] would restore 2 file(s) of 0.1.0 from the cached package:
  bin/pso.cmd
  node_modules/marked/package.json

$ pso repair --full --root <root>
restored 2 file(s) of 0.1.0 from the cached package:
  bin/pso.cmd
  node_modules/marked/package.json
```

> [!NOTE]
> Corrupting `marked/package.json`, a dependency of the installed CLI itself, left the installed `pso` unable to start, so the repair above was run from a **known-good copy** of the CLI (`node <good>/bin/pso.js repair ... --root <root>`). That is a real recovery path: the repair needs any working CLI and the cached package, not the damaged install.

A quick check only compares presence and size; only `--full` finds same-size corruption.

### Update and rollback (Expected output)

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso update check --catalog catalog.json --root <root>
update available: 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1 (stable)

$ pso update install --catalog catalog.json --root <root>
updated 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1. The previous version is kept: `pso update rollback` returns to it.

$ pso integrity check --root <root>
OK  <root>  version 0.1.1  (quick check)
  ok   installation state: install.json lists 2 version(s)
  ...

$ pso update rollback --root <root>
rolled back 0.1.1 -> 0.1.0
```

An update catalog is signed (Ed25519), expires, carries a rising `sequence` (an older catalog is refused as a replay) and lists packages by size and SHA-256. A forged, expired or replayed catalog, a package that does not match its catalog entry, and an unsigned or foreign offline package are all refused (covered by the framework's tests). Between versions nothing is overwritten: the new version is installed beside the old one, expected, and only then activated atomically.

### Uninstall (Expected output)

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso uninstall --root <root>
error: uninstall is destructive and needs --yes
hint: Review the mode first: standard keeps user data, --complete removes all PSO-owned data, --purge also deletes the projects you name

$ pso uninstall --complete --yes --root <root>
complete uninstall: removed 13925 file(s) and 298 director(ies)
```

A foreign file placed in the root is left alone (observed in an earlier installer run: `keep.txt` survived; that run is recorded in the progress record, not re-run here), and the root directory itself is removed only if nothing foreign remains.

## 3. The Windows installer

> [!NOTE]
> The current release, PSO Web V2 `0.2.0-rc.3`, publishes its installer as an **experimental** asset ([Downloads](downloads/index.md)): an unencrypted developer distribution that bundles its private Node.js, needs no signer fingerprint, and installs silently only with the explicit acknowledgement `/VERYSILENT /SUPPRESSMSGBOXES /ACCEPTUNSIGNEDALPHA=1 /DIR=<folder>` (its `INSTALL.md`). Its Windows installation flow is not validated end to end; the portable ZIP is recommended. The encrypted, recipient-pinned flow below (`/SIGNER=`, Node.js on PATH) is the one of the historical `0.1.0-alpha.1` installer, kept as the reference for private encrypted releases.

```bash
pso dist installer --platform windows --package pso.psopkg --bootstrap pso-bootstrap.mjs --trust keys/release.public.pem --name PSO-Web-<version>-win-x64 --out inst
```

With `--publisher "<certificate common name>" --sign-command "<command containing $f>"` the installer is Authenticode-signed while it is built: Inno Setup runs the command on the uninstaller during compilation and on the finished installer (`SignTool=`, `SignedUninstaller=yes`) and refuses a file that comes back unsigned. The release pipeline passes `scripts/psd/codesign.mjs sign` (SHA-256, RFC 3161 timestamp) and then enforces its release gate ([release integrity](infrastructure/release-integrity-and-signing.md#windows-code-signing)). `--sign-command` is refused together with `--dev-distribution`.

The command writes `pso-setup.iss` and compiles it with Inno Setup 6 or 7 (`ISCC` environment variable or the default install locations). Without Inno Setup it reports `BLOCKED` and exits `2`. The output is the installer plus a manifest with its SHA-256.

The installer carries exactly three things, all extracted on demand to a temporary folder and none copied by Inno Setup itself:

| Carried | Purpose |
|---|---|
| the signed `.psopkg` (already compressed; for a private release also **encrypted**) | the product |
| **one** public signing key | to be compared with the signer the developer trusts, never a trust anchor by itself |
| `pso-bootstrap.mjs`, one small readable file | verify, decrypt, extract and activate; it contains none of the CLI, the deployment engine, Studio or any other part of PSO |

Earlier versions of the installer also copied the whole CLI, in plaintext, to a temporary folder to run `pso setup` from it. That made encrypting the package pointless, and it is gone: `--stage` is refused.

What the installer does, in order, **before Inno Setup installs anything**: it checks Node.js 24 or newer; it shows the signing key fingerprint; it runs the bootstrap, which refuses unless the signer is one the developer pinned (or passed as `/SIGNER=<64 hex>`), verifies the Ed25519 signature before decrypting, finds the developer's recipient identity (see [Recipient keys](#recipient-keys-for-a-private-release)), decrypts, checks every file against the signed header and extracts into a staging folder, then activates the version with renames. A refusal returns a message and a non-zero exit code and leaves nothing behind, not even an uninstall entry. Uninstalling from Windows Settings runs `pso uninstall --complete` with the active version's CLI and, if that CLI is itself damaged and cannot, with the previous version's CLI, which is kept side by side (the uninstall works from the signed inventories of every version). The installer is **per user** on purpose: the developer's key is protected for one Windows account, and an installer elevated as a *different* account could not open it.

```text evidence="expected"
$ PSO-Web-0.1.0-alpha.1-win-x64.exe /VERYSILENT /SUPPRESSMSGBOXES /DIR=C:\Tools\pso /SIGNER=<fingerprint> /LOG=setup.log
(exit 0)  install.json, inventory-0.1.0-alpha.1.json, packages/, trust/ under .pso-install; versions/0.1.0-alpha.1/

$ ... the signer is not the one you pinned
(non-zero exit; setup.log: SIGNER_NOT_TRUSTED ... Nothing was installed.)
```

Without `--sign-command` the result is **not Authenticode-signed**: signing needs a publicly trusted code-signing certificate, which no PSO release has yet. Integrity and authenticity come from the SHA-256 and the Ed25519 signature published with the release, checked against a fingerprint you received through a different channel.

### What was verified, and what was not

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| compile with Inno Setup 7 | verified |
| silent install of an encrypted package, as a recipient with a DPAPI-protected key | verified (exit 0, the layout above, `integrity check --full` OK) |
| refusal without an independent trust anchor, with a foreign signer, with a modified package, as a developer who is not a recipient | verified by tests of the bootstrap and by a real run of the compiled installer (non-zero exit, nothing left behind) |
| interrupted installation | verified: a stale staging folder with decrypted files is removed by the next operation |
| Inno uninstaller `unins000.exe` | ran and removed its registry entry in the validation of 2026-11-16; an earlier run on another machine state was blocked by Windows application control because the installer is unsigned |
| a signed installer, SmartScreen behaviour, other Windows versions, a corporate application-control policy | not tested |

> [!WARNING]
> Do not distribute the unsigned installer expecting a clean experience: the operating system may warn about an unknown publisher or block the installer or its uninstaller. Report such a block; do not work around it.

## Recipient keys for a private release

A private release is encrypted for the developers you authorize, one wrapped content key each. **A developer creates their own key pair; the maintainer never sees a private key.**

```bash
# the utility is one file: node pso-recipient.mjs <command>; shown here as pso-recipient
pso-recipient init --label "Ana Souza"            # creates the key pair on this machine, protected by Windows DPAPI (this account only)
pso-recipient show                                # fingerprint, protection, pinned signers
pso-recipient pin-signer --fingerprint <64 hex>   # the maintainer's signing key, received through a different channel
pso-recipient backup --out ana.backup.json        # passphrase-protected backup (recovery)
pso-recipient doctor                              # which account you run as, whether DPAPI works, whether the session is elevated
```

1. The developer obtains the `pso-recipient.mjs` utility and checks its SHA-256 against the value the maintainer published through a second channel. It is a single readable file with no network code.
2. `pso-recipient init` writes `<label>.enrollment.json` (public key and fingerprint only). The private key is stored DPAPI-protected (`CurrentUser`) in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\PSO\recipient`, or, where DPAPI is unavailable (PowerShell in Constrained Language Mode, non-Windows), under a passphrase (scrypt + AES-256-GCM).
3. The developer sends the enrollment file, and reads the fingerprint to the maintainer by another channel. The maintainer compares them and only then adds the public key to the recipients of the next release.
4. The maintainer encrypts the release for all authorized recipients with the unchanged `pso dist pack --encrypt --recipient a.pem,b.pem`. One installer serves them all.
5. The developer pins the maintainer's signer fingerprint once. From then on `pso repair` and `pso update` open the same identity, only when an encrypted package actually has to be read.

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| lost key, no backup | releases encrypted for it cannot be decrypted by anyone; enroll a new key and ask for a release that includes it |
| Windows account changed or profile rebuilt | the DPAPI blob cannot be opened; restore from the backup (`pso-recipient restore`) or enroll a new key |
| new machine | restore from the backup; DPAPI re-protects the key for the new account |
| installer started elevated as another account | the key is not readable there: `DPAPI_UNPROTECT_FAILED`; run it as the account that created the key |
| a recipient is removed | **future** releases are not encrypted for them. Releases they already hold stay readable: removal cannot revoke earlier copies |

Encryption controls who can *install* a release. It does not prevent an authorized developer from inspecting what is installed on their own machine; see [Protection and its limits](#protection-and-its-limits).

## Protection and its limits

The installed framework is a distribution assembled from an explicit, classified allowlist, not a copy of the development repository: no sources, no tests, no source maps, no internal reports. Its proprietary JavaScript is bundled and minified with internal identifiers mangled; the engines that hold the most algorithms receive additional string and control-flow transforms; the public SDK is left readable on purpose because developers build on it. The agent that runs on Linux servers is protected the same way.

This raises the effort of reading and re-creating the implementation. It does **not** make it impossible: the code runs on the recipient's machine, so a determined developer with debugging tools or AI-assisted deobfuscation can still recover its behaviour. No anti-debugging, no antivirus evasion and no destructive anti-tamper is used. Installed files are checked against a signed inventory (`pso integrity check`) and repaired from the authenticated, encrypted package; that detects accidental damage and casual edits, and it is not a security boundary against the device owner.

## 4. Release evidence for npm and Maven

```bash
node scripts/release.mjs npm   --out release-out/npm   [--sign-key <ed25519 private pem>]
node scripts/release-maven.mjs --out release-out/maven [--sign-key <ed25519 private pem>]
node scripts/verify-release.mjs release-out/npm --trust <public pem>
```

Both scripts work on temporary copies, write artifacts to `--out`, and **publish nothing**. Verified stage report of the npm script (one run):

```text evidence="expected"
PASSED   pack - 5 tarballs: @pso/core@0.1.0, @pso/security@0.1.0, @pso/dispatch@0.1.0, @pso/http@0.1.0, @pso/cli@0.1.0
PASSED   reproducible tarballs - two independent packs have identical integrity
PASSED   content policy - no tests, maps, env files or key material in any tarball
PASSED   secret scan - 6 secret patterns, no findings
PASSED   SBOM (CycloneDX) - 39 components, production tree from package-lock.json
PASSED   licence inventory - licences: MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, ISC; own packages UNLICENSED (no licence granted)
NOT RUN  vulnerability audit - --skip-audit
PASSED   checksums + provenance - SHA256SUMS, manifest.json, provenance.json (self-asserted, not an attested SLSA build)
PASSED   signing - Ed25519 signature of SHA256SUMS and manifest.json (verify with signing-key.public.pem)
PASSED   clean install - outside the monorepo from tarballs: cli --help exit 0; imports imports-ok
```

`verify-release.mjs` checks the signature of `SHA256SUMS`, every checksum, the manifest signature and the DSSE provenance envelope against a public key **you** trust, and rejects (expected by tests): an untrusted key, a modified tarball, a modified checksum file, a swapped provenance subject, an unsigned release, and a signing key located inside the repository.

What this evidence does and does not give you:

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| SHA-256 sums, SBOM, licence inventory, secret scan | produced and checked |
| Ed25519 signature over the checksums | only with a key you supply; unsigned otherwise (reported as `NOT RUN`) |
| provenance | **self-asserted** by the build machine; not an attested SLSA build (that needs a hosted builder that signs it) |
| GPG signatures for Maven Central, Authenticode for Windows | not done: they need keys and certificates only you can provide |
| vulnerability scanning | `npm audit` for the production tree; Maven dependencies are not scanned |
| licence | the packages declare `UNLICENSED`; choosing a licence is a decision for the owner (see `docs/commercial/licensing-status.md` in the repository) |


## Variations

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| distribute to a customer you know | `--encrypt --recipient customer.public.pem`, plus the signature |
| air-gapped machine | `pso update install --package <file>` (offline packages are verified the same way) |
| several machines on one version | publish a signed catalog and run `update check` on a schedule |
| a corrupted install | `pso integrity check --full`, then `pso repair` from a good copy |

## Common mistakes

- Trusting a public key you did not receive over a trusted channel.
- Putting the signing key in the repository (the scripts refuse it).
- Expecting `repair` to upgrade (it restores the installed version only).
- Running a destructive uninstall test on your own workstation: use a temporary `--root`.

# Installed CLI and framework development CLI

> Which installation answers to the pso command in a terminal, how an npm-linked development checkout shadows an installed distribution, how to find and resolve PATH conflicts on Windows (PowerShell, CMD, Git Bash), and how to keep pso (installed) and pso-dev (framework checkout) apart.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** on Windows 11 with PowerShell, CMD and Git Bash: an npm-global link to a framework checkout was found shadowing the installed distribution in all three shells and was resolved without deleting the checkout or any other npm package.

Two things can answer to `pso` on one machine:

| | Installed distribution | Framework development checkout |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | a portable folder or an installer installation: a private Node.js runtime, a signed package, `bin\pso.cmd` | `packages/cli/bin/pso.js` of a clone of the framework repository |
| Used for | building applications with a released PSO | changing PSO itself |
| Integrity | `pso integrity check --full`, `pso repair --full` | none: it is source |
| Command | `pso` | `pso-dev` (recommended) or `node <checkout>\packages\cli\bin\pso.js` |

An application should be built with the installed `pso`. Use the checkout only to work on the framework.

## Find out which installation answers

```powershell
Get-Command pso -All | Format-Table CommandType, Source     # PowerShell: the first row wins
where pso                                                   # CMD
type -a pso                                                 # Git Bash
pso --version
```

The installed distribution resolves to `<installation>\bin\pso.cmd` (or `pso-launch.mjs` behind it). A path under `%APPDATA%\npm` (`pso`, `pso.cmd`, `pso.ps1`) is an **npm-global package or link**, often `npm link` run in `packages/cli` of a checkout:

```powershell
npm ls -g --depth=0        # "@pso/cli@0.2.0 -> .\D:\...\pso-web-framework\packages\cli" is a development link
```

Because `%APPDATA%\npm` usually comes before other user PATH entries, that link shadows the installed distribution in every shell, and `pso --version` alone cannot tell them apart (both may say 0.2.0).

## Resolve the conflict

1. Back up first: `reg export HKCU\Environment env-backup.reg` and `npm ls -g --depth=0 > npm-global.txt`.
2. Remove only the global link. The checkout and every other global package stay:

   ```powershell
   npm rm -g @pso/cli
   ```

3. Give the checkout its own name. The framework repository has `tools\dev-bin` (`pso-dev.cmd` for PowerShell and CMD, `pso-dev` for Git Bash), which runs the checkout's `packages/cli/bin/pso.js` with your Node.js. Add that folder to your **user** PATH, after the installed distribution's `bin`.
4. Put the installed distribution's `bin` on your user PATH (the installer does it when its PATH task is selected; for the portable ZIP add `<folder>\bin` yourself).
5. Open a **new** terminal (running terminals keep the old PATH) and check again with the commands above.

A PATH entry that points to a folder that no longer exists (for example a temporary test installation) is harmless but confusing; remove only that entry, after backing up the value.

## What goes wrong

- `pso` still runs the checkout: the terminal was opened before the change, or another `pso` (a second npm prefix, `nvm`, a copied shim) comes first; `Get-Command pso -All` shows it.
- `pso-dev` fails with `Cannot find module`: the checkout is not built (`npm run build` in it).
- `pso integrity check` says `no installation root`: it ran from the development checkout, which is not an installation; an installed `pso` uses its own installation automatically.

# Kubernetes, ECS, Container Apps and Cloud Run descriptors

> Generate hardened deployment descriptors for four platforms, validate them statically, and understand exactly what was and was not verified.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> The descriptors are **generated and statically validated**. They have **not been applied to any cluster or cloud account**. A hardened container run (non-root uid, read-only root file system, all capabilities dropped, health endpoint reachable) was verified locally with Docker; that is not a verification of any cloud platform.

```bash
pso deploy:init --target kubernetes     --registry registry.example.com/pso --tag 1.2.3
pso deploy:init --target ecs            --registry registry.example.com/pso --tag 1.2.3
pso deploy:init --target container-apps --registry registry.example.com/pso --tag 1.2.3
pso deploy:init --target cloud-run      --registry registry.example.com/pso --tag 1.2.3
pso deploy:validate            # add --strict to fail while CHANGE_ME values remain
```

Files go to `deploy/<target>/`. Nothing is applied anywhere and existing files are never overwritten without `--force`.

## What every target gets

| Property | Kubernetes | ECS (Fargate) | Container Apps | Cloud Run |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Non-root, numeric uid | `runAsNonRoot`, `runAsUser` | `user` | image user | image user |
| Read-only root file system, no capabilities | yes | yes | image defaults | platform sandbox |
| Probes on the service health path | readiness + liveness | `healthCheck` | Readiness + Liveness | startup + liveness |
| Resource limits | requests + limits | task cpu/memory | cpu/memory | cpu/memory |
| Secrets | referenced from a ConfigMap/Secret you create | `valueFrom` Secrets Manager ARNs | Key Vault references | Secret Manager references |
| Only the orchestrator is public | NetworkPolicy default deny + allow from the orchestrator | no load balancer for services | `external: false` for services | `ingress: internal` for services |

Images must be pushed by you; tags are fixed versions (`latest` is refused). Services listen on `0.0.0.0` inside the container through `HOST`.

## What `deploy:validate` checks

Run from the files **as they are on disk** (including your edits): root user, writable root file system, privilege escalation, capabilities, seccomp, host namespaces and `hostPath`, missing probes or limits, `latest` tags, secrets written inline, insecure ingress, and unfilled `CHANGE_ME` placeholders (warnings). It is a text-based policy check, not a schema validator for each platform: `kubectl`, `aws` and `az` were not used because they need an API server or an account.

## What the commands print (expected)

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso deploy:init --target kubernetes --registry registry.example.com/pso --tag 1.2.3
created    deploy/kubernetes/gateway.yaml
created    deploy/kubernetes/orders.yaml
created    deploy/kubernetes/namespace.yaml
created    deploy/kubernetes/config.example.yaml
Nothing was applied anywhere. Replace the CHANGE_ME values, then run `pso deploy:validate --target kubernetes`.

$ pso deploy:validate
OK  11 descriptor file(s) in kubernetes, ecs, container-apps, cloud-run
  WARNING deploy/kubernetes/config.example.yaml [placeholder] 3 CHANGE_ME value(s) must be filled in before this can be deployed
  ...
Static validation only: no cloud account was contacted and nothing was deployed.
```

(The file list is abridged and the example used two services; `deploy:validate` reports `OK` while only placeholder warnings remain, and `--strict` turns those warnings into a failure.) A policy violation is an error and exit code 1: for example an edit that changes `readOnlyRootFilesystem` to `false`, or an image tagged `latest`, is reported by rule name (the test suite exercises ten violation classes).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `--tag must be a fixed version, not 'latest'` | pass a real version |
| a conflict for an existing file | you edited it; `--force` overwrites (commit first) |
| `[placeholder] N CHANGE_ME value(s)` | fill them in; `--strict` fails until you do |
| `inline-secret` | a secret value is written in the file: reference a secret store |

## Common mistakes

- Applying a descriptor with `CHANGE_ME` values still in it.
- Assuming validation means a cluster accepted it: no cluster was contacted.
- Publishing the generated services without a network policy or ingress with TLS.

## Next steps

- [Docker](devops/docker.md)
- [Production security checklist](security/checklist.md)

# Logging in the orchestrator and in Spring services

> Readable coloured output in the terminal, structured JSON in production, secrets removed, one correlation id across services, and how to diagnose HTTP and broker problems from the logs.

## What you get

| | Node orchestrator | Spring Boot service |
|---|---|---|
| Terminal (a developer's machine) | `pretty`: time, level, `[component]`, message, `(correlation id)`, `key=value` context, coloured | Spring Boot's console pattern with `[service,correlationId,traceId]` added, coloured by Boot |
| Production / pipes / CI | `json`: one object per line, never any colour codes | structured JSON (ECS) from the `prod` and `staging` profiles |
| Level | `PSO_LOG_LEVEL` | `PSO_LOG_LEVEL` (root logger) |
| Colour | `PSO_LOG_COLOR`, `NO_COLOR`, `FORCE_COLOR` | `PSO_LOG_COLOR=detect|always|never` |
| Secrets | removed from messages and context | removed from every string in JSON output |
| Correlation | `x-correlation-id` accepted when well-formed, else generated | the same header, put in the logging context |

Both sides use the standard facilities of their ecosystem. There is no PSO logging server and no extra logging framework in your Spring service.

## Orchestrator

### See it work

Start the orchestrator and call it (output captured from a real run, `PSO_LOG_COLOR=never` so it can be pasted here):

```log evidence="expected"
2026-11-08 14:18:19.412 INFO  [startup] starting orchestrator  service=gw environment=development logLevel=info logFormat=pretty node=v24.18.0
2026-11-08 14:18:19.428 INFO  [security] security initialized (pem, ES256)
2026-11-08 14:18:19.434 INFO  [http] orchestrator listening  host=127.0.0.1 port=3000 routes=6 modules=2
2026-11-08 14:18:19.530 INFO  request (demo-corr-0001)  traceId=82b1e39923a376ea73ba19a092fca833 method=POST path=/orders status=201 ms=6.56
2026-11-08 14:18:19.536 INFO  request (demo-corr-0001)  traceId=d5bffcb133d75597de34f26b737428d9 method=POST path=/orders status=400 ms=1.17
```

Reading a line: `date time LEVEL [component] message (correlation-id)  key=value ...`.

On a terminal the level is coloured: TRACE grey, DEBUG cyan, INFO green, WARN yellow, ERROR red, FATAL white on red. The colours are standard ANSI palette entries, so a light or dark theme chooses the exact shade.

### Read a failure by its level

The documentation portal colours the level and marks WARN and ERROR lines with a visible edge. This is presentation only: the copied text contains no colour codes, and the level words remain readable without colour. The example below combines messages the runtime can emit; its values are illustrative, not one captured session.

```log evidence="illustrative" title="How a failure stands out in the portal"
2026-11-08 14:18:19.434 INFO  [http] orchestrator listening  host=127.0.0.1 port=3000
2026-11-08 14:18:19.530 WARN  [security] authentication failed  reason=missing_header route="GET /products"
--- separate startup attempt ---
2026-11-08 14:20:02.536 ERROR [dispatch] dispatch initialization failed  detail=broker unavailable
```

![A log example in the portal with INFO in green, a highlighted WARN line and a highlighted ERROR line](../../assets/screenshots/log-severity.png)

*The portal's log presentation after rendering the text above. The words and left-edge markers preserve the severity distinction when colour is unavailable.*

The WARN line tells you a request was rejected before a controller ran: compare the caller's token with the route policy. The ERROR line represents a **different startup attempt**: Dispatch failed to initialize, so that attempt did not start the listener. Check the configured provider and broker connection with `pso dispatch:doctor`. In a real run, use timestamps and correlation IDs to relate lines rather than assuming adjacent lines belong to one request.

### Configure it

| Variable | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `PSO_LOG_LEVEL` | `trace` `debug` `info` `warn` `error` `fatal` `silent` | `info` |
| `PSO_LOG_FORMAT` | `pretty` `json` | `pretty` when stdout is a terminal, `json` otherwise |
| `PSO_LOG_COLOR` | `auto` `always` `never` | `auto` |

Prefer the environment variables. The orchestrator also reads `logging.level`, `logging.format` and `logging.color` from `pso.config.json` (and `PSO_CFG_logging__level`, ...), but only `logging.level` is in the configuration schema today: `pso config:validate` reports `logging.format` and `logging.color` as *unknown key* warnings (verified), although the runtime honours them. Use the variables to avoid the warning ([environment variables](reference/environment-variables.md)). A wrong value stops the start with a message naming the variable; nothing silently falls back.

Colour rules, in order: `json` never has colour; `PSO_LOG_COLOR=never|always` is an explicit decision; then `NO_COLOR` (any non-empty value) turns it off; `FORCE_COLOR` forces it on (`0` or `false` off); otherwise colour is on only for a terminal that is not CI and not `TERM=dumb`.

```bash
PSO_LOG_LEVEL=debug pso dev                 # more detail while you investigate
NO_COLOR=1 pso dev                          # plain text
PSO_LOG_FORMAT=json PSO_LOG_LEVEL=warn node dist/main.js   # what a container should run
```

### JSON in production

```jsonl evidence="expected"
{"ts":"2026-11-08T14:18:19.536Z","level":"info","msg":"request","correlationId":"demo-corr-0001","traceId":"d5bffcb133d75597de34f26b737428d9","method":"POST","path":"/orders","status":400,"ms":1.17}
```

One object per line, `ts` in UTC, lower-case `level`, `msg`, then the context. Parse it with anything (`jq`, a log shipper). The keys `ts`, `level`, `msg` are stable.

### Secrets never reach the output

Before a line is written, the logger replaces: values under keys such as `authorization`, `cookie`, `password`, `secret`, `token`, `apiKey`, `credential`, `jwt`; JWTs and `Bearer`/`Basic` credentials anywhere in text; user and password inside URLs (`redis://user:pw@host` becomes `redis://[REDACTED]@host`); and `password=...`/`token=...` pairs. Errors keep their name, message and `code`; a stack trace (at most 8 frames) appears only at `debug` or `trace`.

This is a safety net, not permission to log secrets. Do not put request bodies or tokens in log context on purpose.

### What is logged at INFO, and what is not

INFO: start-up (environment, log settings), security initialised, configured upstreams, listener, one `request` line per request, shutdown. WARN: refused or degraded things that need attention (a token not forwarded, an upstream that is slow or unreachable). ERROR: failures (start-up refused, broker failure). Per-route registration and internal steps are `debug`. To silence the per-request line in a busy production service use `PSO_LOG_LEVEL=warn` and rely on [metrics](devops/observability.md) for traffic.

## Unexpected errors

An error nobody handled (a bug, an unavailable dependency) always produces the same answer for the client, in every environment: `500` with the problem `PSO_INTERNAL_ERROR` and the correlation id, never the exception.

What the **log** records depends on one setting, because a message can quote request data:

| | Always | With error details |
|---|---|---|
| Error type, stable `code` | yes | yes |
| `component` (controller and action), `route`, `correlationId`, `traceId` | yes | yes |
| `origin`: the first line of your own code on the stack (`file:line:column`) | yes | yes |
| `message`, `stack`, `causes` (after redaction of tokens, JWTs, URL credentials, `key=value` secrets) | no | yes |

Error details are off by default, **on in a `pso dev` session**, and never honoured in production:

| Runtime | Setting | Variable |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | `logging.errorDetails` | `PSO_LOG_ERROR_DETAILS=true` |
| Spring Boot | `pso.observability.error-details` | `PSO_LOG_ERROR_DETAILS=true` (the generated `application.yml` reads it) |

```text evidence="expected"
ERROR [SummaryController.boom] unhandled error in a request (corr-boom-000001)  route="GET /summary/boom" error=Error origin="SummaryController.boom (dist/modules/summary/summary.controller.js:41:11)" message="lookup failed: password=[REDACTED]"
    at SummaryController.boom (dist/modules/summary/summary.controller.js:41:11)
```

Without error details the same line stops after `origin`: enough to find the failing line from a production log. In production the setting is ignored and the log says so once at start-up (`logging.errorDetails is ignored in production`). An upstream call that an action did not handle is logged as `an upstream call failed and the action did not handle it` with `service`, `reason` and `upstreamStatus`, never with the service's response body.

## Spring Boot services

Generated services use Spring Boot's logging (Logback) and its structured-logging support. Nothing is replaced: your own `logback-spring.xml`, if you add one, wins.

### Local profile

```log evidence="expected"
2026-11-08T11:21:55.402-03:00  INFO [orders,,] 40436 --- [orders] [           main] o.s.b.w.embedded.tomcat.TomcatWebServer  : Tomcat started on port 18123 (http) with context path '/'
2026-11-08T11:21:55.413-03:00  INFO [orders,,] 40436 --- [orders] [           main] com.pso.orders.Application               : Started Application in 2.578 seconds (process running for 2.889)
```

`[orders,,]` is `[service, correlationId, traceId]`. The two ids are empty outside a request (start-up) and filled for lines logged while a request is being handled. The local profile sets `com.pso` to `DEBUG`.

### Production profile: structured JSON

`application-prod.yml` and `application-staging.yml` write Spring Boot's ECS JSON format, with secrets removed from every string field:

```jsonl evidence="expected"
{"@timestamp":"2026-11-08T14:21:57.890051500Z","log":{"level":"INFO","logger":"com.pso.orders.Application"},"process":{"pid":39476,"thread":{"name":"main"}},"service":{"name":"orders","version":"0.1.0","node":{}},"message":"The following 1 profile is active: \"prod\"","ecs":{"version":"8.11"}}
```

Inside a request the correlation id (and trace id, when OpenTelemetry tracing is on) are added to the JSON as context fields. To use another Boot format: `LOGGING_STRUCTURED_FORMAT_CONSOLE=logstash` (or `gelf`). To get readable text in production for a short investigation, start with `--logging.structured.format.console=` empty on that instance.

### Configure it

```bash
PSO_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG ./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=local   # root level (TRACE DEBUG INFO WARN ERROR OFF)
PSO_LOG_COLOR=never ...                                                       # detect (default) | always | never
LOGGING_LEVEL_COM_PSO=TRACE ...                                               # one package, standard Spring relaxed binding
```

The redaction is a standard Boot extension point (`logging.structured.json.customizer`), configured in the profile files. The pattern layout used locally is not rewritten: it is for developers, and the framework itself does not log tokens or credentials.

## Following one request across services

The orchestrator reads `x-correlation-id` (8 to 64 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`), replaces anything malformed with a new UUID, forwards it to upstreams, and returns it in the response and in every error body. Spring services do the same. So one id finds everything:

```bash
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/catalog/products -H "x-correlation-id: trace-me-0001" -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# orchestrator terminal:  grep trace-me-0001
# service terminal / JSON: grep trace-me-0001
```

## Diagnose with the logs

| Symptom | Look for | Usual cause and fix |
|---|---|---|
| `400` from a route that validates | the response `errors` list; the `request` line shows `status=400` | field rules; the log never contains the values, so reproduce with the client |
| `401` | `request ... status=401` | missing/invalid token; check `security initialized` at start-up and the issuer/audience variables |
| `503` from the orchestrator | `WARN` lines about the upstream; `status=503` | the service is not running or not reachable at the configured address |
| orchestrator does not start | one `ERROR startup failed ... diagnostics=[...]` line | the message names the route or the setting; nothing was started |
| broker problems | `ERROR [dispatch] dispatch initialization failed code=... detail=...` | broker URL, credentials (they appear redacted), network; check with `pso dispatch:doctor` |
| the same id appears in both runtimes but a field is missing | compare the JSON keys | Spring puts ids in the logging context; the orchestrator prints them as `correlationId` |

## Production checklist

- Run the orchestrator with `PSO_LOG_FORMAT=json` and ship stdout; do not rely on files inside the container.
- Keep `PSO_LOG_LEVEL=info` (or `warn` when traffic is high and you have metrics). Use `debug` for a short time and one instance.
- Never set colour in production. `json` already forces it off; for Spring the structured format has none.
- Treat logs as personal data: ids and paths can identify people. Apply your retention policy.
- Alert on `ERROR` and `FATAL`, and on the absence of the `orchestrator listening` line after a deploy.

## Next steps

- [Metrics, traces and OpenTelemetry](devops/observability.md)
- [Validate request bodies](orchestrator/dto-validation.md)
- [Environment variables](reference/environment-variables.md)

## Colour in `pso dev`

`pso dev` pipes each service's output so it can also be saved to `.pso/logs/<service>.log`. Piped output is not a terminal, so services would normally print plain text. `pso dev` therefore handles colour itself, with no configuration:

- When `pso dev` runs in a terminal, Spring services are started with `PSO_LOG_COLOR=always` (levels are coloured by Spring Boot).
- Structured orchestrator lines (JSON) are re-formatted for the terminal: timestamp, coloured level, component, message and context.
- Each `[service]` prefix has its own colour, so services are easy to tell apart.
- The `.pso/logs` files never contain escape codes, and the orchestrator's JSON stays JSON, so Studio can still parse it.

Turn it off with `NO_COLOR=1` or `PSO_LOG_COLOR=never`. Force it when output is redirected with `FORCE_COLOR=1` or `PSO_LOG_COLOR=always`.

# PSO Web as a Cloud Ecosystem Framework

> How PSO Web covers development, integration, security, infrastructure, deployment and operations, what Cloud Lifecycle and Operations adds, and what is and is not implemented yet.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> Cloud Lifecycle and Operations (CLO) is **implemented and exercised against a disposable Linux server** (a container reached over real SSH) from this repository. It has **not** been validated on an external cloud environment. Treat that as the next acceptance step, not as a finished fact.

**PSO Web is a declarative, cloud-oriented ecosystem framework** designed to simplify the entire lifecycle of distributed web applications. It provides one structural foundation for development, integration, security, infrastructure, deployment and operations, so independent teams can work autonomously while the architecture stays consistent. *Build independently. Integrate seamlessly. Operate securely.*

## The six pillars

| Pillar | What PSO provides | Where it is documented |
|---|---|---|
| Development | Structure by convention, modules, routes, generators | Core Concepts, Orchestrator |
| Integration | Service discovery, contracts, event dispatch | Microservices, Event Dispatch |
| Security | Deny by default, JWT, rate limits, mTLS | Security |
| Infrastructure | Servers, reverse proxy, runtimes, private management plane | this section |
| Deployment | Plans, pipelines, blue-green, rolling, recreate, rollback | this section |
| Operations | Durable state, audit, recovery, logs, service control | this section |

These are one product with one security model, not separate tools. The same declarative idea applies everywhere: you describe the result in a file, PSO validates it, shows you the plan and then makes it so.

## The operational architecture

Four responsibilities, deliberately not four separate products:

- **PSO Studio** is the graphical interface (the *Cloud* section; start it with `pso studio --remote`).
- **PSO Deploy Engine** is the single implementation of planning, validation, preparation, activation, recovery and rollback. It runs **on the target server**, so a deployment survives the end of your SSH session.
- **PSO Runtime Agent** is one bundled file that the engine runs in. It opens **no network port**: you reach it through an authenticated SSH connection, and it offers a fixed list of operations, never a shell.
- **PSO Security Engine** is identity (Ed25519 keys), roles, per-request signatures, rate limiting, secrets and a hash-chained audit log, shared by all of the above.

The CLI and Studio are thin clients of the same calls (`Cloud` in `@pso/deploy`), so they enforce identical policy. There are not two deployment implementations.

```bash
pso connection:add prod --host 203.0.113.10 --user deploy --auth key --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
pso agent:install prod --mode protected --environment production --yes
pso environment:add production --connection prod --repo https://git.example.com/shop.git --domain shop.example.com
pso release:plan production
pso release:deploy production --yes
```

## What is implemented

SSH connections with strict host-key and agent-identity pinning; protected credential storage; environments and static declarations (`DEPLOYMENT.pso.ts`, `PIPELINE.pso.ts`); git and artifact releases pinned to an immutable commit or checksum; blue-green, rolling and recreate strategies; nginx management with ownership markers, validation and graceful reload; Node and Java processes identified by token, not by port; durable deployment state, locks, recovery, rollback; approvals; audit.

Also implemented since: the **systemd** runtime ([systemd runtime](cloud/systemd-runtime.md)), **signed releases and trusted signers** ([release signing](cloud/release-signing.md)), workload and rollback-safety rules ([workloads](cloud/workloads-and-rollback-safety.md)), optional Java dependency scanning, distinct `disabled`/`skipped`/`unavailable`/`failed` check outcomes, and host-administrator recovery ([agent and enrollment](cloud/agent-and-enrollment.md)). A practical guide: [deploy a real application to a VPS](cloud/deploy-to-a-vps.md).

## What is not implemented (read this before relying on it)

- Only **SSH to Linux** is a connection provider. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Kubernetes providers do not exist; the provider interface is where they would attach, and PSO provisions no cloud resources and spends no money.
- No **system-scope** systemd units (only the deploy user's own manager: see [systemd runtime](cloud/systemd-runtime.md)), no automatic TLS certificates or DNS or hosts-file changes, and no resource limits on services.
- The macOS Keychain and Linux Secret Service providers are written but have **not been run** on those systems; only the Windows Credential Manager and the encrypted file were exercised.
- The Java dependency scan needs OSV-Scanner on the server or build host and network access to the OSV database; it was exercised through its adapter with a stand-in executor, not against a real OSV-Scanner run. Without it the result is `unavailable`, never a pass.
- Nothing here has been validated on an external cloud server: see the [external validation guide](cloud/external-validation.md).
- Frontend integration is out of scope for this release.
- Zero downtime is an objective with stated conditions, not a guarantee: see [Deploy a release](cloud/deploy-a-release.md).

## What can go wrong

Most failures are refusals by design: a plan with blockers, a host key that changed, a stale plan, a policy that disallows a strategy. Each refusal names its reason. The [troubleshooting page](cloud/troubleshooting.md) lists them with their fixes.

---

# Connect to a Linux server

> Register a VPS over SSH with strict host identity, choose how you authenticate, and test every layer of the connection.

A *connection* is a named reference to a server: host, port, user, how you authenticate and the SSH host key you approved. It lives on your machine (in `~/.pso-cloud`, or `PSO_CLOUD_HOME`) and holds **references to credentials, never the credentials**.

```bash
pso connection:add prod --host 203.0.113.10 --user deploy --auth key --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
pso connection:test prod
```

## Host identity comes first

`connection:add` asks the server for its SSH host keys and shows their fingerprints. You compare one with what your provider's console shows (or run `ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub` on the server), approve it, and PSO pins it in its own `known_hosts`. From then on every connection uses `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` with `BatchMode`: a changed key is a **hard failure**, never a prompt. In scripts the approval is explicit:

```bash
pso connection:add prod --host 203.0.113.10 --user deploy --auth key --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 --accept-host-key SHA256:AbCd...
```

## Authentication choices

| Choice | How | Where the secret lives |
|---|---|---|
| ssh-agent (default) | `--auth agent` | in your agent; PSO never sees it |
| Private key file | `--auth key --key <file>` | the file stays where it is; PSO stores only its path |
| Passphrase-protected key | add `--passphrase-stdin` | the protected credential store |
| Password (explicit alternative) | `--auth password --password-stdin` | the protected credential store |

Secrets are never arguments (they would appear in shell history and process lists). Pipe them on standard input or type them at the hidden prompt. Private keys are used in place with `IdentitiesOnly`; they are not imported or copied.

## Custom ports, bastions, timeouts, tunnels

```bash
pso connection:add prod --host 10.0.0.5 --port 2222 --user deploy --jump ops@bastion.example:22 --timeout 20 --accept-host-key SHA256:AbCd...
pso connection:tunnel prod --remote-port 20001 --local-port 9001
```

The tunnel forwards a loopback port on your machine to a loopback port on the server, only while the command runs. Controlled reconnection applies to read operations (status, history, logs); a connection lost during a *change* is never retried blindly. See [recovery](cloud/rollback-and-recovery.md).

## The test, layer by layer

`connection:test` reports SSH and host identity, the agent, the agent's pinned identity and your authenticated session, each on its own line, so you know which layer failed.

```text evidence="expected"
OK   ssh             connected as deploy@203.0.113.10:22; host key verified against the pinned SHA256:AbCd...
OK   agent           agent 0.1.0 (management mode: protected)
OK   agent-identity  SHA256:Zx9... verified by challenge-response and pinned
OK   session         authenticated as ana@pso-studio (role superadmin, environment production)
```

## What can go wrong

- *"No protected credential store is available"*: PSO refuses to store a password in plain text. On Linux install `libsecret-tools` with a running keyring, or set `PSO_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER=encrypted-file` with `PSO_CREDENTIAL_PASSPHRASE` or `PSO_CREDENTIAL_KEYFILE`.
- *Exit code 3 from `connection:add`*: a non-interactive shell cannot approve a fingerprint; pass `--accept-host-key` after checking it out of band.
- *Host key verification failed*: the server was reinstalled or someone is impersonating it. Confirm with your provider, then `connection:remove` and add it again.
- The server must have Node.js 24 or newer for the agent. PSO does not install it.

---

# The runtime agent, modes and enrollment

> What the agent is, why it opens no port, how the first administrator is created without a stored password, and how teammates are invited and revoked.

The *runtime agent* is a single bundled file, `pso-agent.mjs`, that PSO uploads to `~/.pso-agent/bin/` over SSH. It needs only Node.js on the server, no `npm install`, and runs as an **ordinary user**, never requiring root.

## A private management plane

The agent has **no listening socket**. Your client starts it through the authenticated SSH connection (`ssh ... node pso-agent.mjs serve`) and speaks newline-delimited JSON on its standard input and output. There is therefore no management endpoint to publish: generated nginx files never mention it, and PSO adds nothing to Docker or the firewall. It is also not a remote shell: the protocol has a fixed list of operations (`release.start`, `service.restart`, `audit.read` ...), and anything else answers `UNKNOWN_OPERATION`.

## Modes

```bash
pso agent:install prod --mode protected --environment production --yes
```

| Mode | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `disabled` | The agent refuses every operation. This is what a server is until someone chooses otherwise. |
| `development` | Relaxed defaults (no approvals required, longer sessions). Authentication is still mandatory. |
| `protected` | Production defaults: approvals required, shorter sessions. |

`--mode` has no default on purpose. A host administrator re-enables a disabled agent with `pso-agent set-mode`, run on the server; the protocol cannot do it for them.

## How the first administrator exists

At provisioning the agent generates its own Ed25519 identity (the private key stays in `~/.pso-agent/identity/`, mode 600) and one **single-use enrollment token** for the role *superadmin*, valid for 30 minutes and stored only as a hash. `agent:install` receives it over the authenticated SSH channel and spends it immediately by presenting **your public key**, which you proved you own by signing a server nonce. Your private key goes into your credential store. No permanent administrator secret exists on the server, none travels to your machine, and nothing is printed to a log. There are no passwords in the agent, so there is no password verifier to leak.

## Recovering administrative access

If the last superadministrator is lost (a laptop gone, a key suspected), recovery is a **host-administrator** action, not a remote one. Someone with a shell on the server as the agent's user runs:

```bash
node ~/.pso-agent/bin/pso-agent.mjs recover-admin --minutes 15
node ~/.pso-agent/bin/pso-agent.mjs recover-admin --revoke-all     # when a client key may be compromised
```

It prints a new **single-use, short-lived** superadministrator enrollment token (at most 60 minutes) and writes an `admin.recovery` audit entry; `--revoke-all` first ends every client and session. You then enroll a **new** client key with `pso agent:enroll` and revoke or rotate the old identities. The operation is **not** in the management protocol (an agent asked for it answers `UNKNOWN_OPERATION`), so it cannot become a remote authentication bypass: it needs the same access as owning the agent's files. It never reveals or resets an existing identity.

## Roles, invitations, revocation

Roles ascend: `viewer`, `operator` (restart services), `deployer` (plan, approve, deploy, roll back), `admin` (audit, secrets, clients, provisioning), `superadmin` (policy, roles).

```bash
pso environment:access production --invite deployer --minutes 15
pso agent:enroll prod
pso environment:access production --revoke SHA256:AbCd...
```

An invitation cannot grant more than its creator holds, is single use and expires. Revoking a client ends all its sessions at once. The last superadministrator cannot be revoked.

## Every request is signed

After a handshake the client signs each request with its key over the session, a growing sequence number, the time, the operation and a hash of the arguments. A captured request cannot be replayed (the sequence only grows) or altered (the hash is signed). Failed authentications are rate limited per client and per source, with growing lock-outs.

## Agent releases and rollback

The agent is installed as **versioned releases**, not as a file that an upgrade overwrites. A release is identified by its semantic version **and** its build (the first 12 hex digits of its SHA-256), so two builds of `0.2.0` are two releases. The file the server runs is a link that is replaced by one atomic rename; the agent's identity, clients, policy, credentials and deployments live in separate directories that a release switch never touches.

```tree title="The agent directory on the server"
.pso-agent/
  bin/
    pso-agent.mjs # a link to the active release, replaced atomically
  releases/
    0.2.0+3f9a1c2b7d10/
      pso-agent.mjs # immutable; its checksum is verified again before it is activated
      release.json # version, build, sha256, installation time, installer, compatibility
    0.1.0+8c01aa42e9b3/ # the file that was installed before releases were versioned: adopted, not discarded
    state.json # the active release, the history and the retention
  identity/ # the agent's identity: never part of a release
  policy.json # the server policy: never changed by an upgrade
```

```flow title="What pso agent:upgrade does on the server"
[upgrade] upload to a temporary name -> verify the SHA-256 -> start the new file (version check) -> store it as an immutable release -> switch the link atomically -> keep the history and apply the retention
[refused] checksum mismatch or a build that does not start -> the running agent stays exactly as it was # nothing is activated
```

`pso agent:releases <connection>` lists the active and previous releases with their checksums, installation times and installers, and the history. `pso agent:rollback <connection> --yes` returns to the previous release, or to one named with `--to`: the target's checksum is verified against the one recorded when it was installed, it must start, and only then is the link switched. A release whose bytes changed on disk is refused. Retention (default 5) never removes the active or the previous release. The first versioned upgrade adopts the plain file that was running as a release, so even a server installed before this existed gets a real rollback point from then on; what was overwritten by older upgrades cannot be recovered and is not reconstructed.

## What can go wrong

- *`enrollment refused`*: the token is invalid, expired or used. The server deliberately does not say which, and repeated attempts lock the source out.
- *`remote management is DISABLED`*: choose a mode with a host administrator.
- *`agent not provisioned`*: run `agent:install`.
- Upgrades are explicit (`pso agent:upgrade --yes`): the agent never updates itself. Every build is kept as a release (see below), so the previous one can always be returned to. Protocol versions are negotiated; if no common version exists both sides say so and nothing proceeds.
- `pso agent:uninstall` removes only management tooling. Applications and their data stay unless `--purge-applications` is given, which is refused while services run.

---

# Environments

> How local, development, testing, staging, production and custom environments stay isolated from each other, and how one project deploys to several of them without copying its source.

An *environment* is one server (or one named slot on it) plus everything decided about it: its identity, connection, deployment policy, runtime requirements, proxy configuration, secrets, history, access and pipeline. PSO treats environments as first-class so that **production never inherits development's credentials, debug settings or insecure defaults**.

```bash
pso environment:add production --connection prod --repo https://git.example.com/shop.git --domain shop.example.com
pso environment:add staging --connection stg --repo https://git.example.com/shop.git --branch develop
pso environment:list
```

This writes `deploy/production.deployment.pso.ts` and `deploy/production.pipeline.pso.ts` (and the staging pair). The same repository is deployed to both: the **source is referenced, not copied**. Each file declares its own `environment`, `connection`, strategy and pipeline.

## What keeps them apart

| Concern | Isolation |
|---|---|
| Identity | each server's agent has its own environment id and a label chosen at install (`--environment production`) |
| Credentials | a connection holds its own SSH secrets and its own client key; nothing is shared between connections |
| Declarations | a declaration for `staging` is **refused** by the production server: the plan reports *"this server is the production environment but the declaration targets staging"* |
| Secrets | named secrets live on the server that uses them (`pso environment:secret`) and are injected only into that server's services |
| Policy | approvals, strategies and retention are set per server and override the project's wishes |
| History and audit | stored on each server, correlated by environment, deployment and release ids |
| Access | enrolled clients and their roles are per environment |

## Reading an environment

```bash
pso environment:inspect production
pso environment:plan production
```

`inspect` is read-only: operating system and architecture, CPU, memory and disk, listening ports, Java, Node.js, git, nginx and Docker availability, existing virtual hosts and PSO applications. `plan` lists what provisioning would do and who must do it (see [nginx and existing infrastructure](cloud/nginx-and-existing-infrastructure.md)).

```text evidence="expected"
Alpine Linux v3.24 x64, 8 CPU, 3010/3920 MB memory free, 18000 MB disk free; agent runs as pso
tools: node 24.18.0, java 21.0.1, git 2.49, nginx 1.30, docker no, systemd no
nginx vhosts: [external] /etc/nginx/http.d/unrelated.conf; [PSO] /etc/nginx/pso.d/pso-shop.conf
no blockers
```

## Several services and repositories

A deployment declares one service (`service`) or several (`services`) and each has its own build, start command, health policy and shutdown grace. Teams that keep one repository per service create one declaration per service (an *application* each) on the same server: they deploy, roll back and restart independently, and find each other through a stable loopback address (`internalPort`), described in [Deploy a release](cloud/deploy-a-release.md).

## What can go wrong

- Two declarations targeting the same environment and name are *ambiguous*: `release:plan` lists the files.
- A **custom** environment name gets no built-in policy defaults; the validator warns.
- The environment label is set once, at `agent:install`. Reinstalling with another label on a provisioned server is refused; remove and reinstall deliberately.
- `local` is a label like the others: it does not turn on a local execution mode. For local development keep using `pso dev`.

---

# Deployment and pipeline declarations

> The DEPLOYMENT.pso.ts and PIPELINE.pso.ts files, what each field means and why they are read as data and never executed.

Deployment follows PSO's declarative idea: you describe the intended result in a typed file, PSO validates and explains it, then applies it. Declarations live in `deploy/<environment>.deployment.pso.ts` and `deploy/<name>.pipeline.pso.ts` (or `DEPLOYMENT.pso.ts` / `PIPELINE.pso.ts` at the workspace root).

```ts
import { defineDeployment } from "@pso/deploy";

export default defineDeployment({
  name: "shop",
  environment: "production",
  connection: { provider: "ssh", credentials: "prod" },          // the NAME of a connection, never a secret
  source: { provider: "git", url: "https://git.example.com/shop.git", branch: "main" },
  service: {
    name: "web", runtime: "node",
    build: [["npm", "ci"], ["npm", "run", "build"]],               // argv arrays: no shell strings
    start: ["node", "dist/main.js"],
    health: { readyPath: "/health/ready", timeoutSeconds: 60 },
    shutdownGraceSeconds: 30,                                       // the application's real shutdown time
    route: { path: "/" },
    secrets: { DB_PASSWORD: "shop-db-password" },                   // env var -> NAME of a server secret
  },
  strategy: { type: "blue-green", proxy: "nginx", rollback: true, drainSeconds: 10 },
  proxy: { nginx: { domains: ["shop.example.com"], listen: { http: 80 } } },
  pipeline: "production",
});
```

## Why they are read as data

Importing a TypeScript file runs it. If merely *inspecting* a project executed its code, cloning an untrusted repository and opening Studio would run that repository's code. So PSO parses the file and evaluates **literal data only**: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, `null`. A function call, a variable, `process.env` or a spread is an error (`PSO-DEC-STATIC`). Secrets are therefore referenced by name and cannot be computed; a value that looks like a credential is rejected (`PSO-DEC-SECRET`).

## The pieces

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `source` | `git` (url plus exactly one of `branch`, `tag`, 40-character `commit`; `credentials` names a server secret) or `artifact` (a path, optional `sha256`) |
| `service` / `services` | `runtime` (`node`, `java`, `command`), `dir` inside the source, `build`, `start`, `port`, `internalPort`, `health`, `env`, `secrets`, `shutdownGraceSeconds`, `instances`, `resources`, `requires`, `dependsOn`, `consumes`/`contract` |
| `strategy` | `blue-green`, `rolling` or `recreate`; proxy, rollback, drain, retention |
| `proxy.nginx` | domains, layout, listen ports, TLS file paths, WebSocket |
| `migrations` | `none` or `expand-contract` with an owner service, a command, and an explicit destructive flag |
| `pipeline` | the name of a pipeline declaration |

`{port}` and `{release}` in `start` and `build` are substituted. `{service:catalog.url}` inside `env` values resolves to the loopback address of that service in the same deployment.

```bash
pso pipeline:validate production
```

Validation is static: no server is contacted and no project code runs. Hooks and custom pipeline stages are the one place project-controlled commands can run, and only when the server policy allows them (see [Pipelines and policy](cloud/pipelines-and-policy.md)).

## What can go wrong

- *`blue-green needs a reverse proxy`*: PSO will not quietly turn a zero-downtime request into `recreate`. Declare `proxy: "nginx"`, or choose `recreate` with `downtimeAcknowledged: true`.
- *`rolling needs at least 2 instances`*: one instance cannot stay available while it is replaced.
- *`credentials must not be embedded in the repository URL`*: use `credentials: "<secret name>"`; the token reaches git through its environment, never an argument or URL.
- A branch is resolved to a commit when you **plan**; the plan records the commit. Writing `commit` pins it in the declaration itself.

---

# Deploy a release

> Plan, approve and run a blue-green deployment of Node orchestrators and Java services, update one service on its own, and understand the conditions zero downtime depends on.

Every deployment starts with a plan you can read. The plan names the server, the services, the commit, the strategy, the expected availability impact, resource needs, configuration changes, which checks are on and off, the permissions needed and whether rollback is possible.

```bash
pso release:plan production
pso release:deploy production --yes
```

## What happens, in order

1. **Plan.** The server inspects itself and resolves `branch: main` to an immutable commit. The commit, not the name, is recorded and deployed. The plan has a hash; approvals bind to it.
2. **Validate.** Environment binding, the deployment lock (one deployment per application), nginx baseline, secrets and resources are checked. These are mandatory and are not pipeline stages.
3. **Prepare.** A new, isolated release directory is created and exactly that commit is fetched into it (never `git pull` in a running release). A manifest with a tree hash is written.
4. **Pipeline stages.** Integrity, compatibility, security, tests and build run as configured, **while the active release keeps serving**.
5. **Start the candidate** in its own slot: its own process identity, port and log.
6. **Verify the candidate.** Readiness must pass (consecutive probes). A candidate that is not ready never receives traffic.
7. **Switch traffic.** The new nginx configuration is validated with `nginx -t`, written, and applied with one graceful reload.
8. **Verify the active release** through the proxy: responses must carry the new release id.
9. **Drain and stop the previous release**, honoring each service's declared shutdown grace plus a margin, then keep it as the rollback target.

```text evidence="expected"
deployment dmz4k1x2 started on the server (release r20261114223601-ce58a814)
  VALIDATING  [integrity:passed compatibility:passed security:passed tests:skipped resources:passed build:running]
  VERIFYING_CANDIDATE
  SWITCHING_TRAFFIC
  VERIFYING_ACTIVE_RELEASE
  COMPLETED
```

If anything fails before step 7 the candidate is stopped and the active release was never touched. If step 8 fails, the previous nginx configuration is restored while the previous release is still running.

## A Node orchestrator and a Java service, independently
