Give the Java service a stable loopback address with `internalPort`, and the orchestrator finds it there while releases are swapped behind it:

```ts
// deploy/production.deployment.pso.ts for the catalog repository
service: { name: "catalog", runtime: "java", build: [["mvn", "-B", "-DskipTests", "package"]],
  start: ["java", "-jar", "target/catalog.jar", "--server.port={port}"],
  health: { readyPath: "/actuator/health", timeoutSeconds: 120 }, shutdownGraceSeconds: 30, internalPort: 21001 }
```

The orchestrator's declaration sets `env: { CATALOG_URL: "http://127.0.0.1:21001" }`. Deploying a new catalog changes nothing in the orchestrator, and the orchestrator is neither rebuilt nor restarted. `pso release:service production restart catalog --yes` restarts one service; PSO signals only processes it started and can prove it started.

## Choosing a strategy

| Strategy | Use when | Honest limits |
|---|---|---|
| `blue-green` | HTTP applications behind nginx | needs memory and ports for two releases; old and new versions overlap briefly |
| `rolling` | 2 or more instances of every service | mixed versions serve together while it runs |
| `recreate` | constrained servers or incompatible workloads | **downtime**, stated in the plan before you confirm |

## What can go wrong

Zero downtime needs: schema changes that both versions tolerate (expand, then contract later), consumers and schedulers that tolerate two versions running briefly, enough resources, and a working `nginx -t`. Long-lived WebSocket connections end on the old release when it stops and must reconnect. Rolling back the application does not roll back the database. PSO never runs destructive migrations without an explicit approval in the declaration **and** a server policy that allows them, and it does not claim exactly-once delivery for any broker: coexisting consumers are your design problem, flagged in the plan.

---

# Pipelines, mandatory protections and approvals

> Which checks a project may turn off, which protections no configuration can disable, how approvals bind to a plan, and how the server's policy overrides the project.

A PSO pipeline is an ordered list of stages declared in `PIPELINE.pso.ts`. It needs no external CI system, and it can run alongside one (see [CI/CD integration](cloud/ci-cd-integration.md)).

```ts
import { definePipeline } from "@pso/deploy";

export default definePipeline({
  name: "production",
  stages: [
    { type: "integrity" }, { type: "compatibility" }, { type: "security" },
    { type: "tests", enabled: false },                       // your choice, recorded in the plan and audit log
    { type: "resources" }, { type: "build", timeoutSeconds: 1800 },
    { type: "health" }, { type: "deploy" },
  ],
});
```

Stages support ordering, `dependsOn`, `timeoutSeconds`, `onFailure` (`fail` or `continue`), environment conditions (`when`), `requiresApproval`, and structured results with a status: pending, running, passed, failed, skipped, blocked, awaiting approval or cancelled. `deploy` must be last and cannot be disabled.

## Optional versus mandatory

You may disable the optional stages: tests, the security scan, compatibility checks, extended health. The plan lists **every** disabled or omitted stage and the audit log records it. An omitted stage is never read as a pass.

These protections are part of the engine, **not stages**, and no pipeline setting can switch them off: authentication and authorization, remote identity verification, credential protection, environment binding, the deployment lock, transfer integrity of the release (the commit or checksum in the plan must match what was fetched), a valid proxy configuration (`nginx -t`), candidate readiness before traffic moves, safety-critical resource checks, and process ownership. Disabling `integrity` still leaves the commit pin and checksum check in force; the validator warns you about that.

## Honest security results

The security stage runs a built-in pattern scan for committed credentials, `npm audit` for Node services and, for Java services, **OSV-Scanner** when it is installed (the executable can be named with `PSO_OSV_SCANNER`). PSO does not ship a vulnerability database or matcher: the adapter detects the tool, runs it with a timeout and a fixed argument list, counts findings by severity and reports the database source and time (OSV is queried live, so freshness is that of the request). The server policy `scanBlockSeverity` (`none`, `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`) decides which severity blocks; it is set per environment, and no declaration can lower it.

Every check ends in exactly one of these outcomes, never merged:

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `passed` | it **ran** and found nothing blocking. The only pass |
| `failed` | it ran and found a problem |
| `unavailable` | it was supposed to run and could not: scanner not installed, advisory database unreachable, timed out, unreadable output. Reported with the reason; never a pass |
| `disabled` | a pipeline setting (or an environment filter) switched it off. Recorded in the plan and the audit log |
| `skipped` | there was nothing for it to do (for example no test steps declared) |

If any scanner of the security stage is `unavailable`, the **stage** is `unavailable` and names what ran and what did not. The server policy `requireSecurityScan` turns that into a blocker. Neither scan is a malware check or a penetration test, and no vulnerability result is ever invented.

## Approvals and the server policy

```bash
pso environment:policy production --set approvalsRequired=1 --set selfApproval=false --yes
pso release:plan production
pso release:approve production --plan 3f9c1a...
pso release:deploy production --plan 3f9c1a... --yes
```

The policy lives **on the server** and wins over the project: allowed strategies, approvals, custom stages, retention, destructive migrations, session lifetimes. A team that forbids self-approval gets a second person; a solo developer keeps `selfApproval` on. An approval is bound to the plan hash, expires, and is rechecked at start: if the branch moved, the active release changed or the policy changed, the start is refused (`PLAN_STALE`) and the latest commit is **not** deployed implicitly.

## Policy compatibility and explicit migrations

The policy belongs to the server's administrator and **fails closed**: a capability the installed agent gained after the policy was written (the `static` strategy for frontends, for example) is refused until someone with authority permits it. An agent upgrade never changes the policy.

```bash
pso environment:policy production --compat
pso environment:policy production --migrate allow-static-frontends
pso environment:policy production --migrate allow-static-frontends --yes
pso environment:policy production --history
pso environment:policy production --revert <entry> --yes
```

`--compat` lists what the agent can do, what the policy permits, the policy version, the unsupported strategies and the pending migrations. `--migrate <id>` without `--yes` only previews: the permissions it would add in words and the exact difference (`allowedStrategies: ["blue-green","rolling","recreate"] -> [..., "static"]`). With `--yes` it applies exactly that difference: the request carries the digest of what was previewed, so a policy that changed in between is refused. It needs the superadministrator role and writes an audit record (`policy.migrated`) and a history entry holding the policy as it was. `--revert` restores the previous values of the keys that entry changed, only while they still hold the value the entry set (`policy.reverted`). Studio's Cloud section shows the same compatibility, read-only, with the command to run. The server also reports a policy version it does not understand and then refuses to act on it.

A static frontend also needs the web server to read its files. The plan refuses (before anything is copied) when a directory of the site root cannot be traversed by other users, which is the case below a home directory with mode 750. The administrator creates a readable directory and sets `--set staticRoot=/srv/pso-sites`.

## Custom stages

A custom stage is an argv array that the agent runs without a shell, as its unprivileged user, in the release workspace. It runs only when the server policy sets `allowCustomStages`; project code cannot weaken any mandatory check.

## What can go wrong

A stage that depends on one that failed is *blocked*, not skipped. `onFailure: continue` is refused for `integrity`, `resources` and `deploy`. Retention keeps the newest releases but **never deletes the active, previous or last known-good release**, whatever `keep` says.

---

# Rollback, interruption and recovery

> How a deployment survives a closed laptop, what INTERRUPTED means, how recovery decides without replaying steps, and what rollback does and does not undo.

The authoritative state of a deployment is a file on the **server**, written by a worker process that is detached from your session. Close Studio, lose Wi-Fi, shut the laptop: the deployment continues, and reconnecting shows where it really is.

```bash
pso release:deploy production --no-follow --yes
pso release:status production
pso release:history production --limit 10
```

## States

`REQUESTED, PLANNING, VALIDATING, PREPARING, BUILDING, STARTING_CANDIDATE, VERIFYING_CANDIDATE, SWITCHING_TRAFFIC, VERIFYING_ACTIVE_RELEASE, DRAINING_PREVIOUS_RELEASE, COMPLETED`, plus the outcomes `FAILED`, `CANCELLED`, `ROLLED_BACK`, `INTERRUPTED` and `RECOVERING`. Each transition is a checkpoint in the deployment file and an audit entry.

## Manual rollback

```bash
pso release:rollback production --yes
```

The previous release (or one named with `--to`) is brought back with the same sequence: start it in a new slot, verify readiness, switch nginx, verify through the proxy, then drain the one being replaced. It needs no build, because the release directory is kept. The plan told you before the deployment whether rollback was possible. If a deployment fails after traffic moved, PSO restores the earlier proxy configuration automatically while the earlier release is still running (`autoRollback`, on by default).

## Interrupted deployments

If the worker dies (a crash, a reboot, `kill -9`), the deployment is reported as `INTERRUPTED` and its lock is *stale*. PSO **never takes a stale lock silently**, and a new deployment is refused until you decide:

```bash
pso release:recover production --yes
```

Recovery inspects what really exists instead of replaying steps: which release nginx is serving (a marker in the managed file), which candidate processes are alive and healthy, what the recorded active release is.

| What it finds | What it does |
|---|---|
| Traffic never moved | stops the candidate; the active release was never touched (`interrupted-before-switch`) |
| Traffic moved and the candidate is healthy | completes forward: drains the previous release, records the new one |
| Traffic moved and the candidate is unhealthy | restores the previous proxy configuration, stops the candidate |
| Anything else | changes nothing and reports `needs-operator` |

```text evidence="expected"
interrupted-before-switch: interrupted before traffic moved: the active release was never touched; the candidate was stopped
```

## Cancel

`pso release:cancel production --deployment <id> --yes` stops at the next safe point. After traffic moved, cancelling is refused because it would leave a mixed state; use rollback.

## What can go wrong

- **Rollback does not undo database changes.** The plan states this when migrations are involved, and you should design migrations as expand-then-contract so the previous release still works.
- A rollback target must still be kept: retention never removes the active, previous or last known-good release, but older ones go.
- `needs-operator` means two views of the world disagree (for example nginx serves a release neither the state nor the deployment explains). PSO stops rather than guess.
- Connection loss during a *change* is never retried automatically: the CLI says the result is uncertain and tells you to read the status. Reads reconnect a bounded number of times.

---

# Credentials and the security model

> Where every secret lives, which guarantees PSO gives, and the limits of each mechanism, written so you can decide what to trust.

This page states what PSO protects and, equally, what it does not.

## Where secrets live

| Secret | Where | Never in |
|---|---|---|
| SSH password or key passphrase | your protected credential store (opaque reference in `~/.pso-cloud/connections.json`) | declarations, git, logs, argv, manifests |
| SSH private key | its own file, used in place | copied or imported anywhere |
| Your client key for the agent | your credential store | the server (it holds only the public key) |
| The agent's identity key | the server, mode 600, never leaves | any response, log or export |
| Application secrets | the server's `secrets/` directory, mode 600, injected as environment variables | plans, manifests, deployment history, the audit log |
| Git deploy key or token | a server secret named by `source.credentials`; reaches git through its environment | repository URLs, argv, logs |

## The credential store

PSO uses the operating system when it can: **Windows Credential Manager** (`windows-credential-manager`), the **Linux Secret Service** through `secret-tool`, the **macOS Keychain**. Secrets are passed on standard input, not on a command line. Where none is available you choose `PSO_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER=encrypted-file`, which uses AES-256-GCM with a key derived by scrypt from `PSO_CREDENTIAL_PASSPHRASE` or a key file (`PSO_CREDENTIAL_KEYFILE`, at least 32 bytes, owner-only). **There is no silent fallback to plain text.** If nothing is available PSO fails with instructions.

| Mechanism | Status |
|---|---|
| Windows Credential Manager | **exercised** on Windows (store, read, replace, remove, no secret in arguments) |
| Encrypted file (AES-256-GCM + scrypt) | **exercised** (wrong passphrase and tampering are refused) |
| Linux Secret Service (`secret-tool`) | written, **not run**: this was not exercised on a Linux desktop session |
| macOS Keychain | written, **not run** on macOS |
| SSH agent (`--auth agent`) | **exercised** against a real server with a running `ssh-agent`: PSO stores no key path or key, and when the agent no longer holds the key the connection **fails** (no fallback to another credential) |
| Passphrase-protected SSH key, password login | **exercised** (the secret reaches `ssh` through the askpass helper below) |
| Git repository credentials | a server secret named by `source.credentials` (a deploy key or token); it reaches git through its environment (an ssh key file in a private temporary directory, or an HTTP header from the environment), never the URL or argv |

**The askpass helper.** For a password or key passphrase PSO creates, per `ssh` child, a temporary directory (mode 700) with a tiny launcher (mode 700/600) and removes it when that child ends. The launcher contains **no secret**: the value is placed only in the child's environment (`PSO_SSH_SECRET`). Verified on Windows and Linux: no file contains the secret, permissions are owner-only, cleanup removes the directory and is idempotent. Residual: on Linux another process of the same user can read a live process's environment.

Isolation, rotation and removal: every connection has its own credential references and an environment never reads another's; `pso connection:rotate` replaces them (the old ones are deleted), `pso connection:revoke` deletes them and ends the client's access on the server, and `pso signer:remove` deletes a signing key from the machine. Studio's renderer never receives a secret: values typed there go to the local Studio process once.

Studio keeps the credential store in its own process. A password you type into Studio goes to that process once, is stored, and is never sent back to the page.

## Rotation, revocation, removal

```bash
pso connection:rotate prod              # new client key enrolled, old one revoked and deleted
pso connection:rotate prod --ssh-secret # replace the stored SSH password or passphrase
pso connection:revoke prod --yes        # end access on the server, delete local secrets
pso connection:remove prod --yes        # forget the connection on this machine only
```

## What PSO redacts

Every log line, error, response and exported record passes through a redactor: registered secret values, credential-shaped keys, bearer headers, PEM private keys, URL user-info and common token shapes. When logs are read back through PSO, all secrets stored on the server are masked too.

## Guarantees and limits

- A native credential store protects against other users and a stolen disk. It does **not** protect against malware running as you: that code can ask the same store.
- The `encrypted-file` provider is exactly as strong as its passphrase or key file.
- Passing a password to `ssh` uses a one-process askpass helper and the child's environment; on Linux another process of the **same user** could read it from `/proc` while that process lives.
- A request signature protects the channel's integrity and prevents replay. It is not end-to-end encryption; SSH provides the confidentiality.
- The audit log is hash-chained and sanitized: edits and accidents are detectable (`pso release:audit production --verify`). A fully privileged administrator of the server can rewrite the entire chain; ship the head hash somewhere they do not control if that matters to you.
- An application that prints its own secret in an unrecognisable form writes it into its own log file; PSO can only mask what it knows or recognizes.
- None of this is a claim that the system cannot be compromised, and no custom cryptography is used: only Ed25519, SHA-256, AES-256-GCM and scrypt from the Node.js runtime.

## What can go wrong

Losing the credential store loses your enrolled client key; an administrator can invite you again. If the encrypted-file passphrase is lost the file cannot be recovered; enroll again.

---

# nginx and existing infrastructure

> How PSO manages nginx virtual hosts without touching anything it does not own, how provisioning splits unprivileged steps from administrator steps, and how to adopt a server that already runs things.

PSO adopts servers that already run applications. It manages only what it can prove it owns, and it tells you everything else it noticed.

## Ownership

A file is *PSO-managed* when its name is `pso-<application>.conf` **and** its first line is `# Managed by PSO Web (app=<application>)`. Anything else is external:

- an existing vhost is listed by `environment:inspect` but never edited;
- a planned file whose name exists without the marker, or with another application's marker, is a **conflict** and blocks the plan;
- a planned `server_name` plus port that an external vhost already serves is a conflict as well.

```bash
pso environment:inspect production
pso release:plan production
```

## Layouts

| `nginxLayout` (server policy) | Files |
|---|---|
| `pso.d` (default) | `/etc/nginx/pso.d/pso-<app>.conf`, a directory owned by the agent's user |
| `sites` | `/etc/nginx/sites-available/pso-<app>.conf` plus a symlink in `sites-enabled/` |
| `conf.d` | `/etc/nginx/conf.d/pso-<app>.conf` |
| an absolute directory | `<dir>/pso-<app>.conf` |

The declaration can name a different `layout`. Each file holds the upstreams, a loopback listener per service (the stable internal address, see [Deploy a release](cloud/deploy-a-release.md)) and, for routed services, the public server with WebSocket forwarding and optional TLS from certificate **file paths you provide**. PSO does not obtain certificates and does not touch DNS.

## Every change is validated

Back up the previous file, write the new one, run `nginx -t`, and only then reload gracefully. If the test fails the previous file is restored and nginx is **not reloaded**, so the running configuration stays the last valid one. If the reload itself fails, the files are restored and a reload is attempted again. Old workers finish their in-flight requests; nothing is stopped.

## Least privilege: provisioning is a plan, not a surprise

The agent runs unprivileged. The few things that need root are listed by `environment:plan`, together with a script you can read and run yourself:

```bash
pso environment:plan production
pso environment:provision production --yes
```

`provision --yes` performs only the steps marked *agent* (directories in the agent's own home, a default policy). The *administrator* steps are creating `/etc/nginx/pso.d` for the agent's user, one `include` line in `nginx.conf` (PSO never edits it), and a sudoers rule granting exactly `nginx -t` and `nginx -s reload`. PSO never installs operating-system packages, changes firewall rules, replaces an existing nginx configuration or restarts unrelated services. Everything is idempotent: running it again converges and removes nothing.

## Paths and links are checked, not trusted

A custom `layout` in a declaration must be an absolute path with no `.` or `..` segments inside the directories PSO may manage (the server's PSO directory, `sites-available`/`sites-enabled`, `conf.d`, `http.d`); anything else, such as `/etc/nginx/../../tmp`, is refused when the plan is made. Before writing, PSO resolves the real location: a symlinked directory that leads outside those roots, or a target file that is itself a symbolic link, is refused (nothing behind the link is touched). An existing `sites-enabled` entry must be the symbolic link to **PSO's own** file; a regular file or a link elsewhere belongs to someone else and stops the change. Concurrent changes are serialized by a lock shared by every deployment on the server, and a failed validation or reload restores the previous files and nginx keeps serving. Verified on Linux (`nginx-safety.test.ts`, run in a Linux container) and in the container end-to-end runs.

## `/etc/hosts` and DNS

Local host resolution (`/etc/hosts`) and public DNS are different things, and PSO changes neither automatically. To test a domain before DNS exists, send the `Host` header yourself (`curl -H "Host: shop.example.com" http://203.0.113.10/`).

## Management is never published

The agent has no network endpoint, so there is nothing for nginx to publish, and no generated configuration mentions it. PSO adds no ports to Docker and no firewall rules.

## What can go wrong

- *`nginx -t fails on the CURRENT configuration`*: PSO refuses to modify a proxy it cannot validate. Fix the existing configuration first.
- *`/etc/nginx/pso.d is missing or not writable`*: run the administrator script from `environment:plan`.
- *The agent cannot run `nginx -t`*: the sudo rule is missing or names a different path to the nginx binary.
- Other software may also listen on the ports you pick; PSO checks ports only against what it can see and against its own reservations.

---

# Studio Cloud section

> Manage connections, environments, deployments, pipelines, infrastructure, credentials and audit logs from PSO Studio, with the same engine and policies as the CLI.

```bash
pso studio --remote
```

Studio normally stays read-only. With `--remote` it gains the **Cloud** section, and only then does it offer any action. Without the flag the section shows your local declarations and connections, says that remote management is off, and offers no button, because a button that cannot work is worse than none.

## One engine, two clients

Studio's local server is the trusted backend: it owns your credential store and your SSH sessions and calls exactly the same operations as the CLI. The browser page receives sanitized data and opaque references, never a secret. A password typed in the *Add connection* form goes to the local process once, into the protected credential store, and is never returned. Mutating requests need the Studio access cookie, a same-origin `Origin` header and a custom header, and each action that changes an environment needs the environment name as confirmation: for **production and staging you must type it**, for the other environments the field is pre-filled.

## Tabs

| Tab | What you can do |
|---|---|
| Overview | See every declared environment with its connection state, and read live status (active, previous and last known-good release, the lock, services running, memory and disk) when you ask for it |
| Environments | Open a declaration with its diagnostics and plan a deployment of a branch, tag or commit |
| Connections | Fetch and approve host keys, add a connection, test every layer, install and enroll the agent |
| Deployments | Follow history, open a deployment live (pipeline stages, the blue-green view, a sanitized log), cancel, roll back or recover |
| Pipelines | See each pipeline's stages and which are off |
| Infrastructure | Read server resources, tools, nginx virtual hosts (PSO-managed versus external) and the provisioning plan with the administrator script |
| Credentials | Rotate or revoke, list who has access and their roles, invite teammates with a single-use token, manage server secret names |
| Signing | Create signing identities on this machine (the private key goes to the credential store and is never shown), see and change the signers an environment trusts, require signed releases, sign a clean checkout, and ask the server to verify a signed manifest (authenticity and integrity shown separately) |
| Applications | The real URLs of each application (read from the nginx file PSO manages), the active release, strategy and runtime, and **Verify accessibility**: process, local health, reverse proxy, reachability from this machine, TLS and an optional authenticated SSH tunnel, each shown on its own |
| Endpoints | The routes published with the active release, complete URLs, required scopes, and a guarded request tester (explicit action, strict TLS, state-changing methods need their own confirmation, the bearer token is never stored) |
| Services | Measured processes, memory, restarts and unit identity of the application, and the infrastructure services of the host listed as *not managed by PSO* |
| NGINX | The nginx files PSO can see (managed or external, effective or not), a guarded editor for PSO-managed files only (lint, preview, `nginx -t`, graceful reload, backup, restore); external files are read-only |
| Network | Every listening socket assessed against the exposure policy, the effective sudo privilege of the agent's user, and a remediation plan that is never applied automatically |
| Audit | The server's hash-chained audit log with chain verification, and the local audit of what you did from this machine |

Production is unmistakable: its name appears as a bordered, uppercase pill with a warning icon, never by color alone, and status is always text plus an icon.

## Pipeline and traffic views

A deployment shows its stages as chips: pending, running, passed, failed, skipped, blocked, awaiting approval, cancelled. The blue-green view shows the previous and candidate releases and which one **currently receives traffic according to the deployment's recorded state**. Both come from the server's deployment file. Nothing is simulated: when live data has not been read, the page says so.

```text evidence="illustrative"
Previous release  r20261114223537-9874ff64   [receiving traffic]   <-->   Candidate release  r20261114223601-ce58a814   [not receiving traffic]
```

## What can go wrong

- *Remote management is disabled*: restart with `pso studio --remote`. The agent's own mode (disabled, development, protected) still applies on top.
- A server that cannot be reached shows an error in the section only; the Studio connection indicator reflects Studio's own server, not the remote one.
- Studio listens on loopback only and requires its one-time URL token; closing the terminal stops it. A deployment you started keeps running on the server.
- The UI cannot weaken policy: an approval requirement, a stale plan or a disabled strategy refuses the action with the same reason the CLI gives.

---

# Integrating with external CI/CD

> Use PSO's deployment engine from GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or any pipeline without duplicating deployment logic, and keep credentials out of the CI configuration.

PSO's pipeline is native, but it does not replace the CI you already use. A CI job builds and tests however it likes, then asks PSO to deploy. The deployment logic (plan, candidate, switch, rollback) stays in one place: the agent.

## The commands are automation friendly

- `--json` prints machine-readable output on every command.
- Exit codes: `0` success, `1` failure, `2` usage error (nothing changed), `3` an action needs explicit authorization (`--yes`), `4` the caller's role is not enough.
- Nothing prompts when standard input is not a terminal. Secrets come from standard input.
- `--dry-run` is available where it applies, and `release:plan` is always a dry run.

```bash
pso release:plan production --commit 9b3c1f0a5d7e2c4b6a8f0e1d3c5b7a9f2e4d6c8b --json
pso release:deploy production --commit 9b3c1f0a5d7e2c4b6a8f0e1d3c5b7a9f2e4d6c8b --yes
```

Deploying an exact `--commit` (the one the CI job just built and tested) removes any doubt about what goes live.

## A CI client is a client like any other

Create a dedicated identity instead of sharing yours:

```bash
pso environment:access production --invite deployer --minutes 15
```

Enroll the CI runner with that single-use token (`pso agent:enroll prod` with the token on standard input) on a runner that has a protected credential store, or use the `encrypted-file` provider with the passphrase held in the CI system's secret manager. The enrolled key lives in the runner's credential store; revoke it with `pso environment:access production --revoke <client-id>` when the runner is retired. Give the CI identity the `deployer` role, not `admin`.

```yaml
# GitHub Actions (illustrative)
- name: Deploy
  run: |
    printf '%s' "$ENROLLMENT_TOKEN" | pso agent:enroll prod
    pso release:deploy production --commit "$GITHUB_SHA" --yes --json
  env:
    PSO_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER: encrypted-file
    PSO_CREDENTIAL_PASSPHRASE: (the value of a secret in your CI secret store)
    ENROLLMENT_TOKEN: (the single-use token, also from the CI secret store)
```

## Approvals still apply

If the server policy requires an approval by someone other than the proposer, the CI job plans, a person approves (`pso release:approve production --plan <hash>`, or in Studio), and the job (or a second job) deploys with `--plan <hash>`. The approval is bound to the plan hash, the commit and the policy, and expires.

## What can go wrong

- *Exit code 3*: you forgot `--yes`. Automation must say it explicitly.
- *`PLAN_STALE`*: the branch moved between planning and deploying. Pin `--commit`.
- *`LOCKED`*: another deployment of the same application is running; two pipelines must not race for one environment.
- A CI runner needs outbound SSH to the server. PSO opens no inbound path; if a bastion is required, register the connection with `--jump`.
- `--json` output contains no secrets, but it is still a record of your infrastructure; treat CI logs accordingly.

---

# Troubleshooting cloud operations

> The refusals and failures you can meet, what each one means, and what to do, from SSH and enrollment to plans, deployments and recovery.

Almost every failure in this area is a deliberate refusal that names its reason. Find it below.

## Connecting

| You see | Meaning | Do |
|---|---|---|
| `Host key verification failed` | the server's SSH key differs from the one you pinned | confirm with your provider; if the server was rebuilt, `connection:remove` and add it again |
| `AGENT IDENTITY CHANGED` | another agent key answers than the pinned one; nothing was sent | same as above; the agent identity is regenerated only by a reinstall |
| `No protected credential store is available` | no OS keyring, and no explicit `encrypted-file` configuration | install `libsecret-tools` or set `PSO_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER=encrypted-file` plus a passphrase or key file |
| `the agent is not provisioned` | `agent:install` has not run | run it with `--mode` and `--environment` |
| `remote management is DISABLED` | the server's mode is `disabled` | a host administrator runs `pso-agent set-mode` on the server |
| `Cannot find module .../pso-agent.mjs` | the agent was not installed | `pso agent:install` |

## Enrolling and permissions

`enrollment refused` covers a wrong, expired and used token alike, on purpose. Create a new one (`pso environment:access <env> --invite <role>`). `RATE_LIMITED` means too many failures from your address or key; wait for the time shown. `FORBIDDEN ... needs the role "deployer"` means your client has a lower role; ask an administrator.

## Planning

A plan with blockers lists each reason. Common ones:

- *this server is the production environment but the declaration targets staging*: use the right declaration for the server.
- *nginx is not installed* / *nginx -t fails* / *not writable*: see [nginx and existing infrastructure](cloud/nginx-and-existing-infrastructure.md); PSO does not install packages.
- *not enough free memory or disk*: the strategy needs room for a second release (blue-green) or the plan blocks.
- *another deployment is in progress (deployment lock held)*: wait, or recover it (below).
- *the server policy does not allow the "blue-green" strategy*: the server's policy overrides the project.

### Signatures and runtime

- *this environment requires releases signed by a trusted signer*: sign the release (`pso release:sign`) and pass `--signed <file>`; see [release signing](cloud/release-signing.md).
- *untrusted-signer*, *revoked-signer*, *expired-signer*, *signer-not-allowed-for-app*: the server's trust store decides; a superadministrator adds a signer with `pso trust:add`. A revoked key is never accepted again.
- *manifest-mismatch*: the signature is genuine but names another commit or checksum than the one the server resolved; sign again after the branch moved.
- *not newer than the last deployed signed release*: raise `--sequence`; to return to an older release use `release:rollback`.
- *systemd is requested but unusable*: the user's systemd manager is not reachable or the server policy does not allow it; the message says which, and lingering is an administrator step (`loginctl enable-linger <user>`).
- *scheduled jobs without leader election* / *applies its own migrations* (blockers): see [workloads](cloud/workloads-and-rollback-safety.md).
- HTTP `429` through a generated gateway during a load test: its rate limiter is working; lower the request rate or raise `PSO_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` for that service on purpose.

## Deploying

| State or error | Meaning | Do |
|---|---|---|
| `CANDIDATE_NOT_READY` | the new release crashed or never answered its readiness path | read `pso release:logs <env> --deployment <id>`; the active release was never touched |
| `PROXY_REJECTED` | nginx rejected the new configuration | the previous configuration is still active; read the logged `nginx -t` output |
| `ACTIVE_NOT_VERIFIED` | after switching, probes through the proxy did not reach the new release | the previous proxy configuration was restored while the old release still ran |
| `PLAN_STALE` | the branch, the active release or the policy changed after planning | plan again; the newest commit is never deployed implicitly |
| `INTERRUPTED` | the worker on the server disappeared | `pso release:recover <env> --yes` |
| `needs-operator` | recovery found contradictory evidence and changed nothing | inspect with `release:status`, then `release:rollback` or deploy again |

## The application is deployed but I cannot open it

1. `pso release:url <app> --verify` shows each layer separately. If the process, local health and proxy on the server are verified but this machine times out, the server is healthy and something on the path (a cloud network security group, a firewall, your own network) is dropping the traffic. That is a hypothesis until the owner of the network confirms it.
2. `pso release:url <app> --verify --tunnel --ca-file <ca.pem>` reaches the application through the authenticated SSH connection with TLS verified: it proves the application works while the public path is closed.
3. Open the rule in your cloud provider's console (inbound TCP 443 from your public IP only) yourself; PSO never changes cloud settings.

## Open the application in a browser

A browser needs two things: a network path to the server and a certificate it trusts. An IP-based environment has no domain, so its certificate comes from a private certificate authority (CA) that no browser knows.

**Trust the CA (public certificate only).** Give the browser the CA *certificate* (`ca.pem`, the public part). Never copy the CA's private key: it is not needed and must not leave the machine that created it.

```bash
# Windows (current user only; no administrator needed). The CA certificate is public.
certutil -user -addstore Root path\to\ca.pem
# macOS
security add-trusted-cert -r trustRoot -k ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db path/to/ca.pem
# Linux (Chrome and Chromium use the user database; Firefox has its own store: Settings, Certificates, Authorities, Import)
certutil -d sql:$HOME/.pki/nssdb -A -t "C,," -n pso-validation-ca -i path/to/ca.pem
```

Check the certificate you are trusting before you trust it: compare the SHA-256 fingerprint the owner gives you (`openssl x509 -in ca.pem -noout -fingerprint -sha256`) with the one in the file. The server certificate must name the address you type (a subject alternative name of type IP): `pso release:url <app> --verify --ca-file ca.pem` checks the chain and the name. Remove the CA from the trust store when the validation ends. TLS verification is never turned off to make a page open.

**While the public port is closed, use the tunnel.** From a machine that holds the connection:

```bash
node scenarios/tunnel.mjs          # in the fixture: https://127.0.0.1:18443 -> the server's HTTPS port, authenticated by SSH, loopback only
```

Then open `https://127.0.0.1:18443/` (the certificate also names 127.0.0.1). This is **temporary private access**, not public access: it exists only while the command runs and only on your machine. Whether the public address works is a different fact: check it with `pso release:url <app> --verify`.

## Verification you can run yourself

```bash
pso connection:test prod
pso environment:inspect production
pso release:status production
pso release:audit production --verify
```

```text evidence="expected"
audit chain intact: 214 entries, head 7f3a91c04b22d8e1…
```

## What can go wrong when troubleshooting

Do not delete lock directories or edit state files by hand: recovery exists because a stale lock may protect a half-finished release. Do not copy a token or log into a ticket without checking it: PSO masks what it knows, and a secret an application prints in an unusual form can survive in that application's own log. If a server was changed outside PSO (a manual `nginx` edit of a managed file), the next deployment will overwrite it; managed files say so in their first line.

## Lessons from the first external validation

- **Several applications in one environment.** Every deployment declaration has a unique `name`; commands and Studio address a deployment by that name (`pso release:plan shop-catalog`), because the environment name (`production`) is shared and would be ambiguous. The typed confirmation still asks for the **environment** name (the server also accepts the application name).
- **A new connection must pin the agent first.** `pso connection:test <name> --pin-agent <fingerprint>` verifies the agent's key by challenge-response and **saves** the pin (it did not before 2026-11-15); only then does `pso agent:enroll` work.
- **After a server restart an application did not come back.** Boot persistence belongs to the *active* release's units. Stopping a service disables it on purpose; starting or restarting it again re-enables it (fixed after the first reboot test: a service restart used to leave it disabled). `loginctl show-user <user> -p Linger` must say `yes`.
- **A JVM stopped for a replacement shows as `failed` in systemd.** It exits with status 143 on SIGTERM; PSO now declares 143 a success so a cleanly replaced release is not reported as a failure.
- **HTTP 301 on the public port, then a failed verification.** When TLS is configured the public HTTP port only redirects; the agent verifies the release through nginx's loopback listener and checks that the redirect exists.
- **A request reset exactly at a traffic switch.** nginx reloads gracefully, but a client that reuses an idle persistent connection can still be reset at that instant (one request in about 100 to 360 in the measured runs; none with one connection per request). Clients should retry idempotent requests. PSO does not claim zero downtime.
- **Packing a directory artifact on Windows** failed when `tar` was Git's GNU tar and the output path was absolute (`C:\...`): fixed. A packaged orchestrator must include `pso.config.json`; there is no public packaging command yet, so omitting it only shows at start-up.
- **The server audit is dominated by `session.open`.** Every Studio or CLI call opens a session and the last 200 entries can be mostly those; filter by event when looking for deployments.

---

# Running services with systemd (no Docker)

> How PSO keeps Node.js and Java/Spring Boot services running on a plain Linux server with the deploy user's own systemd manager, what privilege it needs (one admin command), and what it guarantees across crashes and reboots.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** against a real systemd (Debian 12, systemd 252 as PID 1 of a disposable container, reached over SSH) with Node.js, Java 21 and PostgreSQL. It has **not** been run on an external cloud server, and only the **user-manager** scope exists (see [What is not implemented](#what-is-not-implemented)).

By default PSO keeps your services alive itself: it starts each process, remembers who it is and stops it with the grace period you declared. That works anywhere, but a process the agent started does not come back after a server reboot. When the server runs systemd you can ask for the operating system to do that job:

```ts
export default defineDeployment({
  // ...
  runtime: { supervisor: "systemd", restart: "on-failure" },
});
```

Nothing else about the deployment changes: the same plan, candidate, verification, switch, drain, rollback and recovery apply. Blue-green still starts the new release next to the old one; each instance simply becomes a **unit**.

## Why the user manager, and what an administrator does once

PSO does **not** write units under `/etc/systemd/system`, does not run as root and does not need a sudo rule for systemd. It uses the deploy user's **own** systemd manager (`systemctl --user`), so the agent can only create, start, stop and remove units *inside that user's manager*, and every service runs as that same unprivileged user.

One command, run once by an administrator, makes that manager start at boot without a login session:

```bash
loginctl enable-linger deploy
```

`pso environment:plan <environment>` prints it in the reviewed administrator script (together with the other server-preparation steps); PSO never runs it for you. Without lingering the units stop when the last session of the user ends and are not started at boot: the plan says so as a warning.

## What a unit looks like

One file per service instance and release, named `pso-<application>-<service>-<release>-<n>.service`, in `~/.config/systemd/user/`:

- The first line is the ownership marker `# Managed by PSO Web (app=..., service=..., release=...)` and the file carries a per-slot token. **PSO touches only units that have its shape, the marker and the token.** An unrelated unit of the same user, even one named `pso-...`, is never started, stopped, disabled or deleted.
- `ExecStart` is the argv array you declared, each word quoted for systemd, with an absolute program path (resolved from the agent's `PATH`). There is no shell.
- `KillMode=control-group`, `KillSignal=SIGTERM` and `TimeoutStopSec` = your `shutdownGraceSeconds` plus a margin: systemd sends SIGTERM, waits the real grace period and only then kills. `NoNewPrivileges=yes` is set.
- **Secrets are never in the unit file.** They are in an environment file (mode 600, in the agent's private directory) that the unit reads.
- Output goes to the release's log file; `pso release:logs` returns the journal of the unit when the user's journal is readable, and says which source it used when it is not. Both are sanitized.

## What you get

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| A service crashes (`restart: "on-failure"`) | systemd restarts it; the verified release stays healthy |
| The server restarts (lingering on) | Only the **active** release's units are enabled, so only they start; the previous release does not |
| A candidate fails to start or never becomes ready | Its unit is stopped; the active release is untouched |
| Rollback | The previous release's units are started again with the same verification |
| Independent update of one service | Other services' units are not restarted (their process ids do not change) |

## Verified behaviour

The framework's end-to-end systemd run checks, on real systemd: the plan and the administrator script; the server policy refusing `systemd` when it does not allow it; units with marker, no secret and a private environment file; independent update under traffic without restarting the other service; a failing candidate; rollback; a foreign unit left untouched; restart after `kill -9`; and the application coming back after a server restart with no agent and no operator involved.

## What is not implemented

- **System scope.** Units under `/etc/systemd/system` with a configurable `User=` need a root-owned helper and a narrow sudo rule that PSO does not ship. They are not offered, and PSO does not emulate them. To run services as a different user, install the agent for that user (one agent home per user).
- Resource limits (`MemoryMax` and friends) are not set: the user manager does not always delegate the controllers, and PSO does not claim limits it cannot verify.
- Distributions without systemd (Alpine, containers) keep using the default supervisor.

## Related

- The server decides what is allowed: the policy key `supervisors` (`pso environment:policy <environment> --set supervisors=...`) cannot be widened by a declaration.
- [Deploy a real application to a VPS](cloud/deploy-to-a-vps.md) uses this driver end to end.

---

# Release signing and trusted signers

> How a deployment proves who produced a release (authenticity) separately from whether the bytes are the ones named (integrity), how an environment requires signed releases, and how to generate, enroll, rotate, revoke and recover signing keys.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** with unit tests and an in-process agent (`signing.test.ts`: tampering, wrong release, untrusted, revoked, expired, replay, start-time re-check, no bypass by pipeline or declaration). It has **not** been run against an external environment, and signing is **optional by default**: an environment opts in with `requireSignedReleases`.

## Two different questions

| Question | Called | Answered by |
|---|---|---|
| Are these the bytes that were named? | **Integrity** | an immutable commit id (git) or a SHA-256 checksum (artifact) |
| Did a signer this environment trusts produce that name? | **Authenticity** | a signature checked against the environment's trust store |

A checksum is integrity only: anyone who can change an artifact can change its checksum next to it. PSO reports the two separately in every plan, and never lets one stand in for the other.

## What is signed

A small canonical JSON **release manifest**: the application, the immutable source (the commit id and its git tree, or the artifact's SHA-256), an optional hash of the extracted file tree, a **strictly increasing sequence number** and the time. The signature is Ed25519 (the standard primitive of `node:crypto`; PSO has no custom cryptography) over the manifest with a domain-separation prefix, so a release signature can never be replayed as a request signature or the other way round.

## Where the keys live

- The **private key** is created on the signer's machine and stored in that machine's protected credential store. It is never in a project, a generated application, a package, a manifest, a pipeline or on a server, and PSO has no command that exports it.
- The **server holds public keys only**, in a trust store that **only a superadministrator of that environment** changes, with an audit entry for every change. No declaration, pipeline stage, CLI option or Studio setting can add a signer or switch the requirement off.

```bash
pso signer:generate release-bot
pso trust:add production --signer release-bot --apps shop-catalog --not-after 2027-06-01 --yes
pso environment:policy production --set requireSignedReleases=true --yes
```

## Signing and deploying

```bash
pso release:sign production --signer release-bot --sequence 12 --path ../shop-catalog
pso release:verify production --signed production.release.signed.json
pso release:plan production --signed production.release.signed.json
pso release:deploy production --plan <hash> --yes
```

`release:sign` reads the commit from a **clean** checkout (uncommitted changes are refused: the server deploys the commit, not your working tree). For an artifact release give `--artifact <file>`; the manifest then also carries the hash of the extracted tree, which the server recomputes after unpacking and refuses on any difference.

## What the server enforces (independently of the project)

| Check | Where |
|---|---|
| The signature verifies against a key in **this environment's** trust store | at planning, and **again at start** (a signer revoked after approval stops the deployment) |
| The signer is not revoked, not expired and allowed for this application | same |
| The manifest names exactly the commit or checksum the **server** resolved, for this application | same |
| The sequence is greater than the last signed release deployed (replay and downgrade) | at planning |
| The extracted content matches the signed tree hash | after unpacking, before building |
| A signature that is presented but unacceptable is refused even where signing is optional | at planning |
| Rollback, where signing is required, goes only to a release whose signer still qualifies | at rollback |

Every state has a name: `verified`, `unsigned`, `invalid-signature`, `untrusted-signer`, `revoked-signer`, `expired-signer`, `signer-not-allowed-for-app`, `manifest-mismatch`. Only `verified` is a pass.

## Rotation, revocation and recovery

- **Rotate**: generate a new signer, `trust:add` it, sign new releases with it, then `trust:revoke` the old one. During the overlap both are trusted. A key is never "re-keyed": a new key has a new id.
- **Revoke**: `pso trust:revoke production <key-id> --reason "key leaked" --yes`. It takes effect at once, also for plans already approved and for rollback. A revoked key is never accepted again by that environment, even if re-added.
- **Lost private key**: generate a new signer and trust it. There is nothing to restore, because nothing ever left the machine. If it may have leaked, revoke first.
- **Lost superadministrator**: use the host-administrator recovery in [Agent and enrollment](cloud/agent-and-enrollment.md).

## Limits

- The source of truth for a git release is its commit id, which is a SHA-1 digest unless the repository uses the SHA-256 object format. Use artifact releases where that matters.
- A signature proves who vouched for a release, not that it is free of vulnerabilities or malicious code.
- There is no transparency log and no certificate authority: trust is an explicit list of public keys per environment.

---

# Deploy a real PSO application to a Linux VPS

> A practical, end-to-end guide - prepare the server, enroll your machine, store secrets, deploy a generated PSO gateway and Spring Boot services with PostgreSQL as systemd units behind nginx, update them independently, roll back and recover.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> The steps below were **exercised on a disposable Debian 12 container with systemd, PostgreSQL 15, Java 21, Node.js 24 and nginx, reached over real SSH** (`packages/deploy/test/e2e-real-pso.test.ts`). They have **not** been run on an external cloud server. Where a step needs something your provider controls (DNS, TLS certificates, firewall), PSO documents it but does not do it.

The example is the workspace of the [Build a CRUD API](tutorials/crud-api.md) tutorial: a Node.js **gateway** (the orchestrator), two Spring Boot services **catalog** and **inventory**, each with its own PostgreSQL database, and the tutorial's ES256 JWKS publisher. It was created with `pso create workspace`, `pso create service ... --db postgres`, `pso create orchestrator` and `pso security:keys --generate`; nothing in the framework was changed to deploy it.

## 1. What the server needs

| Need | Detail |
|---|---|
| Linux with systemd | Debian 12 / Ubuntu 22.04+ were used. Without systemd the default supervisor still works, but does not survive a reboot |
| An SSH account for deployment | **Not root**, for example `deploy`. Key login; `PasswordAuthentication` may stay off |
| Node.js ≥ 24 | needed by the agent itself and by Node services. PSO never installs packages |
| Java 21 | for generated Spring services (their `pom.xml` says 21) |
| nginx | blue-green and rolling need it. An existing installation is adopted, not replaced |
| PostgreSQL ≥ 14 | one role and database per service. PSO does not provision databases |
| 1 GB RAM free per JVM you run twice during a switch | blue-green runs old and new side by side |
| Network | inbound SSH from you; inbound 80/443 from clients (yours to open). **PSO opens no port and changes no firewall** |

## 2. Prepare the server once (administrator)

PSO prints what it needs instead of doing it. After enrolling (step 3) run:

```bash
pso environment:plan production
```

It lists each step with its status and prints one reviewable script. Typical content: the PSO-owned nginx directory `/etc/nginx/pso.d` owned by `deploy`, a sudo rule that allows exactly `nginx -t` and `nginx -s reload` and nothing else, and `loginctl enable-linger deploy`. An administrator reads it and runs it as root. Add `include /etc/nginx/pso.d/*.conf;` inside the `http { }` block once (PSO never edits `nginx.conf`).

Create the databases yourself, with a password you keep out of the repository:

```bash
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE ROLE catalog LOGIN PASSWORD '...'" -c "CREATE DATABASE catalog OWNER catalog"
```

## 3. Connect and enroll your machine

```bash
pso connection:add production --host 203.0.113.10 --user deploy --auth key --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
pso agent:install production --mode protected --environment production --yes
pso agent:enroll production
```

`connection:add` shows the server's SSH host-key fingerprint and waits for you to confirm it (compare it with your provider's console). `--auth agent` uses a key held by your `ssh-agent` (PSO never reads it); `--auth key` with a passphrase asks for the passphrase on a hidden prompt and keeps it in the credential store. `agent:install` copies one bundled file, starts nothing and prints a single-use enrollment token; `agent:enroll` reads it from a hidden prompt, generates **your** client key (Ed25519, in your protected credential store) and enrolls its **public** half. Your permanent secret never leaves your machine, and the server never holds anything that lets someone else become you. See [Agent and enrollment](cloud/agent-and-enrollment.md).

Production management stays **disabled** unless the host administrator chose `--mode`. With `protected`, deployments need an approval.

## 4. Secrets

```bash
pso environment:secret production catalog-db-password        # value from a hidden prompt or standard input
```

The value is stored on the server (mode 600), reaches the service as an environment variable, and never appears in a declaration, plan, log, argument list or audit entry.

## 5. Declare and deploy

One `deploy/production.deployment.pso.ts` per application (the gateway, each Spring service, the JWKS publisher). The Spring service, abridged:

```ts
export default defineDeployment({
  name: "shop-catalog", environment: "production",
  connection: { provider: "ssh", credentials: "production" },
  source: { provider: "artifact", path: "artifacts/catalog.tgz" },     // the jar you built, or a git source
  runtime: { supervisor: "systemd", restart: "on-failure" },
  service: {
    name: "catalog", runtime: "java", start: ["java", "-Xmx256m", "-jar", "app.jar"],
    health: { readyPath: "/actuator/health", timeoutSeconds: 150 }, shutdownGraceSeconds: 20,
    internalPort: 8101,                       // the stable address the gateway's workspace file points at
    env: { SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: "staging", DB_URL: "jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:5432/catalog", DB_USER: "catalog", PSO_JWT_ISSUER: "https://idp.example.com", PSO_JWT_AUDIENCE: "shop-api", PSO_JWT_JWKS_URI: "https://idp.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json" },
    secrets: { DB_PASSWORD: "catalog-db-password" },
    workload: { selfMigrates: true },        // Flyway runs at start: see Workloads and rollback safety
  },
  migrations: { mode: "expand-contract" },
  strategy: { type: "blue-green", proxy: "nginx", rollback: true, drainSeconds: 3 },
  proxy: { nginx: { domains: ["catalog.internal"], listen: { http: 8080 } } },
});
```

Declarations hold **references**, never credentials; a value that looks like a secret is refused. Then:

```bash
pso pipeline:validate production
pso release:plan production
pso release:deploy production --yes
```

The plan shows the commit or checksum, the strategy, the resources, who vouches for the release, what is checked, what is switched off, what database changes mean for rollback, and what is enforced no matter what. Nothing changes on the server until you approve it.

For the gateway, point `PSO_WORKSPACE` at the `pso.workspace.json` packaged with it; the ports in that file for `catalog` and `inventory` are their `internalPort` values, so the gateway always reaches whichever release is active.

## 6. Use the application

Through the gateway with a token from your identity provider (the tutorial's `dev-token.mjs` only for development). The services also validate the token themselves against the JWKS, so they do not trust the network. In the exercised run an anonymous request got `401`, a token without the scope `403`, and a valid one `201` with the row in PostgreSQL.

## 7. Update one thing at a time

Deploy only the service that changed. In the exercised run, replacing the catalog (with an additive migration) under authenticated traffic restarted **only** the catalog (the other services kept their process ids) and no request failed; replacing the gateway left both Spring services running. A candidate that the framework's own startup validation refused (an invalid JWT algorithm) never received traffic and the active release kept serving.

## 8. Roll back and recover

```bash
pso release:rollback production --yes
pso release:status production
pso release:recover production --yes        # after an interrupted deployment
```

Rollback restores the previous **code**; it does not undo database changes: the plan said so before you deployed. After a server restart, with lingering on, PostgreSQL and the **active** releases come back by themselves. See [Rollback and recovery](cloud/rollback-and-recovery.md).

## 9. From Studio

`pso studio --remote` opens the same operations: connections, enrollment, policy, plans, deployment progress, logs, rollback, recovery, the audit trail and signers. Studio runs on loopback only and every change goes through the same calls and the same server policy as the CLI.

## 10. An existing VPS

Adopting a server that already runs things is the normal case. PSO reads before it writes: `pso environment:inspect production` reports what is listening, which nginx virtual hosts exist and whether `nginx -t` passes. It writes only files named `pso-<app>.conf` that carry its marker, never edits another virtual host, and refuses a plan that would collide on a name or port. Services it did not start are never signalled.

---

# External cloud validation guide

> What an isolated cloud server must provide, what to run on it in what order, what to record, and how to clean up, so that Cloud Lifecycle and Operations can be validated outside the development machine.

> Status: PARTIALLY implemented — read the limitations.

> [!STATUS]
> **This validation has not been performed.** Everything marked verified in this section was verified on a disposable container on the development machine. Passing this guide is what would justify calling the SSH deployment workflow validated on a real cloud server; it is not a production-readiness certificate.

Use a **new, isolated, disposable** server that you own and can delete. Do not point this at an existing production server, and do not put production credentials in repository files, prompts, logs or documentation. PSO provisions nothing for you: you create and delete the server.

## Minimum server

| | |
|---|---|
| OS | Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 (systemd). Other Linux distributions work with the default supervisor only |
| Size | 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk (blue-green runs two JVMs per Spring service during a switch) |
| Software | Node.js ≥ 24, Java 21, nginx ≥ 1.18, PostgreSQL ≥ 14, git, tar, `sudo` |
| Network | inbound TCP 22 from your address only; 80 and 443 only if you test public access. Nothing else. PSO needs **no** management port |
| Accounts | an administrator account for the one-time preparation, and a **non-root** `deploy` account with key login |

## Order of work

1. **SSH hardening (yours).** Key login for `deploy`, root login off. Record the host-key fingerprint from the provider console.
2. **Connect.** `pso connection:add`, confirm the fingerprint matches, `pso connection:test`. A different fingerprint must fail hard: change it on purpose once and check.
3. **Install and enroll.** `pso agent:install ... --mode protected --yes`, `pso agent:enroll`. Check the token is single use (a second enrollment must be refused) and expires.
4. **Prepare.** `pso environment:plan`, review the script, run it as the administrator. Create the PostgreSQL roles and databases. `pso environment:inspect` must show no blockers.
5. **Secrets.** `pso environment:secret` for each database password. Verify a value never appears in `pso release:plan`, `pso release:logs`, `pso release:audit`, `ps` output or any file under `~/.pso-agent` other than the 600-mode secret.
6. **Initial deployment** of the real applications ([Deploy a real application](cloud/deploy-to-a-vps.md)) with `runtime.supervisor: "systemd"`.
7. **Authenticated flow.** Anonymous `401`, wrong scope `403`, valid token creates and reads rows; check the rows in PostgreSQL.
8. **Subsequent release** of one service under light traffic; confirm the others' process ids did not change and no request failed.
9. **Failure.** Deploy a candidate that cannot start; confirm the active release keeps serving and the candidate has no running unit.
10. **Rollback.** `pso release:rollback`; confirm service and callers; note what it did **not** undo (the database).
11. **Recovery.** Kill the deployment worker mid-build; `release:status` must say INTERRUPTED, `release:recover` must act only on the verified state. Disconnect your SSH session during a deployment; it must continue.
12. **Server restart.** Reboot the server. PostgreSQL and the active release must return with no action from you.
13. **Security verification.** Production mode refuses an unenrolled client; a viewer cannot deploy; `pso environment:access --revoke` ends that client's session at once; a revoked signer's release is refused ([Release signing](cloud/release-signing.md)); nothing listens on a management port (`ss -ltnp` shows only SSH, nginx, PostgreSQL and your services on loopback).
14. **nginx.** An unrelated virtual host must be byte-identical before and after; a deliberately invalid proxy change must leave the previous configuration serving.
15. **Cleanup.** `pso agent:uninstall production --yes` (keeps applications unless `--purge-applications`), remove `/etc/nginx/pso.d`, the sudoers rule `/etc/sudoers.d/pso-nginx` and the user's linger (`loginctl disable-linger deploy`), drop the databases, then delete the server.

## What to record

For each step: the command, the exit code, the relevant output with secrets removed, and the time. Keep `pso release:audit --verify` output (the hash chain) from the end of the run. Record what **failed**; a failed run is evidence, not an embarrassment.

## What can go wrong, and what this guide cannot establish

Sustained production load, a multi-server topology, provider-specific networking and managed databases, TLS issuance, DNS, and long-term operation. Those remain separate milestones.

---

# Workloads, messaging and rollback safety

> What PSO checks when an old and a new release run side by side - scheduled jobs, self-migrating services, message consumers, outbox relays and WebSocket connections - and what an application rollback can and cannot undo.

> [!STATUS]
> **Implemented and verified** as planning rules (`workload-safety.test.ts`) and, for the Flyway case, in the real-application run (an additive migration applied while the previous release served; an application rollback with the schema one version ahead). PSO **cannot see inside your application**: these checks act on what the declaration says. A declaration that omits a workload is not protected against it.

Blue-green and rolling deliberately run two releases at once. That is what keeps the service available, and it is also what makes some workloads unsafe. Say what each service does in `workload`:

```ts
service: {
  name: "orders", runtime: "java", start: ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"],
  workload: {
    scheduledJobs: "leader-elected",     // "none" | "leader-elected" | "singleton"
    selfMigrates: true,                  // Flyway (or similar) runs when the application starts
    consumers: ["kafka"],                // "dispatch" | "kafka" | "rabbitmq" | "redis"
    orderedConsumption: false,
    outbox: true,
    channels: false,
  },
}
```

## What the plan refuses

| You declared | With blue-green or rolling | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `scheduledJobs: "singleton"` | **blocked** | every instance runs the jobs, so they would run twice during the overlap. Make them leader-elected, or use `recreate` with `downtimeAcknowledged` |
| `orderedConsumption: true` | **blocked** | ordering needs one active consumer; two releases consume at once |
| `selfMigrates: true` without `migrations.mode: "expand-contract"` | **blocked** | the migration runs when the candidate starts, *while the previous release still serves*: it must be additive |
| `selfMigrates: true` with a destructive migration | **blocked**, even when approved | it would break the release that is still serving |
| a destructive migration (any strategy) | blocked until `approvedDestructive` **and** the server policy allows it | irreversible changes need explicit authorization |

`recreate` never overlaps, so none of the overlap rules apply to it. PSO does not silently turn a blocked blue-green into a recreate: you choose, and you acknowledge the downtime.

## What the plan states (and does not promise)

- **Messaging stays at-least-once.** While two releases overlap they consume from the same subscription and the broker rebalances; handlers must be idempotent. PSO does not provide exactly-once delivery and does not promise zero downtime for consumer rebalancing.
- **Outbox**: the outbox guarantees no loss, not no repetition; two relays may publish the same row during an overlap.
- **Channels/WebSocket**: connections to the previous release are closed when it stops after the drain; clients must reconnect.
- **Migrations**: concurrent starts are serialized by the migration tool's own database lock, not by PSO. PSO's `migrations` block (a command run once, by one owner service, before the candidate starts) is the alternative when you do not want the application to migrate itself.

## What a rollback can and cannot undo

Every plan carries `rollback.dataSafety`:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `code-only` | this release changed no database structure; rolling back restores the previous code completely |
| `schema-ahead` | an additive migration was applied; rolling back restores the previous code on a database that stays at the newer schema. Safe only because expand-contract promises the previous release tolerates it. The contract step (removing the old column) belongs in a **later** release |
| `forward-only` | a destructive migration is included; rolling back restores the code but **not the data it removed**. Treat the release as forward-only and keep a backup |

In the real-application run, after an additive Flyway migration, rolling the catalog back to the previous jar left the database at version 2, the service started and answered, and the plan had said so before the deployment.

## What can go wrong

A declaration that leaves out a workload is not protected against it: PSO checks what you say, not what the code does. A forgotten `scheduledJobs: "singleton"` runs the jobs twice during a blue-green; a migration that is not really additive breaks the release that is still serving. Treat the `workload` block as part of the review of every release that changes how a service starts, consumes or schedules.

## Graceful draining

The old release keeps its connections for `drainSeconds` after traffic moves; its process then receives SIGTERM and has `shutdownGraceSeconds` (plus a margin) to finish running requests before it is killed. Declare the grace from the application's real shutdown time. The framework's HTTP server closes its listener, finishes accepted requests and only then releases its dependencies; a connection accepted but not yet carrying its request is given a short bounded window instead of being cut.

---

# Why PSO uses directory conventions

> Context, decision, consequences and alternatives.

## Context

Distributed projects accumulate hand-maintained registries: lists of routes, of modules, of services. They drift from the code, and nothing but a running application tells you whether they still agree.

## Decision

Make **location and name part of the declaration**. A file's directory and suffix state what it is; the framework discovers and validates them. Where convention cannot express something (which routes are exposed, which services exist) there is a small explicit file (`ROUTES.pso.ts`, `pso.workspace.json`).

## Consequences

- Tools (CLI, Studio, AI context) can reason about a project without running it.
- A misplaced or misnamed file is an error, not a silent no-op.
- Generators know exactly where to put things, so generated code is predictable and reviewable.
- You give up some freedom of layout. In return, every PSO project looks the same.

## Alternatives considered

A central registry file for everything (drifts, merge conflicts) and annotation scanning (implicit, needs execution). PSO uses conventions for *kinds* and explicit files for *exposure*.

## What it looks like in practice

A misplaced resource is a diagnostic, not a silent no-op (Expected output):

```text evidence="expected"
ERROR   PSO_MODULE_001 gateway: Module declaration missing.
The directory routes/ghost/ contains HTTP code but no MODULE.pso.ts. There is no fallback discovery.
FAILED
```

The message names the module directory `routes/ghost/` in every structure; in the official structure that directory is
`src/modules/ghost/`.

and the same tree gives the same answer on every machine: `pso validate --write-manifest` produced identical manifests on repeated runs ([deterministic manifests](concepts/deterministic-manifests.md)).

## The cost

You cannot choose another layout. Teams used to organising by feature across layers, or by their own scheme, feel it first. The mitigation is that the generators place everything for you, and that the conventions are few ([list](concepts/convention-over-configuration.md)).

## When to revisit

If a convention keeps being worked around, it is probably wrong for real projects; raise it with evidence (a layout that cannot express what teams need), not as a preference.

---

# Why MODULE.pso.ts exists

> Composition as an explicit, validated declaration.

## Context

A directory full of controllers and services does not say which ones belong together, which are public to other modules, or in what order things can be wired.

## Decision

Each module has a `MODULE.pso.ts` that lists its controllers and providers, imports its own route registry and states what it exports. A controller missing from it is never registered.

## Consequences

- Dependency injection is **scoped and checkable**: a controller can only receive providers the module declares or imports (`PSO_MODULE_006`).
- Module boundaries are visible in one small file; `exports` makes sharing deliberate.
- Accidentally adding a controller file does not expose or load anything.
- The cost is one extra file per module, which `pso make:module` and `make:controller` maintain through the AST.

## Alternatives considered

Scanning all `*.controller.ts` files (implicit and unsafe: a stray file would load) and a single global registry (poor locality).

## What it looks like in practice

A controller that exists on disk but is not listed is neither loaded nor exposed. Create `src/modules/ghost/controllers/ghost.controller.ts` without a `MODULE.pso.ts` and validation says so (expected):

```text evidence="expected"
ERROR   PSO_MODULE_001 gateway: Module declaration missing.
```

and a controller file inside a valid module but absent from `controllers` is `PSO_MODULE_003`. Both are found by `pso validate` before the application runs.

## Reproduced

Removing the controller from `controllers: []` is `PSO_MODULE_003` (the controller is never registered) together with `PSO_ROUTE_001` (a route points at a controller that is not part of the module); a deleted `ROUTES.pso.ts` is `PSO_MODULE_002`. The exact messages, with the `Expected` and `Found` lines, are in [Validation errors, one by one](reference/diagnostics-catalog.md).

## The cost

One more file per module, and a rule: adding a controller means updating the module. The generators (`make:controller`, `make:service`) edit it for you, using the TypeScript AST so that your formatting survives.

## When to revisit

If modules become too fine-grained to be worth a file each, group related controllers in one module instead of dropping the declaration; the declaration is what makes dependency injection checkable.

---

# Why ROUTES.pso.ts is mandatory

> Exposure is a security decision made in one reviewable place.

## Context

In annotation-driven frameworks, adding `@Delete` to a method exposes an endpoint. A forgotten decorator, a copy-paste or an AI-generated edit can publish something nobody reviewed.

## Decision

Decorators **describe** actions; `ROUTES.pso.ts` **decides** what is reachable. The route, its method, path, security policy and upstream are declared there, and the runtime activates a route only if the declaration, the module and the decorated action all agree. With no `ROUTES.pso.ts` nothing from the module is exposed, and there is no fallback discovery.

## Consequences

- A security review reads one file per module to know the whole public surface.
- A decorated but undeclared method answers `404`, proven by tests.
- Mismatches (`PSO_ROUTE_004`, `PSO_ROUTE_005`) are caught before deployment and again at start-up.
- Some duplication: method and path appear in the decorator and in the registry. That is the point: they must agree, and `pso make:route` writes both.

## Alternatives considered

Decorator-only exposure (implicit) and registry-only routing without controller metadata (loses the type-checked link between route and implementation). PSO keeps both and validates the pair.

## What it looks like in practice

A method that is decorated but not declared answers `404` (Expected output):

```text evidence="expected"
DELETE /customers/1   (decorated @Delete in the controller, absent from ROUTES.pso.ts)
HTTP 404 application/problem+json
{"code":"PSO_HTTP_NOT_FOUND", ...}
```

and the public surface of the system is one command:

```text evidence="expected"
$ pso routes:list
GET     /products                product.findAll        -> catalog        guard:jwt
GET     /reports/summary         reports.summary                          public
```

## What validation says about it

The consistency checks are real and each one was reproduced on a generated workspace ([Validation errors, one by one](reference/diagnostics-catalog.md)): a registry entry whose method or path differs from the decorator is `PSO_ROUTE_004` or `PSO_ROUTE_005`; an action that does not exist is `PSO_ROUTE_002`; a deleted registry is `PSO_MODULE_002`. And the opposite case, which is the point of this decision: a controller whose actions are decorated but whose registry is empty **validates `OK` and exposes nothing**. Consistent declarations are valid; an endpoint that is not declared does not exist.

## The cost

Two edits for one endpoint (decorator and registry). `pso make:route` writes both, in one all-or-nothing step, and rolls back if validation fails.

## When to revisit

Not as a security trade-off: exposure stays explicit. If the duplication of method and path annoys, improve the generators or the editor tooling, not the rule.

---

# Why controllers use decorators

> Decorators for implementation metadata, with a compiled orchestrator.

## Context

Controllers need to say, next to the code, which HTTP method and path an action implements, how parameters bind, and which providers they depend on.

## Decision

Use TypeScript decorators and emitted constructor metadata (`@Controller`, `@RestController`, `@Get`, `@Param`, `@Body`, `@Injectable`). They are metadata only; exposure still requires `ROUTES.pso.ts`.

## Consequences

- Familiar, readable controllers; dependency injection from constructor types.
- **The orchestrator must be compiled.** Node cannot run decorators or constructor parameter properties directly, so `tsc` (CommonJS, `experimentalDecorators`, `emitDecoratorMetadata`) builds `dist/` and `pso dev` does that for you.
- Type information is erased at run time, so a TypeScript type annotation never validates anything. DTO validation therefore uses explicit field decorators that record runtime metadata (`@Dto`, `@StringField`, ...), and `@Body(MyDto)` opts in ([DTO validation](orchestrator/dto-validation.md)).
- The static validator reads the same decorators from the AST, so build-time and start-up checks agree.

## Alternatives considered

Plain functions with configuration objects (no compile step, but no constructor-type injection) and a decorator-free registry only. Decorators were chosen for ergonomics, with the compile step as the known cost.

## What it looks like in practice

```typescript
@Controller()
@RestController("/orders")
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}          // injected from the constructor's type
```
